46.q: Development of labia majora is from -
46.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Genital swelling [Ref: Inderbir Singh Human Embryology Sth/e p. 256] Embryogical Fate in Fate in male structure female Genital swelling Labia majora Scrotum Genital fold Labia minora Ventral aspect of penis, penile urethra Genital tubercle Clitoris Glans penis

46.q: If the venous drainage of the anal canal above the pectinate line is impaired in a patient with portal hypertension, there may be an increase in blood flow downward to the systemic venous system via anastomoses with the inferior rectal vein, which is a tributary of the:
46.e: The rectal venous plexus is one of the four portal/systemic anastomoses. Blood from the portal system can flow into the venous system at this junction. This means that portal blood, from the superior rectal vein, could flow through the rectal venous plexus, into the inferior rectal vein and into the systemic venous drainage. Now, you just need to figure out what the inferior rectal vein drains into. And it drains into the internal pudendal vein. Reference - Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Pelvis and Perineum, Page number - 226

46.q: A 20-year-old male came to the emergency department with a complaint of sudden onset of severe pain in his left testicle for 2 hours. He had no history of trauma or fever. On examination, the left testicle is tender on palpation, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left side. What is the diagnosis in the above case?
46.e: Explanation: Sudden onset unilateral testicular pain along with an absent cremasteric reflex is the typical presentation of testicular torsion . It mostly occurs without any preceding trauma or fever and is a surgical emergency . The affected testicle appears elevated (Termed as a high-riding testicle ) Varicocele usually presents as a painless , "bag of worms" feeling in the scrotum and does not cause acute severe pain or an absent cremasteric reflex (Option B) . Hydrocele presents as painless swelling of the testis (Option C) . Epididymitis presents with gradual-onset pain, often associated with fever and dysuria, and the cremasteric reflex is usually intact. There is also relief from pain with the elevation of the affected testicle (Option D) .

47.q: Blood supply to the superior portions of the bladder typically arises from the ____________ arteries.
47.e: The umbilical artery supplies the superior part of the bladder by giving off the superior vesical arteries. In males, this artery supplies the ductus deferens via the artery of the ductus deferens. Distal to those branches, the umbilical artery is not patent, and it becomes the medial umbilical ligament. The middle rectal artery supplies blood to the middle of the rectum, while the obturator artery supplies blood to the medial thigh and hip. The inferior gluteal artery supplies blood to gluteus maximus, and the uterine artery supplies blood to the uterus. Reference - Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Pelvis and Perineum, Page number - 237

47.q: A caudal epidural block is a form of regional anesthetic used in childbirth. Within the sacral canal, the anesthetic agent bathes the sacral spinal nerve roots which would anesthetize all of the following nerves except:
47.e: The sacral splanchnic nerves do not come out of the sacral nerve roots--instead, these nerves come from the sacral sympathetic ganglia. So, anesthesia bathing the sacral nerve roots would not affect the sacral splanchnic nerves, which are coming from the sympathetic trunk. The sacral splanchnic nerves contribute to the inferior hypogastric plexus and provide sympathetic innervation to pelvic organs. Reference- Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Pelvis and Perineum, Page number - 266

47.q: Which of the following is not a content of the superficial perineal pouch?
47.e: Bulbourethral glands are not a content of the superficial perineal pouch. They are located in the deep perineal pouch. The superficial perineal pouch is a potential space between the perineal membrane above and the membranous layer of perineal fascia (Colle's fascia) below. Reference- Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Pelvis and Perineum, Page number - 222

48.q: With regard to the head of the femur
o: The arterial supply comes mainly from the inferior gluteal artery
The artery to the head assumes importance after age of 7 years
Psoas lies posterior to the hip joint
The anterior division of the obturator nerve gives partial supply to the hip joint
48.e: The femoral head is the most proximal portion of the femur and is supported by the femoral neck. It articulates with the acetabulum of the pelvis. The femoral head is nearly spherical (two-thirds) but has a medial depression known as the fovea capitis femoris that serves as an attachment point for the ligamentum teres. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 554

48.q: You are in the clinic when a patient presents with varicose saphenous veins in her lower limb. The attending physician asks where the venous valves are located that are defective and cause this condition. Having just studied a clinical case in that regard, you respond. The valves in the:
48.e: Perforating veins are anastamosing channels that shunt blood from the superficial veins to deep veins. These perforating veins have valves to ensure that blood only flows in the superficial to deep direction. If these valves fail, blood will back up in the superficial veins, causing valves to fail in the superficial veins, too. Then, the veins become varicose. Venae commitantes are special veins, usually paired, that accompany deep arteries in the limbs. They surround arteries in an irregular branching network that creates a vascular sheet around the arteries. The veins in the lower limb that are most likely to become varicose are the greater and lesser saphenous veins and their tributaries. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 569

48.q: A patient has been diagnosed with bone cancer in the fibula that necessitates its removal. Which of the following muscles would be least affected following removal of the fibula?
48.e: Flexor digitorum longus is the most medial muscle in the deep posterior compartment of the leg. This means that it takes origin from the middle half of the posterior surface of the tibia and is not attached to the fibula in any way. Biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula and the lateral condyle of the tibia. Extensor digitorum longus is a muscle on the lateral side of the anterior compartment of the leg. This means that it takes origin from the fibula, and would be affected by its removal. Flexor hallucis longus is the most lateral muscle in the posterior compartment, so it originates from the fibula, too. Finally, fibularis (peroneus) longus and brevis, the two muscles of the lateral compartment, both take origin from the fibula. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number: 599

49.q: What is not true about the Chopart ligament?
o: It is also known as bifurcate ligament
It is a strong Y shaped structure
It is part of calcaneonavicular ligament
49.e: The bifurcate ligament (BL) of the foot, also called Chopart ligament, is a strong 1-shaped structure that stabilizes the calcaneocuboid joint. The BL also stabilizes the talocalcaneonavicular and midtarsal joints, and therefore, has been described as the keystone of the transverse tarsal joint. The ligament is anatomically found on the dorsal surface of the calcaneocuboid joint and has a main proximal stem that attaches to the calcaneal sulcus, which then divides distally to attach to the navicular and dorsomedial aspect of the cuboid. Consequently, the BL has two constituent bands: the calcaneonavicular ligament (CNL) and calcaneocuboid ligament (CCL). Reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 3rd Edition, Page Number-668.

49.q: During eversion of the foot, which of the following ligaments is most likely to be injured?
49.e: Explanation: Among the given options, the deltoid ligament, also known as the medial collateral ligament of the ankle, is most likely to be injured during eversion of the foot Inversion injury: An inversion force with the foot in plantar flexion results in the sprain of the anterior talofibular ligament of the ankle. It is the most common ligament injury occurring in the body. Eversion injury: Eversion forces on the foot result in the deltoid ligament injuries. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial malleolus. Explanation of other options: Anterior talofibular (Option A): The most common Injury occurs during Inversion & plantarflexion Posterior talofibular (Option C): Injury happens during inversion Calcaneofibular (Option D): Injury happens during inversion

49.q: Dysplastic hip in a child, investigation of choice
49.e: Answer- C. USG Ultrasonography is the investigation of choice for DDH. It visualizes the cartilage and allows dynamic testing of the hip joint. 1248. Primary pathology in CDH a) Large head of femur b) Shallow acetabulum c) Excessive retroversion d) Everted limbus Correct Answer - B Answer- B. Shallow acetabulum Following changes are seen in dislocated hip :

50.q: Which of the following findings on physical examination is most likely to indicate a tear of the Achilles tendon?
o: Squeezing the calf with the person lying face down causes the ankle to flex.
The area around the ankle is swollen and painful when touched.
When the person bends the knees while lying face down, the ankle is not flexed.
When the person is standing, there is no gap in the Achilles tendon.
50.e: When the person bends the knees while lying face down, the ankle is not flexed. This finding on physical examination usually indicates a tear of the Achilles tendon. Choice A: If squeezing the calf with the person lying face down does not cause the ankle the flex, then the person has a complete Achilles tendon tear. Choice B: Swelling and pain in the ankle could indicate any number of diagnoses, not just an Achilles tendon rupture. Choice D: If a gap is felt in the Achilles tendon with the person standing, then the Achilles tendon is torn. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number: 623

50.q: Compression of the lateral plantar nerve as it passes between the flexor digitorum brevis and quadratus plantae could result in weakness of any of the following actions EXCEPT:
50.e: The medial plantar nerve innervates abductor hallucis, so this muscle would be saved if the lateral plantar nerve was disrupted. The muscles responsible for all the rest of the actions listed are innervated by the lateral plantar nerve, or its branch, the deep lateral plantar nerve: Adduction of the middle toe: plantar interosseus muscles (deep branch); Abduction of the little toe: abductor digiti minimi (lateral plantar); Adduction of the great toe: adductor hallucis (deep branch); Abduction of the middle toe: third dorsal interosseus muscle (deep branch). Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number: 638

50.q: Which of the following nerves originates in the lumbosacral plexus?
50.e: The sciatic nerve originates from both the lumbar and sacral plexus. Specifically, it originates from the fourth and fifth lumbar nerve plexuses and first to the third sacral nerve plexuses. It is the largest nerve in the body formed by nerve roots from the lower spine or lumbosacral plexus. It passes deep in the gluteal region and down the posterior part of the thigh all the way to the heel and sole of the foot. It primarily serves an essential role in the sensory and motor functions of the skin and muscles of the thigh, leg, and foot. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number: 557

51.q: Structure crossing dorsal surface of ischial spine are A/E :
51.e: C. i.e. Obturator nerve Psoas major, iliacus & pectineus muscles, femoral vessels and nerve, femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve, lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh and lymphatics pass below inguinal ligament. 'PIN' structures i.e. Pudendal nerve, Internal Pudendal vessels, Nerve to obturator internus come out of greater sciatic foramen, cross the dorsal surface of ischial spine & enter into lesser sciatic foramen.

51.q: A 19-year-old male suffers a tear to the psoas major muscle during the course of a football game. A scar, which formed on the medial part of the belly of the muscle, involved an adjacent nerve, immediately medial to the muscle. The nerve is called the:
51.e: The obturator nerve runs along the medial border of the psoas major muscle, eventually passing through the obturator canal to innervate muscles of the medial thigh. So, it might be damaged by an injury to the medial portion of psoas major. The femoral nerve runs along the lateral border of psoas major, where psoas major contacts iliacus. The genitofemoral nerve pierces through psoas major at the level of L3 or L4. The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves run under psoas major, emerging at the lateral border of psoas major to run over quadratus lumborum. The way to distinguish between these two nerves is to remember that the iliohypogastric is superior to the ilioinguinal nerve. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Abdomen, Page number - 182

51.q: Which compartment of leg does not have neuro vascular bundles?
51.e: The posterior compartment is divided by deep transverse fascia into deep and superficial sections. The superficial posterior compartment muscles include the gastrocnemius, the plantaris and the soleus. No major arteries or nerves are within this compartment. Pain and a palpable tense and tender compartment suggest the diagnosis. The deep posterior compartment muscles include the popliteus, the flexor digitorum longus, the flexor hallucis longus and perhaps the tibialis posterior. The neurovascular supply to the posterior compartment is provided by the tibial nerve and the posterior tibial artery. Increased pressure in this compartment may cause plantar foot hypesthesia, weakness of toe flexion and pain with passive extension of the toes. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number: 573

52.q: Which of the following is NOT located within the adductor canal?
52.e: The adductor canal contains: the femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve, and nerve to vastus medialis. Adductor longus and magnus make the posterior boundary of the canal, and vastus medialis is the lateral boundary of the canal. The roof of the canal is formed by sartorius. The deep femoral artery branches from the femoral artery in the femoral triangle; it then travels deep in the thigh, posterior to adductor longus. So, it is deep to the canal. The deep femoral artery supplies blood to the posterior compartment of the thigh through perforating branches. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 573

52.q: Regarding the popliteal fossa, which of the following statements is true?
o: The common peroneal nerve slopes downwards lateral to the biceps tendon
The sural nerve is a cutaneous branch of the common peroneal nerve
The middle genicular artery of the popliteal artery supply the cruciate ligaments
The popliteus muscle is supplied by a branch of the common peroneal nerve
52.e: The popliteal fossa is diamond shaped with four borders. These borders are formed by the muscles in the posterior compartment of the leg and thigh: Superomedial - semimembranosus. Superolateral - biceps femoris. Inferomedial - medial head of the gastrocnemius. Inferolateral - lateral head of the gastrocnemius and plantaris. The floor of the popliteal fossa is formed by the posterior surface of the knee joint capsule, popliteus muscle and posterior femur. The roof is made of up two layers: popliteal fascia and skin. The popliteal fascia is continuous with the fascia lata of the leg. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 616

The femoral canal usually contains a deep inguinal lymph node, called the gland or node of Cloquet. This canal opens to the abdominal cavity through the femoral ring, so it might be the site of a femoral hernia. The femoral artery and vein are enclosed in the femoral sheath with the femoral canal, but they are not in the femoral canal. The femoral nerve is also in the femoral triangle, but it is not enclosed by the femoral sheath. It is the most lateral structure in the femoral triangle. The ilioinguinal nerve is not really part of the anatomy of this region. It innervates muscles of the lower abdominal wall and is associated with the superficial inguinal ring. Make sure to remember the difference between the femoral canal and femoral sheath! Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 553

53.q: The tubercle of the 7th rib articulates with which structure?
53.e: The tubercle of a rib is a projection located posteroinferior and lateral to the neck of the rib. It articulates with the transverse process of the vertebra of the same number. So, the tubercle of rib 7 should articulate with the transverse process of the T7 vertebra. The head of the rib is the part of the rib that articulates with the demifacets of two adjacent vertebral bodies. So, the head of rib 7 should articulate with the 6th vertebra superiorly and the 7th vertebra inferiorly. Reference- Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 127

53.q: What does the tip of the T3 spinous process correspond to?
53.e: The tip of the 13 spinous process corresponds to the root of the spine of the scapula Other important surface markings of scapula: Superior angle of scapula: at the level of 2nd rib and vertebra T2. Inferior angle of scapula: opposite the 17 vertebral spinous process. Reference : Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 126

53.q: Which of the following ribs is atypical and doesn't articulate with the vertebra at 3 sites?
53.e: 1st rib is an atypical rib and does not articulate at 3 sites with a vertebra. It has 2 articulations as follows: Circular facet on the head of the rib with the body of the first thoracic vertebra Tubercle of the rib to the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra Reference : Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 124

54.q: The total number of bone present in appendicular and axial skeletal in adults is?
54.e: In the adult, 80 bones are present in the axial skeleton, and 126 bones in the appendicular skeleton. Reference: Textbook of B d Chaurasia's handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Edition, Page number - 57

54.q: Which of the following is not a sesamoid bone?
54.e: Os trigonum is an accessory bone, not a sesamoid bone. Accessory bones, also known as supernumerary bones are not always present. They may arise due to ununited epiphysis developed from extra ossification centres. Clinically, they may be mistaken for fractures. Reference: Textbook of B d Chaurasia's handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Edition, Page number - 57

54.q: Which is true about synovial joint ?

Condyloid joints permit flexion and extension, abduction and adduction, and circumduction. Beyond the synovial membrane, synovial joints have a variety of important characteristics, including: hyaline cartilage to cover the weight bearing surface of the joint, a joint capsule made of accessory ligaments to reinforce the synovial membrane, and accessory structures (such as accessory ligaments, articular discs or menisci, muscles and tendons, and subsynovial fat). 57.q: Glands are classified depending upon their mode of secretion. Sebaceous gland is an example of which of the following type of gland?
57.e: Sebaceous glands are holocrine glands. Holocrine glands are those in which the cell after filling with secretory product dies and is expelled along with its content. Eccrine glands are those in which secretory product is expelled by exocytosis. Eg sweat glands involved in thermoregulation and receiving cholinergic sympathetic innervation. Apocrine glands are those in which the secretory product accumulates in the apical cytoplasm and is expelled out by pinching of the apical plasma membrane. Eg mammary gland and apocrine type of sweat glands that are active after puberty and are found in the skin of axilla and around genital organs. Ref: Clinical Anatomy: (a Problem Solving Approach) By Kulkarni page

69.q: Mechanism of Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation (TENS) for pain management
69.e: Gate control theory is the mechanism behind Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers in the vicinity of the injury. The activity of these cutaneous mechanosensitive afferents reduce the responsiveness of dorsal horn neurons to their input from nociceptive afferent terminals. This is called the gate-control mechanism of pain modulation.

73.q: Shivering is controlled by: September 2012, March 2013
73.e: Ans. B i.e. Posterior hypothalamus Shivering/Shuddering It is a bodily function in response to early hypothermia in warm- blooded animals. When the core body temperature drops, the shivering reflex is triggered to maintain homeostasis. Muscle groups around the vital organs begin to shake in small movements in an attempt to create warmth by expending energy. Shivering can also be a response to a fever, as a person may feel cold, though their core temperature is already elevated. Located in the posterior hypothalamus near the wall of the third ventricle is an area called the primary motor center for shivering. This area is normally inhibited by signals from the heat center in the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area but is excited by cold signals from the skin and spinal cord.

76.q: Airway resistance is lowest in which of the following?
76.e: Airway resistance decreases as lung volume increases because the increasingly subatmospheric intrapleural pressure increases the radial traction on the airways, thereby increasing airway diameter and decreasing airway resistance. Resistances in parallel add as reciprocals. Thus, the large number of small, peripheral airways increases the number of airways arranged in parallel, and lowers the total resistance of the peripheral airways compared to the total cross-section of the central airways. 82.q: Pulmonary vascular resistance decreases if which of the following occurs?

82.e: Increasing cardiac output or pulmonary artery pressure causes pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) to passively decrease due to two mechanisms-distention of the perfused vessels, and recruitment of more parallel vascular beds. At high lung volumes, the pulmonary capillaries ("alveolar" vessels) are stretched and compressed causing an increased PVR. At low lung volumes, the "extraalveolar" blood vessels are compressed, increasing PVR. The lowest PVR occurs near FRC. Decreasing PO2 or increasing PCO2 or H+ concentration causes PVR to rise. The sympathetic nervous system has little effect on PVR under physiologic conditions, but experimentally, stimulation of sympathetic nerves will constrict the pulmonary vessels, causing increased PVR. Approximately 90% of erythropoietin is synthesized in the kidneys , while the remaining 10% is produced in the liver . In the kidneys, fibroblast-like interstitial cells in the cortex and outer medulla are the main sites of production, responding to tissue hypoxia. The liver contributes mainly during the fetal stage , serving as the predominant site of erythropoietin synthesis before birth. When hypoxia occurs, the hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) activates the erythropoietin gene , increasing hormone synthesis to stimulate erythropoiesis in the bone marrow. 100.e: Hexokinase, phosphofructokinase and pyruvate kinase are all catalysing irreversible reactions and are the regulated steps in glycolysis. The conversion of glucose to lactate (anaerobic glycolysis) is a process that does not involve a net oxidation or reduction and, thus, oxygen is not required. Glucokinase (not hexokinase) is important in hepatic glucose metabolism only in the absorptive period following consumption of a carbohydrate-containing meal. Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a potent activator (not inhibitor) of phosphofructokinase. The conversion of glucose to lactate yields two ATP but no net production of NADH. 108.q: As fluid comes down the PCT, what is true ?
108.e: Ans. D. Concentration of inulin decreases

108.q: Which of the following enzyme is not used by liver in urea cycle ?
108.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., CPS-II [Ref Harper 29th / e p. 277-278] Carbmoyl phosphate synthase II (CPS II) is involved in pyrimidine synthesis (not in urea cycle).

109.q: What is true regarding medium chain fatty acids ?
109.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e.,All of the above [Ref Vasudevan 6" p. 160] Metabolism of short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and medium chain fatty acids (MCFAs) is drastically different from long chain fatty acids (LCFAs). SCFAs and MCFAs do not require pancreatic lipase and bile salts for digestion, but required for LCFAs digestion. SCFAs and MCFAs are directly absorbed from intestine into portal circulation, whereas LCFAs are taken by lymphatics, after incorporation into chylomicrons. SCFAs and MCFAs are oxidized by peripheral cells and are not used for storage. LCFAs are esterified with glycerol to form triacylglycerol, storage form of lipid

109.q: In which of the following locations can cardiolipin be found?
109.e: Explanation: Cardiolipin is a unique phospholipid present predominantly in the inner mitochondrial membrane . Functions: Maintains the structural integrity of mitochondria. Stabilizes and optimizes the activity of the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and their supercomplexes. Structure & Synthesis: Has a distinctive dimeric structure with four fatty acid chains. Synthesized within mitochondria from phosphatidylglycerol and CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DAG) . Explanation of other options: Outer mitochondrial membrane (A): Mostly contains phosphatidylcholine & phosphatidylethanolamine, not cardiolipin. Cytosol (C): Cardiolipin is membrane-bound and absent in cytosol. Mitochondrial matrix (D): Not a membrane lipid, hence not present here.

109.q: Glycerophospholipid containing choline is a very important for human body. All of the following statements are correct about it except.
o: Glycerophospholipid containing choline is called as Lecithin
Most abundant phospholipid in mitochondrial membrane.
It represent a large proportion of body's storage of choline.
109.e: Lecithin is a most abundant phospholipids of cell membrane not mitochondrial membrane. Lecithin (Phosphatidylcholine) Glycerophospholipid with Choline as nitrogenous base. i.e. Phosphatidic Acid + Choline. Most abundant phospholipid of cell membrane. Largest body store of choline. Importance of choline Acetylcholine in nerve transmission Transmethylation Dipalmitoyl Lecithin (Di Palmitoyl Phosphatidyl Choline) is a major constituent of lung surfactant. Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 216

110.q: The most common storage form of lipids is?
110.e: Triacylglycerol (TG), which is a neutral fat, is the most common storage form of lipids. They are esters of trihydric alcohol glycerol and fatty acids. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition page 493

110.q: Which among the following is a cardio protective fatty acid?
110.e: Significance of ω3 Fatty Acid Decrease the risk of Cardiovascular Disease Appear to replace arachidonic acid in platelet membranes Lower the production of thromboxane and tendency of the platelet aggregation Decrease Serum Triglycerides Important for Infant Development Lower the risk of various mental illness (Depression, ADHD) Lower the risk of chronic degenerative diseases such as Cancer, Rheumatoid Arthritis, and Alzheimers Disease . Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 239

110.q: Fatty Acid present in human milk
110.e: Docosahexaenoic acid/Cervonic acid (DHA; ω3, 22:6), which is synthesized to a limited extent from α-linolenic acid or obtained directly from fish oils, is present in high concentrations in retina, cerebral cortex, testis, and sperm. DHA is particularly needed for development of the brain and retina and is supplied via the placenta and milk. Patients with retinitis pigmentosa are reported to have low blood levels of DHA. Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 239

111.q: The first step in fatty acid synthesis involves:
111.e: Fatty Acid Synthesis occurs through two enzyme system Acetyl CoA Carboxylase Fatty Acid Synthase Complex Acetyl CoA Carboxylase Converts Acetyl CoA (2C) to Malonyl CoA in the presence of ATP. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase has a requirement for the B vitamin biotin . It is a multienzyme protein. This is the rate limiting step in the Fatty Acid Synthesis. Acetyl CoA carboxylase is not a part FAS Complex Reference : Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 235

111.q: Which of the following is not a part of Fatty Acid Synthase Complex?
111.e: Fatty Acid Synthase (FAS ) Multienzyme Complex The complex is a homodimer of two identical polypeptide monomers in which six enzyme activities and the acyl carrier protein (ACP) Six enzyme activities of Fatty Acid Synthase Complex are Ketoacyl Synthase Malonyl-Acetyl Transacylase Dehydratase Enoyl Reductase Ketoacyl Reductase Thioesterase (Deacylase). Acetyl CoA carboxylase is not a part FAS Complex. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 234

111.q: In a 90-kg man, follows a high carbohydrate meal diet plan, which metabolic pathway is predominantly active and contributes to weight gain? 1. Malonyl-CoA 2. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 3. Mitochondrial carnitine transporter 4. Tricarboxylate transporter (citrate)
111.e: Explanation: After a meal (high-energy state), insulin is elevated, promoting lipogenesis and weight gain. The enzymes responsible for that are: Malonyl-CoA : It is the key intermediate for fatty acid synthesis. (statement 1) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC): Insulin activates ACC (via dephosphorylation), which catalyzes the synthesis of Malonyl-CoA. (statement 2) Tricarboxylate transporter (citrate) : It exports citrate from mitochondria to the cytosol. Citrate is cleaved to provide acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis. (statement 4) Mitochondrial carnitine transporter (CPT-I) is involved in fatty acid oxidation. It helps transport fatty acids into mitochondira for breakdown. Malonyl-CoA potently inhibits CPT-I, blocking fatty acid entry into mitochondria for β-oxidation. (statement 3)

112.q: Thermogenin protein is mainly found in:
112.e: Explanation: Thermogenin , also known as Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1) , is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose tissue (BAT) . (Option A,C and D ruled out) Its primary function is non-shivering thermogenesis . UCP1 acts as a proton channel, allowing protons to leak back into the mitochondrial matrix without passing through ATP synthase. This uncouples oxidative phosphorylation from ATP synthesis, dissipating the proton gradient energy as heat to maintain body temperature, especially in newborns and hibernating mammals. Key Takeaways: Thermogenin (UCP1) is an uncoupling protein found in the mitochondria of brown adipose tissue. It generates heat by uncoupling electron transport from ATP production.

112.q: Which of the following molecules is present in Gangliosides:
112.e: Ganglioside Sphingosine + Fatty acid + Oligosaccharide that contain one, two, three or four molecules of sialic acid. Gangliosides are complex glycosphingolipids derived from glucosylceramide that contain one or more molecules of a sialic acid. Neuraminic acid is the principal sialic acid found in human tissues. Gangliosides are present in nervous tissues in high concentration. They function in cell-cell recognition and communication as a receptor for hormone. Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 218

112.q: Which of the following is a non-phosphorylated lipid?
112.e: Glycosphingolipids are non phosphorylated lipid. GLYCOLIPIDS (GLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS) ARE IMPORTANT IN NERVE TISSUES & IN THE CELL MEMBRANE. All other phospholipids are derivatives of phosphatidic acid, in which the phosphate is esterified with one OH group of glycerol and the other two OH groups are esterified to two long chain fatty acids (glycerophospholipids). Phosphatidic acid is important as an intermediate in the synthesis of triacylglycerols as well as phosphoglycerols but is not found in any great quantity in tissues. Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 215,218

113.q: If there is a Gs alpha subunit gain - of - function mutation, this results in
113.e: Gα S- activates adenylyl cyclase Adenylyl cyclase is the enzyme responsible for formation of CAMP So, if there is Gα S , there is increase in production of cAMP Reference: Ganong 25th edition page No.57

113.q: Glucose transporter present in the RBC:
113.e: Highest level of GLUT1 is present in the RBC Major Glucose transporter in brain is GLUT1 (not present in neurons) Major Glucose transporter in the Placenta is GLUT 1 Major Glucose transporter in the RBC is GLUT1 Major neuronal Glucose transporter is GLUT3 Insulin-responsive glucose transporter is GLUT4, GLUT 8 and GLUT 12 Fructose transporter GLUT 5 (mainly) and GLUT 11 Urate transporter is GLUT 9 Glucose transporter in blastocyst is GLUT 8. Reference : Harper's 32 nd edition, Page no. 191

113.q: All of the following nutrients are considered lipotropic factors that help prevent fatty liver EXCEPT:
113.e: Explanation: Lipotropic factors are substances that promote the export of fat from the liver, preventing hepatic steatosis (fatty liver). Choline , lecithin (which contains choline), and methionine (which can be converted to cysteine and is a methyl donor) are classic lipotropic agents, arginine is not.( Option A,B and D ruled out) Arginine is primarily involved in the urea cycle, nitric oxide synthesis, and other metabolic pathways unrelated to hepatic lipid transport. Key Takeaways: Lipotropic factors prevent fatty liver (e.g., choline, methionine, betaine, inositol). Arginine is not a lipotropic factor.

114.q: Bilirubin in serum can be measured by:
114.e: Option A: Van den Bergh Reaction: Quantitation of bilirubin employs a colorimetric method based on the reddish-purple color formed when bilirubin reacts with diazotized sulfanilic acid. An assay conducted in the absence of added methanol measures "direct bilirubin," which is bilirubin glucuronide. An assay conducted in the presence of added methanol measures total bilirubin. The difference between total bilirubin and direct bilirubin is known as "indirect bilirubin," and is unconjugated bilirubin. Option B: Ehrlich's Reaction is used to detect urobilinogen in urine. Option C: Schlesinger's Reaction is used to detect urobilin. Option D: Fouchet's Reaction is used to detect bile pigment like bilirubin in urine.

Mutations in the gene encoding enzyme ALA synthase cause X-linked Sideroblastic anemia. It leads to anemia with decreased red cell counts and hemoglobin. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine in a pyridoxal phosphate-dependent reaction catalyzed by mitochondrial δ-aminolevulinate synthase (ALA synthase. Succinyl-CoA + glycine → δ-aminolevulinate + CoA-SH + CO2 Humans express two isozymes of ALA synthase. ALAS1 is ubiquitously expressed throughout the body, whereas ALAS2 is expressed in erythrocyte precursor cells. Formation of δ-aminolevulinate is rate-limiting for porphyrin biosynthesis in mammalian liver. So Option A is correct.

114.q: Rate limiting enzyme in heme synthesis ?
114.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e.,ALA synthase [Ref Harper's 29' le p. 309] Heme synthesis takes place in all cells, but occurs to greatest extent in bone marrow and liver. The first step in the synthesis of heme is the condensation of glycine and succinyl Co-A to form 6- aminolevulinic acid (6-ALA), which occurs in mitochondria. This reaction is catalyzed by 6-ALA synthase which requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as cofactor. This is the rate limiting step in heme synthesis.

115.q: Enzymes of glycolysis are found in:
115.e: All of the enzymes of glycolysis are found in the cytosol. Ref: Harper 28th edition, chapter 18.

115.q: Which of the following enzymes participates in the glycolytic pathway?
115.e: Explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is a key enzyme of glycolysis that catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate using ATP and is the main rate-limiting and regulatory step of the pathway. it is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

Ans. C. Deiodinase Selenocysteine is considered as 21 standard amino acid. It is present at the active site of some enzymes that catalyze redox reactions, e.g. thioredoxin reductase, glutathione peroxidase, and the deiodinase (converts thyroxin to triiodothyronine). Biosynthesis of selenocysteine requires cysteine, serine, ATP and a specific t-RNA. Serine provides the carbon skeleton of selenocysteine. Selenocysteine has a structure similar to cysteine, but containing the trace element selenium in place of sulfur atom of cysteine.

116.q: Which of the following is an example of an allosteric enzyme?
116.e: Explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is a classical allosteric enzyme and a key regulatory step of glycolysis, whose activity is modulated by allosteric effectors like ATP and citrate (inhibitors) and AMP, ADP, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (activators). These regulators bind to sites other than the active site (allosteric sites), causing conformational changes and leading to a sigmoidal reaction curve , unlike Michelis-Menten enzymes. Hexokinase shows feedback inhibition by glucose-6-phosphate but is not a classical allosteric enzyme. Chymotrypsin and trypsin are digestive proteases regulated by zymogen activation (proteolytic cleavage) and not by allosteric modulation.

116.q: Which of the following is a ribozyme?
116.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Peptidyl transferase [Ref Harper 29thIe p. 405] Some RNA molecules have intrinsic catalytic activity. The activity of these ribozymes often involves the cleavage of nucleic acid. Two important RNA enzymes or ribozymes are : ? The peptidyl transferase that catalyzes peptide bond formation on the ribosome and Ribozymes involved in the RNA splicing.

Ans. 'D' Nitric acid Xanthoproteic test: The ring systems in phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan undergo nitration on treatment with concentrated nitric acid when heated. The end product is yellow in color which is intensified in strong alkaline medium. This reaction causes the yellow stain in the skin by nitric acid. 319. Taurine is biosynthesized by ? a) Arginine b) Leucine c) Valine d) Cysteine Correct Answer - D Ans. is 'd' i.e., Cysteine [Ref Harper 250/e p. 298-99] Taurine is synthesized from cysteine by 3 enzyme-catalyzed reactions :

117.q: Following is false regarding Vitamin D?
o: The major source of Vitamin D synthesis is the skin.
The major function of Vitamin D is calcium homeostasis.
Its actions are mediated by extranuclear receptors.
Intake higher than that required, reduces the risk of obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cancers.
117.e: Vitamin D is not strictly a vitamin since it can be synthesised in the skin, and in most conditions, this is the major source of the vitamin. Only when sunlight exposure is inadequate, a dietary source is required. Its main function is in the regulation of calcium absorption and homeostasis most of its actions are mediated by way of nuclear receptors that regulate gene expression. It also has a role in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation. There is evidence that intakes considerably higher than are required to maintain calcium homeostasis reduce the risk of insulin resistance, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome, as well as various cancers. Deficiency, leading to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, is a problem in northern latitudes, where sunlight exposure is inadequate Reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd Edition, Page Number- 1297.

117.q: The following are dependent on Vit. K for gamma carboxylation except?
117.e: A number of other proteins undergo the same vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of glutamate to y-carboxyglutamate which include: Osteocalcin Protein C and S Matrix Gla protein in bone Nephrocalcin in kidney and Growth arrest specific gene Gas6, which is involved in both the regulation of differentiation and development in the nervous system, and control of apoptosis in other tissues. All of these y-carboxyglutamate containing proteins bind calcium, which causes a conformational change so that they interact with membrane phospholipids. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition; page 390, Lippincott illustrated reviews 8 th edition biochemistry page 1305

117.q: Haemolytic anemia is due to the deficiency of which vitamin?
117.e: The lack of Vit. E causes the membrane of the RBC to be abnormally fragile and as a result of lipid peroxidation, there is membrane lysis causing haemolytic anemia Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 1302

118.q: How many ATPs are produced by the oxidation of one molecule NADPH in oxidative phosphorylation?
118.e: Option A: NADPH is never used to produce ATP in oxidative phosphorylation, instead it is used for reductive biosynthesis of many compounds. Option B: The oxidation of one molecule FADH2 in oxidative phosphorylation produces 1.5 ATPs. Option C: The oxidation of one molecule NADH in oxidative phosphorylation produces 2.5 ATPs. Option D: It was believed that the oxidation of one molecule NADH in oxidative phosphorylation produces 3 ATPs earlier, but recently it is corrected to 2.5. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 11 PN 108

118.q: Which coenzyme act as reducing agent in anabolic reaction cholesterol?
118.e: Many steps in fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis and steroid hormone required NADPH. NADPH helps in the reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids, Cholesterol and steroid hormones. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 269

119.q: Catabolism of H2O2 is carried out by:
119.e: Peroxisomes (or) microbodies are concerned with three vital functions in a cell namely: Generation and degradation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) Oxidation of very long chain fatty acids (ag, C20 C22) Detoxification of harmful chemicals Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.38

119.q: How many atoms of copper are incorporated in Erythrocuprein?
119.e: Explanation: Erythrocuprein, also known as ceruloplasmin, is a copper-carrying protein in the blood. Each molecule of ceruloplasmin contains one atom of copper that is essential for its enzymatic activity, which includes oxidising iron and functioning in iron metabolism.

119.q: Which of the following sentence is true regarding chemical modification of LDL (Low density lipoprotein) by free radicals?
o: Easily recognized by liver LDL receptor
Not taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors
119.e: Chemical modification of the proteins or lipids in plasma low-density lipoprotein (LDL) leads to abnormal LDL. Option A & Option B: Such modified LDL is not recognized by the liver LDL receptors, and so is not cleared by the liver. Option C: Such modified LDL is highly atherogenic. Option D: The modified LDL is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors. Lipid-engorged macrophages infiltrate under blood vessel endothelium (especially when there is already some damage to the endothelium), and are killed by the high content of unesterified cholesterol they have accumulated. This occurs in the development of atherosclerotic plaques. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 45 PN 542

120.q: In the metabolism of cytosine, what is one of the final products?
120.e: Explanation: Cytosine is a pyrimidine base, and during its catabolism, it is first deaminated to uracil, which is then further broken down via the pyrimidine degradation pathway. One of the final products of uracil (and thus cytosine) metabolism is β-alanine. This distinguishes pyrimidine breakdown from purine metabolism, where the final product is uric acid, and from muscle metabolism, where creatinine is formed

120.q: Allantoin is a more water soluble product of purine catabolism compared to uric acid. But in human, uric acid is not further converted into allantoin due to lack of enzyme:
120.e: Option A: Xanthine oxidase enzyme convert Hypoxanthine into Xanthine and Xanthine into Uric acid. This enzyme presents in mammals and humans both, so both breakdown purines up to uric acid. Option B: HGPRTase is an enzyme involved in the salvage pathway. It converts Guanine & Hypoxanthine into GMP & IMP. Its deficiency can lead to Lesch Nyhan syndrome. Option C: Urease catalyzes the hydrolysis of Urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. It is also not present in humans, so human urea is excreted in urine. Option D: Uricase enzyme convert uric acid into allantoin. Allantoin is more water soluble than uric acid. But in human uricase enzyme is absent, so the end product of purine catabolism is uric acid. Uricase is present in mammals, so they convert uric acid into allantoin. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 33 PN 334

120.q: Which enzyme catalyses the conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides?
120.e: Explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase is the key enzyme that converts ribonucleotides (RNA precursors) into deoxyribonucleotides (DNA precursors), making it essential for DNA synthesis and repair. Ribonucleotide phosphorylase is involved in the breakdown of ribonucleosides during nucleotide metabolism. Nucleoside phosphorylase functions mainly in the salvage pathway by converting nucleosides into nitrogenous bases and sugar phosphates, helping recycle nucleotides. Nucleotidase simply removes phosphate groups from nucleotides to convert them into nucleosides and is mainly involved in nucleotide degradation and regulation.

121.q: A 42 yr old patient with symptoms of premature aging and is diagnosed as Werner syndrome. The most likely mechanism?
o: Short telomere with damaged DNA and loss of helicase
121.e: Werner syndrome is characterized by the dramatic, rapid appearance of features associated with normal aging. Individuals with this disorder typically grow and develop normally until they reach puberty Werner syndrome is characterised by the defective DNA Helicase Enzym, which causes short telomere and damage DNA

121.q: What is the function of DNA ligase ?
o: Unwinding (denaturation) of dsDNA to provide an ssDNA template
Seals the single strand nick between the nascent chain and Okazaki fragments on lagging strand
Initiation of DNA synthesis and elongation
121.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Seals the single strand nick between the nascent chain and Okazaki fragments on lagging strand [Ref Harper 2501e p. 367]

121.q: Radiant damage can lead to following types of DNA damages which leading to cancer, except:
121.e: Some Types of DNA Damage Caused by Radiation Option A: Formation Pyrimidine Dimer (Thymine dimer) - condensation of adjacent thymine Option B: Formation of purine dimer not seen commonly. Option C: Formation of apurinic or apyrimidinic sites by elimination of corresponding bases, Hydrolysis of N glycosidic bond which connect N base with deoxyribose sugar Option D: Formation of strand (chain) breaks or cross-linking of DNA strands Chain break - Disintegration of backbone element, can be single strand or double strand Cross linkage - Between bases in same or opposite strands, also between DNA and protein molecules (eg, histones) Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 56 PN 683

122.q: Which RNA is used in RNA splicing ?
122.e: Ans. is 'B' i.e., Small nuclear RNA [Ref Harper 29th/e p. 378, 390] Splicesome Splicesome is an assembly made up of small nuclear RNA (snRNA), some proteins and hnRNA. snRNA combines with proteins to form small nuclear ribnonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs or snurps) that mediate splicing. It is snRNA component of snurps that catalyzes splicing°. Snurps are U,,U,,U3,U4, U5 and U6

122.q: Which of the following pharmacological agents inhibit protein synthesis due its structural similarity with tyrosyl-tRNA?
122.e: Option A: Tetracycline prevents the binding of aminoacyl-tRNAs to the bacterial ribosome A site. Option B: Chloramphenicol works by binding to 23S rRNA, which is interesting in view of the newly appreciated role of rRNA in peptide bond formation through its peptidyl transferase activity. Option C: Puromycin is a structural analogue of tyrosyl-tRNA. Puromycin is incorporated via the A site on the ribosome into the carboxyl terminal position of a peptide but causes the premature release of the polypeptide. Puromycin, as a tyrosyl-tRNA analog, effectively inhibits protein synthesis in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Option D: Cycloheximide inhibits peptidyl transferase in the 60S ribosomal subunit in eukaryotes, presumably by binding to an rRNA component. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 37 PN 407

122.q: Menke's disease is due to a defect of which enzyme?
122.e: Option A: Menkes syndrome, characterized by kinky hair and growth retardation, results from a dietary deficiency of copper, an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase that functions in formation of the covalent cross-links that strengthen collagen fiber. Option B & Option D: Lysyl and Prolyl hydroxylases are required for the postsynthetic modification of procollagen to collagen. Both this enzyme requires vitamin C. In vitamin C deficiency(scurvy), leading to skin changes, fragility of blood capillaries, gum decay, tooth loss and bone fracture, which can be attributed to impaired collagen synthesis(leading to delayed wound healing). Option C: Prolyl oxidase does not exist.

123.e: Explanation: The anticodon is a sequence of three nucleotides in tRNA that is complementary to a specific mRNA codon. This sequence allows the tRNA to recognize and bind to the corresponding codon on mRNA during translation, ensuring that the correct amino acid is added to the growing polypeptide chain. The anticodon is what primarily determines the tRNA's binding specificity to mRNA.

123.q: In sickle cell anemia, translocation on codon 6 is due to substitution of ?
123.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Valine for glutamate [Ref Harper's 29th/e p. 444] Sickle cell disease, is caused by mutation of a single base out of the 3 x 109 in the genome, a T-to-A DNA substitution, which in turn results in an A-to-U change in the mRNA corresponding to the sixth codon of the 13-globin gene. The altered codon specifies a different amino acid (valine rather than glutamic acid), and this causes a structural abnormality of the p-globin molecule.

123.q: Stickler Syndrome is due to deficiency of which type of collagen?
123.e: Chondrodysplasias are a mixed group of hereditary disorders affecting cartilage. They are manifested by short-limbed dwarfism and numerous skeletal deformities. A number of them are due to a variety of mutations in the COL2A1 gene, leading to abnormal forms of type II collagen. One example is Stickler syndrome (may also be due to mutations in the COL11A1, COL11A2), manifested by degeneration of the joint cartilage and of the vitreous body of the eye. Reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32 nd Edition, Page Number-643.

124.q: In FITC the color emitted after blue light absorption? \
124.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Yellow green Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) is a derivative of fluorescein used in wide-ranging applications including flow cytometry. FITC is the original fluorescein molecule functionalized with an isothiocyanate reactive group (-N=C=S), replacing a hydrogen atom on the bottom ring of the structure. This derivative is reactive towards nucleophiles including amine and sulfhydryl groups on proteins. FITC (fluorescein isothiocyanate) is a fluorochrome dye that absorbs ultraviolet or blue light causing molecules to become excited and emit a visible yellow green light. This emission ceases upon removal of the light causing the excitation.

124.q: Which of the following statements regarding mature cytoplasmic messenger RNA is true ?
o: Has Thiamine in place of Uracil
Its molecular weight is more than hn-RNA
124.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Transcribed from Nuclear DNA [Ref: Lippincott's Biochemistry 5thp.428;Fundamentals of Cytogenetics & Genetics (2010) p. 444] Mesenger RNA (mRNA) is formed by the process of 'transcription' from one of the strands of double stranded nuclear DNA and carries genetic information from the nuclear DNA to the cytosol where it is used as a template for protein synthesis. mRNA comprises only 5-10% of total cellular RNA. It carries the information (massage) from the nucleus to the ribosome. mRNA is synthesized in the nucleus as lieterogenous RNA (hn RNA)', which is processed into functional m RNA.

124.q: Which of the following is the most powerful technique used in transcription factor research which allows identifying genome wide DNA binding sites for transcription factors?
124.e: Option A: Systematic deletion mapping is genetic mapping technique that enables to determine the location of specific genes on chromosomes. Option B: DNAse I sensitivity assay used for discovering regulatory domains. This method maps discrete sites in the genome where the conformation of chromatin renders its DNA hypersensitive to cleavage by endonuclease DNAse I. Option C: Chromatin immunoprecipitation-sequencing (ChIP-seq) is used for simultaneous identification of all of the genomic sites bound by a given transcription factor under a given set of physiologic conditions Option D: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a molecular cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescent probes that bind to only particular parts of a nucleic acid sequence with high degree of sequence complementarity. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 39 PN 447

125.q: Calories from TPN: 100mg dextrose. 30mg amino acids, 40 mg lipids
125.e: Carbohydrates & protein (amino acid) provide energy of 4 Kcal/gm, whereas fats are a concentrated source of energy providing 9 Kcal/gm. So total calorie calculation = (100 x 4) + (30 x 4) + (40 x 9) = 880 So Option D is correct.
The active part of both Glutathione and N-Acetyl Cysteine is the Sulfhydryl group of Cysteine. So N-Acetyl Cysteine replenishes Glutathione. Reference: Harper's 32 nd edition, page 23

125.q: True about Nitric Oxide are all except:
o: Nitric Oxide Synthase has three isoforms
Otherwise called Endothelium derived Relaxing Factor
125.e: Nitric Oxide acts through cGMP Formed from Arginine iNOS, eNOS, nNOS are three isoforms of Nitric Oxide Synthase Nitric Oxide Uncharged molecule has an unpaired electron, so it is highly reactive, free radical. Very short half life (0.1 seconds) Formerly called Endothelium Derived Relaxing Factor. Gaseous molecules. Second messenger is cGMP. Functions of Nitric Oxide Potent Vasodilator. Involved in Penile erection Neurotransmitter in brain and Peripheral Nervous System. Low level of NO involved in Pylorospasm in Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis. Inhibit adhesion, activation and aggregation of Platelets. Reference: Harper's 32 nd edition, page 661

126.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with Jaundice. His laboratory reports show increase in AST, ALT and Serum Bilirubin. Which of the following correlates the condition?
126.e: The condition suggests liver cellular injury. All options other than cell membrane rupture are reversible cell injury. Irreversible injury like cell membrane injury shows elevated serum levels due to leakage of intracellular enzymes. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:37

126.q: Which of the following is/are effect(s) of irreversible cell injury caused by reactive oxygen species?
o: Lesions in DNA, loss of phospholipids
126.e: The production of ROS is increased by many injurious stimuli. These free radicals are removed by spontaneous decay and by specialized enzymatic systems. Excessive production or inadequate removal leads to accumulation of free radicals in cells, which may damage lipids(by peroxidation), proteins and DNA, resulting in cell injury. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 44

126.q: Which of the following conditions is an example of disuse atrophy?
o: Skeletal muscle in patients with limb immobilization
Cardiac muscles in patients with Brown atrophy of the heart
126.e: Causes of atrophy include a decreased workload(e.g., immobilization of a limb to permit healing of a fracture), loss of innervation, diminished blood supply, inadequate nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation and aging(senile atrophy). Although some of these stimuli are physiologic(e.g., the loss of hormone stimulation in menopause) and others are pathologic (e.g., denervation), the fundamental cellular changes are similar. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 50

127.q: Which of the following gives moth eaten appearance in the cytoplasm of necrotic cell?
127.e: Necrosis is characterized by changes in the cytoplasm and nuclei of the injured cells. Necrotic cells show increased eosinophilia(i.e., they are stained red by the dye eosin), attributable partly to increased binding of eosin to denatured cytoplasmic proteins and partly to loss of basophilic ribonucleic acid(RNA) in the cytoplasm(basophilia stems from binding of the blue dye hematoxylin). Compared with viable cells, the cell may have a glassy, homogeneous appearance, mostly because of the loss of lighter staining glycogen particles. Myelin figures are more prominent in necrotic cells than in cells with reversible injury. When enzymes have digested cytoplasmic organelles, the cytoplasm becomes vacuolated and appears "moth-eaten." Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:35

Anti-apoptotic. BCL2, BCL-XL, and MCL1 are the principal members of this group; they possess four BH domains (called BH1-4). These proteins reside in the outer mitochondrial membrane as well as in the cytosol and ER membranes. Regulated apoptosis initiators or sensors. Members of this group, including BAD, BIM, BID, Puma, and Noxa, contain only one BH domain, the third of the four BH domains, and hence are sometimes called BH3-only proteins. The activity of BH3-only proteins is modulated by sensors of cellular stress and damage; when upregulated and activated, they can initiate apoptosis. Reference: Robbins& Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 44

127.q: Which of the following changes are seen in infarction microscopically?
127.e: In most tissues, the main histologic finding associated with infarcts is ischemic coagulative necrosis. Coagulative necrosis is a type of cell death that occurs when blood flow to cells stops or slows (ischemia). It can occur anywhere in the body except the brain. Many conditions can cause ischemia, including atherosclerosis. Treatment and prognosis depend on the extent of the damage to the cells and tissues. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:115

128.q: A 65-year-old male patient having long-standing cigarette smoking (2 pkt/day) and nonfebrile presented to OPD complaints of shortness of breath and cough since many months. His dyspneic duration and intensity increasing these days. His chest is hyperresonant on percussion. Clubbing is also present. X-ray revealed overinflation of lung. Based on the above findings, what will be the histopathological findings in the lung?
o: Destruction of the walls of airspaces without fibrosis
Interstitial fibrosis of the lung parenchyma
Prominent bronchial smooth muscle cell hyperplasia
128.e: Emphysema is a chronic lung disease characterized by enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, with destruction of their walls, but without fibrosis or inflammation. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter-15, Pg 678

128.q: Which concept states that a normal human cell can only replicate and divide forty to sixty times before it cannot divide anymore, and will break down by programmed cell death or apoptosis?
128.e: B and c are realetd to neoplasia and d is related to quality control Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 42

128.q: Which pathological process is the reason of release of cardiac specific enzymes in blood?
128.e: The biochemical mechanisms of necrosis vary with different injurious stimuli. These mechanisms include: Failure of energy generation in the form of ATP because of reduced oxygen supply or mitochondrial damage Damage to cellular membranes, including the plasma membrane and lysosomal membranes, which results in leakage of cellular contents including enzymes Irreversible damage to cellular lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, which may be caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS); and others. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:35

129.q: A 42-year-old man has had increasing progressive muscle weakness in both arms and legs along with dysarthria and difficulty in swallowing for the past 2 years. He is now wheelchair-bound. Physical examination shows 3/5 motor strength in all extremities. He has no muscle pain on palpation, no deformities or loss of joint mobility, and no tremor. A biopsy specimen of the quadriceps muscle is obtained, and microscopic examination shows no inflammation, but only atrophy of the myofibers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
129.e: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is also known as Lou Gehrig disease, named for the famous New York Yankee first baseman affected with the disorder. Lower and upper motor neurons can be affected, resulting in a denervation type of pattern of muscular atrophy. This occurs because an individual neuron innervates a group of muscle fibers. Bulbar (cranial nerve) involvement denotes a more rapid course. Werdnig-Hoffmann disease also is a neuropathic disease with grouped atrophy, but onset is in infancy. The other listed options are not associated with denervation.

Inflammation is never associated with apoptosis and this is one of the major differences between necrosis and apoptosis. Reference: Robbins& Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 44

129.q: Which of the following is/are the morphological feature(s) of acute pancreatitis? i. Microvascular injury and edema ii. Fat necrosis and acute inflammation iii. Destruction of pancreatic parenchyma and blood vessels iv. Infiltration by eosinophils
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
129.e: Acute pancreatitis, is sudden inflammation of pancreas that may be mild or life threatening. The basic alterations in acute pancreatitis are microvascular leakage causing oedema. necrosis of fat by lipases, an acute inflammatory reaction, proteolytic destruction of pancreatic parenchyma, and destruction of blood vessels leading to interstitial haemorrhage. Mild cases are usually successfully treated with conservative measures. Severe cases often require admission in intensive care unit to monitor and manage complications of the disease. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-681

130.q: Which is the first site of scar deposition in liver biopsy under the microscope?
130.e: Scar formation may follow very severe acute injury, but occurs more often as a reaction to chronic injury. The principal cell type involved in scar deposition is the peri-sinusoidal hepatic stellate cell. Following liver injury, stellate cells may become activated and convert into highly fibro genic my fibroblasts, which produce the fibrous scar. Stellate cell activation involves complex interactions between Kupffer cells, hepatocytes, and inflammatory cells. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-639

130.q: Complement complex that attacks cell membrane is:
130.e: The complement complex attacking the cell membrane is membrane attack complex having a composition of C56789. Action of this complex leads to entry of fluid and ions inside the cells leading to cell lysis. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 85

130.q: Lewis triple response is caused by:
130.e: Histamine is vasoactive amine that is located in most body tissues but is highly concentrated in the lungs, skin and gastrointestinal tract. It is stored in mast cell and basophils. When it is injected intradermally, it causes the triple response: Red spot: due to dilatation Wheal: due to exudation of fluid from capillaries Flare: Redness in surrounding area due to arterial dilatation Reference: Goodman and Gilman, 10 th ed, Pg: 650.

131.q: Maximum collagen in wound healing is seen at -
131.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., End of second week During second week there is continued accumulation of collagen and proliferation of fibroblast. Maximum collagen is seen in second week.

131.q: Which of the following contains PDGF?
131.e: Platelets are disc-shaped anucleate cell fragments that are shed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow into the bloodstream. Their function depends on several glycoprotein receptors, a contractile cytoskeleton, and two types of cytoplasmic granules. α-Granules have the adhesion molecule P-selectin on their membranes and contain proteins involved in coagulation, such as fibrinogen, coagulation factor V, and vWF, as well as protein factors that may be involved in wound healing, such as fibronectin, platelet factor 4 (a heparin-binding chemokine), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and transforming growth factor-β. Dense (or δ) granules contain adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate, ionized calcium, serotonin, and epinephrine. Reference :Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 102

131.q: Which of the following is derived from fibroblast cell?
131.e: Interstitial matrix is produced by mesenchymal cells like fibroblasts and is mainly composed of fibrillar and non-fibrillar collagen. TGF-beta is chemotactic for leukocytes and fibroblasts. It induces proliferation of fibroblasts. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 85

132.q: Assertion: Septic infarctions occur when infected cardiac valve vegetations embolize Reason: Septic infarct gets converted into a granuloma.
o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related
The first statement is true and second is false
The first statement is false and second is true
132.e: Septic infarcts occur when infected cardiac valve vegetations embolize, or when microbes seed necrotic tissue. In these cases, the infarct is converted into an abscess, with a correspondingly greater inflammatory response and healing by organization and fibrosis. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:115

132.q: Elevated D-dimer levels are specific for:
132.e: Levels of fibrin degradation products, including crosslinked fibrin degradation products (D-dimer), are usually increased in the presence of acute venous thromboembolism. Absence of an elevated level of D-dimer in patients undergoing an evaluation for acute DVT or PE has an excellent negative predictive value for thrombosis. Reference : Wintrobe's 12th/pg 1437

132.q: Which is the commonest site of thrombosis?
132.e: Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis) are almost invariably occlusive; they frequently propagate some distance toward the heart, forming a long cast within the vessel lumen that is prone to give rise to emboli. Because these thrombi form in the sluggish venous circulation, they tend to contain more enmeshed red cells, leading to stasis or thrombi. The veins of the lower extremities are most commonly affected (90% of venous thromboses); however, venous thrombi also can occur in the upper extremities, periprostatic plexus, or ovarian and periuterine veins, and under special circumstances they may be found in the dural sinuses, portal vein, or hepatic vein. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:110

133.q: Why do all mitochondria DNA of the embryo come from the mother?
o: Head and tail of sperm degrade upon fertilization
Cell division process leaves out mitochondria DNA from sperm
Mitochondrial DNA of sperm is degraded upon entering egg
133.e: During fertilization, the sperm penetrates the outer layer of the egg and fuses with the plasma membrane. Upon fusion, the sperm releases its contents inside the egg and the head and tail are degraded. Mitochondria are heavy in the tail so DNA does not get transferred from the sperm. Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 29

133.q: All of the following features are true pertaining to autosomal recessive disorders EXCEPT:
o: Onset is frequently early in life.
The expression of the defect tends to be uniform
50% reduction in the normal gene product is associated with clinical signs and symptoms.
133.e: 50% reduction in the normal gene product is associated with clinical signs and symptoms is a feature of autosomal dominant disorder. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 246

133.q: ABO blood group is an example of ?
133.e: WHEN BOTH ALLELES EXPRESS THEMSELVES, ITS CALLED CO-DOMINANCE Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th Edition page No.141

134.q: A 10 year old child complaining of abdominal pain and weakness. On examination hepatosplenomegaly noted. In blood investigation pancytopenia was found. Bone marrow shows 'crumbled tissue paper appearance'. This disorder is occur because of accumulation of which of the following molecule.
134.e: Gaucher’s Disease Most common Lysosomal Storage Disorder Enzyme Defect:- Glucocerebrosidase defect Lysosomes filled with Glucocerebroside No cherry red spot in the macula Hematological features: Pancytopenia, bleeding manifestation Hepatosplenomegaly Bone Pain and Pathological Fractures of long bones X-ray Femur Erlenmeyer Flask Deformity Bone Marrow Biopsy Gaucher cell with Wrinkled paper appearance/crumbled tissue paper appearance. Elevated seruml levls of chitotriosidase, ACE & TRAP, also CCL-18/PARC Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 251

134.q: Accumulation of sphingomyelin in phagocytic cells is feature of:
134.e: Niemann-Pick Disease Autosomal Recessive Biochemical defect Deficient activity of acid sphingomyelinase, a lysosomal enzyme encoded by a gene on chromosome 11 Accumulation of sphingomyelin and other lipids in the monocyte-macrophage system. Clinical features Failure to thrive Hepatosplenomegaly Rapidly progressive neurodegenerative course. Treatment Orthotopic liver transplantation Amniotic cell transplantation Bone marrow transplantation Miglustat A phase I trial of enzyme replacement therapy for type B NPD. Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 250-251

134.q: Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with which residue in Golgi apparatus to direct them to lysosome?
134.e: Mannose 6- phosphate is marker for delivering lysosomal enzymes Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing roughly 40 different acid hydrolases (i.e., enzymes that function best in acidic pH - 5). These hydrolases include proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases, phosphatases, and sulfatases. Lysosomal enzymes are initially synthesized in the ER lumen and then tagged with a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) residue within the Golgi apparatus. Such M6P-modified proteins are subsequently delivered to lysosomes through trans-Golgi vesicles that express M6P receptors. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 1 pg 13

o: Accumulation of short chain fatty acids
Accumulation of very long chain fatty acids
Accumulation of medium chain fatty acids
135.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Accumulation of very long chain fatty acids [Ref Harper 29m/e p. 554; Chatterjea 6th le p. 412] Zellweger Syndrome is a rare inborn error of peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation° due to absence of functional peroxisomes in all tissues. As a result, the long chain fatty acids are not oxidized in peroxisomes and accumulate in tissues particularly in brain, liver, kidney and muscle and usually result in death by age six.

135.q: A patient was diagnosed with isolated increase in LDL. His father and brother had the same disease with increased cholesterol. The likely diagnosis is:
135.e: Disease:- Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa) Defect:- Defective LDL receptors or mutation in ligand region of apo B-100. Remarks:- Elevated LDL levels and hypercholesterolemia, resulting in atherosclerosis and coronary disease. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 275

135.q: A child presents with micrognathia and low-set ears. These clinical features are commonly associated with which type of genetic abnormality?
135.e: Explanation: Micrognathia (small jaw) and low-set ears are classic dysmorphic features seen in several chromosomal deletion syndromes, such as: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) Wolf -Hirschhorn syndrome (4p deletion) 2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) 13q deletion syndrome T Translocations, inversions, or amplifications may also cause genetic disorders, but specific features like micrognathia and low-set ears are most characteristically seen with deletions. (option B, C, D) Key Takeaways: Deletions consistently produce the distinct facial dysmorphisms (micrognathia, low-set ears) due to loss of developmental genes. References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4736720/ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1523/?utm_source=chatgpt.com https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1183/

136.q: Which of the following statement is NOT TRUE for invasion and metastasis?
o: Cell-cell contacts are lost by inactivation of E-cadherin
Some tumour show organ tropism due to expression of adhesion or chemokine receptors whose ligands are expressed by endothelial cells at the metastatic site
Sarcomas preferably metastasize through the lymphatic route
SNAIL and TWIST are metastasis oncogenes
136.e: Lymphatic spread is more typical of carcinomas , whereas haematogenous spread is favoured by sarcomas . Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 196.

136.q: Which of the following is MOST suitable definition for Differentiation in context to Neoplasia?
o: The extent to which tumour cells resemble their normal mature tissues in structure
The extent to which tumour cells resemble primitive tissue of the fetus in function
The extent to which tumour cells resemble their normal mature tissue in structure and function
The extent to which tumour cells resemble primitive tissue of the fetus in structure and function
136.e: Differentiation refers to the extent to which neoplasms resemble their parenchymal cells of origin, both morphologically and functionally; lack of differentiation is called anaplasia. In general, benign neoplasms are composed of well-differentiated cells that closely resemble their normal counterparts. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 192.

136.q: Which of the following is an unequivocal sign of malignancy?
136.e: Metastasis is defined as the spread of a tumour to sites that are physically discontinuous with the primary tumour, an event that unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant. The spread of cancer cells from the place where they first formed to another part of the body. In metastasis, cancer cells break away from the original(primary) tumor, travel through the blood or lymph system, and form a new tumor in other organs or tissues of the body. Metastasis is a pathogenic agent's spread from an initial or primary site to a different or secondary site within the host's body; the term is typically used when referring to metastasis by a cancerous tumor. The newly pathological sites, then are metastases. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 272-273.

137.q: Cancer cell survival is enhanced by which of the following events? i. Overexpression of p53 gene ii. Suppression of p53 protein iii. BAX iv. BCL-2
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
137.e: Activation of p53 leads to cell cycle arrest and it also directs the transcription of several pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX and PUMA which are believed to tip the balance in favour of cell death via intrinsic pathway. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 295.

137.q: Which of the following gene is the Governor of proliferation of the cells in neoplasia?
137.e: RB , a key negative regulator of the cell cycle, is directly or indirectly inactivated in most human cancers. The function of the RB protein is to regulate the G1/S checkpoint , the portal through which cells must pass before DNA replication commences. RB exerts anti-proliferative effects by controlling the G1-to-S transition of the cell cycle. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 208-211.

137.q: Which of the following is/are true statement's about p53 i. It regulates the genes involved in cell cycle progression ii. Its increased levels can induce apoptosis iii. Mutations of p53 gene are common genetic alteration seen in variety of human cancers. iv. UV radiation decreases its activity and causes cell cycle stimulation.
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
137.e: UV radiation decreases its activity and causes cell cycle arrest. p53, also known as Tumor protein P53, cellular tumor antigen p53 or transformation-related protein 53 is a regulatory protein that is often mutated in human cancers. The p53 proteins are crucial in vertebrates, where they prevent cancer formation. Activated p53 promotes cell cycle arrest to allow DNA repair and/or apoptosis to prevent the propagation of cells with serious DNA damage through the transactivation of its target genes implicated in the induction of cell cycle arrest and/or apoptosis. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 211.

138.q: Carcinoma of lung, breast marker is -
138.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., CEA Carcinoembryonic antigen is a marker in cancer of colon, pancreas, lung, breast, and ovary.

138.q: All the following are associated with obesity EXCEPT?
138.e: Explanation: Cancers with increased incidence in obesity due to: Hyperinsulinemia, increased IGF-1 , Chronic inflammation , Increased estrogen (from aromatization in adipose tissue) . Cancers associated with obesity include : Adenocarcinomas of the esophagus, gastric(Option C ruled out), colon , rectum , liver , gallbladder , pancreas(Option D ruled out) , kidney , thyroid . In women: endometrium, ovary, breast (postmenopausal) . In men: prostate . Meningioma (Option A ruled out)

138.q: Which of the following growth factors is associated with cancer cachexia? i. PDGF ii. EGF iii. VEGF iv. TNF
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
138.e: It is suspected that TNF and other cytokines produced by macrophages in response to tumour cells or by the tumour cells themselves mediate cachexia. TNF suppresses appetite and inhibits the action of lipoprotein lipase, preventing the release of free fatty acids from lipoproteins.
