Histopathological examination of the lesion after removal shows dystrophic calcification. Which of the following additional complications is she most likely to have?
182.e: Prolactinomas are more common than other hormonesecreting pituitary adenomas. In addition to her galactorrhea and infertility, this patient also may have decreased libido, and her amenorrhea is secondary to the excessive prolactin secretion. Microadenomas might not have pressure effects on surrounding structures such as optic chiasm, but they can be discovered because of their hormonal effects. Acromegaly results from a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma in an adult. Cushing disease occurs when there is an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. A thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-secreting pituitary adenoma is uncommon, but it could account for elevated levels of T4 and TSH in a hyper-thyroid patient. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1066

182.q: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of type 2 diabetes mellitus suffers a massive hemorrhagic stroke and expires. Examination of the pancreas shows hyalinization of many islets of Langerhans. Which of the following characterizes the material within the islets of Langerhans?
182.e: In T2DM, amyloid is often present within the islets of Langerhans, particularly in patients over 60 years of age. This type of amyloid derives from a polypeptide molecule known as amylin, which is secreted with insulin by the β-cell. As many as 20% of aged nondiabetic persons also have amyloid deposits in the pancreas, which is a finding that has been attributed to the aging process itself. None of the other choices show Congo red staining and apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1097

183.q: Which of the following antibodies is most frequently seen in Antiphospholipid Syndrome?
183.e: Anti- beta 2 glycoprotein antibody is most frequently seen in Antiphospholipid Syndrome Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 124; 8th/pg 123

183.q: A patient presented with neck swelling. Cytology showed parafollicular cells along with clusters of plasmacytoid and scant amyloid. What investigation should be done to follow up the patient?
183.e: Parafollicular cells along with clusters of plasmacytoid and scant amyloid are suggestive of medullary carcinoma thyroid gland. Serum calcitonin levels are used as a tumor marker in this case. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1091

183.q: All the following condition can be diagnosed by FNAC; except:
183.e: The hallmark of all follicular adenomas is the presence of an intact, well-formed capsule encircling the tumor. Careful evaluation of the integrity of the capsule is therefore, critical in distinguishing follicular adenomas from follicular carcinomas, which demonstrate capsular and/or vascular invasion. This can be demonstrated by biopsy of the gland and not FNAC which will demonstrate only the morphology of the tumor cells and not the entire gland histology. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th edition, pg631

184.q: A 59-year-old woman has a firm mass with irregular borders felt in her left breast on a routine physical examination. A fine needle aspiration is performed and microscopic examination shows an infiltrating ductal carcinoma. A left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection is performed. A tissue sample of this neoplasm is submitted for analysis by flow cytometry. Which of the following does flow cytometric analysis most likely provide?
184.e: Aneuploidy is defined as a number of chromosomes that is not a multiple of the haploid state; for humans, that is a chromosome number that is not a multiple of 23. Aneuploidy is remarkably common in cancers, particularly carcinomas and was proposed as a cause of carcinogenesis over 100 years ago. Aneuploidy is the presence of one or more extra chromosomes or the absence of one or more chromosomes. The risk of fetal aneuploidy rises with increasing maternal age. Because fetal aneuploidy can affect any pregnancy, all pregnant women should be offered screening. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 203.
Ans. is 'd' i.e., Papilloma Examples include atypical ductal hyperplasia, atypical lobular hyperplasia, and intraductal papillomas.

184.q: A 52-year-old woman feels a lump in her right breast. Her physician palpates an irregular 3 cm mass that is not movable because it appears fixed to the overlying skin, which is retracted. A mastectomy is performed and the pathologist on sectioning the breast finds a 3 x 3.5 cm ovoid mass that does not have discrete borders, but appears to infiltrate into the surrounding fibrofatty breast stroma. The mass is firm, white and has a fibrous consistency. Which of the following features is most likely demonstrated by the gross appearance of this mass?
184.e: Malignant potential is revealed only by invasion into adjacent tissues or metastasis. The stroma carrying the blood supply is crucial to the growth of tumours but does not aid in the separation of benign from malignant ones. The amount of stromal connective tissue does, however, determine the consistency of a neoplasm. Certain cancers induce a dense, abundant fibrous stroma(desmoplasia), making them hard, so-called "scirrhous tumors". Desmoplasia is the result of increased synthesis of extracellular matrix proteins and collagen by stromal cells. It is considered to be a reaction and response of the host tissue against invasive cancer cells.[5] The biological relevance of the desmoplastic response to cancer is still unclear. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 193.

185.q: Most common site of bone metastasis in prostate cancer
185.e: Lumbar spine > Proximal femur > Pelvis > Thoracic spine > Ribs Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 977

Answer- D. All Infection :- Osteomyelitis, Brodie's abscess, syphilis Neoplasms Benign : Osteoid osteoma Malignant : Ewing's sarcoma, osteosarcoma Eosinophilic granuloma Healed stress fracture Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy

185.q: GNAS mutation is associated with malignancy of which cells?
185.e: The mutation of guanine nucleotide-activating alpha subunit (GNAS) gene is the somatic mutation related to the McCune-Albright syndrome. GNAS mutation is also detected in about 30% to 40% of sporadic growth hormone (GH) secreting tumors.

186.q: Which of the following/s is/are seronegative arthritis?
186.e: SERONEGATIVE ARTHRITIS REFERS TO A GROUP OF FOUR CHRONIC DISEASES - ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS, PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS, REACTIVE ARTHRITIS, AND ENTEROPATHIC ARTHRITIS. ALL OF THEM ARE NEGATIVE FOR RHEUMATOID FACTOR, THEY'RE ALL POSITIVE FOR HLA-B27, AND THEY TYPICALLY ALL RUN IN FAMILIES. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number- 822

186.q: Which of the following is involved in the development of rheumatoid arthritis?
186.e: Explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy joint tissues. In genetically susceptible individuals, exposure to specific antigens activates CD4+ T-cells. These T-cells release inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and interferon-γ, which in turn activate endothelial cells, B-cells, and macrophages. This immune cascade leads to persistent inflammation, joint damage, and the characteristic deformities of RA. Explanation of other options: IgE-mediated (Option A): Primarily seen in allergic reactions, not in RA. Defective cellular and humoral immunity (Option B): RA involves targeted autoimmunity rather than a general immune defect. Chronic microbial infections (Option D): May trigger or worsen autoimmune responses but are not the primary cause of RA.

186.q: Which of the following factor is not included in predisposing factors of Gout?
o: Age older than 60 years of age
186.e: Only about 10% of patients with hyperuricemia develop clinical gout. Other factors contribute symptomatic gout: Age of the individual and duration of the hyperuricemia. Gout usually appears after 20 to 30 years of hyperuricemia. Genetic predisposition. In addition to the well-defined X-linked abnormalities of HGPRT, polymorphisms in genes involved with urate or ion transport and possibly inflammation are also associated with gout. Alcohol consumption. • Obesity. • Drugs (e.g., thiazides) that reduce excretion of urate Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number- 824

187.q: Basal cell layer dysplasia associated with hyper and parakeratosis is seen in
187.e: Actinic keratosis may show dysplastic changes that lead to cutaneous SCC. The stratum corneum is thickened (hyperkeratosis) and cells in this layer retain their nuclei (parakeratosis). Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1145

187.q: Regarding histology of dysplastic nevi, all are correct except
o: Linear fibrosis occurs around epidermal rete ridges involved by the nevus
Lymphocytic infiltrate may be seen in the epidermis
Presence of cytological atypia in form of irregular nuclear contours and hyperchromasia
187.e: Lymphocytic infiltrates may be seen in superficial dermis. Release of melanin from dead nevus cells into dermis may occur (melanin incontinence) and this is phagocytosed by dermal macrophages leading to a peculiar fibrosis surrounding epidermal rete ridges that are involved by nevus. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1137

o: These are benign neoplasms that have mutation leading to constitutive activation of RAS or BRAF
Earliest lesion is a junctional nevus
May become more prominent in pregnancy
Lack neurotization, a phenomenon present in melanoma
187.e: At the deepest extent of melanocytic nevi, nevus cells often acquire fusiform contours and grow in fascicles resembling neural tissue, this phenomenon is called neurotization and it is absent in melanoma. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1136

188.q: What is the most common site for Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma?
188.e: Pilocytic astrocytomas are relatively benign tumors that typically affect children and young adults. Most commonly located in the cerebellum , they also may involve the third ventricle, the optic pathways, the spinal cord, and occasionally the cerebral hemispheres. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 883

188.q: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency room 2 hours after being involved in an automobile accident. The patient denies striking his head, although his head was thrust forward and backward. His vital signs are normal, and he returns home. The following day, the patient's wife notices that he is lethargic. By the time the ambulance arrives at the emergency room, the patient is comatose. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the decline in mental status in this patient?
188.e: The consequences of traumatic brain injury may be internal and subtle. The parasagittal cortex is anchored to arachnoid villi, whereas the lateral aspects of the cerebrum move more freely. This anatomical feature, together with the differential density of gray and white matter, permits generation of shearing forces between different brain regions, leading to diffuse axonal shearing injuries, particularly in vehicular accidents. Shearing injuries can distort or disrupt axons, causing them to retract into "spheroids", as well as lose myelin. This type of injury typically occurs in parasagittal white matter and may be accompanied by multiple small hemorrhages. Duret hemorrhage (choice b) occurs in the uncus during transtentorial herniation. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1249

188.q: Which is the most common brain tumour?
188.e: Most common brain tumour is Metastatic tumour and the most common primary brain tumour is meningioma. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 885

189.q: Flow cytometry is used to detect?
189.e: Flow cytometry helps in subtyping hematopoietic cells. Blood cell counters give differential leukocyte count Coagulometers give coagulation profile Antibody quantification is usually done by ELISA Reference: Pathology Outlines - Flow cytometry

189.q: Flow cytometry is routinely utilized for:
189.e: Flow cytometry is used routinely in the classification of leukemias and lymphomas. In this method, fluorescently labeled antibodies against cell surface molecules and differentiation antigens are used to obtain the phenotype of malignant cells. Flow cytometry is a technology that rapidly analyzes single cells or particles as they flow past single or multiple lasers while suspended in a buffered salt-based solution. Each particle is analyzed for visible light scatter and one or multiple fluorescence parameters. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 238.

189.q: What is/are use's of DNA Microarrays?
189.e: The most common method for large-scale analysis of RNA expression in use in research laboratories has been based on DNA microarrays. DNA microarray analysis helps as the bacterial genomic DNA often outlasts the viability of the bacteria and a diagnosis can be made using a small amount of DNA, as opposed to the large numbers of bacteria needed for culture. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 240.

190.q: Resolution provided by light microscope is:
190.e: Resolution power: It is the ability to produce separate images of closely placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power of: Unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm) Light microscope is about 0.2 μm Electron microscope is about 0.5 nm The best resolution for an optical microscope is about 0.2 microns = 200 nm. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 7-8

190.q: Resolution provided by electron microscope is:
190.e: Resolution power: It is the ability to produce separate images of closely placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power of: Unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm) Light microscope is about 0.2 μm Electron microscope is about 0.5 nm Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 11

190.q: Resolution provided by unaided human eye is:
190.e: Resolution power: It is the ability to produce separate images of closely placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power of: Unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm) Light microscope is about 0.2 μm Electron microscope is about 0.5 nm Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 2, Pg 10

191.q: Most potent stimulator of Naive T-cells -
191.e: Mature Dendritic cells Mature B-cells and T-cells before antigenic exposure are called naive-B and T cells respectively. Sequence of events in activation of naive T cells. Immature dendritic cells in the epidermis are called langerhans cell. These immature dendritic cells (langerhans cells) capture the antigen in the epidermis. After capturing the antigen these cells secrete cytokines. These cytokines cause loss of adhesiveness of langerhans cells. Langerhans cells separate from each other and migrate into lymphatic vessels. In lymphatic vessel, maturation of langerhans cells takes place. Then these mature langerhans dendritic cells reach to naive T cells in the lymph nodes and present antigen to these cells and activate them.

191.q: A 20-year-old female presents with history of recurrent episodes of swelling of the submucosal tissue of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts from childhood. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates that her C1 inhibitor level is less than 6% of the reference value. The most likely diagnosis is:
191.e: Hereditary angioedema is caused by deficient levels of C1 inhibitor. This reduces the ability to control activation of the classical pathway. Autosomal-dominant inheritance Gene locus: SERPING1(C1 inhibitor) on chromosome 11 Excessive spontaneous activation of classical complement pathway (especially C2) causing local inflammation of gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts. Swelling of tracheal and bronchial passages can be life-threatening. Nutrition-based immunodeficiencies are not does not presents with severely reduced levels of specific cell types or related molecules. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is caused by a deficiency of CD59. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is caused by a deficiency of the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

191.q: Lysozyme is found in significant quantities in all of the following bodily secretions, EXCEPT:
191.e: Lysozyme is present in tears, saliva, human breast milk and respiratory mucus secretions. It is also present in cytoplasmic granules of the macrophages and the polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). Reduced lysozyme levels have been associated with bronchopulmonary dysplasia in newborns. In certain cancers (especially myelomonocytic leukemia) excessive production of lysozyme by cancer cells can lead to toxic levels of lysozyme in the blood. High lysozyme blood levels can lead to kidney failure and low blood potassium. It is used as a marker of sarcoidosis disease activity and is suitable for disease monitoring. (Sensitive but less specific) Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 14, Page Number: 175

192.e: T-independent antigens can stimulate B cells directly without the need for T-cell help. These antigens are typically polysaccharides or repetitive structures that can cross-link B cell receptors, leading to B cell activation and antibody production. Key Takeaway: T-independent antigens activate B cells directly, bypassing the need for T helper cells. Tag: FMGE 2023 Tag Line: Moderate Reference: Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology , chapter 12 on antigens - antibody reaction.PP-152.

192.q: All of the following interactions occur between antigen-antibody reactions except:
192.e: Antigen-antibody interactions primarily involve ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and Van der Waals forces. Covalent bonds are not typically involved in these interactions. Key Takeaway: Antigen-antibody interactions are primarily mediated by non-covalent forces. Tag: May know Tag Line: Moderate Reference Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology , chapter 12 on antigens – antibody reaction.PP-160.

192.q: Which of the following is very difficult to induce antibody?
192.e: Following antigens have poor immunogenicity (difficult induction of antibody): Smaller size/molecular weight antigens Nucleic acid > Lipids > Carbohydrates (in decreasing order) Antigens not degradable by tissue enzyme self-antigen Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 15, Pg 148-150

193.q: A 30-year-old male presents with headache, fatigue, light-headedness, dyspnea, and tachycardia. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased hemoglobin and a positive direct Coomb's test. The patient is presently on an antibiotic for symptoms of upper respiratory infection. These findings suggest which of the following?
o: Type I, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type II, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type III, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type III, mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies
193.e: Type II reactions involve antibodies directed against self-cells (erythrocytes) or membranes. Certain drugs react with erythrocytes to form neoantigens. Type I responses are against foreign antigens (e.g., allergens), cause IgE responses, and do not invoke a Coomb's reaction. Type III reactions involve soluble antigen-antibody complexes, and type IV reactions do not involve antibody. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

193.q: True regarding Histamine release from mast cell granules:
o: It requires the cells to have IgE of only one antigenic specificity per cell
It cannot occur in the absence of antigen-specific IgE
It occurs after IgE Fc receptor crosslinking
193.e: Basophils and mast cells bind IgE via high affinity Fc receptors, so each cell has IgE of many different specificities on its surface. Ca2+is required Many non-lgE triggers (C3a and C5a) can produce granule release. IgE Fc receptor crosslinking triggers release of granule content from mast cell. Referene: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

193.q: A young student immediately felt difficulty in breathing and tightness in his chest. Hestarted sweating and fainted. His friends found out that a bee had just stung him. The emergency school medical team attended him and within minutes he recovered. Which one of the following drugs was administered by the medical team?
193.e: This patient had a major anaphylactic reaction and his tracheal-bronchial smooth muscle has contracted. Epinephrine is the only treatment in this group to reverse this reaction. It will relax the smooth muscle of the respiratory tree and stimulate the heart to beat stronger to raise the blood pressure. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

194.q: Bence Jones protein are composed of:
194.e: Bence-Jones proteins: Multiple myeloma light chain immunoglobulin - kappa or lambda. Identified in urine by coagulation when heated to 50°C but redissolving at 70° In single patient - kappa/lambda, never both Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 13, Pg 201

194.q: Most effective method to prevent transmission of MRSA in a ward is?
194.e: Single most effective method of prevention of hospital acquired infections is handwashing. DOC in the treatment of MRSA is vancomycin. Nasal carriers are treated with mupirocin. Reference: Essentials of medical microbiology by Apurba sastry 1 st edition Pg no.218

194.q: Treatment for nasal carriers of MRSA is by
194.e: Single most effective method of prevention of hospital acquired infections is handwashing. DOC in the treatment of MRSA is vancomycin. Nasal carriers are treated with mupirocin. Reference: Essentials of medical microbiology by Apurba sastry 1 st edition Pg no.218

195.q: Which of the following is not a step in Pathogenesis of listeriosis?
195.e: Pathogenesis of listeriosis: Intracellular survival : After entry into the intestinal epithelium, it survives inside the host cell, mainly due to lysis of phagosome by forming pores (mediated by listeriolysin O) Then it causes host cell actin polymerization , which helps the bacterium to reach near the cell membrane. Finally, it migrates to the adjacent epithelial cells/ macrophages by direct cell-to-cell spread, mediated by listeriopods . Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 698.

195.q: Periodontal disease form of actinomycosis is caused mainly by:
195.e: Dental caries and periodontal diseases: Mainly caused by naeslundii and A. odontolyticus. Oral-cervicofacial actinomycosis: This is the most common form, usually presented as a painless, slow growing, hard mass with cutaneous fistulas, a condition commonly known as lumpy jaw. Thoracic actinomycosis may present as cavitary lesions and pleural effusion. Abdominal form: It occurs due to spillage of intestinal flora secondary to bowel surgery or other conditions of bowel such as appendicitis. Pelvic form: It occurs following intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUCDs) insertion. Brain abscesses. Bone destruction and soft tissue infections. Disseminated form: It may occur due to hematogenous spread. Lungs and liver are the common sites; where multiple nodules are formed. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 543.

Diphtheria is disease of childhood, it can be of various types. Faucial, cutaneous etc. Faucial is most common. In his patient has white to grey membrane on tonsil which bleeds on touch. Treatment of Diphtheria is diphtheria antitoxin is to be given. It is made up of antibodies used in the treatment of diphtheria. Dose is as below. Less than 48 hrs duration Pharyngeal/laryngeal - 20000 to 40000 units. Nasopharyngeal - 40000 to 60000 units More than 72 hrs duration 80000 to 120000 units. So all the options given are not true. 196.q: Which cleaning agent is recommended for effectively eliminating Clostridium difficile spores from environmental surfaces?
196.e: C. Sodium hypochlorite (bleach): This agent is highly effective at killing C. difficile spores, making it the recommended choice for disinfection in environments where C. difficile is present. Why Not Others: A. Alcohol-based disinfectants: These are ineffective against C. difficile spores, as they do not have sporicidal properties. B. Hydrogen peroxide: While it has some antimicrobial activity, it is not as effective as sodium hypochlorite for specifically eliminating C. difficile spores. D. Quaternary ammonium compounds: These compounds lack efficacy against C. difficile spores, making them unsuitable for this purpose. Key Takeaway: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) is the recommended disinfectant for eliminating C. difficile spores from surfaces, ensuring effective infection control. Tags : good to know Reference: CDC guidelines on disinfection for C. difficile.

196.q: Which serotype of botulinum toxin is known for being the most severe in human disease?
196.e: Serotype A : This serotype is known for being the most severe and is the one most commonly associated with human botulism. Why Not Others : Serotype B does cause disease but lacks the severity associated with serotype A . Serotype E is less severe and not the primary concern in human botulism cases. Serotype G is not recognized for its severity in human infections, unlike serotype A . Key Takeaway : Serotype A of botulinum toxin is the most severe and is commonly linked to human disease . Tags : neet 2020 Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-40 Food poisoning pp-397.

Pseudomembranous colitis is caused by Clostridioides difficile which is an obligate anerobic gram positive spore forming bacilli. The important risk factors associated with it are Prolonged Antimicrobial use. Prolonged hospital stay Old age Intestinal surgery Antacid treatment Reference: Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 492-493

197.q: Primary pulmonary TB is defined as the initial exogenous infection with tubercle bacilli. What is the name of the complex when the primary complex gets calcified?
197.e: Ranke Complex is formed when the primary complex gets calcified. Ghon focus refers to the initial nodular cavitations. When these involve hilar lymph nodes, it is called primary complex. Simon focus is the hematogenous seeding of apex of the lung in post primary TB. reactivated Simon focus with central caseation is called Assman's focus. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 625

197.q: A patient presented to the urology department with urinary frequency, dysuria, nocturia and abdominal pain. The patient is afebrile at the moment but complains of low grade fever at night. Upon urinalysis,pus cells were found but no bacterial agent was isolated. Imaging revealed a thimble bladder. Which specimen should be collected next for establishing a diagnosis?
197.e: The given clinical features, along with sterile pyuria in urinalysis raises a suspicion of genitourinary TB. It is seen when tubercular bacilli are disseminated hematogenously. It is diagnosed by collecting 3 early morning urine samples and processing them via culture in MGIT or LJ media or Genexpert Radiology may show strictures or perinephric abscesses. It is treated well with ATT Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 752

197.q: Isoniazid is one of the first line drugs for the treatment of tuberculosis. Which of the following layers of the cell wall does it inhibit, that also gives Mycobacteria its acid fastness?
197.e: Mycolic acid layer is the principal constituent of the mycobacterial cell wall, made up of long chain fatty acids attached to arabinogalactan. It confers very low permeability to the cell wall and is responsible for acid fastness. Lipoarabinomannan facilitates the survival of tubercle bacilli within the macrophages. It is also used as a target antigen for the TB diagnosis. Peptidoglycan maintains the shape and rigidity of the cell. Lipopolysaccharide is found in gram negative bacteria. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 624

198.q: Which of the following strains has been used for developing the leprosy vaccine?
198.e: The killed Mycobacterium indicus pranii vaccine has been developed in India in 2018. Trials have shown that if given in close contacts, cases can be brought down by 60% in 3 years Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 538

198.q: Which nerve is never involved in Leprosy?
198.e: The medial plantar nerve is never involved in leprosy. The most commonly involved nerve is ulnar followed by post auricular Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 535

198.q: Which is the earliest sensation lost in leprosy?
198.e: Since lepra bacilli grow in cooler areas, they invade cutaneous nerves first, hence thermal sensations are lost earlier. Reference- https://internationaltextbookofleprosy.org/chapter/neurological-manifestations-leprosy

199.q: What is media used to differentiate EHEC from other E coli?
199.e: Sorbitol Mac Conkey agar is used to differentiate EHEC from other E.coli. It does not ferment sorbitol and produces pale colonies. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.482

199.q: Which of the following is a motile bacterium?
199.e: Proteus spp. are motile by peritrichous flagella. Clostridium perfringens is the only clostridium species that produces a capsule in animal tissues and it is non-motile. Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Bacillus anthracis are non-motile. 199.q: A patient is diagnosed with an infection caused by Enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) O157:H7. In this serotype designation, what does the "H" denote?
199.e: Explanation: The "H" antigen in E. coli serotyping refers to the flagellar antigen, which determines the motility of the bacteria. O157:H7 is a strain of Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) known for producing Shiga toxin, leading to hemorrhagic colitis and Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS). Serotyping of E. coli: "O" antigen → Somatic (LPS) antigen (Option D) "H" antigen → Flagellar antigen (Option C) "K" antigen → Capsular antigen (Option A) Fimbriae (Option B) aid in bacterial adhesion , but they are not part of E. coli serotyping as the "H" antigen.

200.e: Heterophile antibodies are typically detected in the Weil-Felix test, which is used to identify certain types of rickettsial infections. The Widal test is used for typhoid fever, and standard agglutination tests are used for various bacterial infections. Key Takeaway: The Weil-Felix test is associated with the detection of heterophile antibodies. 200.q: Investigation of choice in 2nd and 3rd week of enteric fever is?
200.e: Principle: It is an agglutination test where H and 0 antibodies against S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A and B are detected and measured in the patient's sera by using O and H antigens. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.300-301

200.q: Recommended transport medium for stool specimen in a case of bacillary dysentery is:
200.e: Recommended transport medium for stool specimen is: Sach’s Buffered glycerol saline medium (when Salmonella spp. or Shigella spp. are suspected) Venkatraman Ramkrisnan (VR) medium/ Carry Blair (CB) medium (when Vibrio cholerae is suspected). Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 4, Pg 40-45

201.q: Cholera is known to cause diarrhea through its interaction with specific receptors in the human body. Which of the following is known to make it easier for cholera toxin to enter the body through the intestinal mucosa?
201.e: Explanation: Cholera toxin is produced by Vibrio cholerae and is the main factor responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera. The toxin attaches to receptors on the intestinal epithelial surface and enters the cells. The specific receptor is GM1 ganglioside , a glycosphingolipid located in the intestinal cell membrane. Binding to GM1 initiates endocytosis of the toxin. Inside the cell, the toxin disrupts ion transport, causing massive fluid loss and diarrhea. Explanation of other options: GLUT1 (Option A): Facilitates glucose transport across membranes; not a receptor for cholera toxin. GM2 ganglioside (Option B): A glycosphingolipid, but not the binding site for cholera toxin. Cephalin (Option C): A membrane phospholipid, unrelated to cholera toxin entry. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3089049/

201.q: A 25 yr old man presents with history of diarrhea and fever since 5 days.There is a history of consumption of uncooked crabs and oysters on the trip to Bangkok. On culture ,it showed swarming on blood agar and the organism was found to be motile. Identify the culture media which is blood agar with high salt content which shows beta hemolysis
201.e: Halophilic vibrios can withstand higher salt concentration (>6%) in contrast to V. cholerae, which can tolerate upto 6%. They are widespread in marine environment. Kanagawa phenomenon: It causes hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar (a special type of high salt blood agar). Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.487

201.q: DOC for chemoprophylaxis of cholera is?
201.e: Tetracycline is the drug of choice and is indicated in household contacts during epidemic.

202.q: Organism most likely responsible for ventilation associated pneumonia is:
202.e: Baumannii causes widespread hospital infections such as: Ventilator associated pneumonia Central line associated bloodstream infection Post-neurosurgical meningitis Catheter- associated UTI Wound and soft tissue infections Infections in burn patients Acinetobacter can be grouped into several genomospecies. A. baumannii is the most pathogenic species. Most other species such as A.calcoaceticus and A. lwoffii are rarely pathogenic to man. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 646

202.q: In a Microbiology laboratory you were asked to differentiate Burkholderia pseudomallei and Burkholderia mallei on the basis of biochemical properties. Which of the following test would be used for the same?
202.e: Mallei differs from B. pseudomallei in being non-motile and oxidase negative. List of important bacteria which are: Catalase positive: Remember: 'SPACE' Staphylococcus aureus Pseudomonas Aspergillus Candida Enterobacter Urease positive: Remember: 'PUNCH KiSS' Proteus Ureaplasma Nocardia Cryptococcus Helicobacter Klebsiella Saprophyticus Epidermidis Oxidase negative: All enterobacteriaceae Acinetobacter Staphylococci Streptococci Indole positive: Remember: ' M organ the vulgar ox ate E.coli on the indole pasture with Ed' Morganella Proteus vulgaris Klebsiella Oxytoca Coli Pasteurella Edwardsiella Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition.

202.q: Which medium is used for the enhancement of pigment production by pseudomonas?
202.e: King's media is used for enhancement of pigment production by pseudomonas. 203.q: Acellular pertussis vaccine is composed of: a) Pertussis toxoid b) FHA c) Pertactin d) IgA e) Adhesins f) cAMP
203.e: Acellular Pertussis Vaccine: It is composed of pertussis toxoid and 2 or more other bacterial components such as FHA, pertactin or fimbriae. Though the efficacy is same as the WC vaccine, it is associated with fewer side effects as compared with the latter and can be safely given after 5–6 years. It is available as DaPT (along with diphtheria and tetanus toxoid). It is recommended for older children who have missed their primary doses of DPT. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 641

203.q: What is the mechanism of toxin produced by Bordetella Pertussis?
203.e: Mechanism of various bacteria toxins: Inhibition of elongation factor 2: Diphtheria toxin Pseudomonas Increase cAMP: Remember: 'CAEP' Cholera Anthrax ETEC labile toxin Pertussis Increase cGMP: ETEC stable toxin Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 638

203.q: Which of the following special factors are required for Haemophilus? A. Hemin B. Christmas factor C. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide D. Fibrinogen E. Thrombin F. Ca2+ G. Fe2+
203.e: Haemophilus requires two accessory growth factors (factor X and V) in blood for their growth. Factor X is a hemin, present freely in blood. Factor V is nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), which is present inside RBCs. It is also produced by some bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus. Growth surrounding X and XV disks only: Produced by species that require X factor, but not V factor; examples include H. ducreyi and A. aphrophilus. Growth surrounding V and XV disks only: Produced by species that require X factor, but not V factor; examples include H. parainfluenzae, H. parahaemolyticus and A. paraphrophilus. Growth surrounding combined XV disk only: Produced by species that require both X and V factors; examples include: H. influenzae, H. aegyptius and H. haemolyticus. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 612

204.e: Quintana: It is transmitted by louse. It is the agent of - Trench fever: It occurred as epidemics in the trenches during World War I. It is a mild febrile illness which lasts for five days, subsequent episodes occurring every 5 days (hence also called as 5 days fever). Thereafter, it was found to be silent for decades. However, the disease has re-emerged in USA recently. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 315

204.q: Which of the following amino acids is required for isolation of F.tularensis?
204.e: Isolation of F.tularensis is very difficult as it is highly fastidious. It needs Special media, such as: BCG agar (blood cysteine blood agar) CHAB agar (cysteine heart agar supplemented with 9% heated sheep blood). Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 808

204.q: Drug of choice for rabbit fever is:
204.e: Tularemia, also known as “rabbit fever,” is a disease caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis. Tularemia is typically found in animals, especially rodents, rabbits, and hares. Gentamicin is considered as the drug of choice,given 5mg/kg for 7-10 days. Doxycycline or ciprofloxacin can be given as alternatives. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 810

205.q: Two girls in the same class are diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their 12-year-old close friend is in fear of contracting disease. What advice should be given to her-
o: No vaccine needed as exposure has already occurred.
205.e: Meningococcal meningitis can spread from one person to other. Because it stays in nasopharynx of person. Now in the given case 2 girls in the same class are already diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their friend must get two dose of conjugate vaccine to prevent getting infection. Incorrect options : Option A is wrong two dose of polysaccharide vaccine. Option C i s wrong Single dose of meningococcal vaccine. Because meningococcal vaccine has two dose not one. Option D is wrong, vaccine can help in spreading of infection. No matter exposure has occurred or not, vaccine can always help. Key Takeaways: Conjugate vaccines (MCV4) are preferred over polysaccharide vaccines (MPSV4). Close contacts of meningococcal meningitis cases require vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine induces stronger, long-lasting immunity and reduces carriage.

205.q: Which of the following is not the content of the Modified New York city medium used for the culture of Neisseria?
o: Above all are the contents of modified new york city medium
205.e: Thayer martin medium is also known as new york city medium. Thayer Martin medium is chocolate agar added with vancomycin, colistin and Nystatin. It inhibits commensal Neisseria Species. Modified New York City medium: Lysed blood agar and lincomycin, colistin, trimethoprim and amphotericin B. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 696

205.q: Meningococcal vaccine is ineffective against which of the following serogroups?
205.e: Meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines are currently formulated as either bivalent (serogroups A and C) or quadrivalent (serogroups A, C, Y, and Wl35). Dose: 50 µg of each polysaccharide antigen per dose is used, administered as two doses, 2-3 months apart to children of 3-18 months of age or a single dose to older children or adults. No vaccine is available for serogroup B because: Capsule of serogroup B (made up of sialic acid) is less immunogenic. lt is also encephalitogenic due to expression of similar cross reactive antigens on neural cells. Not given below 3 years. Conjugated vaccines can be given below three years. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 697

206.q: Chlamydiae can synthesize all of the following on their own except:
206.e: RBs are also the metabolically active form and can synthesize their own nucleic acid, lipids and proteins except ATP; hence, they are called as energy parasites (as they depend on host ATP for survival). Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 766

206.q: Identify the true statements for C. psittaci. 1. Is sensitive to sulfonamide. 2. man-to-man transmission present. 3. Causes psittacosis by inhalation route. 4. Exclusive human pathogen. 5. Forms diffuse vacuolated inclusions without glycogen matrix.
206.e: C. psittaci: Forms diffuse vacuolated inclusions without glycogen matrix. Resistant to sulfonamide. Natural pathogen of birds. Leaves the host cell by lysis. Has many serotypes. Disease caused by it: Psittacosis (Atypical interstitial pneumonia). Transmission is by inhalation route - pet birds (parrots) and poultry (turkeys and ducks) No man-to-man transmission. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 767

206.q: All are true for Taiwan Acute Respiratory Agent ( TWAR ) except:
206.e: C. pneumoniae - TWAR agent Exclusive human pathogen Forms inclusions without glycogen matrix Resistant to sulfonamide Has Only 1 serotype Causes: Community-acquired atypical pneumonia. Associated with: atherosclerosis and asthma. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 767

207.q: A 20-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy unknown to her treating doctor, was given a single injection of penicillin for the treatment of syphilis. Within minutes, she developed diffuse urticaria, tachycardia, and hypo-tension. This patient has experienced:
207.e: This patient displays the hallmarks of a classical anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. Anergy is the impairment of effector immune responsiveness. Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity is most often localized to tissues bearing epitopes to which the antibody binds. Contact sensitivity results from the epicutaneous application of a reactive antigen/hapten; in the present question, the antigen (penicillin) was administered intramuscularly. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

207.q: Painless genital ulcer in male with everted margin is seen in ?
207.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e.,Syphilis [Ref Harrison 18th/e p. 1382, Jawetz 22"/e p. 642] Painless indurated ulcer with everted margins, h/o of sexual exposure and lack of systemic symptoms favours the diagnosis of syphilis.

207.q: A 27-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant presents to the Obstetrics clinic for prenatal care. She has a history of treatment for syphilis 4 years previously. The results of serologic tests for syphilis are as follows: Non treponemal test RPR: Non-Reactive Treponemal test (TP-PA) reactive Which of the following statements is most correct?
o: The baby is at high risk for congenital syphilis
The mother needs a lumbar puncture and a VDRL test for her CSF for neurosyphilis
The mother needs to be treated again for syphilis
The mother's previous treatment for syphilis was effective
207.e: Non-treponemal tests, such as VDRL and RPR are preferred over treponemal tests for monitoring response to treatment. Antibody titers of treponemal tests remain elevated even after clinical improvement. VDRL has to be done at 3 month's intervals for at least 1 year. For primary and secondary syphilis: Following clinical improvement, there should be at least a fourfold decline in the titer by the third or fourth month and non-reactive by 12 months. For latent or late syphilis, or patients with multiple episodes of syphilis: It may show a gradual decline in titer, low titers may persist for years. Here, Non treponemal tests are negative hence the treatment to the mother was effective. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 761

208.q: Which of the following is primary cell line ?
208.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Chick embryo fibroblast Chick embryo fibroblast is primary cell culture.

208.q: Choose the correct statement with respect to nucleic acid replication in viruses
o: All DNA viruses replicate in Cytoplasm except Poxvirus
All DNA viruses replicate in nucleus except Poxvirus
All RNA viruses replicate in nucleus except Retrovirus
All RNA viruses replicate in cytoplasm except Papillomavirus
208.e: In DNA viruses, the DNA replication occurs in the nucleus except in poxviruses, which synthesize DNA in the cytoplasm. In RNA viruses, the RNA replication occurs in the cytoplasm except in retroviruses and orthomyxoviruses, which synthesize RNA in the nucleus. Option D is incorrect because Papilloma virus is not an RNA virus Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 83

208.q: Which of the following families includes non-enveloped RNA viruses that cause gastroenteritis?
208.e: Reoviridae is a family of non-enveloped RNA viruses that includes rotavirus, a major cause of gastroenteritis. The other options either include DNA viruses or non-gastroenteritis related RNA viruses. Key Takeaway: Identifying Reoviridae as a family of non-enveloped RNA viruses associated with gastroenteritis is essential for understanding and managing outbreaks of this illness, especially in children. Rotavirus vaccination is associated with intussusception. Tags: neet 2023 Difficulty Level: Medium CDC Reference: CDC - Rotavirus

209.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Plaque assay Plaque assay and Pock assay are quantitative infective assays.

209.q: A 40-year-old female with hepatitis C viral infection presents with decreased renal function, hypertension, and anemia. Laboratory findings decreased serum C3 and urine sediment contains leukocytes, erythrocytes, and red blood cell casts. Her renal biopsy demonstrates changes consistent with glomerulonephritis. These findings suggest which type of hypersensitivity?
o: Type 1 hypersensitivity mediated by CD4+ T cells
Type 4 hypersensitivity mediated by IgG and sometimes IgM
209.e: Glomerulonephritis is often associated with immune complex deposition, a type III hypersensitivity. Red blood cell casts are indicative of glomerulonephritis, and reduced C3 levels indicate a high level of cleavage and activation of C3. Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE, not by CD4+ T cells. Type II hypersensitivity responses usually involve IgG. Type IV hypersensitivities do not involve antibodies. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

209.q: A 35-year-old male doctor presents after a needlestick exposure. Additional hepatitis tests are ordered upon patient's request. The patient's results are: HIV Ag/Ab: Negative/Negative HBsAg: Negative HBsAb: Positive Hepatitis C antibody: Negative HBc IgM: Negative HBc IgG: Positive What is the most likely explanation of the results above?
209.e: Hepatitis B serologies can reveal significant information about the status of hepatitis B in any given patient. Major components of the test include HBsAg (surface antigen), HBsAb (surface antibody), HBc IgM (core IgM antibody), and HBc IgG (core IgG antibody). Immunization from a previous infection indicates previous exposure to viral antigens and subsequent development of antibodies against both to the surface and core antigens. Patients who develop antibodies against the viral envelope antigen (HBeAb) are more likely to achieve long-term clearance of the virus. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

210.q: Which of the following is true for IPV (Salk)?
o: Can be given in immunocompromised patient
210.e: Salk (Injectable Polio Vaccine) is prepared by Formalin killed strain. No local & herd immunity Zero chance of VAPP & VDPV Can be given to immunocompromised patient, pregnant and old aged patients Short duration of protection Relatively safer than OPV Sabin (Oral Polio Vaccine) is prepared from live attenuated strain. Provides both local & herd immunity More chances of VAPP & VDPV Cannot be given to immunocompromised patient, pregnant and old aged patients Longer duration of protection Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 711

210.q: Which of the following is the vector for yellow fever
210.e: Yellow fever is an acute febrile illness which is characterized by liver dysfunction which leads to jaundice. Humans get the infection by the bite of Aedes aegypti or tiger mosquito. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.530

210.q: Which antigenic type of polio is responsible for Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis?
210.e: Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is due to an OPV-like isolated strain, which is slightly genetically divergent from parental OPV strain. VAPP is spread among recipient and its close contacts, and it cannot cause an outbreak. Vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPVs) show high level of genetic divergence from parental OPV strain at VP1 sequences. Most VDPV cases occur due to IPV type 2 strain. VDPVs can be classified into 3 types: Circulating VDPVs Immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs Ambiguous VDPVs Reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264410X98004095

211.q: A 2-year-old girl, Aarti, presented with diarrhea, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and weakness. She suffered from chickenpox before 1 week, for which her mother gave her a tablet of Aspirin for fever. What is the girl suffering from?
211.e: Reye’s syndrome commonly occurs in children undergoing recovery phase of viral infections especially Chickenpox and Influenza, and are taking Aspirin. Symptoms in Reye’s syndrome occurs typically due to fatty degeneration of liver. There is no specific treatment, only supportive management is indicated. Hence, Aspirin is avoided as much as possible in infants and children. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

211.q: A 36-year-old male, Rahul, presented with severe fever, impaired awareness, headache and seizures. Neck rigidity was not seen. CSF PCR was conducted which was positive for HSV1. Which lobe is commonly affected in this condition?
211.e: Fever, impaired awareness, headache and seizures without nuchal rigidity and PCR positive for HSV is suggestive of Herpes Encephalitis. Herpes is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis, and it commonly affects Temporal lobe in adults. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

211.q: A 15-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of the sudden appearance of a rash on her trunk that started 6 hours ago and subsequently spread to her extremities. Four days ago, she was taken to the emergency department because of a high fever and vomiting. She was treated with acetaminophen and discharged the next day. The fever persisted for several days and abated just prior to appearance of the rash. Physical examination shows a rose-colored, blanching, maculopapular rash, and postauricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
211.e: Roseola infantum is a self-limited viral exanthem (usually due to HHV-6 and less commonly, HHV-7) that primarily affects infants and young children and is characterized by a high fever for 3–5 days that is immediately followed by a blanching, maculopapular, non-pruritic rash. The rash initially appears on the trunk but may spread to the face and extremities. It is commonly associated with cervical, postauricular, and/or occipital lymphadenopathy and may also cause febrile seizures. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

212.q: Which of the following is Fungi imperfecti
212.e: Taxonomical Classification - Based on the production of sexual spores, the Kingdom Fungi has been divided into four medically important phyla. They are as follows: Phylum zygomycota: They are lower fungi, produce sexual spores known as zygospores and possess aseptate hyphae, e.g. Rhizopus and Mucor Phylum ascomycota: They produce sexual spores known as ascospores and possess septate hyphae, e.g. Aspergillus Phylum basidiomycota: They produce sexual spores known as basidiospore e.g. Cryptococcus Phylum deuteromycota (Fungi imperfecti): In majority of the medically important fungi, the sexual state is either absent or unidentified yet. Hence, they are traditionally grouped as fungi imperfecti. Reference : Sastry 3rd ed pg. 116 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 87

212.q: Which of the following agent is highly infectious requiring bio safety level 3?
212.e: Cultures of Coccidiodes are highly infectious; may lead to accidental inhalation of spores in laboratories and hence require biosafety level-3 precautions Reference : Sastry 3rd Ed pg. 382 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 413

Ans. is 'd' i.e. T. mentagrophytes Zoophilic dermatophytes are the species which primarily infect animals and occasionally transmitted to humans. Zoophilic species of trichophyton are T. montegrophytes and T verrucosum. Other zoophilic species of dermatophytes is M. canis.

213.q: Latex agglutination study of the antigen in CSF helps in the diagnosis of
213.e: Cryptococcal antigens can be detected in CSF, serum and urine by latex agglutination test. Antigen titre in CSF stays for longer duration and is directly proportional to mortality of the patients. Reference : Jagdish Chander 3/e p306, Harrison 18/e p1651,17/e p1252 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 473

Individuals at high risk for cryptococcosis include: Patients with hematologic malignancies, recipients of solid organ transplants with ongoing immunosuppressive therapy, Persons whose medical conditions necessitate glucocorticoid therapy. Patients with advanced HIV infection and CD4+T lymphocyte counts of Reference: Harrison 18/e p1650-51, 17/e p1251

213.q: Galactomannan antigen in patient's sera or urine (by ELISA) is used for
213.e: Detection of Aspergillus specific galactomannan antigen in patient's sera or urine (by ELISA) Reference : Sastry 3rd edition pg. 118

214.q: Which of the following statement is NOT accurate for Microsporidia species -
o: Reproduce in cell by spore formation
Demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin stain
214.e: Option D - Microsporidia are unicellular obligate intracellular parasites. They reproduce in host cells by producing spores. 3 genera and 13 species are associated with human disease particularly, in HIV and other immuno-compromised patients. Infection is caused by an inhalation or ingestion of spores. Though commonly causes diarrhea, it may also lead to extra intestinal infections like sinusitis, cholangitis, bronchiolitis and kerato- conjunctivitis. Because of its intracellular locations, they are not routinely demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin stain. Modified trichrome stain, gram stain and modified acid-fast stain are usually used to demonstrate them. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -106

214.q: An intermediate host whose presence may be required for the completion of a parasite's life cycle but in which no development of the parasite occurs is -
214.e: Paratenic host : An organism that harbors the sexually immature parasite (larva) but is not necessary for the parasite's developmental cycle to progress. Reservoir host : an organism that harbors a pathogen but suffers no ill effects, responsible for continued existence of parasite in area Accidental host : an organism that generally does not allow transmission to the definitive host, thereby preventing the parasite from completing its development. Definite host : An organism in which the parasite reaches the adult stage and reproduces sexually Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -1

214.q: A first-year pathology resident is given exercise to demonstrate various parasitic infections from peripheral blood smear (PBS). He should look for following parasites in PBS EXCEPT
214.e: Option A – L.donovani is present intracellularly in monocytes or macrophages in PBS as L-D body. Option B – T.brucei and T.cruzi are present extracellularly in plasma. Option D – Babesia are present in RBCs. Schistosomes though present in vesical and pelvic plexuses, it is never demonstrable in peripheral blood smear due to its location in capillaries of internal organs. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -7

215.q: Regarding T.cruzi, which of the following is most accurate :
o: Exists as both amastigote and trypomastigote in humans
Complications of chronic diseases are common in children
215.e: Option C - Metacyclic trypomastigotes are infective forms of parasite which after entry through bug bite, enters R-E cells and convert into amastigote forms. Some of them, after converting through epimastigote form, convert to trypomastigote forms inside blood. Reduviid bug is a vector which when feeds on human blood, acquires infection. Option A - Tsetse fly is a vector which transmits T.brucei Option B - Armadillo, cat ,dog and pigs are major reservoir Option D - complications of chronic diseases are common in adults, while in children acute disease is common. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -48

215.q: Best way to differentiate amoebic dysentery stool from bacillary dysentery stool in microscopy is -
o: Presence of trophozoite with ingested RBC
215.e: Option D – the only confirmatory way to diagnose E.histolytica infection (amoebic dysentery) is presence of trophozoites with ingested RBCs. Macrophage can be present in amoebic as well as bacillary dysentery. Though characteristically present in clumps, RBC’s can be present discrete and it is very difficult to identify type of dysentery based on arrangement of RBCs as its not very specific. Charcot-Leyden crystals are present in amoebic dysentery but it is also present in other parasitic infection and allergic conditions. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -20

215.q: Conversion of uninucleate cyst into mature quadrinucleate cyst in E.histolytica is accompanied by all EXCEPT -
215.e: Option C – Uninucleate cyst is spherical about 10-20 µ in size. It has a single nucleus, large glycogen mass and 1-4 chromatoid bodies. With successive nuclear division, glycogen mass is reduced in size and the chromatoid body disappears and the cyst is surrounded by refractile cyst wall. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -16

216.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Laveran . The specific causative agent of malaria was discovered in the red blood cells of a patient in 1880 by Alophonse Laveran, a French army surgeon in Algeria. Remember . Romanowsky developed a method of staining malaria parasites in blood films.

216.e: Answer- D. PNH Red cell surface antigen that offer protection against malaria Duffy blood group system ABO (H) blood group system Glycophorins Gerbich antigen Complement receptor type I Knops blood group Abnormalities of the red cell cytoskeleton which may offer protection include South-east asia ovalocytosis Hereditary elliptocytosis Hereditary spherocytosis Sickle cell HbA/S

216.q: You are performing the ZN staining for your microbiology practicals. You notice that the decolourizer is 5% sulphuric acid. Which of the following will stain acid fast positive with this concentration of sulphuric acid? i. M.leprae ii. MAC iii. Legionella iv. M.tuberculosis v. Oocyst of cryptosporidium vi. Oocyst of tenia vii. Actinomyces
216.e: The above question describes the staining method of modified ZN staining , wherein 5% sulphuric acid is used instead of 20%. The former concentration shows positive with M. Leprae, whereas the latter shows acid fastness for M.TB and Atypical mycobacteria. Oocysts of Cyclospora, Isospora and Cryptosporidium are also acid fast with 5% H2SO4 Nocardia, Legionella and Tenia oocysts are acid fast with 0.5%-1% H2SO4. Actinomyces is not acid fast. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 29

217.q: An example of type I hypersensitivity is:
217.e: a) Lepromin test: Type 4 Hypersensitivity b) Tuberculin test: Type 4 Hypersensitivity c) Casoni's test: Type 1 Hypersensitivity d) Arthus reaction: Type 3 Hypersensitivity Examples of Type I Hypersensitivity: Experiments: P-K reaction Schultz Dale phenomenon Theobald smith phenomenon Systemic anaphylaxis Localized anaphylaxis (atopy) such as: Allergic rhinitis (or hay fever) Asthma Food allergy Atopic urticarial Atopic dermatitis (allergic eczema) Drug allergy Wheal and flare reaction. Parasitic diseases: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia (TPE) Loeffler's pneumonia (Ascaris) Ground itch (Hookworm) Leakage of hydatid fluid Cercarial dermatitis/swimmer's itch (Schistosoma). Parasitic tests: Casoni test (hydatid disease) Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

o: Patient is allowed to swallow a capsule containing coiled thread
Used for demonstration of giardia lamblia
Not used for obtaining eggs of Fasciola hepatica
217.e: Enterotest is a simple method of obtaining duodenal contents. Patient is allowed to swallow a gelatin capsule in which a thread of nylon yarn is coiled. The end of the yarn is affixed to the patient's face. Upon reaching the stomach, gelatin dissolves and a weighted string is carried to duodenum. Secretions are retrieved after 3-4 hours and content adhered to yarn is scraped off and examined under microscope. Traditionally used for Giardia lamblia, it is now used to collect eggs of F.hepatica, larva of S.stercoralis and oocyst of Isospora. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -35

217.q: Intestinal bilharziasis (Schistosomal dysentery) is commonly seen in infection with -
217.e: Option B - S.mansoni resides in venules of inferior mesenteric vein in sigmoido-rectal region. Because of the presence of characteristic eggs having lateral spine, eggs deposited in the intestinal wall leads to erosion, microabscesses, granuloma and dysentry. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 148

218.q: Intestinal re-infection (Hyper infection syndrome) is seen in -
218.e: Option B - in S.stercoralis infection, if patient has defective cellular response - AIDS patient, lepromatous leprosy, corticosteroid therapy or severe malnutrition, rhabditiform larva which are released in intestinal lumen instead of passing into feces develop into filariform larva in intestine which penetrate intestinal mucosa and lodge into lungs and various tissue and organs - condition called as intestinal re-infection or Hyper infection syndrome. Option A & D - intestinal re-infection usually does not occur in these parasites. Option C - auto-infection and retro-infection is a feature of E. vermicularis in which eggs deposited in perianal skin, autoinfects person due to itching and unhygienic habits or larva hatched in perianal skin moves retrograde through anus causing retrograde autoinfection. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -184

218.q: Following statement is INCORRECT about Visceral larva migrans
o: Common mode of infection is ingestion
Larva develops into adults in ectopic sites
Can also be caused by larva of S.stercoralis and A.lumbricoides in ectopic sites
218.e: Option C - Visceral larva migrans (VLM) or toxocariasis is a zoonotic infection usually caused by dog or cat ascarids of the Toxocara genus. The eggs are ingested and then hatch into larvae, which penetrate the intestine and start migrating. These nematodes can infect but not mature in humans so larva is not developed into adults. It is also seen in human nematodes like S.stercoralis and A.lumbricoides, when larvae of these parasites are not able to complete their normal development and enter ectopic sites. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -167

218.q: Unsegmented eggs are in which parasite?
218.e: Ans. a. Trichuris trichura 706. In malaria, sexual cycle is - a) Sporozoite to gametocytes b) Gametocytes to Sporozoite c) Occurs in human d) Responsible for relapse Correct Answer - B Ans. is 'b' i.e., Gametocytes to sporozoite LIFE CYCLE OF PLASMODIUM Plasmodium passes its life cycle in two different hosts ?

219.q: What is one example of a situation where routine environmental microbiological sampling is indicated?
o: Outbreak investigation of a new infection
Assessment of a new method for equipment sterilization
Monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units
Evaluation of a new hospital construction
219.e: Monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units: Correct , routine monitoring is critical to ensure safe water quality for dialysis patients. Why Not Others: A. Outbreak investigation: Focuses on targeted sampling, not routine checks. B. Equipment sterilization: Involves evaluative sampling after changes, not regular monitoring. D. New hospital construction: Involves specific sampling rather than ongoing routine checks. Key Takeaways: Routine environmental sampling is indicated for monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units to ensure safe water quality . Other situations often require targeted or specific sampling rather than routine. Tags : good to know Reference: Guidelines on routine and targeted environmental microbiological sampling.

219.q: Hospital associated infection can be defined as all of the following except:
o: The infection should be incubating at the time of admission
The symptoms should appear at least after 48 hours or after admission
The patient should be admitted for a reason other than the infection in context
Infections acquired in hospital, but symptoms present after discharge
219.e: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) can be defined as- The infections acquired in the hospital by a patient admitted for a reason other than the infection in context , The infection should not be present or incubating at the time of admission , and The symptoms should appear at least after 48 hours of admission. This also include: Infections that are acquired in the hospital but symptoms appear after discharge. Occupational infections among staff of the healthcare facility (e.g. needle stick injury transmitted infections). Infection in a neonate that results while passage through the birth canal (in contrast to congenital infections due to transplacental transmission, which are not HAIs). Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 229

219.q: Patients with similar infections requiring contact precautions can be placed together if single isolation rooms aren't available. This is called Cohorting. What is the minimum distance for a spatial separation of two patients in a room?
219.e: For infection control: Single isolation room with a bathroom facility is preferred. If not available, then cohorting is recommended. Cohorting may be carried out in various ways Patients with similar infections requiring contact precautions can be placed together either in the same isolation room, or in the same cubicle or corner of a ward or Spatial separation of minimum of 3 feet distance between the beds with privacy curtains. Other measures for infection control are: Hand Hygiene should be maintained. Health care workers should wear PPE. Single-use patient-dedicated equipment. Patient movement should be limited only to medically-necessary purposes. Disinfection of rooms should be carried out frequently and adequately. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 236

221.q: An investigator injects 7 mg of an experimental drug into an animal. The drug does not bind to plasma proteins and is eliminated unchanged in urine via first-order kinetics. Two hours later, the investigator obtains laboratory values from the animal that reveal the rate of drug elimination is 0.02 mg/min, the plasma drug concentration is 0.04 mg/mL, and the total amount of drug eliminated in urine is 5 mg. Which of the following is the best estimate of the clearance of the drug in the animal at the time of measurement?
221.e: Plasma clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma cleared of a substance in a period of time. It is estimated by dividing a substance's rate of elimination by its plasma concentration: CL = (0.02 mg/min)/(0.04 mg/mL) = 0.5 mL/min. In first-order kinetics, the rate of elimination of the substance and the plasma concentration of the substance decrease with time, but the CL remains constant. Alternatively, the CL of a substance with first-order kinetics can be calculated by multiplying the volume of distribution (Vd) by the elimination constant (Ke) of the substance. For a substance that is minimally protein-bound and excreted unchanged only in the urine, as in this case, the CL is essentially the glomerular filtration rate. In humans, inulin is such a substance Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.52

221.q: Which pharmacokinetic parameters are used to determine the loading dose of an orally administered drug? 1. Volume of distribution (Vd) 2. Half-life 3. Plasma concentration 4. Bioavailability
221.e: Explanation: Loading dose (LD) = (Desired steady-state plasma concentration × Vd) ÷ Bioavailability. Half-life determines maintenance dosing frequency and time to steady state, but it is not a direct component of the loading dose equation (Statement 2 ruled out) For oral drugs , bioavailability (F) must be accounted for because oral dosing is reduced by first-pass extraction and incomplete absorption. Formula (practical): LD (oral) = (C_target × Vd) / F Where: C_target = desired plasma concentration (therapeutic target) Vd = volume of distribution F = fraction absorbed (bioavailability)

221.q: There is no statistically significant difference in the dose-corrected area under the curve (AUC) for the two routes of administration. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this finding?
221.e: This drug is almost entirely absorbed into systemic circulation when orally administered, as indicated by the lack of difference in the dose-corrected AUCs for oral and intravenous administration. indicating that this drug has near 100% bioavailability. Isosorbide mononitrate does not undergo first-pass metabolism by the liver and thus has approx. 100% bioavailability. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.48

222.q: A researcher for a pharmaceutical company is studying a new medication to treat parkinsonism. The medication is dosed at 10 mg and causes improvement in bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity in 99% of patients. However, 100 mg of this medication causes toxicity manifested as seizures in 1% of the population treated with this medication. What is the standard margin of safety of this medication?
222.e: The standard margin of safety (SMS) is a measure of how much safer a drug's effective dose is compared to its toxic dose. It's calculated using the formula: SMS = (LD1 / ED99) - 1 * 100 In this case: Effective dose (ED99): The dose at which the medication causes improvement in bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity in 99% of patients is 10 mg. Toxic dose (LD1): The dose that causes seizures in 1% of the population treated with this medication is 100 mg. Now, calculate the SMS: SMS = (100 mg / 10 mg) - 1 * 100 = 10 - 1 * 100 = 900 So, the standard margin of safety for this medication is 900. The correct answer is D) 900. This indicates that the medication is 900 times safer at the effective dose (10 mg) than it is toxic at the dose that causes seizures (100 mg). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 37

222.q: Drug A and Drug B are of equal magnitude. If Drug A and Drug B are combined together, And it produces an effect that is equal in magnitude to the sum of effects when both are given individually, this would be an example of which of the following?
222.e: (A) The additive effects of drugs occur when two drugs with the same effect are added together and produce an effect that is equal in magnitude to the sum of the effects when the two drugs are given individually. (B) Neutralization occurs when two drugs combine with another to form an inactive compound. (C) Potentiation occurs if a drug lacking an effect of its own increases the effect of a second active drug. (D) Synergism occurs if two drugs with the same effect, when given together, produce an effect that is in greater magnitude than the sum of the effects when the drugs are given individually. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.9

222.q: Which of the following is not a feature of type B adverse drug reactions?
o: Symptoms and signs of drug allergy
222.e: Adverse drug reactions can be defined as one of the two types: Type A: Dose dependent common extension of known pharmacological effect Type B: Dose independent uncommon symptoms and signs of drug allergy The most important type to the adverse drug reaction is type B, which encompasses both anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions. Reference: Physics, Pharmacology and Physiology for Anaesthetists, Matthew E. Cross, second edition, pg 151.

223.q: A 42-year-old man with a 6-cm right adrenal tumour is going to undergo a laparoscopic surgical procedure to remove the tumour. It is anticipated that the procedure will take approximately 12 h. The patient has a history of hypertension controlled with a alpha-blocker. Which of the following agents, used intraoperatively, will provide efficacious blood pressure control for the duration of the procedure?
223.e: Nadolol has a half-life of 12 to 24 h and would be the best agent for beta-blockade in a patient who is undergoing a long duration surgical procedure. A single intra-operative dose should suffice the entire case. Acebutolol has a 3- to 4-h half-life. Esmolol has a 10-min half-life. It is the shortest acting Beta-blocker. Metoprolol has a 3- to 4-h half-life. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 166.

223.q: Which of the following patients is most likely to be treated with intravenous glucagon?
o: An 18-year-old woman who took an overdose of cocaine and now has a blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg
A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes who has not taken her glyburide for the last 3 days
A 62-year-old man with severe bradycardia and hypotension resulting from ingestion of an overdose of Atenolol
A 74-year-old man with lactic acidosis as a complication of severe infection and shock
223.e: Glucagon acts through cardiac glucagon receptors to stimulate the rate and force of contraction of the heart. Because this bypasses cardiac β adrenoceptors, glucagon is useful in the treatment of β-blocker-induced cardiac depression. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 757

223.q: A 45-year-old woman found obtunded in her apartment. She is hypotensive and bradycardic. Intravenous glucagon is administered, and her condition improves. Which of the following intracellular changes is most likely responsible for the improvement in her condition?
o: Decreased cAMP in vascular smooth muscle
Decreased DAG in vascular smooth muscle
223.e: This patient has most likely overdosed on beta blocker medications. Beta blocker overdose causes diffuse non-selective blockade of peripheral beta adrenergic receptors, causing depression of myocardial contractility, bradycardia, and varying degrees of AV block. The result is a low cardiac output state. Glucagon is the drug of choice for beta blocker overdose. Glucagon acts on G protein-coupled receptors, increasing intracellular CAMP and thus increasing the release of intracellular calcium during muscle contraction. This increases heart rate and cardiac contractility. Improvements in heart rate and blood pressure may be observed within minutes. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 192

224.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic myopia comes to the ophthalmologist for regular check-up. Examination shows bilateral narrowing of peripheral visual fields, cupping of the optic discs, and elevated intraocular pressure. Gonioscopy shows no abnormalities. Which of the following first line of treatment for this patient ?
224.e: The loss of peripheral vision, optic disc cupping, and elevated intraocular pressure in this patient with a normal gonioscopy are diagnostic of open-angle glaucoma. Preferred first-line therapy are topical prostaglandin analogs like Latanoprost. Alternative options are Topical beta blockers alone and/or alpha-2 agonists OR Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. For treatment of Refractory glaucoma, oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are used. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 159.
