In addition, decreased estrogen levels following menopause increase this patient's risk for osteoporosis and osteopenia. Bisphosphonates and denosumab (anti-RANK ligand antibody) are used to treat glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 713

263.q: Romiplostim acts on which of the following receptors:
263.e: Romiplostim: Genetically engineered protein in which the Fc component of a human antibody is fused to two copies of a peptide that stimulates the thrombopoietin receptors; approved for treatment of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura Ref: Katzung 11th edition Chapter 33.

263.q: All of the following are false regarding prasugrel, except:
o: Not much metabolism in the body
Slow onset of action than clopidogrel
263.e: Prasugrel : This is a newer, more potent and faster acting irreversibleP2Y12 purinergic receptor blocker , as when strong antiplatelet action is required.(Option C ruled out) Like its predecessors, it is also a prodrug, but is more rapidly absorbed.(Option B ruled out) It is also more rapidly and more completely activated, resulting in faster and more consistent platelet inhibition.(Option A ruled out) Bleeding complications are also more frequent and more serious. Patients with a history of ischaemic stroke and TIAs are at greater risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Prasugrel is contraindicated in such patients. Key Takeaway: Irreversible P2Y12 blockers(Prodrugs): Clopidogrel, Ticlopidine, Prasugrel Reversible, competitive P2Y12 blocker: Cangrelor Reversible, non competitive P2Y12 blocker: Ticagrelor

263.q: Which of the following most accurately describes the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
o: Clopidogrel directly binds to the platelet ADP receptors
Clopidogrel facilitates the action of antithrombin III
The active metabolite of clopidogrel binds to and inhibits the platelet ADP receptors
The active metabolite of clopidogrel binds to and inhibits the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
263.e: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that is activated by CYP2C9 and CYP2C19. It irreversibly binds to the ADP receptor on the surface of platelets that serves as a key role in platelet aggregation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834

264.q: Which enzyme is involved in the management of thrombotic events by converting plasminogen to plasmin?
264.e: Explanation: Urokinase is an enzyme that promotes the breakdown of blood clots by converting plasminogen into plasmin, which then degrades fibrin, the main component of clots. This fibrinolytic action helps dissolve clots in blood vessels. It is used in Pulmonary embolism, Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) etc to dissolve clots.

264.q: Which of the following drugs acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase?
264.e: Explanation: Methotrexate is a structural analogue of folic acid and acts as a competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, preventing the conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, which is essential for DNA synthesis and cell division. This particularly affects rapidly dividing cells, making it useful in cancer and autoimmune diseases.

264.q: Which one of the following compounds is function as antagonist of Vitamin K, and commonly used to reduce blood clotting in patients with high risk of thromboembolism?
264.e: Option A: Antagonists of vitamin K are used to reduce blood coagulation in patients at risk of thromboembolism; the most widely used is warfarin. Option B: Menadione and menadiol diacetate, synthetic compounds that can be metabolized to phylloquinone. It has vitamin K activity. Option C: Menaquinones, synthesized by intestinal bacteria, with differing lengths of side chain. It has also vitamin K like activity. Option D: Tocopherol have vitamin E activity. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, CH 44 PN 532

265.q: Mechanism of action of leukotriene pathway inhibitors?
265.e: Two approaches to interrupting the leukotriene pathway have been pursued: inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase, thereby preventing leukotriene synthesis; and inhibition of the binding of LTD 4 to its receptor on target tissues, thereby preventing its action. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 349

265.q: A 10-year-old boy with asthma uses an albuterol and low-dose inhaled mometasone. Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate to prevent complications from this treatment?
265.e: Oral rinsing after inhaled steroid use is the most appropriate recommendation. In bronchial asthma, the use of inhaled glucocorticoids such as mometasone results in more targeted steroid delivery to the lungs with much less systemic absorption. However, some of the drug is deposited in the oral cavity, which predisposes patients to local opportunistic fungal infections, especially candidiasis. Gargling or oral rinsing immediately after inhalation is recommended to reduce the local steroid burden and decrease the risk of infection. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 713

265.q: Which of the following is FALSE for deriphyline?
265.e: The methylxanthines have positive chronotropic and inotropic effects. At low concentrations, these effects appear to result from inhibition of presynaptic adenosine receptors in sympathetic nerves increasing catecholamine release at nerve endings. The higher concentrations (> 10 μmol/L, 2 mg/L) associated with inhibition of phosphodiesterase and increases in cAMP may result in increased influx of calcium. At much higher concentrations (> 100 μmol/L), sequestration of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum is impaired. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 345

266.q: A 40-year-old male presents with severe burning chest pain radiating into his neck. His electrocardiogram was normal and test for troponin was negative. A diagnosis of GERD was made and he was sent home with a prescription for a drug that irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase in the parietal cells. Which of the following is not a side-effect of drug?
266.e: Some of the side effects of PPIs Gastrointestinal Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, flatulence ↑ Risk of C. difficile infection Reactive hypergastrinemia ↓ Absorption of iron and vitamin B12 ↓ Absorption of calcium and magnesium → ↑ risk of osteoporosis in long-term use→ ↑ risk of fractures in elderly individuals Neurological Light headedness, headaches Possibly increased risk of developing cognitive impairment/dementia Others Exanthema Visual disturbances (rare) ↑ Risk of pneumonia In rare cases, acute interstitial nephritis Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1095

266.q: A 12-year-old boy is brought due to chronic diarrhea and failure to gain weight appropriately. He has a history of recurrent respiratory infections, and prior sputum cultures have been positive for pseudomonas aeruginosa. His younger brother died from a severe respiratory infection at age 9. Which of the following agents is most likely to improve this patient's condition in the long term?
266.e: This young Caucasian patient has a history of recurrent respiratory infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. These findings, along with a family history of early sibling death from pulmonary infection, suggest a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. Steatorrhea and failure to thrive occur as a result of malabsorption due to obstructive fibrosis and progressive insufficiency of the exocrine pancreas . Pancreatic lipase supplementation is likely to improve this patient's condition by enhancing macronutrient and vitamin absorption. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1092

266.q: Which of the following is a small molecule that polymerizes in stomach acid and coats the ulcer bed, resulting in accelerated healing and reduction of symptoms ?
266.e: Sucralfate is a small molecule that polymerizes in stomach acid and forms a protective coat over the ulcer bed. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1110

267.q: A patient who is taking verapamil for hypertension and angina has become constipated. Which of the following drugs is an osmotic laxative that could be used to treat the patient's constipation?
267.e: A laxative that mildly stimulates the gut would be most suitable in a patient taking a smooth muscle relaxant drug such as verapamil. By holding water in the intestine, magnesium hydroxide provides additional bulk and stimulates increased contractions . A helpful mnemonic is magnesium "magnifies" stool, aluminum halts the stool. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1091

267.q: A 38-year-old woman comes with motion sickness. She is planning a vacation cruise and has previously experienced severe nausea and vomiting while sailing. After the appropriate drug therapy is recommended, this patient should be counselled regarding which of the following side effects?
267.e: Perception of motion and orientation is determined by input from the vestibular, visual, and somatosensory systems. These 3 systems are usually congruent, but conflicting input can lead to motion sickness, characterized by nausea, dizziness, and autonomic symptoms (eg, diaphoresis). Integration of these sensory pathways occurs in the vestibular nuclei via muscarinic M1 and histaminic H1 neurotransmission. As such, antimuscarinic agents (eg, scopolamine) and first-generation antihistamines (eg, meclizine, dimenhydrinate) are most effective for management of motion sickness. Anticholinergic side effects are common with these medications and may include blurry vision, dry mouth, urinary retention, and constipation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1108

267.q: Which drug stimulates chloride secretion into the gut lumen and is used for irritable bowel syndrome?
267.e: Linaclotide is approved for the treatment of chronic constipation and IBS with predominant constipation. Linaclotide activates guanylyl cyclase-C on the luminal intestinal epithelial surface, which leads to activation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) leading to increased chloride-rich secretion and acceleration of intestinal transit. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1103

268.q: All of the following drugs bind to microtubules and thus interfere with their assembly or disassembly, except:
268.e: Option A: Ciprofloxacin is fluoroquinolone class of antibiotic, which inhibits DNA replication by inhibiting bacterial DNA topoisomerase and DNA gyrase. Certain drugs bind to microtubules and thus interfere with their assembly or disassembly. These include colchicine, Vinblastine, Griseofulvin & paclitaxel. Option B: colchicine which is used for treatment of acute gouty arthritis Option C: Vinblastine is a vinca alkaloid used for treating certain types of cancer Option D: Griseofulvin is an antifungal agent Paclitaxel (Taxol) is effective against ovarian cancer. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 51 PN 625

268.q: Which drug is commonly used to treat cancers by inhibiting DNA replication through interference with topoisomerase II?
268.e: Explanation: Etoposide is a chemotherapy drug that targets topoisomerase II in eukaryotic cells. Etoposide stabilizes the topoisomerase II-DNA complex after it has introduced a double-strand break, preventing the enzyme from re-ligating the DNA. This results in DNA breaks, which interfere with DNA replication and lead to cell death. Etoposide is widely used in the treatment of various cancers, such as lung cancer, testicular cancer, and lymphomas, making this the correct answer.

268.q: A 53-year-old woman with breast cancer and pre-existing heart failure requires chemotherapy. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
268.e: Explanation: Epirubicin is an anthracycline known for cardiotoxicity , which can worsen pre-existing heart failure. It is contraindicated in patients with heart failure . Adverse Effects of Epirubicin: Cardiomyopathy Alopecia Anemia Amenorrhea Leukopenia Diarrhea Explanation of Other Options: Methotrexate (Option A): Folate antagonist Not significantly cardiotoxic. Cyclophosphamide (Option C): Alkylating agent Some cardiovascular effects but not strongly cardiotoxic. Can be used cautiously. Cisplatin (Option D): Nephrotoxic primarilyC ardiotoxicity risk is lower. Can be used with monitoring.

269.q: Mechanism of action of basiliximab is:
269.e: IL-2 receptor antagonist The CD-25 molecule is expressed on the surface of immunologically activated, but not resting T-cells. The CD-25 acts as a high affinity receptor for IL-2 through which cell proliferation and differentiation are promoted. Some anti CD-25 antibodies have been developed as IL-2 receptor antagonists to specifically arrest the activated T-cells. Daclizumab: It is a highly humanized chimeric monoclonal anti CD-25 antibody which binds to and acts as IL-2receptor antagonist. Combined with glucocorticoids, calcineurinantagonists and/or azathioprine/MMF, it is used to prevent renal and other transplant rejection reactions. Basiliximab: This is another anti CD-25 antibody with higher affinity for the IL-2 receptor, but shorter plasma t½ (1 week). Clinical use of basiliximab is similar to that of daclizumab.

270.q: A 68-year-old woman had a relapse of breast cancer. The cancer was now unresponsive to standard doses of chemotherapy. The decision was made to treat the patient with high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation. Which of the following drugs is needed for the patient's autologous stem cell transplantation?
270.e: The success of transplantation with peripheral blood stem cells depends on infusion of adequate numbers of hematopoietic stem cells. Administration of G-CSF to the donor (in the case of autologous transplantation, the patient who also will be the recipient of the transplantation) greatly increases the number of hematopoietic stem cells harvested from the donor’s blood. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 842-43

270.q: Which of the following statements about pegfilgrastim is true?
o: It decreases the risk of neutropenia in patients on anti- cancer therapy
It is a short acting drug
270.e: Filgrastim It is a recombinant human granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF). Started one day after myelosuppressive chemotherapy and injected s.c. or i.v. (5 μg/kg) daily, till neutrophil count normalizes, may be used to shorten recovery time from neutropenia. It is a long acting drug due to its pegylated form. It is administered as parenterally(S/C or IV) MOA: Recombinant G CSF drug Uses: Neutropenia in HIV Myelodysplasia Chemotherapy induced agranulocytosis Aplastic anemia S/E: Bone pain Recombinant GM CSF drug: Sargramostim

270.q: Which of the following is most likely to be required by a 5-year-old boy with chronic renal insufficiency?
270.e: The kidney produces erythropoietin; patients with chronic renal insufficiency often require exogenous erythropoietin to avoid chronic anemia. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition by Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 887-89

271.q: A 6-year-old child ingest the iron- containing supplements. What immediate treatment is necessary? Correction of acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities and
271.e: Activated charcoal does not bind iron and thus is ineffective. Oral deferasirox is effective for chronic iron toxicity. Dantrolene inhibits Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is an antidote for malignant hyperthermia induced by inhaled anaesthetics. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834

271.q: A 34-year-old pregnant woman has a young child at home and is taking iron- containing prenatal supplements, she should be warned that they are a common source of accidental poisoning in young children. Toxicity associated with acute iron poisoning usually includes which of the following?
o: Necrotizing gastroenteritis, shock, and metabolic acidosis
Severe hepatic injury, encephalitis, and coma
271.e: Acute iron poisoning often causes severe gastrointestinal damage resulting from direct corrosive effects, shock from fluid loss in the gastrointestinal tract, and metabolic acidosis from cellular dysfunction. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 835-37

272.q: A victim of child trafficking was brought to you by the police for age determination. Which of the following would you use as an accurate method for determining the same?
272.e: From the given options, mineralization of teeth is the more accurate method of age determination in childhood . The relationship between the chronological age and dental age is stronger than between chronological age and skeletal age. Two aspects of tooth development have been used in the estimation of dental age: The emergence of teeth - superior part of the crown of the tooth appearing level with the surface of the alveolar bone The stage of mineralization of crowns and roots during development Mineralization of teeth begins at 14 weeks in utero and lasts for a long time after birth. Two important processes in tooth development, dentinogenesis and amelogenesis, are responsible for the formation of dentin and enamel, respectively. Reference ; Encyclopedia of Forensic and Legal Medicine, Page no. 125

272.q: While examining the skeletal remains from a bomb blast, a forensic expert decides to use the Gustafson's method for identification of the ages of people killed. Which of the following would you not assess in this method?
272.e: Tooth length is not assessed in Gustafson's method. Gustafson's method of estimation of age of an individual is based on physiological changes in teeth. It is mainly useful in adults over 25 years of age. Gustafson criteria includes: Attrition - Wear and tear changes of occlusal surface Periodontosis - Regression of gums surrounding the tooth resulting in loosening of the tooth and falling Secondary dentin formation - Deposition of dentin in pulp cavity Cementum apposition - Deposition of cementum in the root forming incremental lines Root resorption - Involves both cementum and dentin Transparency of the root - This is the most reliable criteria. Canals in dentin get filled with mineral and they become less transparent. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 50, 51.

272.q: A forensic expert is examining the skeletal remains of an unknown individual to determine the sex. Which of the following is regarded as the best source of information for the same?
272.e: Explanation: The pelvis is most reliable single bone for sex determination of an unknown individual. The accuracy in sex determination by the pelvis alone is 95%. The femur is the most useful long bone for sex determination, due to its length and massiveness. Krogman's degree of accuracy in sex determination from adult skeletal remains: Entire skeleton - 100% Pelvis alone - 95% Skull alone - 92% (Option B) Pelvis plus skull - 98% Long bones plus pelvis - 98% Long bones alone - 80% (Option C & D)

273.q: A forensic expert is examining the pelvic bone and lower vertebrae of an unknown individual, to determine the sex. Which of the following is regarded as the best source of information for the same?
273.e: The pubis of the pelvic bone has long been regarded as the best sources of information for determining the sex of an unknown individual. The femur is the most useful long bone for sex determination, due to its length and massiveness. Sacrum is least reliable bone for sex determination. Subpubic concavity is also a good indicator of sex. The subpubic region is located on the pubis, inferiorly to the obturator foramen. In females, the subpubic region is concave, while in males the subpubic region is either straight or convex. Reference : Encyclopedia of Forensic and Legal Medicine, Page No. 131

273.q: You have measured the femur length to be 40cm from the skeletal remains of an unknown person. What is the approximate height of the individual?
273.e: The approximate height of the individual is 150 cm. The stature/femur relationship is 3.74. Thus, stature can be calculated by using the formula, stature = femur length x 3.74 = 40 x 3.74 = 149.6 cm = 150 cm The relationship between the mean stature and the mean length of the femur appears to be fairly stable around the world. However, this factor tends to overestimate tall and underestimate short individuals. Femur length shows a highly statistically significant correlation with stature. (r=0.88 in males and r=0.862 in females). This study revealed that the height of an individual is four times the femur length of the individual, since the femur length is proportional to the height, therefore the taller the individual the longer femur length, while the shorter the individual the shorter the femur length. Reference: Encyclopedia of Forensic and Legal Medicine, Volume 1, Page no: 104,

273.q: Which bone provides the highest accuracy in determining sex during forensic examination?
273.e: Explanation: The pelvis is the most reliable bone for sex determination, offering 95–98% accuracy. It exhibits distinct morphological differences related to childbirth in females: Female pelvis: Wide subpubic angle (>90°), broad sciatic notch, and oval pelvic inlet. Designed for childbirth. Male pelvis: Narrow subpubic angle ( Explanation of other options: Skull (Option A): Accuracy ~80%; males show pronounced brow ridges and square orbits. Long bones (Option C): Accuracy ~70%; depend on length and robustness. Sternum (Option D): Least reliable (~60% accuracy). Key takeaways: Pelvis = most accurate bone for sex estimation. Skull provides secondary confirmation. Useful in skeletal remains identification. References: Bones

274.q: DNA finger printing cannot be taken from ?
274.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Tooth [Ref Parikh 6th le p. 7.2-7.15] DNA finger-printing/ DNA profiling Is a technique employed by forensic scientists to assist in the identification of individuals by their respective DNA profile it is a fool proof method to conclusively fix the paternity/ maternity. The most desirable method of collecting a reference sample is the use of a buccal swab. When this is not available (e.g. because a court order may be needed and not obtainable) other methods may need to be used to collect a sample of blood, saliva, semen, or other appropriate fluid or tissue from personal items (e.g. toothbrush, razor, etc.) or from stored samples (e.g. banked sperm or biopsy tissue)

274.q: A vegetable vendor with no prior criminal record went missing and was discovered dead after a week with advanced decomposition. What methods would be used to identify the body?
274.e: Explanation: DNA profiling is a highly reliable method for identifying a body, even when it is in an advanced state of decomposition. Explanation for other options: General Recognition (Option A): Not reliable due to significant alteration of features from decomposition. Dental Records (Option C): May not be available for a vegetable vendor, making this method less practical. Fingerprints (Option D): More dependable if the deceased has a criminal record; otherwise, fingerprints may not be useful. Reference: https://www.fortunejournals.com/ijabpt/pdf/63045-II-Mahesh%20Singh-forensic%20dentistry[1].pdf

274.q: Identical twins have similarities in all the following except:
274.e: Quetelet's rule: Every nature-made object shows infinite variations of forms, and in the world’s, crime records no two identical fingerprint patterns have been reported. Hence, it is unique to every individual. Fingerprint pattern differs even in identical twins. Blood group, DNA fingerprinting and iris color are same in identical twins Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 104

275.q: First-hand knowledge rule is applicable to:
275.e: The first-hand knowledge rule is applicable to a common witness who gives evidence about the facts observed or perceived by him An expert witness is someone who has been trained or is skilled or has knowledge and experience and is able to draw conclusions from the facts observed by him. Doctors, handwriting/fingerprints/firearms experts etc. come under this category. A hostile witness is a person who is supposed to have some interest or motive for concealing a part of the truth or for giving completely false evidence. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35 th Edition, Page No. 9, 10

275.q: The first-hand knowledge rule applies to:
275.e: Explanation: The first-hand knowledge rule applies to a common witness who gives evidence about the facts observed or perceived by them. An expert witness is someone who has been trained or is skilled or has knowledge and experience , and can conclude from the facts observed by them. Doctors , handwriting/fingerprints/firearms experts etc. come under this category. (Options B and C) A hostile witness is a person who is supposed to have some interest or motive for concealing a part of the truth or for giving completely false evidence. (Option D)

275.q: Criminal negligence by a Registered Medical Practitioner is punishable under Section 106(1) of BNS for a maximum imprisonment of
275.e: Sec. 106. (1) BNS - Causing death by negligence: Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation: For the purposes of this sub-section, "registered medical practitioner" means a medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act. Reference: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023

276.q: Which BNS section denotes the death of the human being, unless the contrary appears from the context?
276.e: BNS Section 2(6) denotes - "death" means the death of a human being unless the contrary appears from the context. Option B: BNS 2(14) defines "Injury". It states that, "injury" means any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property. Option C: BNS 2(17) states that, "life" means the life of a human being, unless the contrary appears from the context. Option D: BNS 2(23) deals with oath and solemn affirmation. It states that, The word "oath" includes a solemn affirmation substituted by law for an oath, and any declaration required or authorized by law to be made before a public servant or to be used for the purpose of proof, whether in a Court or not. Reference: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023

276.q: A person is sitting on fast unto death. As a doctor you will not allow the person to die because of
276.e: Article 21 of Constitution of India: This ensures Right to life but does not include right to die. So forcible feeding of persons going on hunger strike is lawful in India Declaration of Malta This deals with the Respect the autonomy of the patient and suggests that the doctor should not feed forcibly in such cases. Feeding is allowed when the patient has lapsed into coma Article 14 of the Constitution of India: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India". Declaration of Sydney: Deals with the determination of death and the recovery of organs Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 260

276.q: As per the THOA 1994, The burden of proof to diagnose brainstem death rests on
o: Doctor in charge of the patient
Doctor in charge of the hospital
276.e: Brain-stem death should be certified by a Board of medical experts consisting of the following namely: The registered medical practitioner (RMP) in charge of the hospital in which brain-stem death has occurred; An independent RMP, being a specialist, to be nominated by RMP specified in cause (i) A neurologist or a neurosurgeon to be nominated by the RMP specified in clause (i) The RMP treating the person whose brain-stem death has occurred. The burden of proof to diagnose brainstem death rests on the specialist with Neurosciences. Reference: THE TRANSPLANTATION OF HUMAN ORGANS AND TISSUES ACT, 1994 - Amendment 2011 and 2014

277.q: A person died suddenly, and his family is abroad. His viscera were preserved during autopsy. Which of the following substances can still be detected in his visceral organs even if he did not consume them before death?
277.e: Explanation: When a body is preserved, ethanol may be detected in the viscera because of the fermentation of body fluids and tissues after death. This post-mortem alcohol production can result in a positive ethanol test even if the person did not consume alcohol before dying. Morphine (Options A), Aconite (Option B), and Arsenic (Option C) can only be detected if they were consumed by the person

277.q: In medicolegal autopsy, cavity to be opened first is ?
277.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Any of the above [Ref Reddy 30thle p. 97] Depending on type of case, any of the body cavity can be opened first. Spinal cord is routinely not opened. It is convenient to start the examination with the cavity chiefly affected

277.q: An autopsy may be performed at the site of recovery of the body in all of the following cases except?
277.e: In deaths due to RTA, autopsy is usually performed in an equipped mortuary. An autopsy may be performed at the site of recovery of the body, in the following scenarios: Advanced stage of putrefaction as materials of evidentiary value may be lost during transportation. Exhumation If the District Magistrate desires, it to be conducted at the site due to some law-and-order problems. Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice, Krishan Vij, 5 th edition, Page No. 18.

278.q: Which of the following are true statements regarding scalp injuries? 1. Contusions are present in subdural space 2. Contusions are better felt than seen 3. The number of blows inflicted is difficult to determine if contusions join together 4. Subgaleal hematoma does not show any colour change 5. Bruises of the scalp are not associated with edema
278.e: Contusions may occur in the superficial fascia , in the temporalis muscle, in the loose areolar tissue between galea aponeurotica and the pericranium. They are better felt than seen. Multiple contusions of the scalp may join together and it is often difficult to determine the number of blows inflicted. The bruises of the scalp are associated with prominent edema . Subgaleal hematoma remains the same colour till it resolves. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 35 th edition, K S Narayan Reddy, Page No.185

278.q: Which of the following sites is more prone to bruising with blunt trauma?
278.e: The shins are particularly prone to bruising with blunt trauma. Resilient areas, such as the abdominal wall and buttocks , bruise less with a given impact than a region where underlying bone acts as an anvil with the skin between the bone and the inflicting force. The head, chest, and shins are the examples. A direct trauma to the shin bone can damage the periosteum (known as bone bruising of the tibia or periosteal contusion). This causes a collection of blood underneath the periosteum of the shin bone. Reference : Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4 th Edition, Page Number-141.

278.q: What type of injury is scalping?
278.e: Scalping is a type of laceration. Here, a large area of skin and subcutaneous tissue is rolled off the scalp. These lesions could be caused by the traction of hair being trapped in machinery. This was formerly a common industrial accident. Hairnets were worn by women factory workers to prevent this. Flaying is also a type of laceration, caused by shearing force. This is where a large area of skin and subcutaneous tissue is rolled off a limb. Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4 th Edition Page No. 147, 148

279.q: A pedestrian hit by a car hurls up on the windshield following which his head strikes the road. How is the head injury described?
279.e: In this case, pedestrian hit by a car (Primary impact injury) hurls up on the windshield (Secondary impact injury) following which his head strikes the road (Secondary injury. Injuries to pedestrians: Primary impact injuries are the injuries sustained by a pedestrian by the initial impact with the vehicle. Secondary impact injuries are the injuries sustained by a pedestrian by falling over the vehicle. Secondary injuries (Sometimes also called as Tertiary injuries) are the injuries sustained by a pedestrian by falling over the ground after being hit by the vehicle. References: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4 th Edition, Page No. 289; Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 355

279.q: A pedestrian hit by a car hurls up on the windshield following which his head strikes the road. How is the head injury described?
279.e: Explanation: The head injury sustained when the head strikes the road is a Secondary injury . In the scenario described: The pedestrian is hit by the car (The injuries sustained by a pedestrian due to the initial impact are known as Primary impact injury). (Option A) The pedestrian then hurls up onto the windshield (The injuries sustained by a pedestrian by falling over the vehicle is known as Secondary impact injury). (Option B) Finally, the pedestrian's head strikes the road. The injuries sustained by a pedestrian by falling over the ground after being hit by the vehicle is known as Secondary injuries (sometimes also called Tertiary injuries). Key Takeaway: In a vehicular accident involving a pedestrian, the injury sustained from falling onto the ground after being hit by the vehicle is classified as a Secondary injury (also sometimes called Tertiary injury).

279.q: Which of the following statements about extradural haemorrhage is false?
o: Extradural haemorrhage may be ruled out in the absence of a skull fracture
A minimum of 35 ml of blood is required to accumulate for clinical signs to appear
The most common vessel affected is middle meningeal artery
It is the least common type of traumatic brain membrane haemorrhage
279.e: Extradural haemorrhages (EDH) cannot be ruled out in the absence of a skull fracture. Most extradural haemorrhages are associated with fractures of the skull, but about 15 per cent occur in intact skull. They usually occur unilaterally in the parieto-temporal area, caused by the rupture of the middle meningeal artery (usually posterior branch). It is the least common type of brain membrane bleeding. The most common traumatic intracranial haemorrhage is sub-arachnoid haemorrhage. Adams suggests that a minimum volume of 35 ml is needed before clinical signs are apparent, though other writers suggest 100 ml is usually the minimum associated with fatalities. Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition. Page no 182, 183

280.q: Temperature regulation by the hypothalamus completely fails below which body temperature?
280.e: Once the body temperature has fallen below about 85°F (30°C), the ability of the hypothalamus to regulate temperature is lost. For each 10°F decrease in body temperature, the rate of chemical heat production in each cell is depressed almost twofold. This is the reason for diminished temperature regulation. Sleepiness followed by coma, depresses the activity of the CNS heat control mechanisms and prevents shivering. Our internal body temperature is regulated by a part of our brain called the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus checks our current temperature and compares it with the normal temperature of about 37°C. If our temperature is too low, the hypothalamus makes sure that the body generates and maintains heat. Reference: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, 13th Edition, Page No. 921

280.q: An autopsy was done on a burn victim. Which of the following is a reliable indicator that the victim was alive while the fire was in progress?
o: Vital reaction in the burned area
Redness of the exposed skin surface
280.e: Elevated levels of carbon monoxide in the circulating blood and carbon particles in the air passages and lungs are reliable indicators suggesting that the victim was alive while the fire was in progress. Option (A) & (B): The exposed skin surface may be reddened in both ante-mortem and post-mortem burns, the classical distinction of a 'red flare' or 'vital reaction' being unsafe as an index of infliction before death. Option (D): Blisters can form post-mortem, but are pale yellow unless on scorched skin. Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No. 319, 320

280.q: The 'hold-on effect' is characteristically seen in
280.e: The hold-on effect is seen in electrical injuries . When, as most often happens, the entry point is in the hand, the stronger flexor muscles of the arm go into spasm and cause a hold-on effect. This means that any object being held in the hand is involuntarily clenched and, as it is likely to be the faulty electrical appliance or a wire, the object cannot be released and the current thus continues to flow. This adds to the time element and progressively worsens the risk of both cutaneous burns and the risk of cardiac or respiratory arrest. Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology 4th edition, Page No. 326-328

281.q: What is the bullet recovered from the victim of a homicidal shooting known as?
281.e: Bullet collected at surgery or autopsy, from the body of a victim alive or dead is called a crime bullet. In other words, crime bullet is the one which is recovered from the body of a victim. Test bullet is a bullet that is fired from a firearm suspected of being involved in a crime. The test firing is into a gunny bag fixed into a deal wood box. The bullet is then collected for comparison with crime bullet under a comparison microscope, for identifying the crime weapon. The primary markings(Macroscopic) and secondary markings(microscopic) characteristics on the crime bullet are compared with those present over test bullet. This can only be done in relation to rifled weapons. Exhibit bullet is a crime/test bullet, which is presented in the court as evidence. Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, Page No. 296.

281.q: 'Dry Submarine' in custodial torture injuries refer to
o: Tying of a plastic bag over the head
Inserting heated metal skewer into anus
281.e: Beating on the sole of the feet is known as Falanga or Falaka or Bastinado. Dry submarine means head and face are covered with a plastic bag. In Wet submarine (Latina), head is submerged in polluted water. Inserting heated metal skewer into the anus is known as Black slave. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 229

281.q: Which is the most commonly injured part of the spinal cord?
281.e: The cervical spine is the most commonly injured part of the spinal cord. The cervical spine accounts for 60 per cent of the adult spine injuries and the most common part of the spine to be injured is the region of the upper cervical vertebrae (C1–C4), and injury to the C1/C2 complex accounts for 19–25 per cent of the cervical spine injuries. These are followed by injuries to the thoracolumbar (20 per cent), lumbar (10 per cent), thoracic (8 per cent), and sacral level (2 per cent). Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4 th Edition, Page No. 210

282.q: Victim was choked with mouth & nose covered with elbow around neck. It is called as ?
282.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Mugging [Ref Reddy 30th/e p. 321] Mugging: Strangulation is caused by holding the neck of the victim in the bend of the elbow. Garrotting: The victim is attacked from behind. The throat may be grasped or a ligature is thrown over the neck & quickly tightened, by twisting it with a lever, which results in sudden loss in consciousness and collapse. Bansdola: one strong bamboo or stick is placed across the back of the neck & another across the front. Both the ends are tied with a rope due to which the victim is squeezed to death

282.q: While doing an autopsy on a victim of strangulation, you are examining his brain. Which of the following areas of the brain is the most likely to show evidence of hypoxic damage in this victim?
282.e: From the given options, the hippocampus is most likely to show evidence of damage in the case of a hypoxic brain injury like strangulation . However, third and fourth cortical layers are best for displaying the histological changes of hypoxia. The parts of the brain most suitable for seeking evidence of hypoxic damage are: Hippocampus (especially CA1 sector = Sommer's area and subiculum) Cerebellar folia Globus pallidus in the basal ganglia Boundary zones of the cerebral cortex where the grey matter is most vulnerable because it lies at the terminal reaches of the arterial supply (for example, parasagittally at the middle frontal gyrus where the watershed between middle and anterior cerebral arteries lies). The third and fourth cortical layers are best for displaying the histological changes of hypoxia. Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4 th Edition, Page No. 207

282.q: A victim of suicidal hanging is brought to you for examination. All the following lead to the death of this patient except:
282.e: Laryngeal spasm is not a cause of death suicidal hanging. Causes of death in hanging: Asphyxia (Fatal hypoxia → when O2 Level falls Venous congestion Combined asphyxia & Venous congestion Cerebral ischemia Reflex vagal inhibition Fracture or dislocation of cervical vertebrae References: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 369; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 261, 262

283.q: On examining a case of wet drowning, you observe weights that are attached to the body to keep it underwater. What does this suggest?
o: Can be either homicidal or suicidal
283.e: Attachment of weights to the body to keep it underwater is consistent with both homicidal and suicidal drowning. Differentiating points: Suicidal drowning - Determined suicidal person may attach weights to the body or tie his limbs. It is common among women. Homicidal drowning – The assailant may attach weight to his victim’s body to keep it underwater to conceal the evidence. In addition, there may be signs of struggle on the body, or evidence of struggle at the banks of the river from where the body was recovered. Accidental drowning is the most common form of drowning. It is seen among fishermen, bathers, dock workers, intoxicated, and epileptics. Homicidal drowning is the least common. Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 400; Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 402

Paltauf's haemorrhages are mostly found in the lower lobes . Paltauf’s haemorrhages ( Paltauf’s spots): Appearance → Shining, pale pink or bluish red haemorrhages, immediately beneath the pleurae (Subpleural space). Size → Minute or up to 3-5 cm in diameter Incidence → 50%. Location → Lower lobes of lungs (most common). May also be on interlobar surfaces or anterior surfaces of entire lungs. Mechanism → Tearing (rupture) of the interalveolar partitions due to decreased pressure during forced expirations They are found when the alveolar walls rupture as a result of increased pressure during forced expirations. They are described in 50- 60% of drownings. They are mostly found in the lower lobes on the anterior surface and margins of lung. Reference : Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 397

283.q: Characteristic feature of drowning is Specific finding of antemortem drowning:
o: Cadaveric spasm with grass in hand
283.e: Cadaveric spasm with grass in hand is the definite sign of antemortem drowning. (The medico-legal importance of diatoms is controversial) Definite signs of antemortem drowning: Cadaveric Spasm with weeds/grass in the hand Emphysema aquosum Copious amount of white, fine, leathery froth (D/t Emphysema Acquosum) Paltauf’s haemorrhages Diatoms ( The medico-legal importance of diatoms is controversial. If the same species of diatoms present in the drowning media is present in bone marrow and if the victim had not drunk the same water before submersion is the most important internal sign of antemortem drowning) References: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 286, Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 395

284.q: A 27-year-old woman lodges a complaint in the police station that that she was raped by her husband while living separately, under a decree of separation. Which among the following statements is false regarding this situation?
o: Minimum punishment for this offence is 2 years imprisonment
Section 67 BNS deals with such cases
This is a cognizable offence on complaint of victim
284.e: Sexual assault by the husband upon his wife during separation is a bailable offence Section 67 BNS: - Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation: - Whoever has sexual intercourse with his own wife, who is living separately, whether under a decree of separation or otherwise, without her consent, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than two years, but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. This offence is cognizable and bailable on complaint of the victim. This is not marital rape → Marital rape means, sexual intercourse with his own wife without her consent and as of today marital rape is not punishable in India. References: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 322

284.q: A newspaper editor discloses the identity of a victim of rape without prior permission. He would be tried under which section of BNS?
284.e: Sec. 72(1) of BNS deals with punishment for disclosure of the identity of the victim of rape - Up to 2 years of imprisonment and fine. Sec 202: Intentional omission to give information of offense by person bound to inform. Sec 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life. Sec 272: Malignant acts likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life. Reference: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023

284.q: A woman pretends to be pregnant and later presents a child as her own in order to claim financial or property benefits from a man. What is the term used for such a child?
284.e: Explanation: A supposititious child is one fraudulently presented as being born to a woman, typically to extort money, claim inheritance, or establish false paternity. It is a legally recognized term in forensic medicine for cases involving falsified parentage claims. Explanation of other options: Superfecundation (Option B): Fertilization of two ova from separate acts of intercourse in the same cycle → twins with different fathers. Posthumous child (Option C): Child born after the father’s death. Superfetation (Option D): Fertilization of a second ovum during an ongoing pregnancy. Key takeaways: Supposititious child = false claim of maternity/paternity. Relevant in disputes of inheritance and legitimacy. Important medicolegal term under family and inheritance law. References: Supposititious child

285.q: In case of infant deaths, Ploucquet's test is carried out to determine live birth by:
o: Increase in weight of lungs in relation to body weight following respiration
Presence of air in middle ear
Presence of air in stomach following respiration
Change in shape of chest after respiration
285.e: Ploucquet's test: This test helps to demonstrate establishment of respiration. Weight of lungs before respiration → 1/70 of body weight and after respiration → 1/35 of body weight. Fodere's test(Static test): Weight of lungs before respiration → 30-40g and after respiration → 60-66g. Wredin's test: Assesses the changes in the middle ear. The gelatinous substance in the middle ear is replaced by air if respiration has taken place. Shape of the Chest: Before respiration, the chest is flat, and its circumference is one to two cm. less than the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus. After respiration, the chest expands and becomes arched or drum shaped. Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, PC Dixit, Page No. 175-177.

285.q: In both water and food are completely withheld to a person, death usually occurs in
285.e: Total deprivation of water and food results death in about 10 to 12 days. Newborns may survive for 7 to 10 days without food and water. If food alone is withdrawn, death may occur in 6 to 8 weeks or even more. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 259

285.q: An ASHA worker brings the body of a newborn to casualty saying that the child was delivered dead at home. You suspect it as a live birth and request an autopsy. All the following will confirm a live birth except
o: Presence of milk in the stomach
Presence of meconium in the large bowel
285.e: The absence (and not presence) of meconium in the large bowel may be a sign of Live birth but the presence of meconium in the large bowel is not a confirmation of live birth. Confirmatory signs of live birth: Presence of milk in the stomach Absence of meconium in the large bowel, exception being breech delivery. Exfoliation of skin closure of foetal channels Changes in the umbilical cord Live birth can be excluded if: Signs of maceration are present. Signs of immaturity are present. If the child has not attained the viable age (7 months), it could not have been born alive. Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, P C Dixit, Page No. 178

286.q: What acts as both poison & antidote ?
286.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., CuSO4 [Ref: Reddy 30th/e p. 500, 503] Copper sulphate acts as a poison & an antidote for phosphorus poisoning. Copper sulphate when ingested causes burning pain in stomach with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting. In severe cases, hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, methemoglobinemia, jaundice, pancreatitis & cramps & convulsions. Death can occur due to hepatic & renal failure. It is given in gastric lavage for phosphorous poisoning as it coats the particles of phosphorous with a film of copper sulphide which is harmless.

286.q: If father's blood group is A and mother's blood group is B, the child's blood group will be
286.e: There are 4 phenotypes and 6 genotypes in blood group inheritance. If father is phenotype A (Genotype may be AA or AO) and mother is phenotype B (Genotype may be BB or BO), the offspring's genotype can be AB or AO or BO or OO, which will manifest the genotype as AB or A or B or O. A and B are both "dominant" and O is "recessive" to A and B, whereas A and B are equally dominant. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 351

286.q: ABO antigen are found in all except
286.e: 80% of the human population are secretors and 20% are non-secretors. The secretors secrete ABO antigen in all their body fluids except in CSF. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 352

287.q: Mild poisoning by organophosphate occurs when the ChE activity is
287.e: Mild poisoning usually occurs when cholinesterase activity is 20 to 50% of normal. Moderate poisoning occurs when activity is 10 to 20% of normal. Severe poisoning when activity is less than 10% normal. Small, repeated exposures may gradually depress the cholinesterase activity to very low levels, often resulting in minimal symptoms. References: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 396.

287.q: The starting dose of pralidoxime in OP poisoning is:
287.e: Pralidoxime(2-PAM), a nucleophilic oxime, most effective when treatment is started early and if used within 48 hours and helps in regenerating AChE associated with skeletal muscle neuromuscular junctions(overcome the nicotinic effects of OPCs). Dose: 1-2 g IV(20-40 mg/kg) over 5-20 min dissolved in 0.9% normal saline solution, may be repeated at 1-2 hours if muscle weakness is not relieved and again after 8-10 hours. Alternatively, continuous infusion(200-400 mg/h) of 2-PAM is more effective because of shorter duration of action of a single dose. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 655.

287.q: All are true of OPC poisoning, except:
287.e: Atropinization: Atropine blocks the muscarinic manifestations and has no effect on nicotinic receptors(on muscle weakness or paralysis) and does not affect the rate of regeneration of inhibited AChE. Dose: 2-4 mg IV(0.05-0.2 mg/kg in children) repeated after every 5-15 minutes till atropinization, the dose should be adjusted to maintain this effect for at least 24 hours(maintenance dose: 0.02-0.05 mg/kg). Option A: OP compounds are anti-cholinesterase agents(ChE inhibitors) Option B: The muscarinic manifestations may lead to bradycardia or tachycardia; but predominantly bradycardia. Option D: Nicotinic manifestations on striated muscle leads to initial stimulus results in contraction. Later there is paralysis due to persistent depolarisation. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 655.

288.q: A woman found comatose in her house is life-flighted to the nearest regional medical center. Blood gases reveal a normal PaO2 but a lower than normal arterial O2 saturation. Which of the following conditions is most consistent with the findings?
288.e: Hemoglobin has 210 x greater affinity for carbon monoxide than for oxygen. Thus, in carbon monoxide poisoning, the amount of dissolved oxygen, as reflected by the PaO2 may be normal, but the saturation of hemoglobin with oxygen will be lower than expected for a given PaO2. V/Q mismatch with low V/Q units, hypoventilation, and right-to-left shunting are all causes of hypoxemia (decreased PaO2). In anemia, hemoglobin concentration is reduced, but the saturation of hemoglobin O2 is normal. Reference: Ganong, pp 683-691. Levitzky, pp 180-183.

288.q: What is the cause of death in smoke inhalation?
288.e: Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning . In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anaemic hypoxia Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity to haemoglobin compared to oxygen and hence the amount of haemoglobin available for oxygen transport is markedly reduced. It displaces oxygen from its combination with haemoglobin and forms a relatively stable compound known as carboxyhemoglobin . It thus reduces the oxygen content of the blood, and hence, that of the tissues. It acts as a chemical asphyxiant and produces death due to anaemic anoxia. References: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice 5th edition Page no: 113; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 101

288.q: Lee Jones test is used to detect:
288.e: Lee Jones test is used to detect cyanide. Lee Jones test: To 5 ml of stomach contents add few crystals of ferrous sulphate and 5 drops of 2% sodium hydroxide. Boil and cool and add 10 drops of 10% hydrochloric acid. Greenish-blue colour indicates cyanide, and purplish colour salicylates. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 480

289.q: A chronic alcoholic assaulted his neighbour. He had quit drinking 4 days back but now has delirium tremens. He is:
o: Family is responsible for his act
289.e: Medico-legal Aspects of delirium tremens: It is a medical emergency and should be treated on an inpatient basis. When a person is in delirium tremens commits any illegal act, he is not held responsible by the reason that he is considered to be mentally unsound during this state (Sec. 22 BNS). 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind. - Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition. Page No. 606

289.q: An alcoholic patient is brought for medical examination for alleged assault of his neighbour. On examination, abnormal behaviour with irrelevant talk is noted. He has history of abstaining from alcohol for past 4 days and is diagnosed to be a case of delirium tremens. What is true according to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha?
o: He is criminally responsible for his act
He is partially responsible for his act
Have diminished responsible for his act
Not responsible for his act under section 22 BNS
289.e: Sec. 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind.-Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. Delirium tremens is a psychiatric condition arising as a result of abstinence from alcohol. In case of delirium tremens, he doesn't know that what is he doing. So, he is not criminally responsible for his act under section 22 BNS. Reference: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023

289.q: An alcoholic patient is brought for medical examination for alleged assault of his neighbour. On examination, abnormal behaviour with irrelevant talk is noted. He has history of abstaining from alcohol for past 4 days and is diagnosed to be a case of delirium tremens. What is true according to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
o: He is criminally responsible for his act
He is partially responsible for his act
Have diminished responsible for his act
Not responsible for his act under section 22 BNS
289.e: Explanation: Delirium tremens is a psychiatric condition arising as a result of abstinence from alcohol. In case of delirium tremens, he doesn't know what he is doing. So, he is not criminally responsible for his act under section 22 BNS. Sec. 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind. Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.

290.q: The usual fatal dose of white phosphorous:
290.e: The usual fatal dose of white phosphorous is 60-120 mg. Fulminating poisoning (death within 12 hours) may be seen when the patient takes a large dose. Early death is due to cardiac dysrhythmias, secondary to electrolyte abnormalities, such as hypocalcaemia and hyperkalaemia. Death after the first 24 h is due to hepatic failure. Fatal dose: 60-120 mg (1 mg/kg) of white phosphorus. Fatal period: Within 24 hours but may be delayed by 5-7 days. Diagnosis: Oral and skin burns, luminescent 'smoking' vomitus and stools with a garlic odour, and GIT and biliary damage characterize white phosphorus poisoning. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 565

290.q: M/C Heavy Metal poisoning in The World?
290.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e.,Lead [Ref Park 22"'Ile p. 752] More industrial workers are exposed to lead than any other toxic metal.

290.q: Cardiac arrythmias, myalgia and flaccid quadriplegia are characteristic of poisoning by:
290.e: Cardiac arrythmias, myalgia and flaccid quadriplegia are characteristic of poisoning by Barium carbonate. Signs and symptoms of Barium carbonate poisoning: The most characteristic features are areflexia and paralysis. Barium induces hypokalaemia. (Ba 2+ ion is a muscle poison). GIT: Nausea, vomiting, salivation, abdominal pain and diarrhea. Muscular system: Tingling sensation, tremors, cramps, stiffness of the muscles, paralysis of the tongue and larynx, myoclonus, myalgia, flaccid quadriplegia. CVS: Hypertension, arrhythmia, ectopic beats, ventricular fibrillation, irregular pulse, shock, cardiac arrest. RS: Pulmonary edema, respiratory failure. CNS: Mydriasis, vertigo, headache, confusion, convulsions. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 560

291.q: Several children were hospitalized with symptoms thought to be due to ingestion of food containing botulinum toxin. Which one of the following signs or symptoms is consistent with the diagnosis of botulinum poisoning?
291.e: Botulinum toxin impairs all types of cholinergic transmission, including transmission at ganglionic synapses and somatic motor nerve endings. Botulinum toxin prevents discharge of vesicular transmitter content from cholinergic nerve endings. All of the signs listed except cycloplegia indicate cholinomimetic action. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 114

291.q: A girl, otherwise healthy, sleeping on the floor suddenly develops nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, quadriplegia at night. Diagnosis is:
291.e: Krait: Signs and symptoms are similar to cobra poisoning, but less rapid. The signs and symptoms are Abdominal pain Ptosis Dysarthria Dysphagia Chest pain Quadriparesis Respiratory paralysis Death Common krait hunt nocturnally and are quick to bite people sleeping on the floor, often without waking their victims, since the venom is painless. Victims wake up early morning, paralyzed - mistaken for STROKE Option A: GBS will have a preceding history of diarrhoea 6 to 8 weeks before and will have ascending paralysis. Option B: Poliomyelitis will have gradual onset flaccid paralysis. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 581

291.q: In a snake envenomation, antivenom is started by giving a dose of:
291.e: The recommended initial dose of PASV is 8-10 vials administered slowly via IV route over a period of 1 hour Repeat doses for vasculotoxic species is based on the 6 hours rule (depending on the coagulation profile); the maximum recommended dose is 30 vials. Repeat doses for neurotoxicity is based on the 1-2 hours rule (depending on whether patients have not improved, or worsened); maximum dose is 20 vials. Antivenin treatment should be given, as soon as it is indicated. Ideally PASV should be administered within 4 hours, but effective even if it is given within 24 hours. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 584

292.q: A person of interest in a homicide case is on the run from the police. He wishes to remove the tattoo on his left arm which is very prominent. Which of the following methods may be used for the same? 1. Surgical excision 2. Scarification with sandpaper 3. Caustic soda 4. Rubbing with isopropyl alcohol 5. Electrolysis
292.e: Methods for deliberate tattoo removal include Surgical methods: Complete excision and skin grafting Production of burn by means of red hot iron Scarification with sandpaper Carbon dioxide snow Electrolysis Caustic substances remove pigment by producing inflammatory reaction and a superficial scar, e.g., mixture of papain in glycerine, zinc chloride and tannic acid LASER beam: By exposure to laser beams, the particles of the dye get vapourised and expelled from the tissues in gaseous form Confluent smallpox and sometimes chronic eczema in children can obliterate tattoo marks Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 68

293.q: Which structure of the ear develops from all three germ layers?
293.e: The tympanic membrane develops from all three germinal layers. The outer epithelial layer is formed by the ectoderm The inner mucosal layer of the endoderm The middle fibrous layer is formed by the mesoderm. Explanation of other options: External auditory canal (Option B): The External auditory canal develops from the ectodermal layer. Stapes (Option C): The Stapes develop from the endodermal layer. Vestibular labyrinth (Option D): Forms from the otic placode (ectoderm) and surrounding mesoderm, but does not involve endoderm. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number: 15

Scheibe dysplasia Most common inner ear anomaly. Dysplasia of cochlea and saccule; hence also called cochleosaccular dysplasia.(Pars Inferior) Bony labyrinth is normal. Superior part of membranous labyrinth(utricle and semicircular ducts) is normal.(Pars Superior) Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 135.

o: Always occur as an isolated anomaly
Cochlear implants are used in treatment
May be associated with Pendred syndrome & DiGeorge syndrome
293.e: Mondini dysplasia may be seen in Pendred, Waardenburg, branchio-oto-renal, Treacher-Collins and Wildervanck syndromes along with other anamolies. Mondini dysplasia: Inner ear malformation Only basal coil is present or cochlea is 1.5 turns. There is incomplete partition between the scalae due to absence of osseous spiral lamina. Condition is unilateral or bilateral Can be treated by a cochlear implant. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 135.

294.q: A patient with ear wax underwent syringing. During syringing, the patient developed a syncopal episode. Stimulation of which nerve is responsible?
294.e: Auricular branch of the vagus (CN X), also called Arnold's nerve, supplies the concha and corresponding eminence on the medial surface. Vagus nerve has a parasympathetic action on the muscle fibers of the heart, so its stimulation during syringing of the ear canal can cause syncopal episode in some patients. Other Options: By stimulation of the other three nerves given in other three options don't cause syncope on stimulation.

294.q: Which of the following best describes Fissure of Santorini
o: Natural deficiency in cartilaginous part of external auditory canal
Natural deficiency in bony part of external auditory canal
Natural deficiency in fallopian canal of facial nerve
Vertical bony septum in Internal Auditory Canal
294.e: Fissures of Santorini are natural dehiscence in cartilaginous part of EAC. They allow transmission of infection and malignancy from EAC to Parotid gland Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Anatomy of Ear, Page number:3

295.q: Not a true match about the anatomical aspects of ear
o: Korner's septum is remnant of petrosquamous suture
Subiculum is a bony spicule which separates oval and round windows
Processus Cochleariformis indicates the basal turn of cochlea.
Canal for Tensor tympani lies on the anterior wall of middle ear
295.e: Processus cochleariformis is a hook like process on the medial wall of middle ear which marks the first genu of facial nerve. Tendon of tensor tympani takes a turn here to attach to malleus. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page - 5,6, 9

295.q: Infection of CNS spreads to tympanic cavity(=middle ear) through:
295.e: Hyrtl's fissure connects middle ear to middle cranial fossa. Canal of Huguier is the exit point of chorda tympani nerve from middle ear Vestibular aqueduct is the bony cover of Endolymphatic duct Aqueduct of cochlea connects inner ear to CSF in subarachnoid space of brain(not middle ear) Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Some Memorable Nuggets for Rapid Review, Page number: 547

295.q: Which of the following middle ear structure develops from neural crest cells?
295.e: Explanation: Middle ear ossicles begin forming around 6 weeks of development as cartilaginous structures . Malleus and Incus: Derived from mesoderm of the first pharyngeal arch . Stapes: Suprastructure: From mesoderm of the second pharyngeal arch . Footplate: From the otic capsule , which is derived from neural crest cells .

296.q: Which of the following forms lateral wall of mastoid antrum?
296.e: It is a large, air-containing space in the upper part of the mastoid and communicates with the attic through the aditus. Its roof is formed by tegmen antri, a continuation of the tegmen tympani and separates it from the middle cranial fossa. The lateral wall of antrum is formed by a plate of bone which is on an average 1.5 cm thick in the adult. It is marked externally on the surface of mastoid by suprameatal (MacEwen's) triangle Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9 th edition, Pg.no.7,8

296.q: A surgeon while doing mastoid surgery encounters unusual bleeding in the operative site. He can control the bleeding by doing everything except
o: Polish the area with diamond burr
Apply cutting burr to the site of bleeding
Use electrocautery to control the bleeding
Use bone wax to control the bleeding
296.e: Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 566. Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1249.

296.q: Mohan, 22 years old, male gives a history of right sided ear discharge, foul smelling and occasionally blood stained for the last 6 years.For last 3 days patient has developed fever with chills, headache and pitting oedema over mastoid region. The most probable diagnosis is
o: Atticoantral CSOM with sigmoid sinus thrombosis
296.e: Foul smelling and occasionally blood stain discharge, suggest unsafe CSOM also called as Atticoantral CSOM Pitting edema over mastoid is Greisinger sign Mastoiditis do not presents with pitting edema over mastoid or headache Meningitis present with neck, rigidity, vomiting Brain abscess, presence with fever with chills.

297.q: What is capula in the inner ear?
o: Sensory end organ of utricle and saccule
297.e: The sensory end organ of utricle and saccule are called as macula . They are responsible for linear Balance. The sensory end organ of semicircular canals are called cristae . They are responsible for angular Balance. Each semicircular canal have one narrow end and one dilated end. The dilated end is called ampulla. Cristae are present inside ampulla Cristae contains Gelatinous layer which contains cupula.

297.q: Mark the correct statement(s) regarding Inner and Outer hair cells: Inner hair cells are in a single row and transmit auditory impulses.II. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate the function of inner hair cells.III. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of the tectorial membrane. IV. Outer and inner hair cells are present in the ratio of 3:1.
o: I, II and IV are correct
I, II and III are correct
297.e: Explanation: Inner hair cells (IHCs): IHCs are single row cells responsible for transmitting auditory impulses to the brain via afferent fibers . Outer hair cells (OHCs): OHCs are arranged in 3-4 rows and modulate the function of inner hair cells via efferent pathways, amplifying cochlear sensitivity. Outer hair cells and tectorial membrane movement: OHCs do not primarily move the tectorial membrane . Their role is mainly cochlear amplification ; tectorial membrane motion is a passive mechanical response. (Statement 3 is incorrect) Ratio of Outer: Inner hair cells: OHCs (~12,000) outnumber IHCs (~3,500), approximately a 3:1 ratio.

297.q: As per the travelling wave theory of hearing given by Von Bekesy, sound energy creates a wave-like movement in which structure of the inner ear?
297.e: Travelling wave theory of hearing has been given by Von Bekesy which states that - A sound wave depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude on a particular place in the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment. Therefore, higher frequencies are sensed in the basal turn and low frequencies are sensed in the apex of cochlea. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number- 20.

298.q: All are true about malignant otitis externa except
o: Technetium scan is more useful in the prognostic evaluation of this entity
ESR can be used to monitor the progression of disease
Facial nerve is the most commonly involved nerve
298.e: Malignant otitis externa = Skull base osteomyelitis is locally destructive infection of bony EAC which is part of skull base. It is mostly seen in old diabetics and caused by Pseudomonas. Radionucleide gallium(good for prognostic evaluation) and technetium scan(good for diagnosis) are helpful in the management. Also ESR is a good tool to monitor disease activity. \ Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Some Memorable Nuggets for Rapid Review, Page number: 548

298.q: A 62 year old diabetic male with severe pain in ear and granulation with discharge in the external ear. On examination, the patient has facial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
298.e: Malignant Otitis Externa is an inflammatory condition caused by pseudomonas infection usually in the elderly diabetics, or in those on immunosuppressive drugs. Its early manifestations resemble diffuse otitis externa but there is excruciating pain and appearance of granulations in the ear canal.

298.q: Malignant otitis externa is characterised by all of the follwing except
298.e: Necrotizing otitis externa, also called malignant otitis externa, is caused by pseudomonas infection in an elderly patient with diabetes. Symptoms include severe otalgia, facial nerve palsy can occur. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.548

299.q: Most common cause of conductive deafness in children less than 12 yrs:
299.e: In above all the condition we see Hearing loss except in acute otitis media .In Acute otitis media patient present with Ear ache . The most common cause of hearing loss in children less than 12 years is Serous otitis media. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Disorders of Middle Ear, Page number: 75

299.q: The most common site of cholesteatoma in the middle ear cleft is
299.e: Prussak's space is the most common site of cholesteatoma formation in middle ear. It lies between the pars flaccida and the neck of malleus. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 80, 549. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1191.

299.q: CT scan of a patient suffering from atticoantral CSOM shows an abscess at petrous apex. Which of the following is not a likely symptom in this case?
299.e: Spread of infection from the middle ear to petrous bone is called Petrositis or Gradinego syndrome. This is a triad of Ear discharge Deep seated ear or Retro-orbital pain(CN V involvement) Diplopia(CN VI involvement - Lateral rectus palsy) It is a complication of CSOM. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 95.

300.q: A patient of right unsafe CSOM has presented with double vision and pain behind the right eye. What is the name of this entity?
300.e: PETROSITIS- GRADINEGO SYNDROME It is an infection of Petrous apex air cells. It's a complication of ASOM or CSOM. Petrous apex has relation with 5th and 6th cranial nerves. It has 3 features- PNEMONIC GERD. G-Gradinego syndrome E-Ear discharge R-Retro Orbital pain due to 5 th nerve D-Diplopia-due to 6 th nerve. CT scan of temporal bone will show abscess at Petrous apex. Treatment :– Surgical exploration. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Complications of Suppurative Otitis Media, Page number: 95

300.q: A patient of right unsafe CSOM has presented with history of diplopia and pain behind the right eye. What is the further ideal investigation in this clinical scenario?
300.e: Retro orbital pain and diplopia are suggestive of petrositis. Along with otorrhoea, it forms the triad of Gradinego syndrome. Diagnosis of petrous apicitis requires HRCT tempral bone which shows abscess at Petrous apex. Treatment - Cortical, modified radical or radical mastoidectomy + IV antibiotics Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 95.

300.q: Mohan, 22 year old, male gives history of right sided ear discharge, foul smelling and occasionally blood stained for last 6 years. He also complains of hearing loss for last 2 years. For last 3 days patient has developed fever with chills, headache and oedema over mastoid region. The most probable diagnosis is
o: Atticoantral CSOM with Lateral sinus thrombosis
300.e: Scanty, foul smelling ear discharge is seen in atticoantral CSOM. The patient recently developed fever with chills, headache and oedema over the mastoid(Griesinger sign). All these point to a diagnosis of Sigmoid sinus thrombosis(Lateral sinus thrombosis). TREATMENT Modified radical mastoidectomy with opening the sinus wall and removal of thrombus + i/v antibiotics. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 101.

301.q: The best description of Gelle's test
o: With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is decrease in the intensity of bone conducted sound in normal individuals
With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is increase in the intensity of bone conducted sound in normal individuals
With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is decrease in the intensity of bone conducted sound in Otosclerosis patients
With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is increase in the intensity of bone conducted sound in Otosclerosis patients
301.e: Gelle's test Compares intensity of bone-conducted tuning fork sound, without and with, raising pressure on the tympanic membrane with Siegel's speculum. Normally, Gelle's test is positive because intensity of hearing decreases when air pressure is raised in external auditory canal. In ossicular fixation or ossicular discontinuity, increased air pressure makes no changes in the sound intensity(Gelle's negative). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 27.

301.q: Which of the following statements is false about sodium fluoride regarding its use in the treatment of otosclerosis?
o: It acts treatment of choice in patients with positive schwartz sign.
It acts by inhibiting osteoblastic activity
Is contraindicated in chronic renal failure
Is indicated in patients with a positive Schwartz sign
