301.e: SODIUM FLUORIDE Mechanism of action: Inhibitor of osteoclast activity and so a stabilizer of bone turnover. It also leads to increased calcium deposition in otospongiotic foci and decreased bone remodelling. It inhibits the proteolytic enzymes in the cochlea. Uses: Sodium fluoride is the treatment of choice in Schwartz sign positive patients which represents the active stage of the disease. It is also used in cochlear otosclerosis. Contraindications: Chronic nephritis, Flourosis, in pregnant and lactating women and in children. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1074.

301.q: Which of the following is not a feature of Otosclerosis?
301.e: Rising sun sign is seen in Glomus Jugulare. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page -

302.q: A middle age female patient is complaining of transient sensation of rotational movements of surroundings with nausea while lying down on the bed. She has been experiencing this problem for last 3 days. Which part of the inner ear is the site of origin of pathology that is likely to be responsible for the given complaint?
302.e: This is a case of BPPV(Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo). Otoliths or otoconia are calcium carbonate crystals lying embedded in the gelatinous layer of macula. Macula is the sensory end organ of utricle and saccule whose function is linear acceleration. In certain head positions, the displaced otoconia come to rest against the cupula of SCC causing vertigo. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 52.

302.q: One of the following is not the treatment modality for Meniere's Disease
o: Intermittent Inner ear pulse pressure therapy
302.e: Primary treatment is medical management. Refractory patients are offered further treatments. like transtympanic injection of gentamycin using microwicks or microcatheters. Meniett device is external device used for pulse pressure therapy to labyrinth. Donaldson's line is surgical landmark for localisation of endolymphatic sac to conduct endolymphatic sac decompression therapy. Schwartz operation is other name for cortical mastoidectomy which is done in cases of acute mastoiditis. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Meniere's disease, Page number: 124

302.q: Third window effect is seen in:
302.e: In superior semicircular canal dehiscence, the patient will have conductive hearing loss due to leakage of sound waves from the dehiscence which acts like a third window. This is called third window phenomenon. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1192.

303.q: What is the most common benign tumour of middle ear?
o: Carcinoma of middle ear and mastoid
303.e: GLOMUS JUGULARE It is benign non capsulated locally invasive highly vascular tumour. It is more common in females. Site of origin- it arises from glomus cells lying around the jugular bulb. It is skull based jugular foramen tumour. The red vascular tumor erodes the floor of the middle ear and grows into hypotympanum This is called the Rising Sun sign. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Tumours of Middle Ear and Mastoid, Page number: 128, 129

303.q: 73 year old person with mild unilateral sensorineural hearing loss on right side has been diagnosed with ipsilateral Acoustic neuroma on Gadolinium enhanced MRI scan. The tumour size mentioned in the radiologist report is 1.0 cm. Audiogram reveals mild SNHL on right side, What is the further management of this patient?
o: Neurosurgical removal by middle cranial fossa approach
303.e: Since the tumour size is small and age of the patient is 73, it will be appropriate to go for Gamma Knife therapy, a stereotactic radiotherapy. Indications for Gamma Knife Therapy: Patient unwilling for surgery Patient unfit for surgery Old patient with small tumor with residual hearing. Middle cranial fossa approach is preferred for small tumors with residual hearing. It will lead to hearing preservation. If this patient would have been young, we would have gone for choice D. Translabyrithine approach is good for large size tumours with no residual hearing. Hearing preservation is not possible in this. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 134. Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1263.

303.q: Rising Sun Appearance is typically seen in:
303.e: Glomus jugulare is a benign non capsulated locally invasive highly vascular tumour. It erodes the floor of middle ear and start growing in Hypotympanum as red vascular mass(Rising sun sign). Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Tumours of Middle Ear and Mastoid, Page number: 128, 129

304.q: Which of the following is the surgical landmark for first genu of facial nerve?
304.e: Processuscochleariformis Hook like projection on medial wall of middle ear. Surgical landmark for first genu of facial nerve. It demarcates the geniculate ganglion which lies just anterior to it. Tympanic segment of the facial nerve starts at this level. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. - 7, 108.

304.q: Which of the following is not a boundary of facial recess?
o: Tympanic segment of the facial nerve
Mastoid segment of the facial nerve
304.e: Facial recess is the surgical landmark for posterior tympanotomy. Boundaries: Medial boundary - Vertical segment of the facial nerve (mastoid segment) Lateral boundary - Chorda tympani Superior boundary - Fossa incudis (short process of incus) Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number-6.

304.q: Which of the following is surgical landmark of first genu of facial nerve?
304.e: SURGICAL LANDMARKS OF FACIAL NERVE For middle ear and mastoid surgery Processus It demarcates the geniculate ganglion which lies just anterior to it. Tympanic segment of the nerve starts at this level. Oval window and horizontal The facial nerve runs above the oval window (stapes) and below the horizontal canal. Short process of Facial nerve lies medial to the short process of incus at the level of aditus. Nerve runs behind the pyramid and the posterior tympanic sulcus. Tympanomastoid In vertical or mastoid segment, nerve runs behind this suture. Digastric ridge. The nerve leaves the mastoid at the anterior end of digastric ridge. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.108,109

305.q: Not used in the treatment of bell's palsy
305.e: Steroids are the main stay of management. A patient who reports within first three days should be given acyclovir as well. Care of the eye is a very important part of management to prevent exposure keratopathy.Chances of recovery in bell's palsy are 85% and above. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Facial Nerve and its Disorders, Page number: 112

305.q: All of the following are true about temporal bone fractures except
o: Transverse fractures are more commonly associated with facial palsy
Ear bleeding is suggestive of longitudinal fractures
CSF otorrhoea is more common in transverse fractures
Longitudinal fractures more commonly cause conductive deafness
305.e: Temporal bone fracture are two types: Longitudinal fracture This is due to falling on the side. 80% of total fractures. Less dangerous. Cause Ossicular dislocation. Cause CHL Vertigo is uncommon. EAC bleeding and CSF otorrhoea are more Common Facial palsy is less common and delayed, it is due to edema of nerve. So, treatment is or oral steroids. Transverse fracture Due to Fall on front or the back. 20% of total fractures. More dangerous. Damage cochlea. Cause SNHL Vertigo is common. EAC bleeding and CSF otorrhoea less common Facial palsy is more common and immediate it is due to direct injury to nerve by fracture line. So, treatment is immediate Surgery. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Facial Nerve and its Disorders, Page number: 114

305.q: Which of the following is associated with olfactory nerve dysfunction?
305.e: Olfactory deficits have been described in a number of neurological disorders. Olfactory dysfunction may be the first clinical sign of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and idiopathic Parkinson’s disease (PD). In PD, bilateral olfactory deficits occur before the onset of most of the classical neurological signs. Hence smell testing maybe useful. The remaining syndromes are not associated with olfactory nerve dysfunction. Reference – Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition – Volume 1 – Page – 1237

306.q: A 10-year-old child has fever, pain in ear and Otoscopy shows tympanic membrane to be red & bulging, treatment of choice is:
o: Myringotomy with Grommet surgery and antibiotics
306.e: This is a case of Acute Suppurative Otitis Media(ASOM) with bulging ear drum. It is an impending perforation, hence Myringotomy will be needed in poster inferior quadrant. Grommet is only used in glue ear or Eustachian tube dysfunction. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 75.

306.q: A 10 years old child presented to ENT OPD with history of mouth breathing for last 3 yrs. Otoscopy revealed Bilateral retracted TM with air bubbles visible behind the ear drum. Audiological assesment shows Type B Tympanogram and moderate conductive hearing loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
306.e: INDICATIONS Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome or speech abnormalities, i.e. (rhinolalia clausa). Recurrent Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia. Dental Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent its recurrence after orthodontic treatment. The grommet insertion. If myringotomy and aspiration combined with medical measures have not helped and fluid recurs, a grommet is inserted to provide continued aeration of middle ear. It is left in place for weeks or months or till it is spontaneously extruded Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg no. 507

306.q: Which muscle is responsible for the opening of Eustachian tube during swallowing?
306.e: EUSTACHIAN TUBE : It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. Total Length 36 mm → Outer 12mm is bony& Inner 24mm is cartilagenous Angulation at birth it is nearly horizontal tube where as in adults it is 45° with horizontal. Main function of the Eustachian tube is middle ear ventilation. Tensor veli palatini muscle opens the tube during swallowing. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Eustachian Tube and its Disorders, Page number: 67

307.q: The main function of middle ear is
o: Conduction of sound energy to inner ear
307.e: The middle ear converts sound of greater amplitude but lesser force, to that oflesser amplitude but greater force. This function of the middle ear is called impedance matching mechanism or the transformer action. This is to counterbalance the loss of sound energy in the inner ear fluids. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no - 17, 18.

307.q: A 40 year old patient developed sudden hearing loss on right side within a span of 12 hours. On audiometry, the right ear has 70dB hearing loss over 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz. All of the below are proposed management options in this patient except
307.e: This is a case of Sudden SNHL. Treatment(Proposed) : Bed rest Steroid therapy. Inhalation of carbogen(5% CO 2 + 95% O 2 ) Vasodilator drugs Hyperbaric oxygen therapy Caroverine is not used in the treatment of sudden SNHL. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 42.

307.q: A patient presents to the OPD with complaints of bilateral hearing loss with worsened right ear hearing loss. On examination, the doctor diagnoses otosclerosis and recommends stapedectomy as the final resort to the problem. What would be findings of tuning fork tests based on which doctor recommends stapedectomy:
o: Rinne's test - positive: Weber's test - lateralized to left ear
Rinne's test - positive: Weber's test - lateralized to right ear
Rinne's test - negative: Weber's test - lateralized to left ear
Rinne's test - negative: Weber's test - lateralized to right ear
307.e: Hearing loss is a presenting symptom in otosclerosis , usually starts in early twenties, often bilateral conductive type. In conductive type of hearing loss, Rinne's test shows negative result for frequencies (BC>AC) and Weber's test is lateralized to affected (worse) ear. Tuning fork test will show negative Rinne (BC>AC) first for 256 and then 512 Hz and after complete stapes fixation, for 1026 Hz. Weber will be lateralized to ear with greater conductive hearing loss. Absolute bone conduction may be normal.

308.q: A 31 year old female patient complains of bilateral impairment of hearing for the past 5 years. The audiogram shows a bilateral conductive deafness. Impedance audiometry shows As type of curve. All constitute part of treatment, except:
308.e: The history and investigations done suggest the diagnosis as OTOSCLEROSIS. TREATMENT : Rx of choice is surgery called Stapedotomy>Stapedectomy. Other treatment for Otosclerosis Hearing aid- is given for patients unwilling for surgery. Sodium fluoride (NaF) oral therapy. It i is treatment of choice for Schwartz sign (+) patient. (Early stage of disease) Cochlear otosclerosis. NaF leads to stabilization of disease. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 105, 106.

308.q: Abnormal perception of loudness is seen in?
308.e: Abnormal perception of loudness is seen in Meniere's disease. It is called Recruitment phenomenon. It is tested using ABLB testing(alternate binaural loudness balancing test). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 30.

308.q: High frequency audiometry is used in
308.e: Ototoxic drugs involve high frequency more commonly than the low frequencies. Hence high frequency audiometry is useful in its diagnosis. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 39.

309.q: Turbinate that articulates with maxilla is
309.e: Inferior turbinate articulates with the maxilla. Superior and middle turbinates are parts of ethmoid bone. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no 159

309.q: Which of the following is the treatment for atrophic Rhinitis?
309.e: ATROPHIC RHINITIS (OZAENA) is a chronic inflammation of nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The nasal cavities are roomy and full of foul-smelling crusts. Surgical management includes: (a) Young's operation . Both the nostrils are closed completely just within the nasal vestibule by raising flaps. They are opened after 6 months or later. In these cases, mucosa may revert to normal and crusting reduced. (b) Modified Young's operation. To avoid the discomfort of bilateral nasal obstruction, modified Young's operation aims to partially close the nostrils. It is also claimed to give the same benefit as Young's.

309.q: Which structure is most commonly involved in the compression of the anterior ethmoid nerve in Sluder's neuralgia?
309.e: Explanation: The anterior ethmoidal nerve is most commonly compressed at the middle turbinate followed by the inferior turbinate. Compression of the anterior ethmoidal nerve leads to anterior ethmoid neuralgia, also referred to as Sluder's neuralgia. Most common cause is a spur impinging on the lateral wall of nose. It is characterised by neuralgic pain in the lower half of the face with nasal congestion, rhinorrhea and increased lacrimation.

310.q: A 125-lb, 40-year-old woman with a history of nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity since childhood presents to the Emergency Department with status asthmaticus and hypercapnic respiratory failure. She requires immediate intubation and is placed on a mechanical ventilator on an FIO2 of 40%, a control rate of 15 breaths/min, and a tidal volume of 500 mL. Which of the following is her approximate alveolar ventilation?
310.e: Alveolar ventilation ( VA ) equals the tidal volume ( VT ) minus the deadspace volume ( VD ) times the breathing frequency ( f ). The deadspace volume can be estimated as 1 mL/lb of body weight. VA = ( VT - VD ) x f VA = (500 mL - 125 mL) x 15 breaths/min VA = 5625 mL/min Reference: Ganong, pp 658-660. Kasper et al., pp 1508-1516. Levitzky, pp 67-71.

310.q: Maxillary bone does not articulate with:
310.e: Ans: B. Sphenoid (Ref Gray's 41/e p484, 40/e p473-476) Maxillary bone does not articulate with sphenoid. Articulation of maxilla: Each maxilla articulates with nine bones: Two of cranium: Frontal & ethmoid. Seven of the face: Nasal, zygomatic, lacrimal, inferior nasal concha, palatine, vomer & adjacent fused maxilla. Sometimes articulates with orbital surface & with lateral pterygoid plate of sphenoid.

310.q: Frontal sinus can be best visualized by:
310.e: Caldwell view (Occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position) - Frontal sinus – seen best Shows all sinuses except sphenoid sinus Water’s view (occipitomental view or nose-chin position)- Maxillary sinuses (seen best). Shows all sinuses except ethmoid Sphenoid sinus seen only if the film is taken with open mouth Towne’s view is taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis. Schuller’s view is taken for mastoiditis, cholesteotoma, longitudinal fracture of petrous pyramid. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 509- 511

311.q: Which of the following is the best test for olfaction?
311.e: University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test or UPSIT Best test for olfaction. Can be self-administered in 10 to 15 minutes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Clove oil is not a standardized test of olfaction. Option C - Acoustic rhinomanometry records the total air flow and resistance to air flow. It is not a test of olfaction. Option D - Ammonia is an irritant and does not stimulate the olfactory receptors. Reference: Scott-Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery: Volume 1, 8th Edition, Page Number 1232, 991; Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-164.

311.q: Which structure cannot be approached through transnasal endoscopic surgery?
311.e: Think about the anatomy of the eye - lacrimal glands lie in lateral part of orbit . So cannot be approached via transnasal route. Endoscopic surgery can be used to access the orbit, optic nerve, lacrimal sac and pituitary gland in addition to the nose and paranasal sinuses. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 494 Parson's Diseases of the Eye - 23 rd edition - Page - 422, 423 Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition - Volume 1 - Page - 1244, 1283

311.q: The odour receptor is present in:
311.e: Smell is perceived in the olfactory region of the nose, which is situated high up in the nasal cavity (upper 1/3 rd of nasal cavity). Olfactory area is also called the dangerous area of the nose. Esthesioneuroblastoma (Olfactory Neuroblastoma) arises from the olfactory epithelium. Olfactory pathway: Neurons of olfactory epithelium → Olfactory nerves → Pass through the cribriform plate → Mitral cells of the olfactory bulb → Olfactory tract → Prepyriform cortex and amygdaloid nucleus. Olfactory system is also associated with the autonomic system at the hypothalamic level. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-164, 239.

312.q: A patient presents to her GP with recurrent nosebleeds and also complains of facial fullness and facial pain. Over the past 2 months she has developed progressive shortness of breath and on one occasion she coughed up some blood. What would be the most appropriate test to perform?
312.e: The mostly likely diagnosis in this case is Wegeners granulamotosis. Sinusitis is the commonest ENT manifestation of this auto immune disorder. Septal perforation (bony and cartilaginous), saddle nose deformity with epistaxis is commonly seen. The multi-system involvement leads to pulmonary symptoms. The biopsy from the nose reveals necrotising vasculitis in this case. ANCA(Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) testing is further helpful for the diagnosis. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition - Volume 1 - Page - 133

312.q: Which of the following is not ligated in case of epistaxis control?
312.e: Internal carotid artery is a very important source of blood supply to the brain. It is never ligated for control of epistaxis due to the risk of serious cerebral complications and mortality. The following arteries are ligated for control of epistaxis. Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL) is done first. If uncontrolled, ligation of maxillary artery is done. Then ligation of external carotid artery above the origin of superior thyroid artery should be done. If still uncontrolled, ligation of ethmoidal arteries is done. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 210 Gray's Anatomy- The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice - 41 st edition - Page - 280

312.q: Which of the following is not a true statement regarding the Epistaxis?
o: Majority of the bleeds above the middle turbinate are from sphenopalatine artery
Posterior nasal pack has total 3 threads tied to it, one of them is kept hanging in throat
Woodruff plexus is on lateral wall of nose in the posterior part of nasal cavity
312.e: Above middle turbinate , the area is supplied by Internal Carotid Artery through the Ethmoidal arteries . Below middle turbinate , the External Carotid Artery supplies the area through its branches- greater palatine, sphenopalatine and superior labial. Option A – Hypertension and arteriosclerosis lead to posterior epistaxis . Option C - Posterior nasal pack has 3 threads. Two threads are tied at nostril . 3 rd hangs in throat . It helps in removal of pack. Option D - Woodruff is venous plexus in posterior part of lateral wall of nose. It is a site of posterior epistaxis. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 205, 207, 208

313.q: Prussak's space is bounded by all except-
313.e: Boundaries of Prussak's space: Superior - Fibers of lateral malleolar fold Inferior - Lateral process of Malleus Lateral - Shrapnell's membrane Medial - Neck of malleus Trautmann's triangle - This is a triangular space bounded by: Bony labyrinth anteriorly. Sigmoid sinus posteriorly. Dura containing superior petrosal sinus superiorly. Boundaries of Macewen's triangle are as follows: Superiorly: Suprameatal crest Anterior-inferiorly: Posterosuperior wall of external auditory canal. Posteriorly: A tangential line to the posterior canal wall. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number-549.

313.q: The pathway of spread of infection to cochlea in meningitis is
313.e: Venous drainage of labyrinth is through three veins, namely internal auditory vein, vein of cochlear aqueduct and vein of vestibular aqueduct, which ultimately drain into inferior petrosal sinus and lateral venous sinus. Bacterial infections reach labyrinth through the middle ear (tympanogenic) or through CSF (meningogenic). Sensorineural hearing loss following meningitis is a well known clinical entity. Bacteria can invade the labyrinth along nerves, vessels, cochlear aqueduct or the endolymphatic sac. Membranous labyrinth is totally destroyed. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9 th edition, Pg.no.38

313.q: Which ossicle has the least blood supply?
313.e: Incus has no muscle attached to it. Hence it has the least blood supply. Therefore, it is more vulnerable to be eroded in CSOM. Lenticular process followed by Long process of Incus are most commonly involved. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no - 77

314.q: Which of the following is not true about physiology of nose
o: The inspiratory and expiratory air currents pass through middle part of nasal cavity
Sinuses are mainly ventilated during expiratory phase of respiration
Nasal cilia beat 10-20 times per second and the mucociliary clearance time is 10 -20 minutes
The rhythmic congestion and decongestion is seen in vasomotor rhinitis
314.e: Nasal cycle of rhythmic congestion and decongestion is seen in all normal individuals. The duration of this cycle varies every 2.5 to 4 hours . This occurs because of the autonomic nerve supply of the nose. Nasal mucosa has rich blood supply. Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction and shrinkage of mucosa, while parasympathetic stimulation causes vasodilation and engorgement. Autonomic system is unstable in cases of vasomotor rhinitis . So the rhythmic congestion and decongestion is disturbed. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no 162, 198

314.q: Causes of epistaxis are all except:
314.e: Allergic rhinitis presents with watery nasal discharge. Not epistaxis. Causes of epistaxis include- Local causes like trauma (nose picking, intranasal surgery), infections, foreign bodies, high altitude, DNS Adenoids, juvenile angiofibroma, tumors of nose and paranasal sinuses Systemic causes like disorders of blood, liver, kidney, cardiovascular system, general infections, vicarious menstruation. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 194, 205, 206

314.q: All of the following are true about Allergic rhinitis except
o: Type 1 Ig E mediated allergic reaction
Pollen is the most common allergen for perennial rhinitis
Ipratropium is helpful in reducing rhinorrhoea in this condition
Sodium chromoglycate is a mast cell stabliser and is useful in its management
314.e: The pollen is the most common allergens to cause seasonal allergic rhinitis . Allergic rhinitis is type I allergic reaction which is IgE mediated . A] Early phase is due to release of histamine from mast cells. B] Delayed phase is due to leukotrienes and prostaglandins. Sodium Cromoglycate is a mast cell stabilizer and hence helpful in its treatment. The most common allergen for perennial allergic rhinitis is house dust mite . Ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic agent which is helpful in reducing the nasal discharge. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 194, 197

315.q: Which statement is true about Ethmoidal polyp?
o: Endoscopic removal is the first treatment of choice
315.e: Recurrences are more common in Ethmoidal polypi after removal as they are allergic in origin. Antrochoanal (AC) polyp is more common in children and its better seen on posterior rhinoscopy. FESS is the treatment of choice for AC polyp. For recurrent AC polyp (second recurrence), Caldwell Luc’s operation is done. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 200, 202

315.q: The medial maxillectomy is the preferred treatment now a days for the management of
315.e: Medial maxillectomy is the treatment of choice for Ringertz tumor (Inverted papilloma of nose). These days endoscopic approach is preferred. Option a – Surgical approach is the treatment of choice for angiofibroma. The type of approach depends on the stage of the tumor. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy singly or in combination have also been used. Medial maxillectomy alone is not useful. Option c – Antrochoanal polyps is removed via FESS. Option d – Treatment of maxillary sinus malignancy depends on the stage of tumor. Treatment is usually surgery combined with radiotherapy and chemotherapy as needed. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 236

315.q: Lymphatic drainage of cervix is to
315.e: A. i.e. Iliac lymph nodes om 94. Maximum contribution to the floor of orbit is by: a) Maxillary b) Zygomatic c) Sphenoid d) Palatine Correct Answer - A Ans. A. Maxillary The maxillae are the largest of the facial bones, other than the mandible, and jointly form the whole of the upper jaw. Each bone forms the greater part of the floor and lateral wall of the nasal cavity, and of the floor of the orbit "Orbital surface of maxilla is smooth and triangular, and forms most of the floor of the orbit" Also know: Maxilla is also the most commonly fractured bone of orbital floor. The floor (inferior wall) is formed by the orbital surface of maxilla, the orbital surface of Zygomatic bone and the orbital process of palatine bone The seven bones that articulate to the orbit are

316.q: A patient with head injury presents with unilateral conductive hearing loss and bleeding in the ear. Tympanic membrane is intact on examination. The battle sign is positive in the patient. The most probable cause for deafness could be:
o: Collection of fluid in the middle ear
316.e: This is a case of longitudinal fracture of temporal bone. The ear bleeding is a feature of longitudinal fracture. This fracture is due to parietal blow. Battle sign is ecchymosis around the mastoid tip area which is seen in temporal bone fractures. This fracture causes ossicular dislocation and hence conductive hearing loss. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 116.

316.q: A patient of head injury has bluish discolouration over mastoid area, bleeding from EAC and complaining of hearing loss with normal facial nerve function. After three days, patient starts having facial weakness. What is the possible diagnosis?
316.e: Longitudinal fracture This is due to falling on the side. 80% of total fractures. Less dangerous. Cause Ossicular dislocation. Cause CHL Vertigo is uncommon. EAC bleeding and CSF otorrhoea are more Common Facial palsy is less common and delayed , it is due to edema of nerve. So, treatment is or oral steroids. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 116.

316.q: All of the following investigations are helpful in the diagnostic assessment of a patient of CSF Rhinorrhea except
316.e: X ray of paranasal sinuses has no role in the diagnosis of CSF rhinorrhea. Beta-2 transferrin is the best confirmatory test. CT cisternogram - requires intrathecal injection of iohexol and a CT scan to localize the site of leak in cases when beta-2 transferrin cannot be done. Nasal endoscopy can be done to identify the site of leak and for its repair. OTHER TESTS FOR LOCALIZATION OF SITE OF CSF LEAK- High-resolution CT scan - important to see the bony defects. MRI - requires that CSF leak is active at the time of scan. Intrathecal fluorescein study - Dye appears bright yellow but when seen with a blue filter it appears fluorescent green. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8 th edition, page 192

317.q: All of the following are true about nose and sinus malignancy except
o: Tumours of Infrastructure of maxilla carry a poor prognosis.
Nickel exposure leads to squamous cell carcinoma of sinuses
Ringertz tumour of nose is a premalignant condition
Esthesioneuroblastoma is a malignant tumour which originates from the olfactory neuroepithelium of nose.
317.e: Ohngren’s line is from medial canthus of the eye to the angle of mandible. This line divides maxilla into superstructure and infrastructure. The malignancy of superstructure has poor prognosis due to proximity to orbit. In nickel exposed patients, the most common malignancy is squamous cell carcinoma. Ringertz tumour is other name of inverted papilloma of nose. It is a benign but locally invasive and can show malignant conversion. Esthesioneuroblastoma is a malignant tumour which originates from the olfactory neuroepithelium of nose. Also called olfactory placode tumour. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8 th Edition, pg. no – 241,242, 236, 239

317.q: A 15 year old male child presents with right sided nasal mass and profuse epistaxis with hyponasality of voice, findings suggestive of conductive hearing loss and cheek swelling. What is the possible diagnosis
317.e: Angiofibroma is a pink, firm, 1- to 2-mm dome-shaped papule most commonly located over the nasal bridge and cheeks and is a benign tumor made of blood vessels and connective tissue that can appear as small, red bumps on the face, particularly on the cheeks and nose. It's a type of vascular tumor that's common in patients with tuberous sclerosis, a genetic disorder.

317.q: All statements are true about Ringertz tumour of Nose except
o: Arises from upper part of nasal septum
317.e: Ringertz tumor arises from lateral wall of nose. Inverted Papilloma (Transitional Cell Papilloma or Ringertz Tumour or Schneiderian Papilloma) It is a tumour of the non-olfactory mucosa of nose ( Schneiderian membrane ) and paranasal sinuses. Most common site of origin is lateral wall of nose in the middle meatus It is a benign but locally invasive tumour and can show malignant conversion. Human papilloma virus is thought to be responsible for its aetiology. Clinically, men are affected more than women in the age group of 40–70. Treatment - Medial maxillectomy is the treatment of choice. These days endoscopic approach is preferred. Radiotherapy is not advised as it may induce malignancy. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8 th Edition, pg. no – 236

318.q: An ENT surgeon is performing diagnostic nasal endoscopy in a patient of suspected sinusitis. He passes the endoscope at 0 degrees in the middle meatus, what is this pass called?
318.e: Diagnostic nasal endoscopy is done in three passes. First pass – Examination of nasopharynx and inferior meatus. Second pass - Examination of the sphenoethmoidal recess, superior meatus and openings of sphenoid sinus and posterior ethmoidal cells. Endoscope is passed medial to middle turbinate. Third pass - Examination of the middle meatus in detail. Endoscope is passed from the front into the middle meatus. Can examine uncinate process, bulla ethmoidalis, hiatus semilunaris, sinus of the turbinate (cavity on lateral side of middle turbinate) and the frontal recess. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no -492- 493

318.q: A 20 year old male patient with a long standing history of unilateral foul smelling ear discharge presents to the OPD with severe headache, spontaneous nystagmus and a staggering gait. What is the probable diagnosis?
318.e: A long standing history of unilateral foul smelling ear discharge is possibly due to atticoantral CSOM. The onset of severe headache, spontaneous nystagmus and a staggering gait is suggestive of cerebellar abscess. Treatment - High dose antibiotics, neurosurgical approach. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 99, 100.

318.q: A diabetic patient presented to OPD with blood stained nasal discharge and progressive blackish nasal discoloration. Which of the following is the choice of therapy?
318.e: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis . Mucormycosis is acute invasive fungal infection involving nose and paranasal sinuses, where fungal hyphae invade blood vessels causing ischaemic necrosis. Commonly involves lateral nasal walls and turbinates and quickly spreads to orbit, palate, face and cranium. Treatment is surgical debridement and Amphotericin-B.

319.q: Which of the following is not true about ethmoid bone anatomy?
o: Lamina papyracea is a part of the ethmoid bone.
Inferior Concha is a part of the ethmoid Bone
Cribriform plate is a part of the ethmoid bone
Middle concha is a part of the ethmoid bone
319.e: Inferior concha is an independent bone . Superior and middle concha are parts of ethmoid bone. Uncinate process, lamina papyracea and cribriform plate are also parts of ethmoid bone. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-164.

319.q: All of the following are true about anatomy of ear except
o: Tensor tympani tendon arises from anterior wall of middle ear
Jugular bulb lies in relation to floor of middle ear
Endolymphatic sac lies in epidural space and reabsorbs endolymph
Epitympanum is the narrowest part of middle ear
319.e: Middle ear has three parts- epitympanum, mesotympanum and hypotympanum. Mesotympanum is the narrowest part - Epitympanum (Attic) is the deepest part of middle ear Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no - 6, 13

319.q: All of the following are true about anatomy of ear except
o: Internal carotid artery lies in relation to anterior wall of middle ear
Pyramid lies on the posterior wall
Aqueduct of cochlea connects endolymph to the endolymphatic sac
Mesotympanum is the narrowest part of middle ear
319.e: Aqueduct of cochlea connects the perilymphatic space of the inner ear to the subarachnoid space of the brain. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition - Volume 2 - Page - 545 Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no - 6, 13

320.q: A fire breaks out during laser vocal cord surgery. What is not to be done?
320.e: Oxygen will further support the fire being essential for combustion. So never use 100% oxygen when a fire breaks out. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 417

320.q: Rhinolalia clausa occurs in all of the following except:
320.e: Explanation: Rhinolalia clausa is not seen in cleft palate. Instead, a cleft palate causes velopharyngeal insufficiency , leading to hypernasal speech (rhinolalia aperta) due to excessive nasal resonance, rather than the nasal obstruction characteristic of rhinolalia clausa. Rhinolalia clausa Rhinolalia clausa or hyponasality is the lack of nasal resonance for sounds that are normally resonated in the nasal cavity, such as m, n, and ng . It manifests as a nasal or blocked voice caused by obstruction of the nasal passages or nasopharynx. Common causes of hyponasality Common cold Nasal allergy Nasal polyp Nasal growth Adenoid hypertrophy Nasopharyngeal mass (Option A, B, D ruled out)

320.q: Which of the following is not a method for adenoidectomy?
320.e: Dissection and Snare method is used for tonsillectomy . The other three methods are used for adenoidectomy. These are endoscopy based newer procedures for adenoidectomy. Coblation is the best Method of Surgery. The traditional method for adenoidectomy is curettage which is a blind procedure. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no. 503, 507

321.q: A 10 year old child of 2 weeks post tonsillectomy ate a packet of chips, 2 days after surgery and came to hospital with an oral bleed. What will be the best plan of management?
o: urgent surgical exploration and shift to operating room
Intravenous tranexamic acid and semi solid food for 5 days
321.e: Bleeding after tonsillectomy can be primary (within 24 hours after the operation) or secondary (after 24 hours until 2 weeks). The most likely explanation for secondary bleeding is infection with Streptococcus in the granulating tonsil bed. Treatment depends on the severity and potential cause of the bleed. Antibiotics are advised for secondary bleeding. Severe primary or secondary bleeds need to be controlled in there.

321.q: A 7-year-old post-tonsillectomy child was lying in the ward. He started severely bleeding in the ward and is turning pale and sick. What would be your treatment plan as an Intern in this case?
o: Start Intravenous line and Shift to Operation Theatre immediately
Adrenaline-soaked packing in the Tonsillar fossa and observation in the ward
321.e: If a patient is actively bleeding, the patient should be taken urgently for control of the hemorrhage. Until the patient is transferred to the operating room, if hemorrhaging is significant, direct pressure, either with a throat pack or gauze, should be applied to the tonsillar fossa if the patient is cooperative and an intravenous line can be started before the patient is shifted to the OT.

321.q: All of the following are closely related to the bed of the tonsil except
321.e: Palatopharyngeus muscle does not form the bed of the tonsil. Bed of the tonsil- Formed by the superior constrictor and styloglossus muscles . The glossopharyngeal nerve and styloid process , if enlarged, may lie in relation to the lower part of tonsillar fossa. Both these structures can be surgically approached through the tonsil bed after tonsillectomy. Internal carotid artery lies one inch lateral to the tonsillar bed Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 303

322.q: Nasal angiofibroma of nose is common in:
322.e: The tumor is testosterone dependent and hence is more common in adolescent males. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 289

322.q: The investigation of choice for a 12-year-old male child presenting with polypoidal mass in the nose, which bleeds on touch is:
322.e: Angiofibroma is the most common benign tumour of nasopharynx seen in adolescent males. It’s a highly vascular tumour. CECT scan shows Holman Miller(= Antral) sign – It is the anterior bowing of posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. It is pathognomic of angiofibroma. Angiography is also done before surgery to identify the main blood supply source of tumour. Pre-op embolisation will reduce blood loss(Maxillary Artery). Debulking or biopsy of this tumour is never done as it is a highly vascular tumour. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 292

322.q: CECT scan of 13 year old male patient with Angiofibroma shows the tumor involving nasopharynx, nose and occupying the pterygopalatine fossa. What is the Radkowski tumour staging of this patient?
322.e: Radkowski staging of Angiofibroma Stage IA - limited to nasopharynx and nose IB - extension into one or more than one sinus IIA - minimal extension into pterygopalatine fossa IIB - full occupation of pterygopalatine fossa with or without erosion of orbital bones IIC - extending Infratemporal Fossa IIIA - erosion of skull base with minimal intracranial invasion IIIB - extensive intracranial invasion with or without cavernous sinus invasion Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 293

323.q: A 52 year adult patient presenting with right sided hearing loss has been subjected to audiological investigations and was found to have a type B tympanogram. What will be the priority in further management of this patient?
323.e: This is a suspected case of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma(NPC). Type B tympanogram is suggestive of glue ear(serous otitis media). The unilateral serous otitis media(presenting as conductive hearing loss) in an adult patient should always arise the suspicion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Hence, nasopharyngoscopy should be done and biopsy of any suspicious area should be taken. Nasopharyngeal cancer is the occult hidden primary. Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common presentation of NPC. Myringotomy and grommet insertion will be done for glue ear at a later date when NPC is ruled out. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

323.q: A 52 year old patient presenting with right side hearing loss has been subjected to audiological investigations and diagnosed to be a case of right sided serous otitis media. What will be the priority in further management of this patient?
323.e: This is a suspected case of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma(NPC). The unilateral serous otitis media in an adult patient should always arise the suspicion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Hence, Nasopharyngoscopy should be done and biopsy of any suspicious area should be taken. Myringotomy and grommet insertion will be done at a later date when NPC is ruled out. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 75.

323.q: In Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which of the following is true about the hearing loss in the patient?
o: Unilateral Sensorineural hearing loss due to 8 th nerve involvement
Bilateral Sensorineural hearing loss due to 8 th nerve involvement
Unilateral Conductive hearing loss due to serous otitis media
Bilateral conductive hearing loss due to secretory otitis media
323.e: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma will cause unilateral eustachian tube blockage and hence it will lead to unilateral serous otitis media= glue ear. This causes unilateral conductive hearing loss. VIII th nerve is not involved in NPC. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

324.q: Cricoid cartilage lies at which vertebral level ?
324.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., C6 [Ref BDC 5I'Ve Vol. III, p. 237]

324.q: All of the following are true about Juvenile papilloma of larynx except
o: CO2 laser microsurgery is the treatment of choice
324.e: Juvenile papillomas are premalignant. All papillomas should be examined histopathologically to exclude any dysplastic features or malignant transformation. They are caused by HPV-6,11. The infection is transmitted from mother to child at the time of birth. CO2 laser is the treatment of choice. Recurrences are common after surgery. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 356

324.q: Ideal treatment for Keratosis larynx is
324.e: Leukoplakia or keratosis larynx Localized form of epithelial hyperplasia involving upper surface of one or both vocal cords. White plaque or warty growth on the cord without affecting its mobility. Precancerous condition Treatment is stripping of vocal cords followed by histology of tissue for any malignant change. Chronic laryngeal irritants should be eliminated. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 354

325.q: A 55-year-old woman has been suffering from COPD with neuromuscular respiratory insufficiency. 1 week back, she underwent tracheostomy for airway support and bronchial toilet. She is now in the ward. During the morning rounds, you find that the tracheostomy tube is blocked and her SpO2 is 72%. What would be the immediate management you will carry out?
o: Do suction of the tube after putting normal saline in the tube
325.e: This is an acute airway emergency. The tube should be removed immediately and replaced with a new tube. Oxygen will not help the patient as the tube is already blocked. Deriphyllin is a bronchodilator. It has no role in management of a blocked tube. Suction of the tube after putting normal saline helps in clearing the crusts. This helps to prevent blockage of the tube but is not helpful after blockage has occurred. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-372.

325.q: Which drug has role as a local application agent in JORP( Juvenile onset respiratory papillomatosis)
325.e: Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JoRRP) is a condition related to HPV 6 and 11 infection which is characterized by the repeated growth of benign exophytic papilloma in the respiratory tract of children. Cidofovir is used locally in JORP. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra

325.q: Following statements are true about foreign bodies in the air passage in children except:
o: Vegetable foreign bodies are not common.
A normal chest X ray can be seen in early cases within 24 hours.
More common in the right bronchus.
More common in children less than 4 years of age.
325.e: In children, vegetable foreign bodies are common with peanuts being the most common. A normal chest X ray is seen in early cases within 24 hours or when a foreign body causing partial obstruction with full ingress and egress of air does not produce any sign. Most foreign bodies enter the right bronchus because it is wider and more in line with the tracheal lumen. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number-377, 375.

326.q: 1. True about Reinke's oedema: a. Usually unilateral b. Common in smoker c. Corticosteroid is mainstay of treatment d. Involve whole of membranous part of the vocal cords e. Patient has dysphonia
326.e: Reinke’s edema is usually bilateral Usual cause is smoking and vocal abuse Involves whole of membranous part of the vocal cords Patient has a hoarse, low pitched voice Mainstay of treatment – Decortication of vocal cord Re-education in voice production and cessation of smoking Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no – 342, 353 Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery – 8 th edition – Volume 3 – Page number – 952

Reinke's oedema is due to oedema of the subepithelial space of the vocal cord (Reinke's space). TREATMENT- Decortication of the vocal cord (removal of strip of epithelium is done on one side and 3 - 4weeks on the other). Voice rest, speech therapy, cessation of smoking Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 342

326.q: All are true about Reinke's odema except
o: Speech therapy and Proton Pump Inhibitor are the mainstay of treatment
Sub-epithelial cordectomy is the treatment of choice
326.e: Under the epithelium of vocal cords is a potential space with scanty subepithelial connective tissues. It is bounded above and below by the arcuate lines, in front by anterior commissure, and behind by vocal process of arytenoid. Oedema of this space causes fusiform swelling of the membranous cords (Reinke’s oedema). Stopping smoking and Subepithelial cordectomy is the treatment of choice. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.342

327.q: A child presented with ear infection with foul-smelling discharge. On further exploration, a small perforation is found in the pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane. What would be the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Topical antibiotics and decongestants for 4 weeks
IV antibiotics and follow-up after a month
327.e: Foul smelling discharge with perforation of pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane is suggestive of atticoantral CSOM. It is always managed surgically. So tympanomastoid exploration(MRM) is the correct answer. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 85, 87.

327.q: The ideal treatment for T1N0M0 glottic cancer larynx is
327.e: T1N0M0 glottic malignancy - Tumour limited to vocal cord(s) with normal mobility. Carcinoma of the mobile membranous vocal cord is traditionally treated with radiotherapy. Now such lesions are precisely excised with CO2 laser under microscope with the same good results . Laser excision has the advantages of lower cost, lower duration of treatment and morbidity. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 363

327.q: Which is the preferred treatment for verrucous glottic malignancy of larynx stage T1N0M0?
327.e: Carcinoma of the mobile membranous vocal cord is traditionally treated with radiotherapy. Now such lesions can be precisely excised with CO2 laser under microscope with the same good results. Laser excision has the advantages of lower cost, lower duration of treatment and morbidity. Similar T1 lesions of the supra- or infrahyoid epiglottis with or without neck nodes have been treated with CO2 laser. Cervical nodes in such cases are managed surgically with appropriate neck dissection. Endoscopic CO2 laser is getting popular at some centers where facilities of CO2 laser and expertise are available. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-363.

328.q: All of the following are helpful in the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea except -
328.e: Muller's manoeuvre - An endoscope is used to look for collapse of soft tissues in the oropharynx when the patient inspires vigorously. Level of pharyngeal obstruction can be found. It plays a role in the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea but has no role in its treatment. Treatment options for OSA include - A. Lifestyle changes Weight loss Quit alcohol and smoking Dietary modification B. Positional therapy – Sleeping on the side as supine position may cause OSA. C. CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) or BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure) when CPAP is not tolerated. These devices maintain a positive pressure and keep the airway open. D. Surgical -Laser Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty(UPPP) - The aim is to increase the size of airway. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 327, 328

328.q: All of the following are true about cochlear implant except
o: Receiver stimulator is surgically implanted inside the body
Eighth nerve integrity should be established before cochlear implantation
Mondini's dysplasia of cochlea is not a contraindication of cochlear implantation
Veria approach is the classical facial recess approach
328.e: Surgical technique : The classical approach is posterior tympanotomy(facial recess approach) Other surgical technique is Veria approach. This is transcanal approach Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Rehabilitation of the Hearing Impaired, Page number: 145

328.q: All of the following are true about bone anchored hearing aid except
o: It has surgically implantable titanium fixture
It transmits sound directly to cochlea through the bone conduction.
The BAHA device is implanted on the side of deaf ear.
328.e: Osseointegration takes 2-6 months. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 142, 143.

329.q: Iris cloboma is most common in ?
329.e: Ans. C. Inferonasal All clobomas (including iris) are mostly inferonasal.

329.q: What is the anteroposterior diameter of an adult eyeball?
329.e: Dimensions of an adult eyeball Anteroposterior diameter : 24 mm Horizontal diameter : 23.5 mm Vertical diameter : 23 mm Circumference : 75 mm Volume : 6.5 ml Weight : 7 g Reference: Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-1 Anatomy and development of eye

329.q: What is the volume of an adult eyeball?
329.e: Dimensions of an adult eyeball Anteroposterior diameter : 24 mm Horizontal diameter : 23.5 mm Vertical diameter : 23 mm Circumference : 75 mm Volume : 6.5 ml Weight : 7 g Reference : Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-1 Anatomy and development of eye

330.q: True about rigid gas-permeable lenses are
o: Copolymer of PMMA and silicone and cellulose acetate butyrate.
They resist deposits and are less likely than soft contact lenses to harbour bacteria.
330.e: Oxygen-permeable or rigid gas-permeable lenses are made of a firm, durable plastic that transmits oxygen, e.g., a copolymer of PMMA and silicone and cellulose acetate butyrate. As they do not contain water, they resist deposits and are less likely than soft contact lenses to harbour bacteria. Oxygen-permeable lenses are easy to clean and disinfect, do not dehydrate and last longer than soft lenses. The rigidity of oxygen permeable lenses also means that they are easier to handle than soft lenses. As they retain their shape better, they provide sharper vision. Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 87

330.q: A 15-year-old girl experiences blurry vision OS and a frontal headache. Her acuities are 20/20 OD and 20/60 without correction OS. With -2.00 D refraction she sees 20/20 OS. In the light, pupils measure 6 mm OD and 1 mm OS and in the dark they measure 7 mm OD and 1 mm OS. The right pupil is briskly reactive; the left does not react to light or near stimuli. Her examination is otherwise unremarkable. What type of drop did she use?
330.e: A sympathomimetic drop would dilate the pupil, not constrict the pupil. It would not produce a myopic shift, and the pupil would remain reactive to light and near stimuli. A prostaglandin inhibitor would have no effect on the pupil, and an alpha adrenergic agent would have the same effect as a sympathomimetic. Only a parasympathomimetic drop would constrict the pupil and induce the myopic shift. Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 222/424.

330.q: An emmetropic 12 year old child has a near point of 10 cm. So amplitude of accommodation is
330.e: 1/ 0.1 - 1 / infinity = 10 D Range of accommodation Distance between far (infinity) and near point (30 cm) Power of accommodation Refractive power of eye in fully accommodative state - power at rest = power to focus at near - power to focus at far. The amplitude of accommodation is a measure of the closest point at which the eyes can focus: it is the range from the far point to the near point in dioptres. Because it is measured from the far point, the measurement needs to be taken with the distance correction in place. The amplitude of accommodation (Am) is mathematically expressed as the dioptric difference between the far point (fp) and the near point (np) of the eye and it is related to the maximum power variation that can perform an eye. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: Calculate amplitude of accommodation where patient is myopia - 2D, near point 10 cm
331.e: 2 D is already given as power to focus at far so Amplitude will be 1/ 0.1 - 2 = 10 -2 = 8 D Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: One millimeter decrease in axial length of the eyeball leads to hypermetropia of:
331.e: Shortening of eyeball induces a hypermetropia of + 3 D Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

Pseudo Myopia: This type of myopia is called as false appearance of myopia that occurs due to excessive accommodation and spasms of accommodation.This type of myopia usually manifest the execessive amount of myopia and decreased amount of hypermetropia. It could cause severe headache with asthenopic complaints. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

332.q: While performing subjective verification of refraction, the cross cylinder is used to check:
o: Axis of the cylinder to be prescribed
Power of the cylinder to be prescribed
332.e: Cross cylinder examination (otherwise known as Jackson's cross cylinder, JCC) is an examination used to refine the astigmatic refraction by fine-tuning the axis and strength of astigmatism. While a rough estimate can be obtained via retinoscopy or automated refractometry, cross-cylinder examination remains invaluable in fine-tuning the refraction for best vision. It confirm the axis and power of cylinder both Eg of types of JCC 0.25 JCC = +0.25DS/-0.50DC X 90 0.50 JCC = +0.50DS/-1.00DC X 90 1.00 JCC = +1.00DS/-2.00DC X 90 Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

332.q: Causes of premature presbyopia include all of the following except:
332.e: Rather in uncorrected myopia presbyopia occurs late, as they already have a good near vision without glasses Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

332.q: If the youth is in poor health or does much near work the perpetual overaction of the ciliary muscle is likely to produce symptoms; the condition is often called
332.e: In the young, the condition may cause no symptoms. When symptoms are present or arise, they are chiefly referable to the abnormal amount of accommodation to which these eyes are subjected, and to the lack of balance between accommodation and convergence. A healthy youth has an ample reserve of accommodation, and if hypermetropic, can accommodate for distant and near objects without being conscious of the act. If the youth is in poor health or does much near work the perpetual overaction of the ciliary muscle is likely to produce symptoms; the condition is often called accommodative asthenopia or 'eye strain' Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 79

333.q: Which of the following are indications for Pterygium surgery?
333.e: A pterygium is best left alone unless it is progressing towards the pupillary area, causes excessive astigmatism, a restriction of ocular motility or is disfiguring. Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

333.q: Which of the following is/are indications for Pterygium surgery?
333.e: Explanation: Indications for removal of Pterygium: Progression towards the pupillary area Excessive astigmatism Restriction of ocular motility Cosmetic disfigurement

333.q: Which is false regarding viral conjunctivitis
o: Topical antibiotics are treatment of choice
333.e: Topical antibiotics have a role in bacterial conjunctivitis In viral they can be given for prophylaxis from secondary bacterial infection Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

334.q: Sclera is outer coat of eye ball. It is
334.e: The sclera is the white outer coating of the eye. It is tough, fibrous tissue that extends from the cornea(the clear front section of the eye) to the optic nerve at the back of the eye. The sclera gives the eyeball its white color. Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 67.

334.q: Sclera is not transparent due to
o: Collagen bundles in sclera are of varying sizes and are irregularly arranged
334.e: The sclera proper, also known as the scleral stroma, is also called the substantia propria. Ultrasructurally, sclera is composed of: Collagen bundles Elastic fibers Fibroblasts Ground substances These components are responsible for its non-transparent nature. The ground substances consist of proteoglycans and glycoproteins. The collagen bundles in the sclera vary in size and are irregularly arranged, which is why the sclera is not transparent like the cornea. These variations in scleral collagen fibers are more pronounced in the mid-sclera, where the diameter of the fibers ranges from 50 to 400 nm. Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 45.

334.q: Most common systemic association of scleritis is
334.e: RA is the most commonly associated with scleritis, which is an inflammation of the sclera characterized by vasodilation of the superficial and deep episcleral vessels. Occasionally, scleritis may present before the onset of joint symptoms in the RA patient. It may also occur as a manifestation of systemic vasculitis. However, The most common eye-related symptom of rheumatoid arthritis is dryness. Reference: parson's 22/e section II chapter 16 diseases of the sclera. Pg 228.

335.q: Most common protozoan causing keratitis is
335.e: Ans. is `b' i.e., Acanthamoeba [Ref Kanski 8th/e p. 197] "Acanthamoeba keratitis is the most common keratitis caused by a protozoan especially in contact lens users".

335.q: All of the following microbial organisms are implicated in development of ICK except?
335.e: It is hypothesized that commensal organisms from periocular skin or the ocular surface gain access to the stroma via suture tracks or through compromised unhealthy corneal epithelium. Microorganisms that can produce this type of infection include α haemolytic Streptococcus, Peptostreptococcus, Pseudomonas and Candida, and prolonged treatment with topical vancomycin, moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin eyedrops with discontinuation or minimization of topical steroid use is generally required. Recurrence of infection and stromal scarring are common which may then require keratoplasty. Neisseriae Gonnorhoea is a highly virulent micro-organism that can invade healthy corneal epithelium whereas ICK is caused by low grade (low virulent) commensal micro-organisms that affect damaged corneal epithelium. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

335.q: Which of the following organisms is not implicated in development of marginal corneal ulcers?
335.e: Marginal/ Catarrhal ulcers occur near the limbus, especially in old people. Aetiology: As an immune reaction to toxins produced by staphylococcal organisms residing in the conjunctival sac or lids in patients with chronic meibomianitis or blepharitis; they also occur in association with a chronic conjunctivitis and may be caused by Moraxella or Haemophilus. Pseudomonas is implicated in development of contact lens induced keratitis. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

336.q: Which drug is implicated in development of Argyrosis?
336.e: Pigmentation may occur from the prolonged topical use of silver nitrate (argyrosis). It is due to the permanent impregnation of the elastic fibres, particularly the Descemet's membrane, with metallic silver. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 - Diseases of Cornea

336.q: Which of the following investigations / results support diagnosis of keratoconus?
o: Topography: cone shaped lesion with astigmatism
336.e: Keratometer: The keratometer mires are malformed, malaligned and malfocussed. Corneal topography: In the early stages, the condition is diagnosed with corneal topography, which demonstrates the cone and typical astigmatic pattern. Corneal thinness can also be measured with ultrasonic pachymetry or the Orbscan II corneal topography system. With the ophthalmoscope or a plane mirror at a distance of 1 m, a ring of shadow, concentric with the margin, is seen in the red reflex (resembling a droplet of oil), which alters its position on moving the mirror. It is due to a zone through which a few rays pass into the observer’s eye, as the emergent rays in the centre are convergent while those on the periphery are divergent. Refraction: irregular myopic astigmatism Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

336.q: Which of the following tests are performed as part of donor screening for eye donation?
336.e: Cadaveric allograft corneal tissue and sclera are made available for transplantation by eye banks by the process of eye donation organized by eye banks. With consent of the legal next of kin (parents/spouse/sibling/progeny/grandparents/grandchildren), the eyes are harvested and tissues processed before releasing for transplantation. Donors are screened for known contraindications by medical and social history, clinical examination and serological screening of a donor blood sample for transmissible infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS, HbsAG, hepatitis C and syphilis. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

337.q: A 78-year-old man experienced unilateral sudden loss of vision 1 year previously. Currently, he complains of severe pain in that eye. Examination reveals no light-perception vision, intraocular pressure of 72 mm Hg, iris neovascularization and evidence of a central retinal vein occlusion. What would the least helpful topical therapeutic agent be at this time?
337.e: The management of a painful blind eye with end-stage glaucoma can include topical cycloplegia (anticholinergic agent) and a corticosteroid agent for comfort. A topical beta blocker may provide relatively little intraocular pressure lowering but may provide some increased comfort. Eyes with end-stage iris neovascularization and neovascular glaucoma have completely or near completely closed angles. A cholinergic agent, such as pilocarpine, will not successfully reduce intraocular pressure in these eyes and will often increase pain and inflammation. Reference: Parsons 22nd Edition/303

337.q: Which statement regarding Muller cells is false?
o: They are modified glial cells that provide structural framework supporting neural elements in the retina.
Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer
Their basal processes extend out to form the inner surface of the retina (inner limiting membrane).
The apical or outer cell processes extend beyond the outer nuclear layer, where they are connected to the photoreceptors by a system of terminal bars that comprise the external limiting membrane.
337.e: The nuclei of the Muller cells lie in the inner nuclear layer, whereas the nuclei of the photoreceptors lie in the outer nuclear layer. Reference : kurana 3/e,p. 46

337.q: Which statement about the RPE is false?
o: The RPE interdigitates with the apical processes of the rod and cone segments.
RPEs are densely adherent to Bruch's membrane
RPEs comprise the inner blood-retinal barrier
RPE cells are taller and contain a greater concentration of pigment in the macula
337.e: RPE cells comprise the outer blood–retinal barrier; the inner blood– retinal barrier consists of the endothelium lining the retinal blood vessels. Reference : kurana 4/e, p. 40

338.q: All of the following are seen in RP except
338.e: Rather the vessles become thin and attenuated in retinitis pigmentosa. This is most consistent sign in RP also. Reference: parson's 22/e section IV, chapter 20. pg. 328.RP

338.q: A patient is suffering from gyrate atrophy of choroid which is due to the deficiency of enzyme Ornithine aminotransferase. Which of the following is beneficial for the patient?
338.e: Ornithine aminotransferase deficiency (also known as gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina) is an inborn error of ornithine metabolism, caused by decreased activity of the enzyme ornithine aminotransferase. Biochemically, it can be detected by elevated levels of ornithine in the blood. Clinically, it presents initially with poor night vision, which slowly progresses to total blindness . It is believed to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Research suggests there can be some adverse effect on muscles and also the brain. The cause of this is somewhat unclear but may relate to very low levels of creatine often found in this population. Treatment may include vitamin B6, lysine or dramatic dietary change to minimize arginine from patient's diet . Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 473.

338.q: Which of the following is not a common ocular association in retinitis pigmentosa?
338.e: Ocular associations of retinitis pigmentosa include myopia, primary open-angle glaucoma, microphthalmos, conical cornea (keratoconus) and posterior subcapsular cataract. Reference: Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th edition – A.K.Khurana, Chapter-12 Diseases of retina.

339.q: What is not a cause of monocular diplopia
339.e: Monocular Diplopia Monocular diplopia is usually attributable to refractive or media abnormalities. Common causes include uncorrected astigmatism, corneal irregularities, tear film abnormalities, cataract, etc. The hallmark of monocular diplopia from refractive abnormalities is improvement with pinhole. KIDS(pneumonic) Keratoconus/astigmatism Incipient cataract Double pupil/trauma Subluxated lens Reference: kanski, 5 th Edition, Page no. 544.

339.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Wagner's syndrome ?
339.e: Wagner's syndrome has an autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance with following features: Vitreous is liquified with condensed membranes. Retina shows narrow and sheathed vessels, and pigmented spots in the periphery. Choroid may be atrophied. Cataract may develop as late complication. Reference : Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-12 Diseases of retina

339.q: The most frequent cataract type seen in adult retinitis pigmentosa patient is
339.e: Cataracts are recognized as the most common anterior segment complication of RP. The opacity of lens generally happens at the mid stage of the disease course with obvious clinical symptoms and signs, and the major symptom is glare, especially in bright light. As these are complicated cataracts and are posterior subcapsular cataracts the most common prob is that of glare. Reference: parson's 22/e section IV, chapter 20. pg-327-328. RP

340.q: Intraocular lens (IOL) which can correct astigmatism is
340.e: Toric IOLs have an integral cylindrical refractive component to compensate for pre-existing corneal astigmatism . The main potential problem is rotation within the capsular bag (rare), and may be corrected by early surgical repositioning. Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 368

340.q: Endophthalmitis involve all the layers of the eyeball except
340.e: Endophthalmitis is the most dreaded and worst possible complication of cataract surgery. It is a suppurative inflammation starting from the vitreous which extends to all the parts of the eye except the sclera . If the sclera also becomes involved , the condition is then called as panophthalmitis . Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 724/725

340.q: Which of the following is/are not complications noted in early post-operative period of keratoplasty?
340.e: Complications in the early postoperative period include wound leak, shallow anterior chamber, persistent or nonhealing epithelial defect, secondary glaucoma, graft oedema, uveitis, graft infection, inflammatory ‘sterile’ suture infiltrates and primary graft failure. In the late postoperative period (after 3 weeks), complications include graft rejection, graft infection, secondary glaucoma, loose sutures and high astigmatism. Very late complications (after 1 year) include graft rejection and wound dehiscence from minor trauma and recurrence of the primary disease. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

341.q: All are considered emergencies in eye except
341.e: CRVO is not an emergency in eye The ocular emergencies are Ischemic optic neuropathy: rule out giant-cell arteritis (GCA) Central retina artery occlusion: rule out GCA and causes of emboli/thrombus Mac-on rhegmatogenous retinal detachmen Acute third nerve palsy: rule out intracranial aneurysm Open globe: rule out intraocular foreign body Acute angle closure glaucoma Endophthalmitis Alkali injury: requires urgent and copious irrigation Orbital cellulitis Reference: kanski 9/e chapter 22 pg. 892-916

341.q: In what condition are cycloplegic agents contraindicated during refraction?
o: Adverse side effects to anticholinergic drugs
341.e: The use of cycloplegic agents for cycloplegic refraction is an important part in the evaluation of patients with complaints pertaining to binocular vision and ocular motility. Adverse reactions to cycloplegic agents(anticholinergics) include allergic or hypersensitive reaction with conjunctivitis, eyelid edema and dermatitis. Psychological effects have been observed in children receiving the drug. Adverse reactions occur more frequently with atropine compared to other agents. Systemic intoxication from atropine manifests as dry mouth, fever, flushing of the face, rapid pulse, nausea, dizziness, delirium and erythema. Patients with previous adverse side effects are at risk for adverse reactions to further use of the offending cycloplegic agents. In none of the other conditions are cycloplegic drops contraindicated. Reference: Kanski, 6th edition, Pg no. 756.

341.q: Not a risk factor for angle closure glaucoma ?
341.e: Ans. D. Small lens Predisposing factors for PACG :- i) Shallow anterior chamber,ii) Short eye (short axiallensth),i1i) Smaller corneal diameter, iv) Anterior location of iris-lens diaphragm, v) Hlpermetropic eye, vi) Large lens (older cataractous).

342.q: Recurrent anterior uveitis with increased intraocular tension is seen in ?
342.e: Ans. A. Posner schlossman syndrome Glamatocyclitic crisis (posner - Schlossman syndrome) is a unilateral recurrent non- granulomatous iritis that is associated with an elevated ocular pressure during the attacks'

342.q: All are complications of anterior uveitis except
342.e: Complications of uveitis Early: Secondary glaucoma - angle closure, trabeculitis Seclusio pupillae Occlusio pupillae Late: Secondary glaucoma - synechiae formation, steroid induced Cataract - complicated cataract Band shaped Keratopathy, Hypotony, Cystoid macular edema: cause of low vision in uveitis Optic neuritis, Phthisis bulbi: In chronic disorders of eye sometimes there is shrinkage of eyeball, architecture is lost, IOP becomes very low, sclera gets thickened and there is calcification. Reference: parson's 22/e, chapter 17 pg. 241 sequelae

342.q: Which ocular disease is generally characterized by normal intraocular pressure interrupted by recurrent episodes of markedly elevated intraocular pressure associated with low-grade anterior chamber inflammation?
342.e: Glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome) is a rare form of open-angle glaucoma characterized by recurrent attacks of mild anterior uveitis and marked elevation of intraocular pressure, often to 40-60 mm Hg. The condition is usually unilateral and affects middle-aged patients. The iritis is generally mild with small, discrete, round keratitic precipitates. The acute attack usually resolves within a few weeks. The intraocular pressure typically returns to normal between attacks, but a chronic glaucoma may develop over time with recurrent episodes. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis, pseudoexfoliation glaucoma, and pigmentary glaucoma are generally associated with chronic pressure elevation. Reference: Parsons 22nd edition/300pg

343.q: Uveal effusion syndrome may be associated with all of the following, except
343.e: Uveal Effusion Syndrome(Ciliochoroidal Effusion) is an idiopathic disease of the retina and choroid characterized by abnormal accumulation of serous fluid in the outer layer of ciliary body or choroid. Clinical Features: Structurally abnormal sclera(Thick Sclera) Abnormal accumulation of serous fluid in the outer layer of ciliary body and choroid leading to Detachment of Ciliary body(Exudative) Detachment of Choroid(Exudative) Deep Ciliochoridal detachments Detachment of Retina(Exudative) Absence of inflammation or neoplastic disease Eyes maybe nanopthalmic (small) or hypermetropic Phthisis and hypotonia is usually due to ciliary body shutdown from chronic detachment which compromises the blood supply to the ciliary processes Mottling of pigment epithelium( Leopard spots ) may be seen after spontaneous resolution. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 484.

343.q: Head light in fog appearance is seen in ?
343.e: Ans. B. Toxoplasmoss On fundoscopic examination, there is diffuse "headtightinthe fogappearance, in congenital toxoplasmosis. This is due to combination of active retinal lesion in the center with depigmentation (the headlight) and severe vitreous inflammation (the fog).

343.q: Which of the following is true about Birdshot Chorioretinopathy?
