343.e: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is an uncommon idiopathic chronic/recurrent bilateral disease which predominantly affects females . Over 95% patients are positive for HLA A29 . The disease involves both the retina and choroid independently. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 429, 467.

344.q: Most common malignant tumour of eyelid is ?
344.e: Ans, b. Basal cell carcinoma Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the eyelids and constitutes 85-90% of all malignant epithelialeyelid tumours.
The most common malignancy of the eyelid is basal cell carcinoma. Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 1308

344.q: Extra row of cilia in the lid margin is
344.e: Distichiasis is a rare condition in which there is an extra posterior row of cilia , occasionally in all four lids. The posterior row of cilia arise from the orifices of the Meibomian glands . Reference: Kanski 8/e, Pg. 32.

345.q: Which structure divides the lacrimal gland into two lobes?
345.e: The lacrimal gland is split into two lobes by the lateral extent of the levator aponeurosis. Reference : kurana 4/e, p. 35

345.q: What is the most common site of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction?
345.e: Congenital dacryocystitis is the inflammation of the lacrimal sac in a newborn, most commonly due to delayed/incomplete canalization of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD), most often at the lower end of NLD and near valve of Hasner - occlusion is membranous. Presents with epiphora, swelling and purulent discharge at inner canthus. Treatment Massage over lacrimal sac with topical antibiotics -initial treatment of choice for 1 year. Syringing is attempted usually by 9-12 months of age. Most of us do it after 1 year only Probing of NLD should be undertaken after 12 months of age, as spontaneous resolution is likely to occur by 12 months. Dacryocystorhinostomy after 4 years of age. Reference: Parson's 21/e p. 464, 466

345.q: What is the initial management of congenital dacryocystitis?
345.e: Congenital dacryocystitis is the inflammation of the lacrimal sac in a newborn, most commonly due to delayed/incomplete canalization of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD), most often at the lower and near valve of Hasner -occlusion is membranous. Presents with epiphora, swelling and purulent discharge at inner canthus. Treatment Criggler Massage over lacrimal sac with topical antibiotics -initial treatment of choice. Syringing is attempted usually by 9-12 months of age Probing of NLD should be undertaken after 12 months of age, as spontaneous resolution is likely to occur by 12 months. Dacryocystorhinostomy after 4 years of age. Reference: Parson's 21/e p. 464, 466

346.q: True about chemical injury to eye all except
o: Acid injury are more severe in eye
Wash is to be done by ringer lactate
Steroids are given to decrease inflammation
IOP can be high in initial period
346.e: Alkali (penetrate inside) burns are more severe as compared to acid(coagulate on surface) Corneal epithelial and stromal damage by coagulase enzyme released by damaged epithelium and cause a lot of inflammation. Limbal ischaemia results from loss of stem cells. Vascularisation and conjuctivalisation of cornea occurs. Severe cases can have corneal ulceration and perforation. Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 912 chemical injury

346.q: Most dangerous intraocular foreign body is
346.e: Chalcosis, also called chalcosis bulbi, is a chronic reaction to a copper-containing intraocular foreign body (IOFB) When copper enters the eye, it is oxidized from its uncharged elemental form, Cu, to Cu 2+ ions. Though the ions are free to diffuse throughout the vitreous, they have a propensity to deposit in intraocular basement membranes including Descemet's membrane of the cornea (KF ring) and the internal limiting membrane (ILM) Foreign bodies containing less copper ( 85%) show a generalized pattern of intraocular copper deposition and are associated with more devastating outcomes such as suppurative endophthalmitis and phthisis bulbi. Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 911 IOFB

346.q: Cherry Red spot in children after trauma is seen in
346.e: Commotio retinae Commotio retinae is caused by concussion of the sensory retina resulting in cloudy swelling that gives the involved area a grey appearance. It most frequently affects the temporal fundus. If the macula is involved, a 'cherry-red spot' may be seen at the fovea. Severe involvement may be associated with intraretinal haemorrhage that can involve the macula. The prognosis in mild cases is good, with spontaneous resolution in around 6 weeks. Sequelae to more severe commotio may include progressive pigmentary degeneration and macular hole formation Reference: Kanski 8th edition/873

347.q: Cavernous sinus syndrome can be differentiated by orbital apex syndrome by
347.e: Early vision loss; visual loss is early in orbital apex syndrome as apex has optic canal optic nerve also Orbital apex syndrome (inflammation of the posterior orbit, including the superior orbital fissure through which cranial nerves III, IV, V, and VI and the superior ophthalmic vein traverse, as well as the optic canal involving the ophthalmic artery and optic nerve and characterized by less edema and proptosis but more vision loss than cavernous sinus thrombosis) Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 476

347.q: Which of the following is common feature of Orbital Apex Syndrome and Cavernous sinus thrombosis?
347.e: Total ophthalmoplegia: In this condition all extraocular muscles including LPS and intraocular muscles, viz., sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle are paralysed. It results from combined paralysis of third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves. It is a common feature of orbital apex syndrome and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Reference: A k Khurana, 5th edition, Pg: 333.

347.q: A child of 10 year age presented with UL painful proptosis following nasal congestion. After two days he developed diplopia while looking at left side and severe headache and decreased vision. What could be the diagnosis
347.e: Cavernous sinus thrombosis; diplopia occurs because of 6th nerve involvement in cavernous sinus Nasal congestion suggests it might be sinusitis leading to orbital cellulitis and finally to cavernous sinus thrombosis Cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually caused by a bacterial infection that spreads from another area of the face or skull. Many cases are the result of an infection of staphylococcal (staph) bacteria, which can cause: sinusitis Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 482

348.e: AMBLYOPIA Amblyopia is a unilateral or bilateral reduction of best corrected visual acuity in the absence of any organic cause. Clinical Features: Unilateral or bilateral reduced vision Crowding phenomenon may be seen: The patient is able to identify a Snellen's chart character with the amblyopic eye when the character is presented in isolation. If the character is shown along with other letters, the patient may not be able to recognize it. Neutral Density Filter Test(NDF): When the patient is asked to read through a NDF, the amblyopic eye shows no change, while in the normal eye, there is a drop in visual acuity Amblyopia treatment should be tried till the child is 12 years old. Best results are seen between 5-8 years of age. Reference: Kanski, 8th Edition, Page no. 746.

348.q: Angle evaluation can be done by
348.e: Angle evaluation is clinically done with Gonioscope but there are machines available for the same They are Anterior Segment OCT Ultrasound Biomicroscopy(UBM) Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th Edition, Pg No. 1024

348.q: Which of the following test programmes on the Humphrey's automated perimeter is best suited for evaluation of visual fields in neurologic disease?
348.e: Visual field defects are best detected by Goldmann kinetic perimetry (full field) and Humphrey automated threshold perimetry (30-2 programme for central field or neurological programmes). 10-2, 24-2 are used in evaluation of fields in glaucoma. 120-2/ full fields can be used for neurological evaluation but very time consuming/ poor compliance by patients due to attention fatigue. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye 23rd edition-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

349.q: A regular contact lens user presents with complaints of severe pain, redness, photophobia and blurring of vision for more than two weeks not responding to standard treatment. On examination, a paracentral ring shaped lesion with stromal infiltrates and overlying epithelial defects is observed in the affected eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis
349.e: A history of contact lens usage and a corneal ulcer not responding to standard treatment ( antibiotics and cylcoplegics ) suggest acanthamoeba ulcer. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

349.q: Which of the following patient scenarios is/are not suitable for keratoprosthesis implantation?
349.e: A keratoprosthesis is a device designed to replace the cornea. Unfortunately, an ideal keratoprosthesis has not yet been devised. Implantation of a keratoprosthesis is considered only as a last resort where penetrating keratoplasty is not possible or has repeatedly failed. Implantation of a keratoprosthesis is reserved for bilaterally blind patients suffering from severe ocular surface disorders such as following chemical burns, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, severe dry eyes and recurrent graft rejections. Preoperative prerequisites include a minimum vision of light perception and absence of gross posterior segment disorders as evaluated by ultrasonography. Advanced keratoconus: first line of treatment : keratoplasty Fungal endophthalmitis: requires vitrectomy, not keratoprosthesis Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

349.q: Which of the following is the treatment of Candida endophthalmitis?
349.e: Treatment of Candida endophthalmitis includes: Antifungal treatment : Agent is decided based on culture sensitivity. Intravenous amphotericin-B in combination with oral flucytosine is given, but resistance is a concern. Voriconazole orally or intravenously has a broad spectrum of antifungal action with low reported resistance and high ocular penetration; adjunctive intravitreal treatment may be given(100 µg in 0.1 ml), with serial injections probably needed. Pars plana vitrectomy should be considered at an early stage, especially for severe or unresponsive disease. Along with providing a substantial culture specimen, it reduces fungal and antigen load, facilitates therapeutic agent penetration and clears the ocular media. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 454.

350.q: A 40-year old woman develops blurred vision at near in the left eye. She has a mid-dilated pupil that reacts only to near stimulus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
350.e: An isolated dilated pupil that reacts to near better than light is typically from a tonic(Adie) pupil. Loss of accommodation frequently occurs with pupillary dilation. Accommodative insufficiency and accommodative spasm are not associated with pupillary dilation. Third nerve palsy would be expected to have other features, including ptosis and an ocular misalignment. In Adie's Tonic Pupil, the affected pupil is larger(anisocoria). Its exact cause is not known. It is usually unilateral, associated with absent knee jerk and occurs more often in young women. Adie's pupil constricts with weak pilocarpine(0.125%) drops, while normal pupil does not. Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 293.

350.q: Swinging light test is positive in ?
350.e: Ans. C. Retrobulbar neuritis Swinging flash light is used for relative efferent pathway defect (RAPD) which is most characteristic of Iesions in the optic nerve. Thus it is positive in retrobulbar neuritis.

350.q: A 42-year-old woman has anisocoria that is greater in light. The right pupil is sluggishly reactive to light and she has normal ocular motility, alignment and normal eyelid position. What would be the best next step?
350.e: The findings suggest a problem with the pupillary sphincter(greater anisocoria in light). Normal lid position, alignment and eyelid position make third nerve palsy unlikely. Cocaine is useful in the diagnosis of Horner syndrome. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy would be the most helpful to distinguish abnormalities in the iris that might suggest a tonic pupil or trauma as the cause of anisocoria. Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 293, Parsons, 22nd, Edition, Pg: 33.

351.q: Which clinical condition shows most resemblance to IIH?
351.e: Retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates and disc edema may be seen in many retinal vascular pathologies. Features characterisitic of each are as follows: Diabetic Retinopathy: Hard exudates and micro-aneurysms involving posterior pole. Malignant Hypertension: Changes centred around disc +/- exudative retinal detachment CRVO: Disc edema plus tortuous veins plus hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants CRAO: Retinal pallor plus cherry red spot at macula Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

351.q: A 30-year-old woman is referred to you by her neurosurgeon after removal of a cerebellar hemangioma. Which of the following are you most likely to find?
351.e: Capillary hemangioma of the retina is associated with cerebellar and other central nervous system hemangiomas as part of the Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Choroidal hemangiomas are seen in Sturge-Weber syndrome. Racemous angiomas of the retina and cavernous hemangiomas of the retina most commonly occur as isolated entities. Reference: Kanski, 8th Edition, Page no. 506.

351.q: Which of the following blood vessels are compromised in Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy?
351.e: Posterior ischemic Optic neuropathy This entity shares the features of AION except for the site of involvement. Posterior optic nerve ischaemia is believed to occur due to disorders affecting the small pial vessels which supply the intraorbital portion of the optic nerve away from the eyeball. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

352.q: A young man aged 30 years, presents with difficulty in vision in the left eye for the last 10 days. He is a rural community and gives history of trauma to his left eye with vegetative matter 10-15 days back. On examination, there is an ulcerative lesion in infiltrate. Ulcer margin is feathery and hyphate. There are a few satellite lesions also. The most probable etiological agents is
352.e: This is a typical presentation of fungal corneal ulcer. The only fungus given in the option is fusarium. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

352.q: Leucocoria can be seen in all except
352.e: D/D of LEUCOCORIA France TRIP to C DR Fungal endophthalmitis Toxocariasis ROP Inflammatory cyclitic membrane PHPV Congenital cataract, coloboma, Coats's disease Dysplasia of retina Retinoblastoma Reference: leucocoria

352.q: Most common distant site of metastasis in malignant melanoma
352.e: Uveal melanoma is a malignant tumor arising from melanocytes in the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, or choroid). It is the most common primary intraocular tumor in adults with an age-adjusted incidence of 6 per million. The choroid is the most common site involved and gives rise to 90% of uveal melanomas. Melanomas arising within the ciliary body comprise 7% and melanomas of the iris account for 2% There is a strong tendency for metastasis, particularly to the liver, and prognosis is poor when the tumor has disseminated. Reference: Kanski's Synopsis of Clinical Ophthalmology (Fourth edition) 2023, Page 322

354.q: Chronic use of systemic steroids most commonly leads to which ocular complication?
354.e: Injudicious use of systemic steroids leads to the following ocular complications: Cataract - most common Delayed wound healing Infections of eye Papilloedema Central retinal vein occlusion Glaucoma - more often associated with topical ocular or periocular steroids Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 461.

354.q: Which of the following is not used as local injection for ophthalmic use?
354.e: All of the following are examples of steroids. Methylprednisolone is administered only systemically . The remaining steroids can be administered locally or systemically. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 459.

356.q: Burden of disease in a society is best indicated by
356.e: Disability-adjusted life years (DALY) : DALY is a measure of overall disease burden, expressed as a number of years lost due to ill-health, disability or early death. The DALY is becoming increasingly common in the field of public health and health impact assessment. The Global Burden of Disease project combines the impact of premature mortality with that of disability. It captures the population impact of important fatal and nonfatal disabling conditions through a single measure. It is calculated by formula : DALY = YLL + YLD The DALY relies on an acceptance that the most appropriate measure of the effects of the chronic illness is time. One DALY, therefore, is equal to one year of healthy life lost.

356.q: Human development index(HDI) values range from
356.e: PQLI→ ranges from 0 to 100 HDI→ ranges from 0 to 1 Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th Edition, Chapter Concept Of Health & Disease.

356.q: Which of the following is a mortality indicator
356.e: Life expectancy is a positive mortality indicator Notification rate is a morbidity indicator DALY is a disability indicator Bed turn over ratio (eg: hospital discharges/ average bed) is a Health ultilisation indicator Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

357.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Early stage of disease Primordial prevention → Before risk factor present. Primary prevention → Before onset of disease (risk factor present). Secondary prevention → In early stage of disease. Tertiary prevention → Late stage of disease.

357.q: Highly sensitive test, when ___________, rules out a disease.
357.e: Highly sensitive test, when negative, rules out a disease. Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25 th Edition, pg- 153

357.q: Information especially of a biased or misleading nature used to promote a political cause or point of view is?
357.e: Correct answer is Option A Propaganda is communication that is primarily used to influence or persuade an audience to further an agenda, which may not be objective and may be selectively presenting facts to encourage a particular synthesis.

358.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Sentinel surveillance o Sentinel surveillance in India is done in national AIDS control programme.

Ans. is 'a' i.e., Population genetics Hardly-Weinberg law The hardly-weinherg law states that "The relative frequencies of each gene allele tends to remain constant from generation to generation". o Thus, the study of gene frequencies, and the influences which operate to alter the "gene pool" and their long term consequences is the central theme in population genetics.

358.q: If an association is found between the incidence of a disease and a certain genetically determined character
o: Disease is clearly genetic in origin
Genetic factors are at least implicated in all cases of disease
Genetic factors are implicated in at least some of the cases of disease
A role for environmental factors is excluded

359.q: Berkesonian bias is a type of ?
359.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Selection bias Berksonian bias is a type of selection bias. Bias o It is any systemic error in the analysis of study that results in a mistaken estimate of an exposure's effect on the risk of disease. o Mainly biases are of following types.

359.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Measures incidence rate o Incidence rate can not be measured by case-control study as denominator (population at risk is not available).

359.q: To find out the incidence of deafness in factory workers, the suitable study design is
359.e: ANALYSIS OF COHORT STUDY The data are analyzed in terms of : a.Incidence rates of outcome among exposed and non exposed, b.Estimation of risk. INCIDENCE RATES In a cohort study, we can determine incidence rates directly in those exposed and those not exposed. Estimation of risk Estimation of risk of outcome (e.g., disease or death) in the exposed and non-exposed cohorts is done in terms of two well-known indices: (a) relative risk, (b) attributable risk.

361.q: Disease imported to a country which was not there otherwise
361.e: EXOTIC Diseases which are imported into a country in which they do not otherwise occur. ZOONOSES An infection or infectious disease transmissible under natural conditions from vertebrate animals to man. May be enzootic or epizootic - e.g., rabies, plague, bovine tuberculosis, anthrax, brucellosis, salmonellosis, endemic typhus, hydatidosis, kyasanur forest disease, monkeypox, lassa fever, etc EPIZOOTIC An outbreak (epidemic) of disease in an animal population. Eg: the agents of anthrax, brucellosis, rabies, influenza, Japanese encephalitis. EPORNITHIC An outbreak (epidemic) of disease in a bird population ENZOOTIC An endemic occurring in animals e.g., anthrax, rabies, brucellosis, bovine tuberculosis, endemic typhus and tick typhus Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

362.q: Which statement accurately describes the single exposure point source epidemic?
o: Has more than one incubation period
362.e: Explanation: A single exposure point source epidemic occurs when a group of people are exposed to an infectious agent simultaneously (e.g., contaminated food, water). The outbreak shows a sudden, explosive rise in cases, followed by a rapid decline once the exposure ends. (Option D ruled out) The epidemic curve typically displays a sharp single peak , corresponding to a single incubation period. (Options A & B ruled out)

362.q: The area is declared free of epidemic
o: No new case reported for the incubation period of disease since last case
No new case reported for twice the incubation period of disease since last case
No new case reported for six months since last case
362.e: An area is declared free of epidemic till no new cases are reported for twice the Incubation period of disease from last case Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

362.q: Migration study is used to study
o: Socio-demographic reasons for migration of a population
Prevalence of disease in a population
Environmental and genetic factors in a disease in population
362.e: Migration studies is the academic study of human migration. Its a method of understanding the relative importance of inherited genetics and environmental factor in medical conditions whose incidence varies around the world Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

363.q: Prophylaxis for HIV is optimally effective if started upto ..... hrs of exposure
363.e: Answer- A. 1 goal is to start within one to two hours or earlier after exposure often using a starter pack with appropriate drugs as immediately available. The median time to initiation of postexposure prophylaxis is 1.8 hrs. The centre for disease control and prevention (CDC) recommendations are to offer prophylaxis upto 24-36 hrs after exposure, for longer time lapses, the recommendations is to seek advice from an expert

363.q: Which vaccine follows open vial policy
363.e: Explanation: Pentavalent vaccine (which protects against Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, and Hib) is a liquid vaccine that comes in multi-dose vials and does follow the open vial policy . If stored correctly (2-8°C), not expired, unopened vials are clean, and aseptic technique is followed, it can be used up to 28 days after opening. Explanation for other options: BCG (option A): Does not follow open vial policy. It is a lyophilized (freeze-dried) vaccine that must be reconstituted and used within 4-6 hours. After that, it must be discarded. JE (option C): incorrect it is also a lyophilized vaccine, and once reconstituted, it must be used within a short time (usually 4 hours). Does not follow open vial policy. MMR (option D): incorrect it is also lyophilized, and must be used within 4 hours of reconstitution. Does not follow open vial policy.

364.q: Which of these vaccines are not covered under the open vial policy?
364.e: Explanation: The measles vaccine does not follow the open vial policy. The open vial policy states that vaccine vials, once opened, can be used for multiple sessions over a period of up to 28 days, as long as they are kept under proper cold chain conditions to minimize vaccine wastage. This policy applies to all liquid vaccines, such as Hepatitis B , DPT, Pentavalent, OPV, IPV, PCV, and Td. However, reconstituted vaccines like MMR, BCG, JE , Yellow Fever, and Rotavirus vaccines do not follow the open vial policy.

366.e: Highly specific test, when positive, rules in a disease. Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25 th Edition, pg- 153

366.q: A researcher finds a sensitive test to be positive for a person. For diagnosis, which of the following will hold true?
o: It confirms that the person does not have the disease
it suggests that if the disease is rare, the person surely has the disease
it confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common
it is an expected finding in case the disease is prevalent
366.e: Sensitivity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who have the disease. It confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common. Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25 th Edition, pg- 152

366.q: A test for Hepatitis C is performed on 200 patients with biopsy-proven disease and 200 patients free of the disease. The test shows positive results on 180 of the patients with the disease and negative results on 150 of the patients without the disease. Which of the following is appropriate?
o: Has a positive predictive value of 90%
Has a negative predictive value of 75%
366.e: To determine the appropriate statement, let's define the terms: Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The probability that a person with a positive test result truly has the disease. Negative Predictive Value (NPV): The probability that a person with a negative test result truly does not have the disease. Sensitivity: The proportion of true positive cases that the test correctly identifies. Specificity: The proportion of true negative cases that the test correctly identifies. Given the information: True positives (TP): 180 True negatives (TN): 150 False positives (FP): 50 (200 - 150) False negatives (FN): 20 (200 - 180) Sensitivity=TP/(FN+TP)=180/(20+180)=180/200=0.9 = 90% Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25th Edition, pg- 152

368.q: A pregnant woman with a 2-year-old child reports that she completed all recommended antenatal vaccinations during her previous pregnancy. Which of the following is recommended for her current pregnancy?
o: Give a booster dose of TT
Give a booster dose of Td
368.e: Explanation: The Td vaccine (Tetanus and Diphtheria) is recommended as a booster during pregnancy for women who have completed the required tetanus immunizations in previous pregnancies. Current Indian guidelines emphasize the following points: Td vaccine provides immunity against both Tetanus and Diphtheria , whereas the older TT (Tetanus Toxoid) vaccine only targets tetanus. For women with a history of prior antenatal TT vaccination, a single booster dose of Td is sufficient in the current pregnancy to maintain protective immunity. (Options A, C & D ruled out) Timing: The first dose is administered at the start of pregnancy (preferably before 20 weeks). The second dose is scheduled between 20-26 weeks if the first dose was given early or if additional coverage is required.

368.q: Which of the following disease is known as "Barometer of Social Welfare"?
368.e: Barometer of Social welfare→ TB Breakbone fever→ Dengue Monkey fever→ KFD 5 day fever→Trench fever 8 th day fever→Tetanus neonatorum 100 day cough→Pertussis Slim’s disease→HIV/AIDS Black Sickness→Kala-Azar Black Death→Plague Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th Edition, Chapter Concept Of Health & Disease.

369.q: Organism included in Category A Bioterrorism is/are a. Vibrio cholerae b. Clostridium botulinum c. Yersinia pestis d. Bacillus anthracis
369.e: Category A bioterrorism agents are those that pose the highest risk to national security because they can be easily disseminated or transmitted from person to person, result in high mortality rates, and have the potential for major public health impact. Explanation for why not the other options: a. Vibrio cholerae: Vibrio cholerae is the bacterium responsible for causing cholera, a severe diarrheal disease. While cholera can cause significant morbidity and mortality, it is not typically considered a Category A bioterrorism agent due to its lower potential for deliberate dissemination and widespread impact compared to other agents in Category A. Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page no.:982

369.q: The causative agent of endemic typhus is:
369.e: Explanation: Endemic typhus (also called murine typhus ) is caused by Rickettsia typhi . Transmission: Flea bite (commonly from rats). Clinical features: Mild febrile illness, headache, myalgia, sometimes rash. Usually self-limiting. Differentiation from epidemic typhus: Epidemic typhus → caused by Rickettsia prowazekii , transmitted by body lice , more severe. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Rickettsia prowazekii (Option A): Causes epidemic typhus , not endemic typhus. Salmonella typhi (Option C): Causes typhoid fever , a bacterial enteric fever, not a rickettsial infection. Orientia tsutsugamushi (Option D): Causes scrub typhus , transmitted by chiggers , not fleas.

369.q: What is the correct composition and dosing schedule of the Shanchol vaccine?
369.e: Explanation: Shanchol is a bivalent oral cholera vaccine given in 2 doses This refers to a vaccine that targets two different strains of Vibrio cholerae and requires two doses for complete immunisation. The Shanchol vaccine is bivalent, meaning it covers two different strains of Vibrio cholerae (01 and 0139) and typically requires two doses for full protection.

370.q: There is an outbreak of encephalitis in school children due to lack of proper childhood vaccination. According to universal immunization schedule, Which of the following type and route of vaccine that could have prevented this
370.e: JENVAC is a single dose inactivated Japanese Encephalitis (JE) Vaccine. This Vero cell derived vaccine is prepared from an Indian strain (Kolar- 821564XY) of the JE virus. JENVAC has been developed in collaboration with the National Institute of Virology, India. It is a safe and highly-effective vaccine that protects against all known strains of Japanese Encephalitis. Data of 2-dose study shows that a single dose of JENVAC is sufficient to elicit the immune response as the subjects who received a single dose were 98.67% sero-protected and the 4-fold sero-conversion was at 93.14% for the ≥1 year to ≤50 years age group. Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 111

371.q: Sachin visited the Emergency Department after he had received a Category 3 wound by a cat at his Veterinary centre. He had received pre-exposure prophylaxis. What should be the next line of management?
371.e: In case a person has received Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis, HRIg is not needed to be given. Hence, in this case, Wound management + ARV is only given. Post-Exposure prophylaxis in a person who has already received Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis: Cat 1: Wound Management Cat 2: Wound Management Cat 3: Wound Management + ARV (only 2 doses are administered on Day 0&3) Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis: 3 doses on Day 0, 7 & 21/28 Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

371.q: In a CHC area in a particular day, in which of the following diseases the prevalence may be zero though the incidence may be quite high in the area
371.e: All new cases of rabies (Incidence) are dying fast, so Prevalence will be zero at one point Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

371.q: A patient presents with a history of category 3 dog bites. He received rabies prophylaxis for a monkey bite 6 months ago. What is the next step in management?
o: Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3
371.e: Explanation: For patients who have previously completed rabies vaccination (within the last 3-6 months), management after a new category 3 exposure includes: Immediate wound cleaning Booster rabies vaccination on days 0 and 3 This approach triggers a rapid anamnestic immune response , providing sufficient protection without additional interventions like rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) . Explanation of Other Options: Wound cleaning only (Option A) : Category 3 bites require vaccination even in previously vaccinated individuals. Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0, 3 & 7 (Option C) : Only 2 booster doses are needed for previously vaccinated patients. Wound cleaning + IM vaccine + RIG (Option D) : RIG is reserved for rabies-naive patients or those without prior vaccination.

372.q: True about source of leptospirosis (contaminated) EXCEPT:
372.e: Surface water reservoirs : True. Contaminated water, especially during floods, is a primary source of Leptospirosis . The bacteria can survive in water, and humans can get infected through direct contact. Mud and soil : True. Soil and mud contaminated with the urine of infected animals, particularly rats , can be a source of Leptospirosis . Food : True. Although rare, Leptospirosis can be transmitted through contaminated food, especially when food is exposed to infected animal urine. Bite of carrier animal : Incorrect. Leptospirosis is primarily transmitted through direct contact with contaminated water, soil, or food, not by the bite of infected animals. Key Takeaways: Tags: INICET JUNE 2020 Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive & Social Medicine, K.park, 27 th Edition, Chapter-5, Page no: 338-339.

373.q: Second most common STD after gonococcus ?
373.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Chlamydia [Ref Park 2151/e p. 304] Five classical STDs are syphilis (T. pallidum), gonorrhoea (N. gonorrhoeae), chanchroid (H. ducreyi), lymphogranuloma venerum (chlamydia trachomatis), and donovanosis (calymmatobacterium granulomatosis). Most common STD in India is herpes genitalis (20%) followed by chancroid (11%), viral warts/HPV (11%), syphilis (11%) and gonorrhoea (9%). Overall (in world) most common STD is chlamydia followed by gonorrhoea.

373.q: Blood screening is not done for ?
373.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e.,EBV Screening recommended in all Selective screening in some countries countries HIV Malaria HBV HTLV HCV CMV Syphilis Chagas disease

373.q: Five clean practices under strategies for the elimination of neonatal tetanus include all except?
373.e: The "Five Clean Practices" are part of the WHO-recommended strategies to prevent neonatal tetanus , especially during home or non-institutional deliveries. These practices are focused on ensuring cleanliness during delivery and cord care, which are the primary sources of Clostridium tetani infection in newborns. The Five Clean Practices include: Clean surface for delivery Clean hands of the birth attendant Clean cord-cutting instrument (e.g., new or sterilized blade) Clean cord tie Clean cord care (e.g., avoiding the application of unclean substances) Additional practices include: Clean water : For washing hands, the perineal area, and cleaning the newborn. Clean towel : To dry and wrap the baby immediately after birth (reduces risk of hypothermia and infection). Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 261

374.q: Which of the following is not included in the STEP approach?
374.e: Explanation: The WHO STEPwise approach (STEPS) is a standardized framework for countries to collect, analyze, and disseminate data on key risk factors for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) . It is designed to be simple and flexible, gathering information in three sequential "steps." Step 1: Questionnaire-based assessment of demographic, behavioral, and historical risk factors (e.g., tobacco use, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity). Step 2: Simple physical measurements (e.g., height, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure ). (Option B ruled out) Step 3: Biochemical measurements (e.g., fasting blood sugar , blood lipids like cholesterol). (Options C & D ruled out) Blood group is a fixed genetic characteristic and is not considered a modifiable risk factor for NCDs in the context of this surveillance tool. Therefore, it is not included in the STEPS approach.

375.q: Jowar is Pellogerogenic due to excess of -
375.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Leucine o Similar to maize, Jowar also Contains excess of leucine. o Leucine interferes with conversion of tryptophan to niacin. o Pellagra has been reported in India in Telangana area of Andhra Pradesh because of Sower (Sorghum vulgare) consumption.

375.q: Maximum linolenic acid is present in ?
375.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Safflower oil [Ref Park 22"d /e p. 566] The richest source of linoleic acid is safflower oil. Sources of linoleic acid in decreasing order are safflower oil > cornoil > Sunflower oil > Soyabean oil > Sesame oil > ground nut oil.

375.q: Cervical cancer screening using the co-test includes:
o: Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) and Pap smear together
Pap smear and HPV DNA test together
Blood test for antibodies and Pap smear together
375.e: Explanation: Co-testing for cervical cancer involves performing both a Pap smear (cytology) and HPV DNA testing Purpose: Pap smear: Detects cellular abnormalities (pre-cancerous changes). HPV DNA test: Detects high-risk HPV strains associated with cervical cancer. Recommended for women ≥30 years for improved sensitivity compared to either test alone. Explanation of Incorrect Options: VIA and Pap smear together (Option A): VIA is a visual screening method ; co-testing specifically refers to cytology + HPV DNA. Blood test for antibodies and Pap smear (Option C): No role of blood antibodies in cervical cancer screening; not part of co-testing. VIA alone (Option D): VIA is a stand-alone screening method , not a co-test.

376.q: Which of the following drugs are used for clinical cure of malaria? Artemether Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine Chloroquine Primaquine
376.e: Explanation: Clinical cure refers to the treatment that clears the parasite burden from the blood, relieving the acute symptoms of malaria. This is achieved by schizonticidal drugs . Artemether (an artemisinin derivative), Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (a sulfa drug combination), and Chloroquine are all blood schizonticides and are used for clinical cure. Primaquine is a tissue schizonticide (acts on hypnozoites in the liver for P. vivax and P. ovale) and a gametocidal It is not used for clinical cure of the acute attack but for radical cure (preventing relapse) and preventing transmission. Key Takeaways: Blood schizonticides (e.g., Chloroquine, Artemisinin, SP) are for clinical cure. Primaquine is for radical cure and gametocidal action.

376.q: In a town with population of 1,00,000, the number of slides examined is 50,000. Out of these, 100 slides were positive for malaria. The API is-
376.e: The Annual Parasite Index (API) is a measure used to assess the intensity of malaria transmission in a specific area. It is calculated by the formula: API = (Number of positive blood slides for malaria / Total population) × 1,000 Given: Total population = 100,000 Number of slides examined = 50,000 Number of slides positive for malaria = 100 API= (confirmed cases during one year/population under surveillance) x 1000= (100/100000) x 1000= 1 Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 306

376.q: According to WHO, what proportion of a country's Gross National Product (GNP) should ideally be allocated to health services?
376.e: Explanation: The WHO recommends that 5% of a country's GNP be spent on health services. This allocation is intended to: Ensure adequate healthcare delivery to the population Strengthen public health infrastructure Meet the healthcare needs of the community effectively

377.q: HIV post exposure prophylaxis should be started within?
377.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., 1-2 hrs Anti-retroviral drug for post-exposure prophylaxis should be initiated as soon as possible after the exposure within the first few hours and no later than 72 hours. So, the best answer here is 1-2 hours (first few hours).

377.q: A patient diagnosed to have both HIV and TB, which of the drug regimen should be followed
o: Start ART first followed by ATT
Start ATT first followed by ART
377.e: If a person is positive for both HIV and TB, Treatment for TB should be started first . In a person positive with both HIV and TB, signs and symptoms of TB are less prominent due to decreased cellular immunity (due to decreased CD4 count ) If ART is given 1st to this person, the cellular immunity will be increased, there will be flare up of signs and symptoms of TB. This is known as Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome ( IRIS) . Hence, ATT is given first to prevent this. ATT is given for minimum of 2 weeks followed by ART . With rifampicin containing regimen : Additional dose of DTG 50mg should be taken after 12 hours on the same day, as rifampicin decreases the bio-availability of dolutegravir ( DTG) Reference -Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 235

378.q: For a population of 70,00,000 with 30% of it belonging to the slum population, how many Urban PHCs are required for the slum population according to NUHM?
378.e: Explanation: According to NUHM, 42 U-PHCs are required for this scenario. According to NUHM guidelines, an Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) is typically established for every 50,000-60,000 population. When targeting slum areas specifically, one U-PHC is recommended for approximately 25,000-30,000 slum population. In exceptional cases, such as highly dense or isolated slum clusters, one U-PHC may be set up for populations as low as 5,000-10,000. In the given question, the total population is 70,00,000. Out of this, 30% is the slum population, which means the slum population is 21,00,000 (30% of 70,00,000). Using the standard norm of one U-PHC per 50,000 people, we divide the slum population by 50,000. 21,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 42 Therefore, to serve the slum population of this city, 42 Urban PHCs would be required.

381.q: Mr. X married Mrs. Y, and the couple had two children, born in 2002 and 2005. In 2020, Mr. X's father, who was employed with the State Bank of India (SBI), retired and moved in with Mr. X and his family, accompanied by his wife. Which of the following best describes the family transition?

386.q: Results of any study are better defined in ?

392.q: What is the term used to describe the process that occurs in an oxidation pond?
o: Aerobic during day, anaerobic during night
Anaerobic during day, aerobic during night
392.e: Explanation: Oxidation ponds (also called stabilization ponds or lagoons) are large, shallow basins used for sewage treatment. Their functioning depends on the interaction between algae and bacteria . Daytime: Algae perform photosynthesis → release large amounts of oxygen into the pond. This oxygen supports aerobic bacteria , which break down organic matter into simpler, non-toxic compounds. Hence, the pond environment is predominantly aerobic . Nighttime: Photosynthesis stops in the absence of sunlight. Microorganisms continue to consume oxygen through respiration . Oxygen levels fall rapidly, and anaerobic conditions may develop, particularly at the bottom layers. This daily oscillation between aerobic (day) and anaerobic (night) conditions is a characteristic feature of oxidation ponds and helps in effective sewage stabilization. (Options A, B & D ruled out)

Flea (Option D): Fleas are vectors for diseases like plague (Yersinia pestis) and endemic/murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi). Key Takeaways: Scrub Typhus = Orientia tsutsugamushi = Vector is Mite (chigger).

403.q: If the prevalence of a disease is 10%, the probability that either one among three will have diabetes
403.e: To find the probability that at least one person among three will have diabetes, we can use the complement rule, which states that the probability of an event happening is equal to 1 minus the probability of the event not happening. Given: Prevalence of the disease (diabetes) = 10% = 0.10 Number of people selected at random = 3 The probability that none of the three people have diabetes can be calculated using the binomial probability formula: P (none have diabetes) = (1 - 0.10) 3 = 0.90 3 = 0.729 Therefore, the probability that at least one person among the three will have diabetes is: P (at least one has diabetes) = 1 - P(none have diabetes) = 1 - 0.729 = 0.271 Rounding off =0.3 So, the probability that either one among three will have diabetes is approximately 0.3, which corresponds to option (b). Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 977

404.q: Quartiles and tertiles are measures of:
404.e: Explanation: Quartiles (dividing data into four equal parts: Q1, Q2, Q3) and tertiles (dividing data into three equal parts) are positional measures or measures of location . They describe the position of a value within a dataset but are not measures of central tendency (which identify the center) or dispersion (which describe spread). (Options A,D ,B ruled out) Q2 (the second quartile) is the same as the median , a measure of central tendency, but quartiles/tertiles as a group are classified as locational measures. Key Takeaways: Quartiles and tertiles are measures of location, describing specific points in a data set.

404.q: What is the chromosomal translocation in AML M3 -
404.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., T(15,17) Class Chromosomal abnormalities Mz t (8 : 21) M3 t (15: 17) M4 inv (16)

405.q: For a population of 10000, sex ratio of more than 1000 means
405.e: Sex ratio is number of females as per 1000 males in the population A sex ratio of more than 1000 indicates that for every 1000 males, there are > 1000 females. That means more than 50% are females. Therefore, if the total population is 10000, and the sex ratio is more than 1000, it means that the number of females are more than 5000 and males are less than 5000 Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 558

405.q: Mean weight of 100 children was 12kg and SD was 3. Calculate the percent Coefficient of variation
405.e: The coefficient of variation (CV) is a measure of relative variability, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation (SD) to the mean, multiplied by 100. Given: Mean weight of 100 children = 12 kg Standard deviation (SD) = 3 kg The formula for the coefficient of variation (CV) is: CV = (SD/MEAN) × 100 CV = (3/12) × 100 = .025 * 100 = 25% So, the correct answer is a. 25% Therefore, the correct percent coefficient of variation for the given data is option A. 25%. Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 980

405.q: If the mean of a normal distribution is 20 and its standard deviation is 5, then 95% of the data lie within which of the following ranges?
405.e: If mean is 20, +- 1 SD = 20+5 to 20-5 = 25 to 15. This covers 68% of all data. Thus, we know 95% of data is covered in mean +/- 2SD, thus the range shall be 20 +/- 2*(SD) = 20+/- 2*(5) = 20 +/-10. Thus the final range comes out to be 10-30. Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 976

407.q: A test with high specificity has a low
407.e: A test with high specificity has a low probability of falsely classifying individuals without the disease as positive (Type I error). Explanation for why other options are wrong: b. Type II error: Type II error refers to the probability of incorrectly failing to reject a false null hypothesis, which is more related to sensitivity than specificity. High specificity reduces the likelihood of Type I errors, not Type II errors. c. 1-β represents the power of a statistical test, which is related to sensitivity rather than specificity. Higher specificity does not directly influence the power of the test. d. 1-α Represents the significance level of a statistical test, which is determined by the researcher and is not directly influenced by the specificity of the test. Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 156

407.q: In a 3x4 contingency table, the number of degrees of freedom equals to
407.e: In a contingency table, the number of degrees of freedom is calculated using the formula: Degrees of freedom = (r - 1) * (c - 1) where r is the number of rows and c is the number of columns in the contingency table. Given that the contingency table in this scenario is 3x4 (3 rows and 4 columns), the calculation for degrees of freedom would be: Degrees of freedom = (3 - 1) * (4 - 1) = 2*3 = 6 Therefore, the correct answer is c. 6 Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 980

407.q: While applying chi square test to a contingency table of 4 rows and 4 columns, the degrees of freedom would be
407.e: In a chi-square test for a contingency table, the degrees of freedom (df) are calculated using the formula: df = (number of rows - 1) × (number of columns - 1) In this case, the contingency table has 4 rows and 4 columns. So, applying the formula: df = (4 - 1) × (4 - 1) = 3 × 3 = 9 Therefore, the degrees of freedom for a contingency table of 4 rows and 4 columns would be 9. Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 980

408.q: Best study for definitive cause of disease ?
408.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Cohort Amongst the given options Cohort study is best to test the association between risk factor and disease. Here are the different epidemiological studies with decreasing order of accuracy to test the association between risk factor and disease :- Systematic review and meta-analysis --> Overall most reliable Randomized controlled trials (controlled clinical trails) --> Most reliable individual study. Retrospective (Non-concurrent/historic) Cohort study. Prospective (concurrent) Cohort study. Case control study Cross-sectional study Ecological study

408.q: Organize the following steps in the correct sequence for conducting research: Conduct data analysis Selecting population Setting research question Setting research objective
408.e: Explanation: The logical sequence of research steps is: Setting research question : Identifying the broad problem area. Setting research objective : Defining specific, measurable goals based on the research question. Selecting population : Choosing the target population and sample after knowing what to study. Conduct data analysis : Analyzing the collected data is one of the final steps. Key Takeaways: The research process begins with defining a question and objectives before any data collection or analysis.

410.q: To prevent Neural tube defects in a woman with history of NTD, dose of folic acid to be given to woman is
410.e: FOLIC ACID SUPPLEMENTATION IN PREGNANCY Should be started ideally 3 months prior to pregnancy and continued throughout the pregnancy Folic acid supplementation has been proven to reduce the incidence of Neural tube defects in newborns Prophylactic dose of Folic acid: 400µg Therapeutic dose of Folic acid: 4mg INDICATIONS FOR THERAPEUTIC DOSE OF FOLIC ACID Megaloblastic anemia Hemolytic anemia Overt Diabetes mellitus Anti epileptic drugs Previous history of Neural tube defects In this case, women have a previous history of Neural tube defects, hence have to be given 4mg of Folic acid

410.q: The United Nations had suggested that universal children's day may be celebrated every year on
410.e: Universal Children's Day is indeed celebrated every year on November 20th. This day was established by the United Nations General Assembly in 1954 to promote international togetherness, awareness among children worldwide, and improving children's welfare. It is observed as a day of action for children, by children, to advocate for their rights and address issues affecting their well-being. Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 629

410.q: Additional daily energy requirement during first six months of lactation
410.e: Option D : 600 calories During the first six months of lactation, breastfeeding women require additional energy to support milk production and sustain their own nutritional needs. The recommended additional daily energy requirement during this period is approximately 600 calories above the woman's pre-pregnancy energy intake. This additional energy is necessary to ensure that breastfeeding mothers have an adequate nutrient intake to support the demands of lactation without depleting their own energy reserves. Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 748

412.q: A patient presents to the casualty with multiple contusions on the chest. He is hypotensive. Arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.3, PCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3- 16 mEq/L, base excess -12, Na+ 130 mEq/L, Cl- 84 mEq/L. Which of the following explains the underlying abnormality?
o: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis with an anion gap of 12
Chronic respiratory acidosis with anion gap 30
Acute metabolic acidosis with anion gap 16
412.e: Explanation: This patient's labs show acidemia (pH 7.3), low bicarbonate (16), and a normal PCO2 (44), suggesting that the primary abnormality is metabolic acidosis (not compensated by respiratory alkalosis/hyperventilation). The anion gap is: Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 130 - (84 + 16) = 130 - 100 = 30 This is a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The findings are consistent with acute severe tissue hypoperfusion (due to shock or trauma), leading to lactic acidosis. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis with an anion gap of 12 (Option A): PCO2 is not elevated, and the anion gap is much higher than 12. Chronic respiratory acidosis with anion gap 30 (Option B): The primary problem is metabolic, not respiratory, as PCO2 is not high but HCO3- is low. Acute metabolic acidosis with anion gap 16 (Option D): The actual anion gap is 30, not 16.

412.q: A case of Acid-base imbalance can be confirmed by? A) pH arterial blood B) pH venous blood C) O2 venous blood D) CO2 venous blood
412.e: Acid-base imbalance can be confirmed by pH arterial blood, pH venous blood, CO2 venous blood. Alternatives to ABG include VBG, end tidal carbon dioxide, transcutaneous carbon dioxide.

412.q: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is associated with metabolic alkalosis?
412.e: Metabolic alkalosis is established by an elevated arterial pH, an increase in the serum [HCO3 -], and an increase in Paco2 as a result of compensatory alveolar hypoventilation. It is often accompanied by hypochloremia and hypokalemia . The arterial pH establishes the diagnosis, because it is increased in metabolic alkalosis and decreased in respiratory acidosis. Metabolic alkalosis frequently occurs as a mixed acid base disorder in association with either respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, or metabolic acidosis Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 55, Pg: 359

413.q: A 14 year old boy develops red eye and rhinitis frequently during the start of the summer. What is the likely triggering agent?
413.e: Grass pollen is released late May till August, and willow pollen is released from March till June. As the allergic rhinitis is triggered during the start of summer, this is most likely to be due to grass pollen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:288 Pg 2160

413.q: Diurnal variation of ACTH depends on ?
413.e: Ans. A. Suprachiasmatic nucleus The biologic clock responsible for the diurnal ACTH rhythm is located in the suprachiasmatic nuclei of the hypothalamus.

413.q: A 14-year-old girl is seen at the endocrine clinic because her mother is concerned that her daughter's periods have not yet started. In reviewing her history, which of the following would be most typical of the first sign of onset of puberty?
413.e: Breast-bud enlargement (thelarche) is the first sign of puberty in girls. The average age of pubertal onset is earlier in girls than boys. The order of pubertal progression in females is thelarche, pubarche followed by menarche. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3031

414.q: Which of the following is an action of IGF-I?
414.e: The growth promoting effects of GH is largely mediated via IGF1. The metabolic actions of GH like hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, nitrogen retention and lipolysis is independent of IGF1. GH impairs glucose tolerance by antagonizing insulin action. IGF-1 apart from binding to its own receptor, can also act on insulin receptor which is responsible for the hypoglycemic episodes. While, injected IGF-I induces hypoglycemia, and lower doses improve insulin sensitivity in patients with severe insulin resistance and diabetes. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2894

414.q: A 56 year old patient with known acromegaly is reviewed during a 6 monthly outpatient appointment. Which one of the following clinical features is an indicator of disease activity?
o: Increase in the loss of visual field
414.e: In acromegaly, the features of disease activity are: headache progressive deterioration of visual field uncontrolled diabetes increased sweating increasing joint pain uncontrolled hypertension Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2913

414.q: A 57-year-old man who has received previous surgery for acromegaly is receiving lanreotide medical therapy as his growth hormone is persistently elevated. What is the mode of action of lanreotide?
o: Inhibition of the growth hormone receptor
Stimulation of the dopamine D2 receptor
414.e: Lanreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue which specifically stimulates SSTR 2. Stimulation of the somatostatin receptor leads to inhibition of production of a number of hormones including gastrin, cholecystokinin, glucagon, growth hormone, insulin and secretin. Somatostatin analogues are used for the medical treatment of acromegaly, pre-surgery or after surgery of radiotherapy for persistently elevated growth hormone levels. They are also used for symptomatic relief of the carcinoid syndrome. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2913

415.q: HPV positive Head and neck SCC differs from HPV negative tumors in all except
o: Increased risk in patients with oral sexual practices
415.e: HPV associated head and neck tumors are seen in: Younger age Multiple sexual partners Oral sex Better prognosis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 77, Pg: 590

415.q: Which of the following is not seen in pituitary apoplexy?
415.e: Pituitary apoplexy is an endocrine emergency characterized by hypotension, hypoglycemia, head ache, bilateral visual symptoms, ophthalmoplegia and coma and death in severe cases. It occurs in a pre existing adenoma of the pituitary or spontaneously in post partum, sickle cell anemia, diabetes, hypertension or shock.

415.q: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with a history of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. She is keen to become pregnant and has been trying for 12 months to conceive without success. She is of normal weight and has no other constitutional symptoms. Which of the following is most likely to be the reason for her symptoms?
415.e: Her symptoms are consistent with hyper-prolactinaemia . Raised prolactin has many causes including pituitary tumors (micro- and macroadenomas), drug treatment (some antidepressants like tricyclic antidepressants, antiemetics and cimetidine), pregnancy, stress, hypothyroidism (because thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates TSH and prolactin in primary hypothyroidism) and renal failure (prolactin accumulates in renal failure but not in hepatic impairment). While hyperprolactinemia can be present in hypothyroidism, it is usually associated with menorrhagia rather than amenorrhoea. Polycystic ovarian syndrome may be associated with amenorrhea and mildly raised prolactin levels, but unlikely to result in galactorrhea. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2909

416.q: Hamman crunch sign is seen in?
416.e: The three main causes are Alveolar rupture with dissection of air into the mediastinum; Perforation or rupture of the esophagus, trachea, or main bronchi; and Dissection of air from the neck or the abdomen into the mediastinum. There is severe substernal chest pain with or without radiation into the neck and arms. The physical examination usually reveals subcutaneous emphysema in the suprasternal notch and Hamman's sign, which is a crunching or clicking noise synchronous with the heartbeat and is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position. The diagnosis is confirmed with the chest radiograph. Usually no treatment is required, but the mediastinal air will be absorbed faster if the patient inspires high concentrations of oxygen. If mediastinal structures are compressed, the compression can be relieved with needle aspiration.

416.q: Oral thrush is most commonly seen in which part of the oral cavity?
416.e: Oral thrush (due to Candida infection appears as a white, cheesy exudate, often on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. While most commonly seen on the soft palate, early lesions are often found along the gingival border Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 216, Pg: 1672

416.q: A patient presents with a five-day history of nausea and vomiting and watery diarrhea after eating crabs. He appears ill and is orthostatic. Serum Na is 129 mmol/L. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Urine Na will be less than 20 mEq/U
Serum osmolality is likely to be high
416.e: This patient has developed hypovolemia from fluid losses from vomiting and diarrhea. There is no evidence that other osmotically active compounds have been ingested, thus serum osmolality is likely to be low. Because of hypovolemia, ADH (and aldosterone) will be stimulated, and serum ADH levels will be high. The kidney will be resorbing water and Na, and urine Na concentration will be low. Intravenous volume repletion with normal saline is advisable. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 342

417.q: An 86-year-old woman presented with her first episode of urinary tract infection. Urine examination confirmed blood and proteinuria and E. coli was grown on culture. What is the next step in management after treating her with antibiotics?
o: Re-testing of urine with cytological examination after antibiotics
417.e: Urinary tract infection is common in females between the age of 20-40 years owing to their sexual activity. But UTI occurring in elderly females is usually due to anatomical factors. Urothelial malignancies present with hematuria and may be mistaken for UTI. Hence further work up is always needed. A concurrent UTI, if suspected, should be treated and urine should be re tested for persistent hematuria . If confirmeb, she should first be subjected to bladder cystoscopy. Along with this the kidneys and upper urinary tract should be visualized with CT Urogram. Retrograde pyelography is not routinely used, as CT urograms use very minimal contrast agents Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:86, 135, Pg:677, 1071.

417.q: The ideal time for taking thyroxine tablet is:
o: Along with first bite of food in the morning
417.e: Thyroxine should be taken at morning in an empty stomach (1 hour before food) as presence of food interferes with absorption from the gut Around 70-80 % of orally administered levothyroxine is absorbed and it occurs within 3 hours of intake after an overnight fast Reference: Liwanpo L, Hershman JM. Conditions and drugs interfering with thyroxine absorption. Best Pract Res Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2009 Dec;23(6):781-92.

417.q: Which of the following laryngeal cartilage is hyaline?
417.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Cricoid Hyaline cartilages Elastic cartilages (do not ossify) Thyroid cartilage Epioglottis Cricoid cartilage Corniculate Basal part of arytenoid cartilage Cuneiform Processes of arytenoid

418.q: A 13-year-old boy is brought to your clinic with a complaint of delayed pubertal changes. While examining the patient, which of the following features is the first change to indicate that pubertal change may have commenced?
418.e: The first clinical sign of the onset of puberty in boys is an increase in testicular volume (> 4 ml). This is followed by growth of external genitalia, pubic and axillary hair growth, growth of external genitalia and deepening of voice The first sign of pubertal onset in girls is thelarche (breast development) followed by pubic hair growth and menarche. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3011

418.q: A 48-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of a lump in the neck which becomes particularly more prominent when she swallows. On examination there is a thyroid nodule at the base of the neck. Leukocyte screening of two other family members who suffered thyroid carcinoma has revealed the ret proto-oncogene. Which type of thyroid carcinoma is linked to the ret-proto-oncogene?
418.e: The ret proto-oncogene encodes for a receptor tyrosine kinase. In medullary thyroid carcinoma the mutation is associated with hyperfunction. Ret is associated with familial cases of medullary thyroid carcinoma and the MEN-2 syndrome. Formerly the condition was screened for with the pentagastrin suppression test, although a DNA probe for ret is now readily available and patients can be screened via a leukocyte sample. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:378 Pg:2714-17

418.q: A 48-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of a lump in the neck which becomes particularly more prominent when she swallows. On examination there is a thyroid nodule at the base of the neck. Genetic testing of two other family members who suffered thyroid carcinoma has revealed mutation in RET proto-oncogene. Which is the most likely cancer in this patient?
418.e: The RET proto-oncogene encodes for a receptor tyrosine kinase. Activating mutation in RET gene can lead to MEN 2A and MEN 2B syndromes Medullary thyroid cancer is present in 100% of MEN2A and MEN 2B syndrome cases Serum Calcitonin is used as a tumor marker in screening patients with suspected Medullary thyroid cancer. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 2953

420.q: Conn syndrome is seen due to increased production of
420.e: Most common cause of Conn's syndrome is aldosterone- producing adrenal adenomas Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.369

420.q: Which of the following syndromes is associated with development of pheochromocytoma?
420.e: MEN 2 is associated with pheochromocytoma, not MEN 1 Syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma: MEN 2 (Both 2A and 2B) Von Hippel-Lindau disease Neurofibromatosis 1 Carney's triad Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition,page number2966

420.q: A 34-year-old woman presents with extreme lethargy a couple of weeks after the birth of her third child by emergency cesarean section. She complained to the health visitor of increasing problems some 7 days earlier, but was told that this was to be expected after the birth of her child. Her lactation was normal. On admission via casualty she was noted to have a sodium concentration of 127 mmol/l, a potassium concentration of 6.8 mmol/l and a urea of 70 mg/dl. What is the likely diagnosis?
420.e: One should always think of the possibility of Sheehan syndrome when a postpartum female presents with fatigue and hyponatremia. This is attributed to secondary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperkalemia is not seen in Sheehan syndrome as low ACTH doesn't impact aldosterone production from adrenal gland. However, absence of lactation is the most specific feature associated with Sheehan syndrome. The presence of normal lactation along with presence of hyperkalemia in the patient makes the diagnosis of Sheehan syndrome unlikely. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2971

421.q: A 22-year-old young woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with a temperature, dehydration and altered consciousness. Her initial biochemistry shows sodium 130 mmol/l, potassium 4.5 mmol/l, bicarbonate 6 mmol/l, urea 50 mg/dl, creatinine 1.2 mg/dl and hydrogen ion 80. What is the most important immediate treatment?
421.e: The patient has diabetic ketoacidosis , a condition still associated with mortality in patients with type-1 diabetes mellitus. There is a total body deficit of fluid and electrolytes. The most important initial treatment is intravenous saline as the hypovolaemia is the factor most likely to cause the patient to die. Intravenous insulin is required at an early stage; and, although it is normal, the potassium level will rapidly fall with fluid and insulin treatment and the patient will require potassium replacement. Intravenous bicarbonate should not be used immediately as it can cause massive fluid shifts and precipitate cerebral oedema. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Pg:3115

421.q: A 18-year-old female with Type 1 Diabetes mellitus with history of treatment default presented to the emergency room with vomiting and abdominal pain. Investigations revealed a GRBS of 536 mg/dl with ABG showing pH of 7.1 and bicarbonate of 11 mEq/L, positive urine ketones, Na-130 mEq/L, K-3 mEq/L, Creatinine - 1.1 mg/dl. What would be the next step in your management?
o: Start IV fluids and Insulin infusion; Avoid bicarbonates
Start IV fluids and insulin infusion; Administer bicarbonate at 50 mmol/hr
Start IV fluids; Give Potassium supplementation; Insulin infusion after K+ correction
Start IV fluids and potassium supplementation; Start Insulin infusion simultaneously
421.e: If initial serum K+ is 3.3 mEq/L If initial K+ > 5.3 mEq/L, insulin therapy can be started without K+ administration. Potassium values to be monitored every 4 hours If initial K+ is between 3.3 and 5.3 mEq/L, insulin infusion to be started along with potassium supplementation because ongoing insulin supplementation would result in lowering of serum K+ due to transcellular shift Reference: ISPAD consensus guidelines on management of Young Diabetes mellitus, Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 3115

Ans. is a and b i.e. Gestational diabetes and Maternal obesity Macrosomia is the term used to describe a large fetus. The recommended definition is fetal (neonatal) weight exceeding two standard deviations or above 90th centile for the appropriate normal population. According to ACOG : birth weight of > 4500gm is called as macrosomia. In Indian context Birth weight of > 4000 gm is called as macrosomia.

422.q: Which of the following is an intermediate acting insulin?
422.e: Ultra short acting Aspart Lispro Glulisine Short acting Regular insulin Intermediate acting NPH Lente Long acting Detemir Glargine Degludec Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 3108

422.q: A 46-year-old diabetic man on oral hypoglycemic drugs is found to have hyponatremia. Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause this complication?
422.e: Up to 5% of patients taking chlorpropamide may develop inappropriate ADH-like syndrome resulting in dilutional hyponatremia. Drugs causing SIADH : ( 5C + SVOT ) C yclophosphamide C hlorpropamide C arbamazepine C hlorpromazine C lofibrate S SRI V incristine O xytocin T ricyclic antidepressants Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2924

422.q: A 54-year-old female with type 2 diabetes is admitted with diarrhea and vomiting. She has noticed small amounts of blood in her stools. The vomiting had commenced one day after having a non-vegetarian diet. The patient's type 2 diabetes is treated with diet alone. Stool cultures taken by the GP reveal Campylobacter jejuni.Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
422.e: Campylobacter is a leading cause of diarrhoeal illness, often caused by ingestion of undercooked meat harboring the pathogen. It is also a major cause of traveller's diarrhea . The use of antibiotic therapy for the management of Campylobacter infection in adults is controversial. Antibiotic of choice in this infection is erythromycin, though ciprofloxacin and tetracycline may also be appropriate. However, appropriate fluid replacement and anti-emetics are initially indicated - most units advocate no antibiotic treatment. Antibiotics are not recommended in patients with nontyphoid Salmonella, Campylobacter, STEC, Aeromonas, or Yersinia, except in severe disease, because they do not hasten recovery or reduce the period of fecal bacterial excretion Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 133, Pg: 1065

423.q: A 12-year-old girl presents with short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea.Given the likely clinical diagnosis, which hormone would be most appropriate to treat this condition?
423.e: This girl most probably has Turner's syndrome , which is most commonly associated with absence of one X chromosome (XO pattern). Characteristic features in this condition include streak ovaries and absent internal genitalia. Estrogen administration will develop female secondary sex characters and life-long therapy will be required. Growth hormone may be useful for a limited period to increase her height. As the ovaries are absent, pulsatile GnRH and luteinising hormone would be of no use. Progesterone would be useful for inducing withdrawal bleed in females sufficiently treated with estrogen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3000

423.q: Kallmann's syndrome is due congenital synthesis defect of?
423.e: Kallmann's syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia. It is due to defective hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)synthesis. KAL gene defect on chromosome Xp22.3 is the culprit. Embryonic migration of GnRH neurons from hypothalamic olfactory placode to hypothalamus is prevented due to this genetic defect. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3013

423.q: Most common cause of anovulation in females is:
423.e: Five most important causes for anovulation in females include PCOS and other hyperandrogenic disorders, hypothalamic anovulation, hyperprolactinemia, POI and chronic illnesses Reference : Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14th edition Page 601

424.q: A 50-year-old overweight woman constable presents with amenorrhoea of 6 months' duration. There is no family history of osteoporosis or fracture. She does not smoke and is a teetotaler. Blood tests: FSH 35 IU/l (postmenopausal level > 30), LH 57 IU/l (Postmenopausal level > 30). Bone density measurements with a DEXA scan are within normal limits. What is the chief reason that this woman has not developed osteoporosis?
424.e: All the options contribute to a decreased incidence of osteoporosis. However, the fact that she is overweight suggests that her estrone levels are high due to higher expression of aromatase enzyme present in adipose tissue. Estrone is the main sex hormone produced after the menopause. Ovarian thecal androgens are converted to estrone in adipose tissue by the enzyme aromatase. High levels of estrone in this woman may thus be the main factor preventing the occurrence of bone resorption and osteoporosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3195

424.q: Amiodarone contains which of the following elements?
424.e: Amiodarone is structurally related to thyroid hormone & contains 37% iodine by weight. 1 tablet of 200 mg Amiodarone contains around 75 mg of iodine. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Pg:2945

424.q: True about Psammoma bodies are all except ?
424.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Seen in teratoma o Psammoma bodies represent a process of dystrophic calcification. o Single necrotic cells may constitute seed crystals that become encrusted by the mineral deposits. The progressive acquisition of outer layers may create lamellated configurations, called psammoma bodies because of their resemblance to grains of sand. o Psammoma bodies are seen in : papillary cancer of thyroid, meningioma, papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary.

425.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Rotor syndrome Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is seen when ? i) Impaired secretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile -> Dubin Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome. ii) Impaired bile flow —> Obstructive jaundice, primary biliary cirrhosis, Neonatal cholestasis, e.g. Extrahepatic biliary atresia/neonate idiopathic hepatitis, Choledocal cyst, Sclerosing cholangitis, Caroli disease, Metabolic (Tyrosinemia, Wolman disease, Nieman pick disease, Galactosemia, Fructosemia).

Answer- D. All of above Impaired bile flow → Obstructive jaundice, primary biliary cirrhosis, Neonatal cholestasis, e.g. Extrahepatic biliary atresia/neonate idiopathic hepatitis, Choledocal cyst, Sclerosing cholangitis, Caroli disease, Metabolic (Tyrosinemia, Wolman disease, Nieman pick disease, Galactosemia, Fructosemia).

425.q: A 42 year old man has worsening jaundice and has deranged liver function tests which have worsened over the last 3 months. He has positive IgG to hepatitis C. Which of the following investigations is most useful for management of the condition?
425.e: Liver biopsy is useful to determine the severity of the disease and for monitory progression when treatment with ribavirin and interferon is instigated. Cirrhosis develops in 20-25 percent of patients with chronic hepatitis C after 10 years. It is also important to rule out liver carcinoma which may be a complication of long standing hepatitis C infection Hepatitis C is an RNA virus and hence option C is incorrect. ERCP is done in cases of obstructive jaundice. CT abdomen is not going to help in this patient Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2592

426.q: Which blood group is more prone to helicobacter and cholera infection?
426.e: In most people (80%), A, B, and H antigens are secreted by the cells and are present in the circulation as well as in various secretions such as saliva ( Se phenotype ). Others, called "nonsecretors" do not secrete A, B, and H antigens ( se phenotype ). ABO and Se/se systems influence the susceptibility to a variety of diseases. Malaria is less severe in O than non O patients. Group O is associated with enhanced susceptibility to Helicobacter pylori (and gastric ulcer) as well as to cholera bacillus or to norovirus . Group O individuals exhibit a lesser procoagulation phenotype when compared to non O individuals. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 113, Pg: 884

426.q: A patient has been diagnosed as having epidemic typhus. By which vector is he most likely to have become infected?
