426.e: The chief vector of epidemic typhus is the human body louse. The hard tick is a vector for a number of rickettsial diseases. Larval trombiculid mites spread scrub typhus. Rat fleas are responsible for the spread of endemic (murine) typhus. The Aedes aegypti mosquito is the vector for dengue fever Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition, Ch:187 Pg:1435

426.q: Which of the following secondary causes of hyperlipidemia result in predominantly hypercholesterolemia, as opposed to hypertriglyceridemia?
426.e: Hypercholesterolaemia rather than hypertriglyceridaemia : nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, hypothyroidism Hyperlipidaemia: secondary causes Causes of predominantly hypertriglyceridemia diabetes mellitus (types 1 and 2) obesity alcohol chronic renal failure drugs: thiazides, non-selective beta-blockers, unopposed estrogen liver disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:400 Page number:2897

427.q: An obese 55 year old woman with Type II diabetes is referred as she has been found to have raised ALT and AST levels. She does not have a history of pruritus or jaundice. She is not on any medication and does not take alcohol. On examination, she has a smooth hepatomegaly of 3 cm edge. There are no xanthelasma and she does not have signs of chronic liver disease. What is the likely diagnosis?
427.e: This diagnosis is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. The mildest type is simple fatty liver (steatosis), an accumulation of fat within the liver that usually causes no liver damage. This disease is usually nonprogressive and rarely causes liver cirrhosis. A potentially more serious type, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), is associated with liver fibrosis. NAFLD is the most common chronic liver disease in many parts of the world, including the United States. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease affects more women than men, and is associated with insulin resistance /diabetes and obesity . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 343Pg: 2621

427.q: Which of the following is not a cause of necrotizing myopathy?
427.e: IMNM, or autoimmune necrotizing myopathy, is characterized by the acute or insidious onset of symmetric, proximal more than distal weakness. Specific autoantibodies associated are: (anti-3-hydroxy-3methyl-glutaryl-coenzyme reductase [HMGCR] and anti-signal recognition particle [SRP]). Anti-HMGCR myopathy can be seen in patients receiving statins, inhibitors of HMGCR, particularly in patients aged >50 years. However, anti-HMGCR myopathy can develop in children and young adults without a history of statin use and can mimic a limb girdle muscular dystrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 365,: 2822

427.q: Most common microbial trigger for Type 1 DM are all except
427.e: Numerous environmental events have been proposed to trigger the autoimmune process in genetically susceptible individuals; however, none have been conclusively linked to diabetes. Identification of an environmental trigger has been difficult because the event may precede the onset of DM by several years(Putative environmental triggers include viruses (coxsackie, rubella, enteroviruses most prominently), bovine milk proteins, nitrosourea compounds, vitamin D deficiency, and environmental toxins. Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 403, Pg: 3100

428.q: Which site is Most commonly involved in gastrointestinal TB among the following?
428.e: Although any portion of the gastrointestinal tract may be affected, the terminal ileum and the cecum are the sites most commonly involved in gastrointestinal TB Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1366

428.q: A 35-year-old man is admitted following a serious attempt at paracetamol overdose. Despite efforts to treat him he develops liver failure. Which of the following is most likely with the ensuing liver failure?
o: Better prognosis in those with high alcohol consumption
Hypoglycaemia rarely happens within 12 hours of onset of encephalopathy
428.e: Lactic acidosis is due to decreased hepatic lactate clearance,compounded by poor peripheral perfusion and increased lactate Use of intravenous N-acetylcysteine reduces morbidity and mortality in fulminant hepatic failure. Severe hypoglycemia affects 40% of patients with fulminant liverfailure, which exacerbates encephalopathy. Reference: Harrison 20 th pg. 2370

428.q: A 25-year-old woman is referred from the Emergency department with a paracetamol overdose.Which of the following is an indication for liver transplantation in acute liver failure as a result of paracetamol overdose?
428.e: Prothrombin time > 100 seconds in acute liver failure with paracetamol poisoning is one of the selection criteria for liver transplantation. The remainder of the selection criteria for liver transplantation in acute liver failure with paracetamol overdose are as follows: Arterial pH Creatinine > 2.5 mg/dL Grade III or grade IV encephalopathy. Serum bilirubin > 15 mg/dl is part of the selection criteria for liver transplantation in non-paracetamol induced acute liver failure. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 340, Pg: 2589

429.q: A 59-year-old man presents with a painful swollen left knee as well as pain and stiffness of both his hands. On examination his skin is pigmented. There is tenderness and swelling of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, he has hepatomegaly of 8 cm below the costal margin. His knee is swollen and aspiration of the joint yields turbid, straw coloured fluid. Which one of the following diagnoses is likely?
429.e: The patient has haemochromatosis as evidenced by the pigmentation and the hepatomegaly. Hemochromatosis involves joints mainly the second and the third MCP joints. It mainly causes chondrocalcinosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st ed, Ch: 374, Pg: 2871

Ans. is 'c' i.e., Increased copper in liver Diagnosis of Wilson disease The gold standard for diagnosis is liver biopsy with quantitative copper assay --> concentration of copper in a liver biopsy sample > 200 mg/g dry weight. Other tests are ? Serum ceruloplasmin level --> low o Urine copper excretion --> increased KF rings o DNA Haplotype analysis.

429.q: A 15-year male child presented with hepatomegaly, involuntary movements, poor scholastic performance. His sister died at 5 years of age. Eye examination is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
429.e: The presence of hepatomegaly, involuntary movements points to Wilson's disease. Wilson Disease is an inherited condition that causes the body to retain excess copper. The copper buildup leads to damage in the kidneys, brain, and eyes. If not treated, Wilson Disease can cause severe brain damage, liver failure, and death.

430.q: A 22-year-old male is evaluated by his primary care physician for dysuria. A urethral swab is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. He receives appropriate antibiotic treatment. He returns to the clinic four weeks later complaining of pain in the knees, ankles, and lower back. Repeat testing is negative for both Chlamydia and Neisseria gonorrhea. Which additional finding might be expected on examination?
o: Right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly
Nontender subcutaneous nodules over several large joints
430.e: Conjunctival injection mainly affects the posterior conjunctival blood vessels. Because these vessels are more superficial than the ciliary arteries, they produce more redness, move with the conjunctiva, and constrict with the application of topical vasoconstrictors. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition Page number - 822

430.q: A 35 year old woman has abdominal pain, jaundice and worsening ascites. She drinks 20 units of alcohol each week, and takes the oral contraceptive pill. Which of the following findings would make a diagnosis of Budd Chiari syndrome likely?
430.e: Budd-Chiari syndrome is an uncommon condition induced by thrombotic or nonthrombotic obstruction to hepatic venous outflow.The classic triad of abdominal pain,ascites, and hepatomegaly is observed in the vast majority of patients but is nonspecific. Ascetic fluid protein may be high or low in Budd Chiari syndrome. Tender hepatomegaly on examination is one of the hallmark signs. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch:50, Pg: 323

430.q: A 37 year old man presents with 2 bowls full of hematemesis. He drinks 10 pints of beer a day and has done so for 10 years. Upper GI endoscopy reveals oesophageal varices. Which of the following is effective in reducing the rates of rebleeding in the future?
430.e: Non selective beta blockers (propranolol, nadolol) can be used for reducing rebleeding in oesophageal varices. They work by decreasing hepatic venous pressure gradient and thereby decreasing portal hypertension. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 344, Pg: 2630

431.q: A 34 year old patient has had a hepatitis test for investigation of jaundice. He has a positive Hep BsAg (HBsAg) and has IgM antibodies to Hep B Core (anti-HBc). What is he likely to have?
431.e: The positive anti-HBc (IgM) and HBsAg suggests acute infection. When the infection resolves, HBsAg becomes negative and anti-HBc (IgG) is positive. In patients who have been vaccinated, HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs is positive. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 339, Pg: 3577

431.q: Which of the following enzyme elevation is/are less specific for the cholestasis jaundice?
431.e: ENZYMES THAT REFLECT CHOLESTASIS The activities of three enzymes-alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)-are usually elevated in cholestasis. Alkaline phosphatase and 5′-nucleotidase are found in or near the bile canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, whereas GGT is located in the endoplasmic reticulum and in bile duct epithelial cells. Reflecting its more diffuse localization in the liver, GGT elevation in serum is less specific for cholestasis than are elevations of alkaline phosphatase or 5′- nucleotidase. Some have advocated the use of GGT to identify patients with occult alcohol use.

431.q: A 47 year old man has painless jaundice. He has pale stools and dark urine. On examination he is deeply jaundiced and has scratch marks all over his body. On palpation of the abdomen Courvoisier's sign is positive. Where is the level of biliary obstruction?
431.e: Courvoisier's sign is a palpable distended gallbladder on examination of the abdomen. Obstruction below the level of the cystic duct causes this, probably due to carcinoma of the pancreas. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine Ch:83, Pg: 659,

432.q: A 29 year old lady presents with abdominal pain to the GP who suspects irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following is a recognized feature of irritable bowel syndrome?
432.e: Irritable bowel syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterized by- Abdominal pain relieved by defecation Bloating Alternating bowel habits - constipation, diarrhoea - alone or alternating with each other. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 327 pg: 2490

432.q: A 66-year-old lady presents with symptoms suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following would represent a 'red flag' indicator and prompt further investigation?
o: Change in bowel habit for last two years
More frequent stools last two months
432.e: The 'red flag' indicators listed in the NICE guidelines as: Unintentional and unintended weight loss Rectal bleeding A family history of bowel or ovarian cancer A change in bowel habit to loose and / or more frequent stools persisting for more than six weeks in a person aged over 60 years. Also, on clinical examination the other 'red flag' indicators are: Anaemia Abdominal mass Rectal mass Inflammatory markers for inflammatory bowel disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 327 Pg: 2493

432.q: What is the differentiating feature between IBS and organic GI disease?
432.e: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional bowel disorder which is non inflammatory. The unifying feature of inflammatory diarrhea due to any cause is the presence of leukocytes or leukocyte derived protein Calprotectin in stools. Another inflammatory marker in stool is Fecal Lactoferrin, which is also present in activated neutrophils. Both of them can be used in diagnosis of relapses of inflammatory bowel disease from IBS or bacterial overgrowth. Fecal calprotectin is also having the advantage of being a sensitive marker of Colonic or ileocolonic inflammation rather than isolated ileal inflammation. Abdominal pain, diarrhea and presence of mucous in stools can be seen in IBS as well as inflammatory diarrhea. Blood in stools, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss is uncommon in IBS.

433.q: A 44 year old man has a diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis. He was incidentally found to have positive anti smooth muscle antibodies by the GP who sent an autoimmune screen. Which is the next recommended test for this patient?
433.e: A positive anti smooth muscle antibody test is suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis . Liver function tests may demonstrate elevated levels of bilirubin, AST and ALT. A liver biopsy may then be warranted. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2482

433.q: A 44 year old man has a diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis. He was incidentally found to have positive anti smooth muscle antibodies by the family doctor who sent an autoimmune screen. Which is the next recommended test for this patient?
433.e: The features are suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis. Liver function tests may demonstrated elevated levels of bilirubin, AST and ALT. A liver biopsy may then be warranted. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch:341 , Pg: 2613-2615

433.q: A 43 year old man has recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea and lower abdominal cramping. Histologic evaluation of a biopsy from flexible sigmoidoscopy reveals acute inflammation without architectural distortion consistent with ulcerative colitis.Which of the following conditions is associated with the condition?
433.e: 75% of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis have inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease of unknown etiology. In the absence of underlying bile duct abnormalities, a generalized beading and stenosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree characterize PSC. PSC is usually progressive, leading to cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and liver failure.Typically, a cholestatic jaundice picture is seen with the liver function tests. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 344, Pg: 2627-2628

434.q: A 55-year-old man on no current treatment for his quiescent ulcerative colitis (UC) is found to have an ESR of 95 mm/hr (0-20mm/1st hour). Investigations show: Haemoglobin 13.2g/dL (13.0-18.0) WCC 4.5 x 10^9/L (4-11) Platelets 160 x 10^9/L (150-400) Corrected Calcium 8.8 mg/dl IgG 25g/L(6-13) IgA 1.8g/L(0.8-3.0) IgM 1.6g/L(0.4-2.2) What is the most appropriate next investigation?
434.e: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate ( ESR) is not raised in quiescent UC . Hence there must be another reason in this case. The only abnormal result given is a raised IgG . This suggests that myeloma is a possible diagnosis. Plasma immunoelectrophoresis to look for an M band is the most appropriate next investigation. A bone marrow trephine is the definitive investigation but is traumatic and painful to the patient and so is not the next investigation of choice. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st d, Ch:111 Pg: 867

435.q: A patient who has had a subtotal thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism is on thyroxine replacement. She has a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), normal tri-iodothyronine (T3) and low free thyroxine (T4) levels. What is the most likely reason for those results?
o: The patient's results are as expected - no change in treatment is required
435.e: Once on a full replacement dose, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels should be checked at intervals of 1-3 years, depending on their stability. Fluctuating or elevated TSH levels in a previously stable patient, or thyroxine requirements in excess of 200 mg/day, usually indicate compliance problems. It is important to rule out malabsorption or abnormal thyroxine kinetics caused by drugs: cholestyramine, ferrous sulphate, lovastatin, aluminium hydroxide, rifampicin, amiodarone, carbamazepine, and phenytoin all alter the absorption or clearance of thyroxine. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:377 Pg:2705-07

435.q: A 24 year old woman has type 1 diabetes. She has weight loss over the past 3 months, and irregular menstrual cycles. Her bowel habit has been unchanged. On examination her BMI was 24 kg/m2. Investigations show: haemoglobin of 8.1 g/dl with a MCV of 69 fl. Which is the likely diagnosis?
435.e: This patient has type 1 diabetes – an autoimmune condition. She now presents with iron deficiency anemia along with weight loss. So the possibility of celiac disease should be ruled out as people with type 1 diabetes are at up to six times greater risk of having celiac disease. Dietary deficiency of iron and heavy menstrual loss will not cause weight loss there is no abdominal pain or blood in stools to suggest a Chron's Disease. Antibodies to gliadin should be sent and the diagnosis of celiac disease can be confirmed by a biopsy of small intestine which will show villous atrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

435.q: A 44 year old man has drunk 50 units a week of alcohol for 20 years. During investigations, she has :Haemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 110 fL (80-96), white cell count 2.1 x 10^9/L (4-11), platelet count 75 x 10^9/L (150-400). What might explain these results?
435.e: The haematological picture is that of macrocytic anemia (most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency). Folate deficiency occurs in the majority of binge-drinking alcoholics and is a common cause of anemia. Inadequate dietary intake, intestinal malabsorption, and impaired folate storage in the liver all contribute to folate deficiency. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine21 st ed, ch: 99, Pg: 773

436.q: During an epidemic of hepatitis E, fatality is maximum in
436.e: In outbreaks of waterborne hepatitis E in India and Asia, the case-fatality rate is 1-2% and up to 10-20% in pregnant women. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 339 pg. 2577

436.q: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute monocular visual loss. Fundoscopy reveals a swollen pale optic disc in the affected eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
436.e: The presence of a swollen optic disc suggests ischaemic optic neuropathy. In elderly people giant cell arteritis is a common presentation of acute monocular visual loss. Optic neuritis is very rare in people over the age of 50. You would expect bilateral swollen optic discs in raised intracranial pressure. In central retinal vein occlusion you would expect diffuse retinal haemorrhages. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3343

436.q: What is the Most common source of E. coli bacteremia?
436.e: The urinary tract is the most common source of E. coli bacteremia, accounting for one-half to two-thirds of episodes Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1071

437.q: A patient with Wegener's glomerulonephritis presents with sinusitis and hemoptysis. His chest radiograph shows several large cavitary pulmonary nodules, consistent with ventilation- perfusion imbalance with low V'/Q' units. Which of the following will be greater than normal in a patient with a low V'/Q' ratio?
437.e: Areas with low V/Q ratios produce hypoxemia or a decreased PaO2, which leads to A decrease in the dissolved oxygen content of the blood and A decrease in PaCO2, due to stimulation of the peripheral chemoreceptors. At lower PaO2 levels, arterial oxygen saturation is decreased, which decreases the oxyhemoglobin content. Because the mixed alveolar PO2 is normal and the arterial PO2 is less than normal, the A-a gradient is greater than normal. Reference: Levitzky, pp 113-116, 122-123.

437.q: Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma after HCV infection are:
o: Infection in infancy or early childhood.
437.e: HCC usually occurs after three decades of disease. And occurs exclusively in patients with cirrhosis. 50-70% - Develops chronic HCV 20-25% - Develops Cirrhosis. 1-4% - Develops HCC Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition page Ch: 341 Pg 2615

437.q: Which of the following is true regarding laboratory findings of Zieve's Syndrome?
437.e: A unique form of hemolytic anemia (with spur cells and acanthocytes) called Zieve's syndrome can occur in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease, reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism. Serum total bilirubin can be normal or elevated with advanced disease. Prothrombin times are often prolonged and usually do not respond to administration of parenteral vitamin K. Serum sodium levels are usually normal unless patients have ascites and then can be depressed, largely due to ingestion of excess free water. Transient hyperlipidemia may also be seen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2625

438.q: All of the following statements regarding Atopic kerato-conjunctivitis are true except?
o: Associated history of Asthma/ allergic rhinitis frequently noted
438.e: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis: Demographics: Generally seen in young adults. Associated Atopic Diseases: Often associated with a history of other atopic diseases such as: Asthma Allergic rhinitis Atopic eczematoid dermatitis in the patient or their family. Disease Characteristics: Responsible for an extremely severe and chronic form of ocular surface disorder. The disease spectrum varies in range of severity: Ranging from mild cases to chronic and persistent inflammation. Comparison to VKC (Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis): Similar in nature to VKC but tends to be more: Severe Chronic Extends into adulthood. Reference: Parson's Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

438.q: A 50 year old male with history of SSc, complaints of fatigue and exertional dyspnoea of 3 months duration. He has also noted malena. On examination, he was pale with spooning of nails. What will be the likely finding on upper GI endoscopy?
438.e: The cause of chronic GI blood loss in a patient with SSC is Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia. The endoscopic appearance is Water melon stomach. Reference : Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2781

438.q: A 40 year old lady has tightening of the skin around her hands and mouth. She has several telangiectasia on her hands, and complains of severe cold hands in winter. She was noticed to be pale. Investigations show : Hb 4.5 g/dl MCV 105 fl WCC 6 x 10^9/L platelets 230 x 10^9/L Iron 22 (14-29) μmol/l Ferritin 155 (15-200)μmol/l total iron binding capacity 50 (45-72) umol/l Folate 11 (3-20) ng/l Vitamin B12 - 85 (120-700 pmol/l) What is the likely cause of anaemia?
438.e: Scleroderma can cause folate deficiency due to malabsorption. However, in this case, the folate levels are normal and there is B12 deficiency. B12 deficiency can occur in conditions where there is bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine (blind loop syndromes) such as jejunal diverticulosis, Crohns disease, fistulas and scleroderma. The anaerobic organisms metabolise vitamin B12 and impair absorption. When systemic sclerosis (SSc) involves the small intestine, normal peristaltic movements are lost and motility is impaired leading to stasis and dilatation. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2781

439.q: Which of the following genotypes is associated with the lowest levels of alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT)?
439.e: α-1antitrypsin deficiency is due to the insufficient plasma activity of the enzyme that degrades several proteins like neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G and proteinase 3. It is an AR disease and is characterized by emphysema and cirrhosis. The wild genotytpe is PiMM seen in > 90% of individuals. The clinically significant mutation is PiZZ, which is associated with The null phenotype (not in the list of options) is the least common but the most severe form of the disease where there is no detectable AAT in the serum. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2615

439.q: Which one of the following statements is true of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
o: Patients show at least a 15 % improvement in the FEV1 after nebulised bronchodilator
Inhaled corticosteroid usage does not improve long-term prognosis
Breathlessness is uncommon until the FEV1 falls to approximately 50 % of predicted
Emphysema is associated with increased transfer factor
439.e: 15% improvement in FEV1 level of improvement would mean the presence of asthma. High dose inhaled steroids have been shown (ISOLDE) to improve quality of life and reduce hospitalisation rates by reducing the number of exacerbations, but it does not slow the rate of decline of FEV1 (hence does not affect prognosis). Breathless is common but subjective. Mild COPD (60 - 79% predicted FEV1) are often unknown to their GP. Those with moderate COPD (40 - 59% predicted) are seen intermittently seen by GP, whilst those with severe disease ( It is asthma which is associated with normal or increased transfer factor. COPD is associated with decreased transfer factor. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: Ch:202, Pg: 2187

439.q: A 70 year old man attends the hospital with a history of proximal muscle weakness. He also gives a history of cough of 12 weeks duration and complains of pain of the small joints of the hands. He has small haemorrhages in the nail folds, but is not clubbed. On examination of the chest he has bibasal crackles, and a chest radiograph reveals diffuse reticular infiltrates. Lung function tests confirm a restrictive pattern. What is the likely cause of his interstitial lung disease?
439.e: The patient has a restrictive lung disease with proximal muscle weakness and arthritis. Arthritis and ILD can be seen in diseases like RA and SLE, Sarcoidosis, Systemic Sclerosis etc. But here there is proximal muscle weakness and the patient is an elderly male with nail bed hemorrhages, which could indicate telangiectasia. So the diagnosis is Dermatomyositis. In polymyositis and dermatomyositis patients often develop proximal muscle weakness and of pain in the small joints of the fingers. They may have ragged cuticles and haemorrhages at the finger nail folds. Interstitial lung disease can occur. Underlying malignancy (lungs, ovaries, breasts and stomach) is present in 5% Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 365, Pg: 2820

440.q: Organisms commonly causing Non gonococcal urethritis in males are all except:
440.e: C.trachomatis caused ~30-40% of cases of non- gonococcal urethritis (NGU). M. genitalium - probable cause of many Chlamydia-negative cases. U. urealyticum but not U. parvum is associated with NGU. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 136, Pg: 1080

440.q: IVC filter is used in following except -
o: To prevent progress of native blood vessel disease
440.e: Answer is 'b' i.e. Negligible size of emboli

440.q: A 34 year old lady has developed worsening pruritus and jaundice over the past year. Investigations revealed a positive antimitochondrial antibody and a liver biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis. Which of the following is associated with the condition?
440.e: Primary biliary cirrhosis is more common in females and is usually associated with raised IgM levels. Xanthelasma are present due to cholestasis. Connective tissue disorders such as Sjogren's syndrome are associated. A positive antimitochondrial antibody and liver biopsy are the best ways to confirm the diagnosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2627

441.q: Which is the antibody associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
441.e: Explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disease characterized by marked lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid, follicular atrophy, and fibrosis . The disease is primarily mediated by T-cell-induced thyroid cell destruction , but autoantibodies serve as important clinical markers . The most relevant antibodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis are: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies → most commonly present, clinically useful for diagnosis. Anti-thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies → also present in many cases. (vs Option C) TSH-receptor blocking antibodies → seen in some patients, especially in thyroid atrophy, but less common. (vs Option B) Among these, anti-TPO antibodies are the most strongly associated and are the standard diagnostic marker. Anti-CCP (Option A): Seen in rheumatoid arthritis , not thyroid disease.

441.q: A 66 year old man is investigated for lower back pain. He also complains of weight loss and fevers. On reviewing his history, he has been told before that he has ankylosing spondylitis. On admission, his blood tests show a urea of 66 mg/dl and a creatinine of 3.50 mg/dl. An ultrasound of the kidneys shows hydronephrosis bilaterally. CT scan shows fibrotic para-aortic masses. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
441.e: The symptoms of fevers, weight loss and lower back pain are classical for retroperitoneal fibrosis. There is an association with inflammatory conditions such as SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and glomerulonephrosis. CT or MRI shows fibrotic para-aortic masses causing ureteral obstruction. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 319 Pg: 2375

441.q: Which of the following drugs used in RA is given orally?
441.e: Among the newer agents, JAK inhibitors are the drugs that are given orally among the options. Conventional DMARDS are also oral agents. Biologicals are all parenteral agents. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761-2764

442.q: A patient complains of paroxysmal episodes of not being able to catch her breath. When no abnormalities are detected with conventional pulmonary function screening, the pulmonologist orders a methacholine challenge test. Which of the following will increase as a result of stimulating cholinergic receptors on the bronchial smooth muscle?
442.e: Methacholine is a cholinergic agonist, which causes constriction of bronchial smooth muscle. Bronchoconstriction reduces airway radius, which increases airway resistance, and thus the resistive work of breathing. Methacholine-induced bronchoconstriction decreases the anatomic deadspace but has no significant effect on the lung compliance, and thus does not affect the elastic work of breathing. Reference: Ganong, pp 649-650, 654, 657-659. Levitzky, pp 34-36, 49-50.

442.q: A 68-year-old man who has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to his pulmonologist with fatigue, dyspnea at rest, and peripheral edema. His blood gases on room air are PaO2 = 60 mmHg, PaCO2 = 60 mmHg, and pH = 7.36. His alveolar-arterial (A-a) O2 gradient, at a barometric pressure of 760 mmHg and a respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, is approximately what?
442.e: The A-a O2 gradient is the partial pressure difference between the alveolar gas and arterial blood. The PaO2 has been measured. The alveolar oxygen tension must be calculated using the modified alveolar gas equation PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/ R PAO2 = [0.21 x (760 - 47 mmHg)] - 60 mmHg/0.8 PAO2 = 150 mmHg - 75 mmHg = 75 mmHg (A-a) O2 gradient = 75 mmHg - 60 mmHg = 15 mmHg The patient's low arterial oxygen tension (hypoxemia; hypoxic hypoxia) results from a low PAO2 due to hypoventilation (as evidenced by the elevated PaCO2), and thus the (A-a) O2 gradient is within the normal range. Reference: Levitzky, pp 75, 180-181, 262.

442.q: A 28-year-old man presents with symmetrical tremor, worsens with voluntary movements, and resolves completely at rest. He has history of asthma. Which of the following drugs is most suitable for management?
442.e: This patient having essential tremor which is symmetrical, worsens with voluntary movements, and resolves completely at rest. Increased activation of β adrenoceptors has been implicated in essential tremor, and management commonly involves administration of propranolol. However, the more selective β1 blocker metoprolol may be equally effective and is more suitable in a patient with pulmonary disease like asthma. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 511

443.q: Which of the following is the most sensitive test for diagnosing tubercular pleural effusion?
443.e: The fluid is straw-colored and at times hemorrhagic; it is an exudate with a protein concentration >50% of that in serum (usually ~4&6 g/dL), a normal to low glucose concentration, a pH of ~7.3 (occasionally 45 IU/L) is the most sensitive test for pleural effusion. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21th edition, ch: 178 Page no 1364

443.q: A 72-year-old man presents with an acute onset of severe pain and swelling of the left elbow. He mentions that he had a chest infection 3 weeks ago. On examination, he had a temperature of 38°C and the left elbow was erythematous, swollen and tender. What is the most appropriate investigation?
443.e: The differential diagnosis of acute monoarthritis includes- septic arthritis, crystal induced arthritis and hemarthrosis. The management of acute monoarthritis is always joint aspiration followed by appropriate therapy. In the context of an elderly male presenting with monoarthritis after a recent history of pneumonia should make us raise suspicion of a septic arthritis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 370, Pg: 2852 20th edition Ch:355 Pg:2570

443.q: A 63-year-old diabetic presents with pyrexia, productive cough, and shortness of breath for 5 days. She has RLL consolidation and a small unilateral pleural effusion on CXR. Which is a marker of poor prognosis?
443.e: Indicators of poor prognosis in pneumonia include: Age >65 Co-existing morbidity including diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure, stroke, coronary artery disease. Respiratory rate>30 Mental impairment Biochemical/haematological markers which include white blood count 30,000/µL; hypoxia needing CPAP or FiO2>60%, positive blood culture and blood urea>7 mmol/L. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:126Pg 1015

444.q: A 48-year-old coal miner complains of shortness of breath and a productive cough. The history reveals that he has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day since he was 16 years old. Pulmonary function studies are ordered including an esophageal balloon study to measure intrapleural pressures. Normally, intrapleural pressure is negative throughout a tidal inspiration and expiration because of which of the following?
o: The lungs have the tendency to recoil outward throughout a tidal breath
The chest wall has the tendency to recoil inward throughout a tidal breath
The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil away from each other throughout a tidal breath
The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil in the same direction throughout a tidal breath
444.e: When the pleura, and hence the lung-chest wall system, are intact, the inward elastic recoil of the lung opposing the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall results in a subatmospheric (negative) pressure with the pleural space. When one reaches lung volumes in excess of ~70% of the total lung capacity, the chest wall recoil is also inward. Reference: Ganong, pp 665-655. Levitzky, pp 17-23, 29-31.

444.q: Tinea capitis occurs Most commonly in Which age group?
444.e: Tinea capitis occurs most commonly in children 3-7 years old. Children with tinea capitis usually present with well-demarcated scaly patches in which hair shafts are broken off right above the skin; alopecia can result. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 219 Pg 1691

444.q: A 35 year old male presents with history of weakness of both the lower limbs of insidious onset, for the past 2 years. He has mild difficulty in swallowing liquids too. There are no sensory symptoms. On examination, he has fasciculations and areflexia. You also notice gynecomastia. He is also undergoing investigation for infertility. What is the likely molecular abnormality be seen in this patient?
444.e: The given patient has an LMN type of weakness without any sensory symptoms and with associated androgen insensitivity as evidenced by the gynecomastia and the sub fertility. This is classical of the Spinobulbar muscular atrophy or the Kennedy syndrome. It is an X linked disorder and is associated with CAG trinucleotide repeats on the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. CGG trinucleotide repeats is seen in Fragile X syndrome. It is associated with mental retardation. There may be ataxia and ovarian failure associated with it. GAA trinucleotide repeats are seen in Friedrich's Ataxia. CTG trinucleotides are seen in Myotonic dystrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 347, Pg: 3415

445.q: A 30 year old man gives a six-month history of worsening breathlessness and coughs up half a cupful of sputum daily. He was occasionally wheezy with viral illnesses as a young child, works in a factory and has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for the last four years. The most likely diagnosis is:
445.e: Bronchiectasis is most likely due to the extensive amounts of sputum production. In a young person, cystic fibrosis and hypogammaglobulinemia should be considered. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 290 Pg 2173

445.q: The most common extra intestinal manifestation of Amebiasis is?
445.e: Extraintestinal infection by E. histolytica Most often involves the liver. Of travelers who develop an amebic liver abscess after leaving an endemic area, 95% do so within 5 months. Young patients with an amebic liver abscess are more likely than older patients to present in the acute phase with prominent symptoms of Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1716

445.q: The most common complication of Amebiasis is?
445.e: Pleuropulmonary involvement, which is reported in 20-30% of patients, is the most frequent complication of amebic liver abscess. Rupture into the pericardium, usually from abscesses of the left lobe of the liver, carries the gravest prognosis; it can occur during medical therapy and requires surgical drainage. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1717

446.q: The wife of a recently married 24-year-old medical student reports that even though her husband doesn't snore, he stops breathing for periods of 1 to 2 minutes while he is sleeping. His physician refers him for a polysomnography study and pulmonary function testing, including ventilatory response curves. The tests confirm the apneic episodes during sleep and show depressed ventilatory responsiveness of both the peripheral and central chemoreceptors. Peripheral and central chemoreceptors both contribute to the increased ventilation that occurs as a result of which of the following?
o: A decrease in arterial oxygen content
A decrease in arterial blood pressure
An increase in arterial carbon dioxide tension
A decrease in arterial oxygen tension
446.e: Both the central chemoreceptors, located on or near the ventral surface of the medulla, and the peripheral chemoreceptors, in the carotid and aortic bodies, cause an increase in ventilation in response to an increase in PaCO2. The peripheral chemoreceptors also cause an increase in ventilation in response to a decrease in arterial pH and a decrease in PaO2, but the central chemoreceptors are unresponsive to hypoxemia and do not cause an increase in ventilation in response to a decrease in arterial pH because the blood-brain barrier is relatively impermeable to hydrogen ions. Neither the central chemoreceptors nor the carotid bodies are stimulated by a decrease in arterial blood pressure or O2 content. Reference: Ganong, pp 662, 672-677, 686-688. Levitzky, pp 114-116, 180-182, 201-210.

446.q: A patient with congestive heart failure, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is referred for pulmonary function testing in the supine and upright positions. Which of the following is higher at the apex of the lung than at the base when a person is upright?
446.e: The alveoli at the apex of the lung are larger than those at the base so their compliance is less. Because the compliance is reduced, less inspired gas goes to the apex than to the base. Also, because the apex is above the heart, less blood flows through the apex than through the base. However, the reduction in airflow is less than the reduction in blood flow, so that the V/Q ratio at the top of the lung is greater than it is at the bottom. The increased V/Q ratio at the apex makes PACO2 lower and PAO2 higher at the apex than they are at the base. Reference: Ganong, pp 643-644, 662-663, 686-688. Levitzky, pp 123-128. Stead et al., pp 25-27.

446.q: Which extrapulmonary site is Most commonly involved in TB ?
446.e: In order of frequency, the extrapulmonary sites most commonly involved in TB are the lymph nodes , pleura , genitourinary tract , bones and joints, meninges, peritoneum, and pericardium. Reference :Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1364

447.q: A 27-year-old man develops adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) after near-drowning. Conventional mechanical ventilation on 100% O2 together with inhaled nitric oxide do not provide sufficient oxygenation. Porcine surfactant is instilled via fiberoptic bronchoscope, and the PaCO2, fraction of inspired oxygen (FIO2), and shunting improve impressively. The improvements in respiratory function occurred because surfactant increased which of the following?
o: The pressure gradient needed to inflate the alveoli
447.e: Pulmonary surfactant increases lung compliance by lowering alveolar surface tension. As a result, the pressure gradient needed to inflate the alveoli decreases, as does the work of breathing. Reference: Ganong, pp 654-6558. Kasper et al., pp 1583, 1592-1595. Levitzky, pp 26-28. Stead et al., p 270.

447.q: A 6 feet 3 inches tall, 140-lb, 20-year-old male was watching television when he felt pain in his shoulder blades, shortness of breath, and fatigue. His father noticed how pale he was and took him to the Emergency Department, where a chest X-ray revealed a 55% pneumothorax of the right lung due to rupture of a bleb on the surface of the lung. Which of the following is true?
o: The intrapleural pressure in the affected area is equal to atmospheric pressure
The chest wall on the affected side recoils inward
There is hyperinflation of the affected lung
The V/Q ratio on the affected side is higher than normal
447.e: When air enters the pleural space due to interruption of the pleural surface through either the rupture of the lung or a hole in the chest wall, the pressure in the pleural space becomes atmospheric, the lung on the affected side collapses because of the lung's tendency to recoil inward, and the chest wall on the affected side recoils outward. Because the intrapleural pressure is atmospheric, the mediastinum shifts farther to the normal side with each inspiration. With collapse of the lung, the V / Q ratio on the affected side decreases. Reference: Ganong, p 688. Kasper et al., p 1568. Levitzky, pp 12, 116-Stead et al., pp 273-274.

447.q: A hospitalized patient is found semicomatose. Arterial blood gases reveal hypercapnia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the high arterial PCO2?
447.e: Profound hypoxia depresses the central nervous system, including the medullary respiratory centers. As a result, alveolar ventilation may decrease, resulting in an increased PaCO2. A decrease in metabolic activity would decrease the rate of production of carbon dioxide (VCO2), which would decrease PaCO2, assuming that alveolar ventilation does not change. If an alveolar capillary block is severe, retention of CO2 could briefly occur, but the coexistent hypoxemia would cause reflex hyperventilation with a decrease in PaCO2. At a constant tidal volume and respiratory rate, a decrease in the deadspace volume would increase alveolar ventilation, and thus lower the PaCO2. Reference: Kasper et al. pp 209-210, 1624-1637. Levitzky, pp 66, 73-74, 136-138.

448.q: A 27-year-old man is noted to have cyanosis of the lower limbs and clubbing of the toes but not the fingers. The blood pressure in the arm and lower limb is the same. Which of the following statements is true?
o: He has coarctation of the aorta.
He is likely to have a loud continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle.
He is likely to need urgent surgery.
448.e: Differential cyanosis (cyanosis only in lower extremities) is seen in a patient with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) when there is reversal of shunt. There is a right-left shunt from the pulmonary artery to the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. This is Eisenmenger's syndrome. Coarctation causes radiofemoral delay and a lower blood pressure in the leg as compared to the arm. It may be associated with PDA but there is no suggestion in this patient. Continuous machinery murmur is the classic murmur of PDA but when the shunt reverses (as in patients with a large PDA and/or pulmonary disease) the murmur becomes softer and shorter. When Eisenmenger's syndrome has developed surgery is associated with a very high mortality. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264 pg:1838,1839

448.q: Which of the following concerning congenital heart disease is correct?
o: ASD is the commonest cardiac malformation at birth
Congenital complete heart block is always associated with Anti-Ro antibodies in the mother
Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is characterised by a large, dilated left ventricle
448.e: Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate in the first trimester . It causes malformed tricuspid valve leading to tricuspid regurgitation. Option 1 - VSD is the most congenital heart disease. Option 2 - In the vast majority of cases of neonates with complete heart block the cause is unknown but in the minority it may be caused by autoimmune disease, particularly Anti-Ro antibodies, in the mother. Option 4 -In hypoplastic left heart syndrome, LV hypolasia occurs as the left sided chambers fail to develop and blood enters the systemic circulation from the right ventricle via the pulmonary artery and a patent ductus arteriosus. Reference: Braunwald's heart disease 12 th edition, page no.1559

448.q: Small cell lung cancer are associated with
448.e: Nearly 90% of SCLCs harbor mutations in TP53 and RB1. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 78, Pg: 597

449.q: A 36-year-old man visits his doctor because his wife has long complained of his snoring, but recently observed that his breathing stops for a couple of minutes at a time while he is sleeping. He undergoes polysomnography and ventilatory response testing to ascertain the extent and cause of his sleep apnea. The activity of the central chemoreceptors is stimulated by which of the following?
o: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain
A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain
An increase in the pH of the CSF
A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue
449.e: The central chemoreceptors, located at or near the ventral surface of the medulla, are stimulated to increase ventilation by a decrease in the pH of their extracellular fluid (ECF). The pH of this ECF is affected by the PCO2 of the blood supply to the medullary chemoreceptor area, as well as by the CO2 and lactic acid production of the surrounding brain tissue. The central chemoreceptors are not stimulated by decreases in PaO2 or blood oxygen content but rather can be depressed by long-term or severe decreases in oxygen supply. Reference: Ganong, pp 675-678. Levitzky, pp 206-208.

449.q: A 30-year-old male presents with hematuria and hemoptysis of two weeks duration. His urinalysis showed 2+ protein and dysmorphic RBC. His physician suspected a pulmonary renal syndrome and performs a renal biopsy. The pathologist uses a special stain to visualize the basement membrane. What is it?
449.e: Referring to the previous question, this patient is also suffering from a pulmonary renal syndrome. If the pathologist wants to stain the basement membrane, he might be suspecting Goodpasteur's syndrome. Jone's Methanamine silver is the stain used for basement membrane. Congo red is used for Amyloid. Masons Trichrome for collagen PAS for staining carbohydrate moiety in the cell membranes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2336.

449.q: Most common symptom of the Pertussis is
449.e: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 160, Pg: 1257

450.q: You review a 67-year-old man for dyslipidemia. He is taking atorvastatin 40 mg/day. Which of the following drugs should be used with caution?
450.e: The risk of statin induced myopathy is high when drugs like Erythromycin, anti fungals, immunosuppressive drugs and gemfibrozil is used along with statins, as these drugs interfere with the metabolism of statins. Statins will increase the drug levels of warfarin and digoxin too. Hence A,.B And C are right options. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, ch: 407, Pg: 3149

450.q: A 37-year-old woman presents to her GP with a vaginal discharge. She has been taking the combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP). What is the most common infection associated with the use of the OCP?
450.e: Women on oral contraceptives have a higher incidence of chlamydial endocervicitis. Vaginal warts are also common in these women. However, it is believed that human papillomavirus infection may occur even before the woman starts taking the pill, and that there is no actual increase in the risk of acquiring infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:389 P page number :2814-15

450.q: Which of the following is the functional effect of Hypokalemia on kidney function?
450.e: The functional effects of hypokalemia on the kidney can include Na+-Cl- and HCO3 - retention, polyuria, phosphaturia, hypocitraturia, and an activation of renal ammoniagenesis. Bicarbonate retention and other acid-base effects of hypokalemia can contribute to the generation of metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemic polyuria is due to a combination of central polydipsia and an AVP-resistant renal concentrating defect. Structural changes in the kidney due to hypokalemia include a relatively specific vacuolizing injury to proximal tubular cells, interstitial nephritis, and renal cysts. Hypokalemia also predisposes to acute kidney injury and can lead to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in patients with long-standing hypokalemia due to eating disorders and/or laxative abuse. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 350

451.q: Helmet cells are characteristic of anemia of?
451.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Hemolytic uremic syndrome Schistocytes, helment cells, triangle cells, burr cells are seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). Changes in erythrocyte morphology

451.q: Which of the following is a cause for secondary hypertriglyceridemia?
451.e: Causes of secondary hyperlipidemia include: Type 2 diabetes mellitus chronic renal failure alcoholism (hypertriglyceridemia) drugs including: thiazides, glucocorticoids, oestrogens, cyclosporine, protease inhibitors hypothyroidism (Hypercholesterolemia) nephrotic syndrome. (Hypercholesterolemia) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:400 Page number:2897

451.q: Renal papillary necrosis is almost always associated with one of the following conditions: March 2004
451.e: Ans. A i.e. Diabetes mellitus `Renal papillary necrosis, an accompaniment of acute pyelonephritis is most often seen in diabetics and is characterised by necrosis of renal papillae of one or both kidneys with sharped demarcation between necrotic and living tissue' — Dorlands Thus while papillary necrosis is a feature of more than one conditions mentioned in the question, it is most commonly seen with diabetes mellitus.

452.q: A 27-year-old woman is in end-stage renal disease. She has been started on regular haemodialysis. She complains of pain in her fingers. An X-ray shows digital subperiosteal erosions. What is the primary metabolic cause for her bony condition?
452.e: Digital sub periosteal resorption is classical of Osteitis fibrosa cystica of hyperparathyroidism. In CKD secondary hyperparathyroidism may progress to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. The series of events that happen in CKD is: Declining GFR leads to reduced excretion of phosphate and thus, phosphate retention The retained phosphate stimulates increased synthesis of both FGF-23 by osteocytes and of PTH and also stimulates growth of parathyroid gland mass PTH production is stimulated by decreased levels of ionized calcium, which in turn, result from decreased levels of renal calcitriol production with reduced kidney mass and suppression of calcitriol production due to phosphate retention and elevated levels of FGF-23, which also increases degradation of calcitriol. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2313

452.q: A 60-year-old man with long-standing type-2 diabetes, who has recently started on peritoneal dialysis, is admitted with a fractured femoral neck. His serum calcium concentration is 2.9 mmol/l, phosphate is 2 mmol/l and PTH is 5.6 pg/ml(normal range 25-65). Medications include alfacalcidol 0.5 mg daily and calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily. What would a bone biopsy show?
o: Aluminium deposition at the osteoid bone interface
452.e: Referring to the above question, we can clearly say that this patient is suffering from adynamic bone disease. Note that the calcium and phosphorous given here are in mmol/l. Ca value has to be multiplied by 4. So the Ca is 11.6mg/dl. Phosphorous has to be multiplied by 3. So the value is 6mg/dl. Aluminium deposited can cause osteomalacia like picture and is seen with use of aluminium as phosphate binder and Al in dialysate. Osteitis fibrosa cystica is severe secondary hyperparathyroidism. An increase in plasma cells cause hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:410, Pg:3181, 3182.

452.q: Which of the following statements are true regarding the management of Lupus nephritis? 1. HCQS should be included as treatment for all classes since it reduces the accrual of tissue damage. 2. Management of class I and Class II should be guided by the extra renal manifestations. 3. Class III and IV requires aggressive immunosuppression. 4. Isolated Class V has got better prognosis than class IV. 5. Isolated class V without nephrotic range proteinuria requires only supportive management.
452.e: The question deals with the management and prognosis of Lupus Nephritis. HCQ should be in the management of allclasses of lupus nephritis. Class I and II should be treated mainly based on the extra renal manifestations. Class III and IV are the proliferative and serious forms and require aggressive immunosuppression with high dose glucocorticoid with either MMF or Cyclophosphamide. Isolated Class V presents with proteinuria alone and has got better outcome than class IV. But class V often co exists with class III and IV. Class V with nephrotic range proteinuria should be treated with immunosuppression, usually steroid with calcinurin inhibitors. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2739-2747 KDIGO guidelines

453.q: What is the most common etiology of complicated UTI?
453.e: In complicated UTI (e.g., CAUTI), E. coli remains the predominant organism Organisms causing UTI: SEEK PP Staph saprophyticus coli Enterococcus Klebsiella Proteus Pseudomonas Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1071

453.q: A 35-year man has been referred for management of hypertension. On examination, he had palpable kidneys. This was confirmed by abdominal ultrasound which showed multiple cysts. Which of the following is likely to be associated?
453.e: A young hypertensive with palpable kidneys and cysts on ultrasound points to the diagnosis of ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease). Polycystic kidney disease is associated with increased levels of EPO which lead to polycythemia. Associations of ADPKD: Cardiovascular: Intracranial aneurysm (5 times more common than general population), can rupture to cause subarachnoid hemorrhage. Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the anterior and posterior cerebral circulation → predisposed to arterial dissection and stroke. Mitral valve prolapse. Insufficiency of the mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves. Gastrointestinal: Colonic diverticula Abdominal wall hernia Polycystic liver disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number 2350-2354.

453.q: A 52 year old man presents with lower back pains and lethargy. Investigations subsequently confirmed obstructive nephropathy and retroperitoneal fibrosis. His medication is reviewed on the ward round. Which medication is well known to cause retroperitoneal fibrosis?
453.e: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a disease featuring the proliferation of fibrous tissue in the retroperitoneum, the compartment of the body containing the kidneys, aorta, renal tract and various other structures. It may present with lower back pain, renal failure, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis and other obstructive symptoms. It may have an autoimmune etiology. 1/3 rd cases are secondary to malignancy, medications, aortic aneurysm or certain infections. Methyldopa, methysergide, amphetamines, beta blockers, cocaine and LSD are drugs which cause retroperitoneal fibrosis. Azathioprine is used to treat the condition. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 319 Pg: 2375

454.q: A 75-year-old man visits his GP for a new-patient screen. His only previous complaints have been type-2 diabetes and mild long-standing back pain. Screening tests reveal an elevated serum creatinine of 2.15 mg/dl and anaemia with Hb of 10.1 g/dl. A back X-ray shows collapse of the lumbar spine and there is a monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis. What is the most likely cause of his deteriorated renal function?
454.e: This patient is suffering from Myeloma as evidenced by the presence of anemia, renal impairment and bone involvement. Myeloma can affect the kidney in several ways - the filtered light chains are toxic to the tubules and can cause acute obstruction: Cast nephropathy The light chain impairs the proximal tubular function and cause RTA Hypercalcemia can cause tubulointerstitial disease Amyloidosis LCDD All forms of renal involvement is reversible to a certain extend with treatment of myeloma. Among the given options Amyloidosis is the best pick Amyloidosis presents predominantly between the ages of 60 and 70 years. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:111, Pg:870.

454.q: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension has renal impairment. His creatinine is 2.8 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows blood ++ and protein +. What is the most useful investigation?
454.e: A urinalysis of 2+ blood and 1+ protein are strong pointers towards glomerular disease. Hence among the options, biopsy is the most useful investigation. Renal ultrasound may be useful in assessing the kidney size and echoes, but it may not help us arrive at a diagnosis. IV urogram is used in the investigation of Obstruction to urinary tract and DTPA nucleide scan is used to asses the functional status of kidneys. Indications of Renal biopsy(when suspected): Glomerulonephritis Nephrotic Syndrome Vasculitis Interstitial nephritis Myeloma kidney HUS and TTP Allograft rejection Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition, Ch: 310, Pg: 2305.

454.q: Which of the following drugs cause renal impairment by causing interstitial nephritis?
454.e: Quinolones, penicillins, cephalosporins, sulphonamides and rifampicin are antibiotics that cause interstitial nephritis. Vancomycin, Aminoglycosides, Amphotericin B, Acyclovir, Foscarnet, Tenofovir and Cidofovir are toxic to the tubules of kidney. Vancomycin and acyclovir cause intra tubular obstruction. Amphotericin B causes RTA like picture with hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia. Hypomagnesemia is also seen with Aminoglycosides. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Chap 310, Pg. 2300

455.q: Which of the following denotes normal cardiac axis?
455.e: The cardiac axis represents the overall direction of electrical activity as it spreads through the cardiac conduction system The normal cardiac axis is directed downward and slightly to the left. It falls within the range of -30° to +90°. Left Axis Deviation (LAD): When the QRS axis is less than -30°. Right Axis Deviation (RAD): When the QRS axis is greater than +90°. Extreme Axis Deviation: Occurs when the QRS axis lies between -90° and 180° ("Northwest Axis") Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1870

455.q: A 24-year-old patient is admitted after falling asleep drunk in a toilet cubicle. On examination his BP 130/70, pulse 98 bpm and there is no pericardial rub. There is 'boggy' tenderness of his right calf and both thigh muscles. Biochemistry reveals urea 125 mg/dl, creatinine 4.0 mg/dl, bicarbonate 15 mmol/l, pH 7.1, potassium 7.8 mmol/l and creatine kinase 17 000 IU/l. (Ref values: s. creat: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17- 43 mg/dL; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mmol/l; S. bicarbonate: 22 to 32 mmol/L; S. creatine kinase: 5 to 25 IU/L IU/l) What is the most appropriate form of treatment?
455.e: This patient was immobilized for prolonged period, which can lead to rhabdomyolysis and renal failure, as evidenced by the high Creatine kinase levels. In addition, he has hyperkalemia and severe metabolic acidosis. Also, he has boggy swelling and tenderness of his muscles, suggestive of compartment syndrome or bilateral DVT. So he is having multiple issues that requires rapid correction. Hence hemodialysis is the best treatment Forced alkaline diuresis may renal failure is established with life-threatening hyperkalemia and acidosis, it is inappropriate. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, chp:310, pg: 2307.

455.q: All of the following are the side effects of cocaine toxicity. Except?
455.e: Cocaine is a psychostimulant . The other agents belonging to this group are, Methamphetamine, MDMA and Cathinone. There are certain therapeutically used psychostimulants too. These include Methylphenidate and Dextroamphetamine, used in the treatment of ADHD. Phenylpropanolamine was a psychostimulant used previously for weight reduction and is now withdrawn due to the risk of intracerebral bleed. The table depicts the symptoms of overuse of all the psychostimulants. Their cardiovascular effects produce tachycardia and not bradycardia. Withdrawal produces hypersomnia, depressed mood and increased appetite.

456.q: Mr. Kohli is a 26-year-old cricketer comes to you for regular check-up. On your assessment, you note a resting heart rate or 45 bpm with an occasional pause of up to 2 seconds. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. He feels well and reports no syncopal or presyncopal episodes at rest or during exercise. ECG is normal. Which of the following would be next step ?
o: Follow-up after 1 week. Avoid cricket for a week
He should undergo a treadmill stress ECG to determine the presence of chronotropic competence.
456.e: Sinus bradycardia and pauses up to 3 seconds are common in young individuals, particularly in highly trained athletes. (You know Mr. Kohli) Given the normal ECG, lack of symptoms, and normal physical examination, no further testing is warranted. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 245

456.q: A 74-year-old woman presents with a feeling of shortness of breath and choking on lying down. Around 4 months earlier she had been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and was started on aspirin and digoxin by her physician. On examination her physician could feel a goitre. Plain radiography confirmed retrosternal extension, which was presumed to be contributing to her shortness of breath. Her TSH level was less than 0.05 mU/l. Thyroid autoantibodies were negative. What diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?
456.e: Toxic multinodular goitre usually occurs in women over 55 years of age and is more common than Grave's disease in the elderly. Her atrial fibrillation may well be related to this. Her goitre is obstructing, with significant retrosternal extension, and surgery is the treatment of choice. Initially, however, she should be rendered euthyroid with antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2948

456.q: A 56 year old chronic alcoholic is found on the street with a low conscious level. His GCS is 3/15 on arrival in casualty. On examination, his BP is 110/65 and he is jaundiced. There is marked ascites and he has 7 spider naevi. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 120. Which is the most practical test to elucidate why he is unconscious?
456.e: In a patient with liver disease, it is important to exclude hypoglycemia as a cause of unconsciousness. Following confirming that baseline observations and BM is normal, the next best step is to perform a CT of his head to exclude a central neurological cause of decreased conscious level. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 28, Pg: 187

457.q: -30° to -60° left axis deviation is seen in
457.e: Answer- A. Left ventricular hypertrophy Normally, QRS axis ranges from -30° to 90°C An axis more negative than -30° is referred to as left axis deviation and an axis more positive than +100° is called right axis deviation Left axis deviation Axis more negative than -30° Associated with Left ventricular hypertrophy Left anterior fascicular block Inferior M.I.

457.q: A 60-year-old man has had a myocardial infarction. His pulse rate is 45/min and he is feeling lightheaded. Blood pressure is 90/65 mm Hg. In which one of the following conditions is temporary pacing indicated even when symptoms are absent?
457.e: Asymptomatic patients with first- or second-degree Mobitz type I AV block do not require any specific therapy. Patients should undergo treatment of any potentially reversible cause (ie, myocardial ischemia or medication effect) Symptomatic patients with any degree of heart block should be treated urgently with atropine (initial dose 0.5 mg given intravenously) or temporary pacing (transcutaneous or transvenous). Indications for permanent pacing: Symptomatic Brady arrhythmias with any degree of AV block Asymptomatic high-degree AV block (second degree Mobitz type II or third- degree heart block) with slow ventricular rates (less than 40 beats/min). Patients with presumed cardiac syncope with normal heart rates and rhythm but bifascicular or trifascicular block on ECG Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1883

457.q: A 52-year-old man had a ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest whilst at a railway station. He was successfully resuscitated by a co-passenger. Further evaluation at the hospital including coronary angiography showed no stenotic lesions in the coronary arteries. Which is the most appropriate step for long term management?
457.e: A cardiac electrophysiological study would be necessary to help confirm whether this patient has inducible ventricular tachycardia, and ablation of the pathways if so. However in a young patient with no coronary artery disease demonstrable to revascularize, ICD is necessary to treat a possible further cardiac arrest. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1873

458.q: Which of the following is not a described association for Mitral valve prolapse?
458.e: Syndromes with MVP as a feature Marfan syndrome Ehler Danlos syndrome Klinefelter syndrome Osteogenesis imperfecta Autosomal dominant Polycystic kidney disease Pseudoxanthoma elasticum Barlow syndrome is synonymous with Mitral valve prolapse Noonan syndrome is associated with peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and atrial septal defect. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2000

458.q: A 65-year-old man has renal bruits, renal impairment and hypertension. Which one of the following tests is most appropriate?
o: Magnetic resonance angiography(MRA) of renal arteries
458.e: From the options above, For renal artery stenosis, MRA remains the best investigation with high sensitivities and specificities. MRI is not effective for detecting stent thrombosis. CT angiography provides excellent imaging of the vessels and is less affected by stents. Risk of contrast nephropathy in renal impairment. Though Intra Arterial angiography remains Gold standard for diagnosis of Large vessel diseases. Doppler is very less expensive but is operator dependent and not useful for distal renal arteries and Fibromuscular dysplasia. Captopril renography has strong negative predictive value. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 278, Pg: 2088-2089.

458.q: A 34-year-old man presented for a routine check-up from company. He was symptom free, but clinical examination suggested a small ventricular septal defect. Which one of the following findings was most likely to have been present?
o: A short systolic murmur at the right sternal edge
A systolic murmur maximal at the apex
A systolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge
458.e: Typically, a small VSD generates a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border(LSB) accompanied by a thrill. The murmur may be heard at the apex but is usually loudest at the LSB . Very small defects may generate an early/late systolic murmur. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:234,264 pg:1673,1833

459.q: Which one of the following sets of components of cigarette smoke is a causal agent of coronary artery disease -
o: Nicotine and carbon monoxide and tar
459.e: Ans. is `b' i.e., Nicotine and carbon monoxide and tar Mechanisms for smoking-induced Coronary heart disease Carbon monoxide induces atherogenesis. Nicotine stimulation of adrenergic drive raising both BP and myocardial oxygen demand. Lipid metabolism with fall in protective high-density lipoproteins. Note : Tar is associated with carcinogenesis (not atherosclerosis). But amongst the given options option b is the best answer as it consists of both nicotine and CO.

459.q: The earliest ECG abnormality in a patient with hyperkalemia is:
459.e: ECG changes start to manifest usually when serum K > 6 mEq/L The earliest ECG finding in a patient with hyperkalemia is tall, tented T waves It is followed by other changes like P wave flattening, PR prolongation, QRS widening, appearance of sine wave pattern Hypokalemia is characterised by ECG changes like T wave flattening/inversion, ST segment depression, appearance of 'u' wave and prolonged QU interval. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1911

459.q: A 62-year-old smoker is admitted with nausea, sweating and central crushing chest pain. A 12 lead ECG reveals ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely to have been affected in this case?
459.e: Right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, the posterior third of the interventricular septum, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and a portion of the posterior wall of the left ventricle. (leads II, III, aVF corresponds to inferior wall) Occasionally the posterior interventricular septum may be supplied by a branch of the of the left circumflex artery, called left dominant circulation. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries arise at the left main coronary artery bifurcation and supply the anterior left ventricle, the bulk of the interventricular septum (anterior two thirds), the apex, and the lateral and posterior left ventricular walls. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2035

460.q: A 68-year-old man has a 2 cm adenoma removed from his sigmoid colon. The biopsy results confirm an adenocarcinoma in situ with moderately differentiated dysplastic cells. The pathology report confirms total excision with clear resection margins. What is the most appropriate follow up management for this patient?
460.e: The first thing to note is the question is about planned management. This patient has been picked up early and has had a tumor resected. His CEA would be normal and would not be expected to be elevated until the disease was quite established on the TNM scale. However, this patient'' prognosis would be excellent but he is by definition someone with increased risk. Therefore, he should continue to be reviewed with colonoscopy annually for at least two years. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:81 Pg: 640

460.q: Which of the following drug-eluting stent belongs to first generation with higher rates of stent thrombosis?
460.e: First generation drug eluting stents include Sirolimus and Paclitaxel which have higher risk of restenosis and late stent thrombosis. Second generation stents including Biolimus, Zotarolimus and Everolimus have lower chances of these complications. Reference: Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2067

460.q: A patient presents with sudden onset aphasia and hemiparesis. The Deficit resolved within 2 hours and the CT Scan of the patient is normal. On examination BP is 160 /110 mm Hg. What is the next best step in management?
o: MRI head to check for ischemia
CT Angiography to look for occlusion in vessel
460.e: The patient in the question has a TIA(Transient Ischemic Attack). The next best step is to find out the source of the thrombus and treat it to prevent the recurrence and stroke. CT angiography of vessels in the head and neck to find the source of the clot.

461.q: Which is not correct regarding RA?
o: The incidence of RA increases between 25 and 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 and then decreases
The most common pattern of joint involvement is symmetrical and polyarticular.
Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark of RA
Macrocytic anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in RA
461.e: A normochromic, normocytic anemia often develops in patients with RA and is the most common hematologic abnormality. Macrocytic anemia may occur in RA due to Methotrexate toxicity. Flexor tenosynovitis can occur in RA. It causes trigger fingers. The most common tendon involved is Flexor Pollicis Longus. The age of onset of RA is between 25 to 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 , after which it decreases. The most common pattern of involvement is symmetrical, polyarthritis. DIP is usually not involved, but if so, it is often due to OA. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2753

461.q: Which of the following drugs target TNF ?
461.e: Etanercept is an Anti TNFα agent used in the management of RA. TNFα agents used in the management of RA includes: Monoclonal antibodies: Infliximab, Adalimumab, Golumumab and Certrolizumab pegol Etanercept is a soluble fusion protein comprising of TNFα receptor 2 in covalent linkage with Fc portion of IgG. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761

461.q: Which drugs are unsafe and unequivocally contraindicated during pregnancy in a RA patient? 1. HCQ 2. Methotrexate 3. Sulfasalazine 4. Leflunomide 5. TNF alpha inhibitors 6. Glucocorticoids Choose the correct combinations of unsafe drugs?
461.e: Flares during pregnancy are generally treated with low doses of prednisone; hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are probably the safest DMARDs to use during pregnancy. Methotrexate and leflunomide therapy are contraindicated during pregnancy due to their teratogenicity in animals and humans. Biologicals are thought to be safe in the second trimester. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch:358, Pg:2765

462.q: A 52-year-old patient who has had chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer 6 months earlier comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath on exertion. Her BP is 125/78 mmHg, her pulse is 94/min and her apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line. CXR - Cardiomegaly, increased shadowing consistent with mild pulmonary oedema at both bases Which chemotherapeutic agent is most likely to be responsible for this patient's symptoms?
462.e: Doxorubicin can be associated with cardiac failure, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and tachyarrhythmias. Platinum based chemotherapies are associated with peripheral neuropathy, and bleomycin with interstitial pneumonitis and a specific skin lesion called 'flagellate dermatitis'. Drugs causing dilated cardiomyopathy Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) Trastuzumab (Herceptin) Tacrolimus Zidovudine Drugs like NSAIDs, Thiazolidinediones can cause fluid retention and thus worsen heart failure in patients with underlying disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 737,1964

462.q: A 52-year-old man suffers an extensive anterior myocardial infarction but recovers well in hospital. His pre-discharge ECHO shows him to have an ejection fraction 35%. He is otherwise asymptomatic. His medications on discharge should include which of the following?
o: Aspirin, metoprolol, ramipril and a statin
Aspirin, atenolol, ramipril, furosemide and a statin
Aspirin, isosorbide mononitrate, ramipril and a statin
Aspirin, nitrate, losartan and a statin
462.e: Following a myocardial infarction, patients with LV dysfunction benefit from taking β-Blockers and RAAS blockers. There is strong evidence supporting the use of aspirin and a statin post-MI. In the absence of anginal pain, prophylactic use of nitrates is not mandatory. Diuretics is indicated for patients with symptomatic heart failure and those with fluid overload. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2048-50

462.q: Kussmaul's sign is classically described in:
462.e: Answer is C (Constrictive pericarditis) Kussmaul's sign is classically described in association with Constrictive Pericarditis.
