Kussmaul's sign refers to paradoxical elevation of JVP/CVP during inspiration (In healthy persons venous pressure falls during inspiration because pressures in the right heart decrease as intrathoracic pressures fall) The Kussmaul's sign is classically described in association with Constrictive pericarditis. Kussmaul's sign is however also seen in association with Right Ventricular Infarction, Restrictive Cardiomyopathy, Pulmonary Embolism and Advanced Systolic Severe Heart Failure

463.q: A 24-year-old woman collapsed in a New York City subway station. An autopsy showed that a blood clot had travelled to her lung and caused her death. The medical examiner ultimately ruled that the blood clot was caused by the use of a birth control patch. Which of the following occurs if the blood flow to an alveolus is totally obstructed by a pulmonary thromboembolism?
o: The V/Q ratio of the alveolus equals zero
The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to that in the inspired air
The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to the mixed venous PO2
There will be an increase in shunting (venous admixture) in the lung
463.e: A pulmonary thromboembolism results in areas of the lung that are ventilated, but not perfused, yielding V/Q ratios of infinity and an increase in alveolar deadspace. When the V/Q ratio equals infinite, the PAO2 of the affected alveoli will be the same as that in the humidified inspired air because atmospheric air enters the alveoli via the process of ventilation but no gas exchange takes place because the alveoli are not perfused. Areas of the lung that are perfused but not ventilated constitute areas of shunting (venous admixture), characterized as a V/Q ratio equal to 0, and having PAO2 values that equilibrate with the mixed venous blood. Reference: Kasper et al., pp 282, 1561. Levitzky, pp 114-117. Stead, pp 272-273.

463.q: Causes of a small pupil include which of the following?
463.e: Causes of small pupils include: Horner's syndrome Old age Pontine haemorrhage Argyll Robertson pupil Drugs and poisons (opiates, organophosphates). Causes of dilated pupils include: Holmes-Adie (myotonic) pupil Third nerve palsy Drugs and poisons (atropine, cobalt [CO], ethylene glycol). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 216

463.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a small amount of haemoptysis and breathlessness. He does not have pleuritic chest pain and has normal oxygen saturation. In considering the potential diagnosis, haemoptysis can occur with which of the following diagnoses?
463.e: Haemoptysis can be caused by pulmonary embolism, tuberculous infection, aspergilloma, bronchial carcinoma, good pasture's syndrome and Wegener's granulomatosis. Interstitial lung disease presents with dry cough along with progressive dyspnoea. Asthma presents with episodic breathlessness and cough in exposure to cold or allergens. Goitre presents as neck swelling; if large, it may compress the trachea causing stridor and breathlessness; retrosternal extension causes venous congestion due to compression of superior vena cava. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 39, Pg:270-272

464.q: Kluver bucy syndrome is due to the lesion in which of the following structure
464.e: Kluver-Bucy Syndrome Occurs due to Bilateral Ablation of the Amygdala Characterized by, Not able to recognize objects by sight - Visual agnosia Tendency to examine objects excessively by mouth Hyperorality Compulsion to intensively explore the immediate environment - Hypermetamorphosis No longer show fear or anger, even when such a reaction is appropriate - Placidity Eat excessively even when not hungry, or may eat objects that are not food - Hyperphagia Augmentation in sexual behavior - Hypersexuality Reference: Guyton, 13th edition page no.760

464.q: A 74-year-old man developed ataxia, then exhibited incontinence, frequent confusion, and difficulty with memory. Neurologic examination shows a bradykinetic, broad-based, magnetic gait, prominent memory loss, and decreased executive functioning. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
464.e: This patient has normal pressure hydrocephalus (PH), which is a clinical syndrome produced by the build-up of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Patients have enlarged ventricles often with normal opening pressures on lumbar puncture. It is characterized by the classic triad (with the accompanying mnemonic): "Wet": urinary incontinence "Wacky": dementia (memory loss, slowed thought) "Wobbly" gait abnormality (apraxic "magnetic" gait) PH is thought to be caused by impaired CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations. It is idiopathic in half of the cases. Secondary causes include meningitis, brain trauma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or prior brain surgery. The treatment for NPH is ventricular shunting. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt drains excess CSF to the abdomen, where it is absorbed. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 503-504

464.q: Unable to consolidate long term memory. Which lobe of the brain is involved
464.e: Answer- C. Parietal Medial temporal lobe is the area of brain responsible for consolidation, i.e. processing of short term memory into long term memory. 1043. Gerstmanns syndrome all except a) Acalculia b) Agraphia c) Aphasia d) Agnosia Correct Answer - C Answer- C. Aphasia Gerstmann syndrome consists of :

465.q: A 58-year-old woman with epilepsy refractory to medical therapy is hospitalised for deep brain stimulation. This new modality uses a pacemaker-like device to stimulate which of the following structures?
465.e: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) therapy uses a pacemaker-like device to deliver targeted electrical stimulation to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. The therapy is FDA-approved with conditions for adjunctive treatment for partial-onset seizures in adults with medically refractory epilepsy. DBS is also FDA-approved for treatment of advanced Parkinson disease and essential tremor. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number. 417

465.q: A 26-year-old woman with lifelong epilepsy controlled with medication has just found out that she is pregnant. She has seizures once a month but seem to be controlled at present. Which of the following statements about epilepsy in pregnancy is true?
o: Valproate is considered a drug of choice
She should be taking high doses of folic acid
She will likely have no change in seizure activity during pregnancy
465.e: Women with epilepsy are often very concerned about pregnancy and what effect the medications might have on fetal development. Planning is the most important component. All women considering pregnancy should be on high doses of folic acid prior to conception. Valproate and barbiturates should be avoided. Those women already on valproate and barbiturates should be switched to other drugs before pregnancy when possible. When seizures are controlled, maintenance medication may be reduced, if possible, to the lowest dose that provides control. If seizures are not controlled, medications and dosages will need to be adjusted prior to pregnancy, if possible. The frequency and severity of seizures may change during pregnancy. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number 430

465.q: A 66-year-old man presents with seizures. Past medical history includes a smoking history of 30 cigarettes a day for many years. His family report a weight loss over the past 8 months.Serum electrolytes show: Sodium 109 mmol/L (135-145) Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) Glucose 126 mg/dL Urea 3.0 mmol/L (3.2-8.1) Urine sodium : 68 mmol/ L These findings are most likely to be due to:
465.e: The biochemistry points to a syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, with a low serum osmolality [2(Na + K) + urea + glucose]. The clinical picture is consistent with small cell carcinoma of the lung, which is often associated with SIADH. SIADH should be diagnosed only after ruling out hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency. Diuretic use associated hyponatremia could be associated with low normal serum potassium. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2924

466.q: A patient with parkinsonism is being treated with levodopa. He suffers from irregular, involuntary muscle jerks that affect the proximal muscles of the limbs. Which of the following statements about these symptoms is most accurate?
o: Coadministration of muscarinic blockers prevents the occurrence of dyskinesias during treatment with levodopa
Drugs that activate dopamine receptors can exacerbate dyskinesias in a patient taking levodopa
Dyskinesias are less likely to occur if levodopa is administered with carbidopa
The symptoms are usually reduced if the dose of levodopa is increased
466.e: The form and severity of dyskinesias resulting from levodopa may vary widely in individual patients. Dyskinesias occur in up to 80% of patients receiving levodopa for long periods. With continued treatment, dyskinesias may develop at a dose of levodopa that was previously well tolerated. Muscarinic receptor blockers do not prevent their occurrence. They occur more commonly in patients treated with levodopa in combination with carbidopa or with other dopamine receptor agonists. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 506-508

466.q: Extrapyramidal syndrome like side effects are seen in -
466.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Haloperidol Drugs causing extrapvramidal effects o Butyrophenones (Haloperidol) o Methyldopa o OCP'S o Reserpine o Levodopa o Metoclopromide o Phenothiazines o Tricyclic Antidepressants

466.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with slowed mentation, lack of coordination, and brief writhing movements of her hands that are not rhythmic with delusions. Her mother has had similar symptoms. Genetic testing shows mutation on chromosome 4. It is very likely that the most appropriate drug for treatment will be
466.e: Although further diagnosis is desirable, choreo-athetosis with decreased mental abilities and psychosis (paranoia) suggests that this patient has the symptoms of Huntington’s disease. Drugs that are partly ameliorative include agents that deplete dopamine (eg, tetrabenazine) or that block dopamine receptors (eg, haloperidol). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 509-511

467.q: All of the following drugs worsen myasthenia gravis except:
467.e: Drugs that may exacerbate myasthenia gravis and potentiate the action of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants are: Antibiotics Aminoglycosides e.g Streptomycin Tetracyclines Quinolones e.g ciprofloxacin Macrolides e.g erythromycin Non-depolarizing muscle relaxants e.g d-Tubocurarine Beta-blockers like propranolol, atenolol, metoprolol Local anaesthetics Botulinum toxin Quinine derivatives like quinine, quinidine, chloroquine, mefloquine Magnesium Penicillamine

467.q: A 50 year old patient has a 2 year history of weight loss and diarrhea. He also gives a history of episodes of flushing. VIP syndrome is considered by the admitting physician. Which one of the following is a feature of VIPoma syndrome?
o: Induction of VIP release by somatostatin
467.e: VIPomas [vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) originate in amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation (APUD) cells of the gastroenteropancreatic endocrine system and in adrenal or extra-adrenal neurogenic sites. Features of VIP syndrome include watery diarrhea (100%), hypochlorhydria (70% in adults), hyperglycemia (20-50% in adults), hypercalcemia (20-50% in adults), flushing (20% in adults) and hypokalemia due to diarrhea. Initial treatment is directed toward correcting volume and electrolyte abnormalities by using potassium chloride and sodium bicarbonate. Octreotide controls diarrhea in 80% of cases. Glucocorticoids reduce symptoms in 50% of patients with VIPoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 84 Pg: 665

467.q: A 56-year-old man presents with a history of abdominal discomfort that is relieved by passing stool. In the past month his stools have been looser in nature and he has had a feeling of urgency and incomplete evacuation. His symptoms seem to be worse with eating. He has also noticed that he has passed mucus per rectum. He is overweight with a BMI of 28 kg/m2. His weight has fallen. He says that he has adjusted his diet in the last six months. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
467.e: Weight loss, tenesmus and a recent change in bowel habit all point towards an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer. Onset of symptoms in later life and a relatively short duration (that is, weeks rather than years) also point towards a 'biological' cause rather than irritable bowel syndrome. The passage of mucus per rectum is a normal physiological function and not indicative of underlying pathology. The symptoms are not suggestive of malabsorption. Diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease are both potential diagnoses but given the duration of symptoms less likely than a colonic neoplasm. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, CH: 81, Pg: 639

468.q: A 22 year old female patient presents with a 5-day history of ascending muscle weakness in both hands and feet. EMGs confirm acute demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy. What treatment should be started?
468.e: The diagnosis is Guillain Barre syndrome . It is preceded by diarrhea (e.g. campylobacter) or chest infections (e.g. mycoplasma) in two thirds of cases. Autonomic dysfunction and hyporeflexia are associated. P rogressive symmetric ascending weakness is characteristic . Management: Plasma exchange (OR) IVIG (IV immunoglobulins) - 2 g/kg/day for 5 days. As effective as plasma exchange. Easier to administer and fewer side effects. No benefit in combining both treatments. Steroids and immunosuppressants have not been shown to be beneficial. Regular FVC (Forced vital capacity ) to monitor respiratory function and assess need for ventilation. ICU admission is recommended when FVC is less than 20 mL/kg and intubation is recommended in most cases when FVC is less than 15 mL/kg . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 ST Ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3503

468.q: Which type ofAmyloidosis is caused by mutation of the transthyretin protein ?
468.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy Transthyretin (TTR) is normal serum protein that binds and transport thyroxine and retinol. TTR can cause following types of amyloidosis :? Mutant TTR : - Mutation in TTR can cause syndrome of familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy or familial amylodotic cardiomyopathy. Wild (non-mutant) TTR : - There is no mutation of TTR and wild type TTR forms fibrils which results in senile systemic amyloidosis (senile cardiac amyloidosis).

468.q: The basic abnormality in increased fasting blood glucose is:
468.e: The basic abnormality in increased fasting glucose is high hepatic glucose output mainly due to reduced basal secretion of insulin or hepatic insulin resistance Raised post-prandial glucose values is due to decreased peripheral utilization (muscle and adipose tissue) First and second phase insulin secretion occurs in response to meals Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 3096-3099

469.q: In multiple sclerosis slow conduction of sensory and motor pathway is due to
469.e: Autoimmune inflammation and demyelination of CNS (brain and spinal cord) with subsequent axonal damage. Most often affects females aged 20-40 Symptoms may exacerbate with increased body temperature (eg, hot bath, exercise). Relapsing and remitting is most common clinical course. ↑IgG level and myelin basic protein in CSF. Oligoclonal bands aid in diagnosis. MRI is gold standard. Periventricular plaques A (areas of oligodendrocyte loss and reactive gliosis). Multiple white matter lesions disseminated in space and time.

469.q: patient underwent adrenalectomy and developed pigmentation and fatigue diagnosis?
469.e: Removal of adrenal gland leads to Addison's disease. Deficiency of mainly 3 hormones Due to mineralocorticoid deficiency: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, small heart, nausea, vomiting Due to glucocorticoids deficiency: Hypoglycemia, fatigue, anorexia, skin pigmentation, weight loss, myalgia Due to adrenal androgen deficiency: Lack of energy, dry & itchy skin, loss of libido in women & loss of axillary & pubic hairs in women.

469.q: With regard to a patient with a neuromuscular disorder on the critical care unit which is true:
o: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be avoided in patients with hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
Rocuronium use should be avoided in patients with myasthenia gravis
Patients with motor neurone disease typically require double the standard dose of suxamethonium to provide optimum intubating conditions.
Local anesthesia can exacerbate symptoms of multiple sclerosis
469.e: The use of suxamethonium is challenging in patients with neuromuscular disorders. Key points to remember include relative resistance to depolarisation in myasthenia gravis, often requiring an increased dosage, and the development of extrajunctional receptors in many of the myotonias, leading to extensive depolarisation and potentially fatal hyperkalemia with the use of depolarising neuromuscular blockade. In addition, there are disease-specific aspects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade that should be noted,including the relative sensitivity in conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome. Hence dose reduction to 10-20% should be considered in addition to ongoing monitoring of blockade. Reference: Harrison 20 th 3188-3200

470.q: A 37-year-old female presents with headaches. Examination reveals papilloedema. Which of the following would make the diagnosis of benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) unlikely?
o: Normal ventricles on CT or MRI scan
470.e: BIH is typically associated with papilloedema, reduced venous pulsation and normal appearances of the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A VIth nerve palsy is a recognised association. Reflexes are preserved and plantars are flexor. Extensor plantars suggest an alternative diagnosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 16Pg: 116

470.q: A 30 year old male comes to you with history of recurrent retro orbital pains that occurs once or twice in a day, each lasting for around an hour, associated with ipsilateral lacrimation. He has had similar episodes before which occurred for a period of 1week, after which he remains asymptomatic for around 6-8 months. Which of the following statements is false regarding the preventive therapy of the above condition?
o: Since the episodes lasts only for around 3 weeks, steroids are a good option for preventive therapy
Verapamil is the first line treatment for episodes that lasts longer
Lithium is a drug that is of proven benefit in preventing the episodes of this head ache
CGRP monoclonal antibody is useful in chronic cluster head ache
470.e: The patient in the question suffers from cluster head ache. The bouts or episodes occur for a very short period of 1 weeks. The preventive therapy of cluster head ache depends up on the duration of bouts. For shorter bouts the drugs that are approved are: Prednisolone CGRP monoclonal antibody Galcanezumab Great Occipital nerve injection with lignocaine or steroids Verapamil For bouts that are longer, the drugs that are approved are Verapamil 160-960mg/day Lithium 400-800mg/day Non invasive vagal stimulation Deep brain stimulation Melatonin, Topiramate and Gabapentin are of unproven benefits So among the options, the CGRP monoclonal antibody is useful not for chronic cluster head ache or longer bouts, but for shorter bouts of head ache. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3367

470.q: Which of the following statements regarding CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy) is correct?
o: Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain is diagnostic
It is associated with an abnormality of the X chromosome
470.e: CADASIL is a diffuse disease of small arteries, predominantly in the brain. It starts during mid adulthood and is characterised by: Recurrent ischaemic events (transient or permanent) Attacks of migraine with aura Severe mood disorders Sub-cortical dementia and A wide spread leukoencephalopathy on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). CT brain is not diagnostic. Characteristic MRI changes include T2 weighted hyperintensity of the periventricular white matter. A family history is almost always present, as it is an autosomal dominant condition, located to chromosome 19. Infarcts are subcortical, and the thalami and basal ganglia are usually involved. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3343

471.e: Transferrin saturation , which is normally 25-50%, is obtained by the following formula: Transferrin saturation = (Serum iron × 100) ÷ TIBC, where TIBC is total iron binding capacity. Iron-deficiency states are associated with saturation levels Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 63, Pg: 436

471.q: Microcytic erythrocytosis is seen in all except
471.e: Only three situations cause microcytic erythrocytosis: β-thalassemia trait, hypoxic erythrocytosis, and PV. With β-thalassemia trait, the RDW is usually normal, whereas with hypoxic erythrocytosis and PV, the RDW may be elevated due to associated iron deficiency. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 103, Pg: 804

Vitamin B6 dependency syndromes that require pharmacologic doses of vitamin B6 are cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, pyridoxine-responsive (primarily sideroblastic) anemias, and gyrate atrophy with chorioretinal degeneration due to decreased activity of the mitochondrial enzyme ornithine aminotransferase. In these situations, 100-200 mg/d of oral vitamin B6 is required for treatment.

472.q: Most common infectious agents that cause facial palsy is?
472.e: The most common infectious agents that cause facial palsy are herpes simplex virus type 1 (Bell's palsy) and varicella-zoster virus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 193, Pg: 1480

472.q: A 44 year old bank clerk presents with a headache, nausea and ptosis of the left eye with blurred vision. She does not have fatiguability of her eye movements. Examination revealed swelling on the left side of face, proptosis and chemosis of the left eye, left mastoid swelling and left ophthalmoplegia involving cranial nerves. The pupil sizes were equal. A CT of her head is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
472.e: A history of headache and no other obvious cause of ptosis is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Third nerve palsy is associated with dilated pupil and Horner's syndrome is associated with miosis. A CT can be normal, and diagnosis is confirmed with MRI. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3444

472.q: An 80 year old lady is admitted complaining of acute onset weakness in both legs and low back pain for the previous 4 weeks. She has lost 5 kg of weight recently, and has a Hb of 8.5 g/dl. Her cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal but she has reduced power in both lower limbs of 3/5. She has a sensory level at T12 and plantar reflexes are upgoing. Rectal tone was normal. Which is the best next investigation?
472.e: This patient is likely to have cord compression from a metastases to the spine. Urgent MRI scan is required to confirm the diagnosis and a referral for either surgery or radiotherapy can then be made. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3447

473.q: A 25-year-old female presented with a sudden onset of left sided head and neck pain. 24 hours later she presents with sudden onset of right hemiparesis, facial weakness and homonymous hemianopia and left Horner's syndrome. A CT brain showed a left middle cerebral artery territory infarction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
473.e: The presence of neck pain on the left side, followed by a right sided weakness points to the diagnosis of carotid dissection. The two commonest causes of young onset stroke (less than 40 years) are cardio-embolism and carotid artery dissection. Carotid artery dissection is either spontaneous or traumatic. Facial/head/neck pain and Horner's syndrome are characteristic features. Migrainous stroke usually affects the posterior circulation (posterior cerebral artery territory is the commonest). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3341

473.q: A 72-year-old woman presented with an acute, severe occipital headache, unsteadiness of her gait and vomiting. She had a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On examination there was nystagmus to the left, ataxia of the left limbs and gait ataxia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
473.e: Cerebellar haemorrhage The most common symptoms are of severe nausea and vomiting and ataxia. Headache may be severe. Patients with cerebellar haemorrhage can rapidly become comatose within hours after the onset from herniation, because of its limited space in the posterior fossa. Pontine haemorrhage There are numerous nuclei located within the pons. Rapidly deteriorating level of consciousness, impaired extraocular movement and extensive sensorimotor deficits are clinical clues to pontine haemorrhage. Basal ganglia haemorrhage Contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, or hemi-inattention. Aphasia, especially non-fluency and impaired comprehension, is frequently seen if haemorrhage occurs in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 428, Pg: 3350

473.q: A 41 year old man complained of a severe headache. Following this, he then developed nausea and vomiting and came to the ER to be assessed. A CT scan demonstrated blood in the left sylvian fissure. Which of the Following is the most likely cause?
473.e: The history is consistent with a subarachnoid haemorrhage, caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm. Migraine will not cause blood in the Sylvian fissure. Carotid dissection will result in ischemia in the brain rather than bleed. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

474.q: An 18-year-old college student living in a dormitory contracts meningitis, which causes a centrally mediated increase in his respiratory rate. The basic respiratory rhythm is generated in which of the following regions of the brain?
474.e: The main components of the respiratory control pattern generator for the automatic control of breathing are located in the medulla. The basic respiratory rhythm is initiated by a small group of synaptically coupled pacemaker cells in the pre-Botzinger complex on either side of the medulla between the nucleus ambiguus and the lateral reticular nucleus. This basic rhythm can be modified by many factors, including higher centers in the cerebral cortex and hypothalamus and input from the reticular activating system and pontine respiratory centers, including the pneumotaxic center in the nucleus parabrachialis. Reference: Ganong, pp 192-193, 671-673. Levitzky, pp 188-194, 200.
Enterococci are well-known causes of nosocomial UTI-the most common infection caused by these organisms. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 149 Pg: 1199

474.q: Which is true of herpes simplex encephalitis?
474.e: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is associated with high signal in one or both temporal lobes (limbic encephalitis). Seizures are commonly present in HSE. Herpes simplex virus type 1 is the causative virus (not type 2 which is associated with genital herpes). PCR for herpes simplex virus on cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) is a highly specific test. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch:137 Pg: 1095-1097

475.q: PNH patients will be having deficient surface proteins that normally protect the red cells from activated compliments. What are the two deficient surface proteins?
475.e: The definitive diagnosis of PNH is based on the demonstration that a substantial proportion of the patient's red cells have an increased susceptibility to complement (C), due to the deficiency on their surface of proteins (particularly CD59 and CD55). Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th Edition, Page

475.q: A 65 year old man presents with an immune-mediated thrombocytopenia. He has been treated with antibiotics during a recent hospital admission. Which of the following is most likely implicated in the new development?
475.e: Drugs causing Thrombocytopenia Trimethoprim/ sulfamethoxazole Penicillin Vancomycin Rifampin Ethambutol Amphotericin B Quinine Heparin Digoxin Amiodarone Ethanol Quinidine H2 -antagonists NSAIDs Acetaminophen Chemotherapy Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 115, pg. 908

475.q: A 71 year old patient has a set of investigations due to lethargy. She complains of polyuria and generalised back pains. Upon investigation, she has the following results: Hb 8 g/dl MCV 100 fl Platelets 190 x 10^9/L total protein 9 g/dl Albumin 3.4 (3.7-4.9) g/dl calcium 12 mg/dl phosphate 1.8 mg/dl What is the appropriate next investigation?
475.e: The patient in this question has bone pains, hypercalcemia with impaired renal function and AG reversal, all pointing to the diagnosis of Myeloma. Hence the next best step would be a serum protein electrophoresis. 24 hour urine albumin or protein and LFT is of little use in this clinical scenario. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 111 Pg : 865-867

476.q: A 36 year old man presents with acute stiffness swelling of his knees and ankles, a painful rash on his legs. The ESR was 107 mm/hour. Chest Xray showed hilar lymphadenopathy bilaterally. What is the likely progression of the arthralgia?
476.e: The description typical of acute sarcoidosis - erythema nodosum, oligoarthropathy and hilar lymphadenopathy. This usually has a good prognosis, with resolution over 6-8 weeks. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 367, Pg: 2833

476.q: Which of the following is false :
o: Cystitis is a risk factor for recurrent cystitis and pyelonephritis.
Recurrent infection leads to renal failure.
ASB is common among elderly but does not in itself increase the risk of death.
Infection plays prime role for development of Chronic Interstitial Nephritis
476.e: Cystitis is a risk factor for recurrent cystitis and pyelonephritis. ASB is common among elderly and catheterized patients but does not in itself increase the risk of death. infection does not play a primary role in chronic interstitial nephritis; the primary etiologic factors in this conditions are analgesic abuse, obstruction, reflux, and toxin exposure. In the presence of underlying renal abnormalities Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1078

476.q: A 25-year-old man has symptoms of lethargy. Blood results reveal a urea of 55 mg/dl and creatinine of 3.9 mg/dl. Which of the following indicates chronic(rather than acute) renal failure?
476.e: The clinical clues to chronicity of renal impairment is symptoms of azotemia > 3 months, renal osteodystrophy, bilaterally scarred kidneys and broad cast in urinary sediments. Anemia can occur in both AKI and CKD. Disorders of Calcium and Phosphorus homeostasis can also be seen in AKI and CKD. Renal osteodystrophy(bone changes) and small sized kidney with a destroyed renal parenchyma, with increased echogenicity and thinned out cortex with isosthenuria and broad cast are the only conclusive findings of chronicity. However, anemia and Ca Phosphate levels in AKI are not the rule but exception. Hence anemia is the best option here. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 52, Pg: 332, 333.

477.q: A 36-year-old man with a history of AIDS and Pneumocystis infection presents to the Emergency Department with severe respiratory distress. The patient is placed on a ventilator at a rate of 16, tidal volume of 600 mL, and FIO2 of 1.0. An arterial blood sample taken 20 minutes later reveals a Po2 of 350 mmHg, a Pco2 of 36 mmHg, and a pH of 7.32. At a barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, and assuming a normal respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, the patient's alveolar oxygen tension is approximately which of the following?
477.e: The alveolar air equation is used to calculate the PAO2. PAO2 = PIO2 - (PaCO2/ R ) Given the barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, FIO2 = 1.0 (100% O2), PaCO2 = 36 mmHg, and R = 0.8, then PAO2 = (1.0)(757 - 47) - (36/0.8) = 710 - 45 = 665 mmHg Pneumocystis is an opportunistic fungal pulmonary pathogen that is an important cause of pneumonia (pneumocystosis) in immunocompromised hosts. HIV patients with a CD4 + cell count below 200/μL have an increased risk of developing Pneumocystis pneumonia. According to new, and still evolving nomenclature, Pneumocystis carinii is the name of the organism derived from rats, and Pneumocystis jiroveci is the name of the organism derived from humans. Reference: Ganong, p 660. Kasper et al., pp 1194-1196, 1583, 1592-1595. Levitzky, p 75. Stead et al., pp 202-204.

477.q: Which is the most common form of localized lymphadenopathy in adults?
477.e: In adults, the most common localized form is inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy In children, it is cervical lymphadenopathy Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 66 Pg: 458

477.q: Which of the following statements is true? 1. In the context of a decreased GFR, autoregulatory mechanisms lead to prostacyclin mediated dialation of afferent arteriole and ACE mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. 2. NSAIDS cause inhibition of afferent arteriolar vasodilation and a decrease in GFR 3. NSAIDS cause inhibition of efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and a decrease in GFR. 4. NSAIDS cause inhibition of efferent arteriolar vasodilation and a decrease in GFR.
477.e: This question deals with renal autoregulatory mechanism. Under circumstances of reduced perfusion pressure, within the autoregulatory range, the GFR is maintained by the dialation of the afferent arteriole and constriction of the efferent arteriole . The former is mediated by prostaglandins and the latter by Angiotensin II. So drugs that inhibit the production of vasodilatory prostaglandins, eg NSAIDS, will reduce the GFR by inhibiting prostaglandin mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation. ACEI or ARBs reduce the GFR by inhibiting Angiotensin II mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Hence statements 1 and 2 are correct. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Chap 310 Pg. 2298

478.q: At what intervals should monitoring of patients on HAART should be done?
478.e: CD4 cell count and viral load have to be monitored every 3-6 months to monitor the response to treatment. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 334

478.q: A 38-year-old man presents with a 16 week history of indigestion. Five years previously he had been treated for a duodenal ulcer. Investigations reveal: Fasting gastrin 120 pmol/l (<55) Which one of the following statements regarding gastrin is correct?
o: It acts upon the G cells of the stomach
It inhibits the secretion of pancreatic bicarbonate
It is produced by the parietal cells of the stomach
Its release is stimulated by gastric luminal peptides
478.e: Gastrin is produced in response to Stimulation by neural reflex pathways By the direct effect of digested peptides on the G cells themselves. Gastrin is mainly produced by the G cells of the gastric antrum. Gastrin stimulates the production of bicarbonate by pancreas. It stimulates the parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 324, Pg: 2435

478.q: A 44-year-old woman presents with a mass in her neck and symptoms of choking/ shortness of breath when she lies down. Investigations; Hb 14.1 g/dl WCC 5.4 x 10^9/L PLT 235 x 10^9/L Na+ 140 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 0.6 mg/dl TSH 0.9 U/l You suspect that she may have retrosternal extension of the goitre. Which of the following would be the investigation of choice for this patient to determine the degree of retrosternal involvement?
478.e: Whilst a plain radiograph may be used to demonstrate retrosternal thyroid extension and tracheal deviation, a CT of the chest is more sensitive and specific in determining the extent of disease. Thyroid ultrasound is most useful for determining the nature of thyroid nodules. Radioisotope scanning has a role to play in determining the uptake of thyroid hormone and as such the underlying diagnosis behind thyrotoxicosis, or in identifying cold nodules within the gland which may raise the suspicion of an underlying neoplasm. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2946

479.q: The most significant risk factor for cancer is
479.e: The most significant risk factor for cancer overall is age. 2/3 rd of all cases were seen in those aged >65 years. Reference: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 72, Pg: 508

479.q: Overall % of developing cancer in males during lifetime is
479.e: Overall, men have a 40.5% risk of developing cancer at some time during their lives; women have a 38.9% lifetime risk Reference: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 69, Pg: 482

479.q: A 74-year-old man was admitted with pallor, light-headedness and loss of energy. On the day prior to admission he had reported loose dark stools. Examination revealed a pulse of 110 per minute and a blood pressure of 106/70 mmHg. Investigations revealed: Haemoglobin 6.2 g/dl (14-18) MCV 72 fl (80-96) White cell count 11.3 x 10^9/L (4-11) Platelet count 480 x 10^9/L (150-400) What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
479.e: This patient has significant microcytic anaemia with a hemoglobin of He should be resuscitated with blood transfusion and then sent for upper GI endoscopy. Red cell administration may be a part of volume replacement even without hemorrhage in order to optimize oxygen delivery if hemoglobin content is A barium meal will not help a bleeding vessel. Parenteral iron administration is for chronic anaemia, not acute bleeds. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch : 303, Pg: 2240

480.q: All of the following can be seen in refeeding syndrome except:
480.e: This is characterized by shift in fluid and electrolyte shift in malnourished patients undergoing refeeding. It is more common with parenteral fluids . It results in hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 25, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 338

480.q: Early management of shock focuses on restoring circulating volume, maintaining perfusion and using appropriate fluids. Several principles guide initial resuscitation. One of the following statements is false. Identify the incorrect statement.
o: First line therapy is putting a short wide bore intravenous cannula and start infusion
Albumin should not be the start in immediate period
Ringer lactate is most physiological fluid and ideal crystalloid
It is ideal to give inotropic agents regardless of preload to heart
480.e: Explanation: Inotropic agents should never be started without ensuring adequate preload. In shock, the first step is to restore circulating volume with crystalloids. Starting inotropes before correcting hypovolemia can worsen ischemia, increase oxygen demand and cause arrhythmias. Principles of fluid therapy in shock: The first step is to gain rapid venous access with a short, wide-bore cannula and begin crystalloid infusion. (Option A) Ringer lactate is considered the most physiological crystalloid solution due to its electrolyte composition. ( Option C) Colloids (like albumin) are not recommended in the immediate resuscitation period because crystalloids are faster, safer and more accessible. (Option B) Inotropes are only considered after adequate fluid resuscitation if hypotension persists. (Option D)

480.q: Calculate the calories from TPN containing 100 grams of dextrose, 30 grams of amino acids and 40 grams of lipids:
480.e: 100*3.4=340 kcal from dextrose 40*10=400 kcal from lipid 30*4=120 kcal from aminoacid Total 860 kcal Reference: https://jamieberray.weebly.com/uploads/5/3/0/9/53090885/parenteral nutrition calculations.pdf

481.q: A child was brought to the ER with a lesion on the forearm as seen. As a surgery resident, you decide to excise the lesion in emergency ot. Which of the following investigations will test for the entire coagulation?
481.e: Thromboelastography can be used for guiding intra operative transfusion. But it cant be employed in other disorders of bleeding and thrombosis. It has some role in venom induced coagulopathy

481.q: What would be maintenance fluid rate in case of shock in a man with 65 kgs of weight?
481.e: For patient weighting more than 40 kgs simple rule to calculate maintenance water is = weight in kgs +40 So, in our patient maintenance fluid would be 65 + 40=105 ml/hour. Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 4, Edition: 21 st

481.q: Which of the following is not the complication of massive transfusion?
481.e: Complications from massive transfusion Complications from massive transfusion include: coagulopathy; hypocalcaemia; hyperkalaemia; hypokalaemia; hypothermia.

482.q: Best gas used for creating pneumoperitonium at laparoscopy is :
482.e: CO2 CO, is the gas used to create pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopy. Other option is - N20 : But it is expensive, less soluble in blood and supports combustion. Also know : Instrument used for creating pneumoperitoneum is veress needle. Flow Rate of CO, for creating pneumoperitoneum 200 - 2000 ml/min & pressure between 15 - 25 mm of Hg.

482.q: Which among the following is a false statement for physical structure of suture material?
o: Monofilament sutures have poor knotting ability
Multifilament sutures have good knotting ability
Multifilament sutures have less bacterial contamination
482.e: Physical structure . Suture material may be monofilament or multifilament. Monofilament suture material is smooth and tends to slide through tissues easily without any sawing action, but is more difficult to knot effectively. Such material can be easily damaged by gripping it with needle holder or forceps and this can lead to fracture of the suture material. Multifilament or braided sutures are much easier to knot, but have a surface area of several thousand times that of monofilament sutures and thus have a capillary action and interstices where bacteria may lodge and be responsible for persistent infection or sinuses. In order to overcome some of these problems, certain materials are produced as a braided suture, which is coated with silicone in order to make it smooth. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 90

482.q: Which among the following is an absorbable suture material?
482.e: Polygalactin also known as vicryl is a monofilament synthetic absorbable suture used in CBD, ureter and bowel surgeries Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 92

483.q: A 16-year-old boy was brought to the emergency ward with wheeze and an extensive rash after eating at a Chinese restaurant. On examination, he had extensive wheezes in his chest, stridor, as well as urticaria covering his upper and lower limbs. His BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
483.e: The scenario is consistent with a food allergy, e.g. nuts, leading to an anaphylactic reaction. The patient should be treated with hydrocortisone (IV or IM) as well as antihistaminic drugs. Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant condition caused by C1 esterase deficiency which leads to recurrent attacks of angioedema Bronchitis presents with a productive cough, fever and dyspnoea. It is usually caused by a viral infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-2728.

483.q: Which of the following defines sepsis according to SEPSIS-3 criteria?
o: Suspected or documented infection & increase in any two of the SOFA points
Suspected or documented infection plus vasopressor therapy needed to maintain MAP>65 mmHg and serum lactate >2.0mmol/L despite adequate fluid restriction
Suspected or documented infection plus two SIRS criteria
483.e: Sepsis is defined by SEPSIS-3 criteria as suspected or documented infection and an acute increase in >2 sepsis-related organ failure assessment (SOFA) points. Documented or suspected infection + Need for vasopressors to maintain MAP more than or equal to 65mmHg and elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L ) defines the septic shock according to SEPSIS -3 criteria.SIRS criteria were included in earlier criteria (SEPSIS I & II). Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20th Ed chap 297, pg.2045

483.q: All electrolyte abnormalities are seen in immediate postoperative period except:
483.e: Option A : Due to increased catabolism in response to surgical stress there will be Negative nitrogen balance occuring. Option B : There is frequently shifting of potassium into cells as well as losses occur in postoperative period that leads to hypokalemia. Option C : Following surgical stress there will be increased glucose production but decreased glucose utilization at tissue level due to insulin resistance, that leads to glucose intolerance. Option D : Following surgery there will be shifting of fluid into extracellular space seen that leads to Hypernatremia. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 1, Edition: 28 th

484.q: All of the following are component of revised trauma score except
484.e: The Revised Trauma Score is another well-studied physiologic scoring system that characterizes the condition of the injured patient by incorporating - Glasgow Coma Scale Systolic blood pressure Respiratory rate. These scores have been of value for research purposes and have been successfully used to make triage decisions. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 389

484.q: Which one of the following is the first priority if you are performing a primary survey on a patient?
o: Ensuring patient is oriented to time place and person
484.e: Ensuring a patent airway is the first priority in the primary survey. This is essential, because efforts to restore cardiovascular integrity will be futile unless the oxygen content of the blood is adequate. Simultaneously, all patients with blunt trauma require cervical spine immobilization until injury is excluded. This is typically accomplished by applying a hard collar or placing sandbags on both sides of the head with the patient's forehead taped across the bags to the backboard. Soft collars do not effectively immobilize the cervical spine. For penetrating neck wounds , however, cervical collars are not believed useful because they provide no benefit, but may interfere with assessment and treatment Reference : Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 11th, Pg: 184

484.q: Injury severity score to categorise an injury as a severe injury is?
484.e: Baker and colleagues presented the ISS, calculated by summing the squares of the AIS severity codes for the three most severely injured body regions. The ISS ranges from 1 to 75 , with severity groupings being defined as - Minor injury (ISS less than 9) Moderate injury (ISS between 9 and 16) Serious injury (ISS between 16 and 25) Severe injury (ISS more than 25). Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 389

485.q: Inferior thyroid artery supplies which structures 1. Esophagus 2. Thyroid 3. Parathyroid 4. Thymus
485.e: The inferior thyroid artery (ITA) is considered the principal blood supplier of the thyroid gland . The ITA gives rise to the ascending cervical artery, the inferior laryngeal artery, and also gives pharyngeal, tracheal , and esophageal ITA also supplies the four parathyroid glands . Blood supply of esophagus: Cricopharyngeal muscle (inlet of esophagus) is supplied by superior thyroid artery Cervical esophagus: predominantly by inferior thyroid artery Thoracic esophagus: aorta, both right and left bronchial artery, along with descending branch from inferior thyroid artery, intercostal artery and ascending branch from inferior phrenic artery Abdominal esophagus: left gastric artery and inferior phrenic artery Blood supply to the thymus comes from the internal thoracic artery .

485.q: Gold standard investigation for a patient having signs of multiple injuries
485.e: Explanation: Whole-Body CT (WBCT) in Severe Blunt Trauma WBCT (head-to-pelvis with IV contrast) is the gold standard for evaluating the severely injured adult with blunt trauma. Selective (region-specific) imaging has no role in these patients due to the high likelihood of multisystem injury and the need for comprehensive assessment. WBCT is time-critical and should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation to guide timely interventions. If a patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy without prior WBCT , Apply a pelvic binder and do not remove it until a pelvic fracture is excluded. Obtain an immediate pelvic X-ray , either in the emergency department or on arrival to the operating theatre. Key Takeaways: Whole-body CT is the preferred investigation when there are signs of multiple injuries or deranged physiology.

485.q: All of the following statements are incorrect regarding evaluation of patient with chest injury except
o: CT chest is almost universally performed during the initial evaluation of patient with risk of thoracic injury
Deviation of trachea at sternal notch suggest intrathoracic pressure on same side of deviation
Thoracic MDCTA is useful for evaluation of pericardium
Thoracic MDCTA has become the standard approach to evaluation of chest injury
485.e: Thoracic MDCTA has become the standard approach to evaluation of the chest and provides superior visualization of the chest wall, vasculature, pleural spaces, and lung parenchyma. Option A : Chest radiography is almost universally performed during the initial assessment on patients at risk for thoracic injuries. Option B : Deviation of the trachea at the sternal notch may reveal intrathoracic tension on the side opposite the trachea. Option C: Thoracic MDCTA is unreliable for evaluation of pericardium, given cardiac motion degradation. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 405

486.q: Which of the following statement about breast tissue is false?
o: Fibrous stroma is absent beneath the areola
Alveolar epithelium is columnar in the resting phase
15-20 lactiferous ducts open in the nipple
Myoepitheliocytes facilitates the passage of the milk along the ducts
486.e: Alveolar epithelium is cuboidal in the resting phase, and columnar during lactation. The fibrous stroma forms septa (suspensory ligaments of Cooper) which anchor the skin and gland to the pectoral fascia. It forms the major part of the gland but is absent beneath the areola and nipple. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 749

486.q: In lymphatic drainage of the breast, the major portion (about 75%) enters eventually into which group of nodes?
486.e: About 75% of the lymph draining the breast goes to the axillary lymph nodes, via the pectoral lymph nodes. All of this lymph from the pectoral lymph nodes must drain to the central lymph nodes as well. This is why it is so important to examine all these groups of axillary lymph nodes when performing a breast exam. Most of the rest of the lymph drainage from the breast goes to the parasternal nodes, although a small amount goes to the opposite breast and a small amount drains to the abdominal wall. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 737

486.q: Which among the following flaps is not used in breast reconstruction surgery?
486.e: Autologous tissue reconstruction in breast surgery is done using the following muscle flaps- Latissimus dorsi flap - based on the thoracodorsal pedicle Muscle-preserving perforator abdominal flaps - Ex: Deep inferior epigastric perforator flap Transverse rectus abdominis flap - based on superior or inferior epigastric artery or both. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 53, Edition: 27th, Pg: 879

487.q: For which type(s) of cancer is prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) typically given? 1. Lung cancer 2. Liver cancer 3. Prostate cancer 4. Breast cancer
487.e: Explanation: Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) is primarily used to reduce the risk of brain metastases in cancers that have a high likelihood of spreading to the central nervous system. Lung Cancer: PCI is most commonly administered in small cell lung cancer (SCLC) due to its aggressive nature and high tendency to metastasize to the brain. It has been shown to improve overall survival and decrease the incidence of brain metastases in patients who respond to initial treatment. Breast Cancer: PCI may be considered in select cases of breast cancer, particularly in patients at high risk for brain metastases. This includes aggressive subtypes such as HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer . Options A, B, and D are incorrect. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9020164/ https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4477380/

487.q: Where is the most common skeletal metastasis seen in the patient of breast tumour?
487.e: Skeletal metastases occurs via the bloodstream in breast carcinoma. The commonly involved sites in order of frequency include - Lumbar vertebrae - most common Femur Thoracic vertebrae Ribs Skull The deposits are generally more osteolytic than osteoblastic . Metastases may also commonly occur in the liver, lungs and brain and, occasionally, the adrenal glands and ovaries via the bloodstream. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 53, Edition: 27th, Pg: 873

487.q: Which among the following is not a clinical finding of the fibrocystic disease of the breast?
487.e: Nipple discharge is not a feature of fibrocystic disease of the breast. Fibrocystic disease of the breast - Common during the fourth and fifth decades of life , generally lasting until menopause. There is an exaggerated response of breast stroma and epithelium to various circulating and locally produced hormones and growth factors. Characterized by the constellation of premenstrual cyclic breast pain, tenderness, and nodularity. As per Bailey it is not seen, so go with choice 3 Reference: Bailey & Love's SHORT PRACTICE of SURGERY, 28th edition, PART 8: ENDOCRINE AND BREAST, Chapter no.58

488.q: Best diagnostic method for parathyroid adenoma is
488.e: Preference investigations for parathyroid diseases in terms of reliablity ( from best to least ) PET - CT - MOST RELIABLE Sestamibi SPECT - better than Tc99m sestamibi scan Tech 99m - Sestamibi scan- most commonly used USG - LEAST RELIABLE The sensitivity of sestamibi SPECT is 79% for Parathyroid adenoma. The sensitivity of PET\CT is 93 % for Parathyroid adenoma.

488.q: A 45 year old female patient on examination of her breast a 4.5cm * 3cm size irregular mass is felt in the left upper quadrant of the right breast which is not fixed to the pectoralis major muscle and no skin changes, a 2cm*1.5cm lymph node is also palpated in the right axilla. No mass felt in the opposite breast. What all investigations will you do to this patient? 1. Mammography 2. PET scan 3. Biopsy of the breast mass 4. USG guided biopsy of the enlarged axillary lymph node
488.e: According to the case scenario-staging of breast carcinoma - T2N1 - early breast cancer Mammography in two planes and ultrasonography are the first line investigations for imaging the breast, it is done for both the breast and also to look for multicnetricity PET scan is done for locally advanced breast cancer TRU CUT biopsy of lump is the gold standard investigation as it is a tissue diagnosis USG guided biopsy of the enlarged axillary lymph node is of no use as, if axillary lymph node are enlarged itself indicates local metastasis, which should be managed by axillary dissection.

489.q: Which among the following statements is false for inflammatory carcinoma of the breast?
o: Presents with painful, swollen breast with cutaneous oedema
It results from blockage of intramuscular lymphatics with carcinoma cells
489.e: Inflammatory carcinoma - Rare Highly aggressive Presents as a painful, swollen breast, which is warm with cutaneous oedema. Due to blockage of the subdermal lymphatics with carcinoma cells. Inflammatory cancer usually involves at least one-third of the breast and may mimic a breast abscess. A biopsy will confirm the diagnosis and show undifferentiated carcinoma cells. It used to be rapidly fatal but with aggressive chemotherapy and radiotherapy and with salvage surgery the prognosis has improved considerably. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 53, Edition: 27 th , Pg: 872

489.q: Which among the following is not the modality for staging carcinoma?
489.e: The goals of preoperative staging are to gain information on prognosis, to counsel the patient effectively, and to determine the extent of disease to decide the most appropriate course of therapy. The three main treatment pathways are upfront resection (with or without subsequent adjuvant therapy), neoadjuvant therapy followed by resection, or treatment of systemic disease without resection The main modalities for staging gastric adenocarcinoma are upper endoscopy; EUS; cross-sectional imaging such as CT, MRI, and/or positron emission tomography (PET); and diagnostic laparoscopy. Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 49, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1222

490.q: After mastectomy, breast reconstruction is done by
490.e: Answer- B. latissimus dorsi If the skin at the mastectomy site is poor (e.g. following radiotherapy) or if a larger volume of tissue is required, a musculocutaneous flap can be constructed either from the latissimusdorsi muscle (an LD flap) or using the transversusabdominis muscle (a TRAM flap as). The latter gives an excellent cosmetic result in experienced hands but is a lengthy procedure and requires careful patient selection.

490.q: What is the most prevalent condition that leads to the occurrence of heartburn and chest pain in a patient?
490.e: Explanation: Esophagitis refers to inflammation of the esophageal mucosa. It presents with chest pain, heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia. Proton pump inhibitors are the mainstay of treatment. Explanation of other options: Barrett's esophagus (Option A): Involves squamous-to-columnar mucosal change in the lower esophagus, usually after long-standing reflux. Pneumonia (Option B): A lung infection causing cough, fever, and infiltrates, not isolated heartburn or chest pain. Myocardial infarction (Option C): Due to ischemia; presents with crushing chest pain radiating to the arm/neck, not relieved by PPIs.

491.q: A 27-year-old female presents with a thyroid swelling. Which of the following symptoms is unlikely to occur due to compression of adjacent structures?
o: Hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression
491.e: Explanation: Thyroid enlargement can compress adjacent structures, producing multiple clinical manifestations. Hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression (Option A): The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs posteromedial to the thyroid. Compression may cause hoarseness , vocal cord paresis, or paralysis. Dysphagia due to esophagus compression (Option B): The esophagus lies medial and posterior to the thyroid. Compression can lead to difficulty swallowing or dysphagia. Superior vena cava syndrome (Option C): Although the SVC is located in the superior mediastinum and is rarely affected, large substernal goiters or massive thyroid enlargements can rarely cause SVC compression, leading to facial and upper limb edema, dyspnea, and facial plethora.

491.q: In a 35-years old pregnant female with hyperthyroidism, which antithyroid drug should be given in the first trimester?
491.e: Antithyroid drugs Those in common use are carbimazole and propylthiouracil : these are ANTI-TPO drugs. Antithyroid drugs are used to restore the patient to a euthyroid state and to maintain this for a prolonged period in the hope that a permanent remission will occur, i.e. that production of TSH-RAb will diminish or cease. Propylthiouracil has no teratogenicity effect. Antithyroid drugs cannot cure a toxic nodule. The overactive thyroid tissue is autonomous and recurrence of the hyperthyroidism is certain when the drug is discontinued. Anti-thyroids in pregnancy: 1 st trimester: propylthiouracil is used (carbimazole not used because it's teratogenic and may cause aplasia cutis) 2 nd trimester onwards: carbimazole (propylthiouracil not used throughout pregnancy due to risk of hepatitis)

491.q: Which among the following radioactive substance is not used in the thyroid scintigraphy technique?
491.e: Thyroid scintigraphy is performed using either technetium-99m pertechnetate or a radiolabelled iodine nuclide (typically 123I or 131I). Depending on the specific study, the tracer can be administered intravenously, orally, or via inhalation, and images are obtained anywhere from 30 minutes (for intravenous [IV] injection) to 24 hours (for oral administration) afterward. The thyroid normally displays symmetric uptake bilaterally. Nodular disease can be classified into whether there is increased focal uptake (the so-called "hot" nodule) or not (the "cold" nodule). Classically, "hot" nodules in the setting of hyperthyroidism are thought to be benign toxic nodules with extremely low risk of malignancy, whereas "cold" nodules carry a 15% risk of malignancy. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 882

492.q: Which among the following thyroid malignancy shows the symptom of diarrhoea?
492.e: Are tumours of the parafollicular (C cells) derived from the neural crest. rather than the cells of the thyroid follicle as are other primary thyroid carcinomas. The cells are not unlike those of a carcinoid tumour and on histological analysis a characteristic amyloid stroma is seen. High levels of serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are produced by many medullary tumours, which should be tested for in suspected cases. Calcitonin levels fall after resection and rise again with recurrence, making it a valuable tumour marker in the follow-up of patients with this disease. Diarrhoea is a feature in 30% of cases and this may be due to 5-hydroxytryptamine or prostaglandins produced by the tumour cells. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 870-871

492.q: Which among the following cancer shows the presence of psammoma bodies?
492.e: Explanation: Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common type of thyroid cancer overall, comprising 84% of all incident cases. Histologically, PTC is characterised by complex branching papillae with pseudo-inclusions, nuclear grooving, and psammoma bodies. The so-called follicular variant of PTC (fvPTC) has a similar prognosis to classical PTC and histologically has well-defined follicles with minimal papillary projections. Other less common but more aggressive histologic subtypes of PTC include tall cell, hobnail, diffuse sclerosing, and columnar variants, which together comprise less than 1% of all PTCs.

492.q: Which among the following is the most aggressive thyroid malignancy?
492.e: This is one of the most aggressive malignancies in humans. Thankfully it is rare. It may develop de novo , or present as dedifferentiation of a papillary or poorly differentiated carcinoma. The disease is characterised by rapid growth, visceral invasion and distant metastases. The surgeon’s role in this disease is crucial. Thyroid lymphoma can be incorrectly diagnosed as anaplastic cancer and so biopsy is critical. This can be done using a core or open technique. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 868

493.q: A 44 year old Asian man presents with epigastric pains of burning nature. The pain was worst at night. He was prescribed combinations of antacids for a year and but this did not relieve his symptoms entirely. He had an endoscopy which did not show any significant abnormalities 3 months ago. Which is the best test for further investigation for this patient?
493.e: This patient presents with features of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). In some cases of GERD, endoscopic signs may be absent due to- A partially treated disease In nonerosive reflux disease - most common cause. In such instances, 24 hour oesophageal pH study can demonstrate excessive esophageal exposure to refluxed gastric fluid, the physiologic abnormality of GERD. Urease breath test is done to identify Helicobacter pylori. Gastric biopsy is done in cases of suspected gastric carcinoma. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2424

493.q: A 38 year old man presents with epigastric pains which are burning in nature and worse at night. He undergoes endoscopy and the investigation confirms a diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). Which of the following is most likely to relieve his symptoms?
493.e: The most effective drugs in Gastro-oesophageal reflux are proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole. Treatment for GORD includes - Lifestyle changes - Avoiding foods that reduce LES pressure like coffee, alcohol, fatty foods Avoiding acidic foods like citrus fruits, tomato based foods Weight loss Pharmacological treatment -PPI like omeprazole >> H2 receptor antagonists like ranitidine Surgical management -Nissen fundoplication -In refractory cases Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st , Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

493.q: A 58-year-old male presents with dysphagia, retrosternal discomfort and weight loss. Studies reveal achalasia. Which of the following is most definitive way to provide symptomatic relief?
493.e: The only durable therapies for achalasia are pneumatic dilation and LES myotomy (Heller myotomy). The patient shows excellent symptom improvement. Reflux is the most common side effect and a concomitant anti-relfux procedure (Nissen's fundoplication) may be performed. Both calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and nitrates relax the lower oesophageal sphincter. However the effect on symptoms is variable, short-lived and usually suboptimal. Use is frequently limited by adverse effects. Consequently medical therapy is typically limited to those patients too frail or unwilling to undergo definitive treatment or other therapies. Latest treatment is POEM. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

494.q: Which is the first line investigation for oesophageal cancer?
494.e: Investigation Endoscopy is the first-line investigation for most patients. It provides an unrivalled direct view of the oesophageal mucosa and any lesion allowing its site and size to be documented. Cytology and/or histology specimens taken via the endoscope are crucial for accurate diagnosis. The combination of histology and cytology increases the diagnostic accuracy to more than 95%. The chief limitation of conventional endoscopy is that only the mucosal surface can be studied and biopsied. Other investigations are therefore usually required to define the extent of local or distant spread. The improved image resolution of modern endoscopes and novel techniques involving magnification and the use of dyes to enhance surface detail may lead to more early lesions being recognised. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1136-1137

494.q: What is the margin of resection in oesophageal cancer?
494.e: PRINCIPLES The principle of oesophagectomy is to deal adequately with the local tumour in order to minimise the risk of local recurrence and achieve an adequate lymphadenectomy to reduce the risk of staging error. Although studies in Japan would indicate that more extensive lymphadenectomy is associated with better survival, this may simply reflect more accurate staging. A number of studies support the view that the proximal extent of resection should ideally be 10 cm above the macroscopic tumour and 5 cm distal. When such a margin cannot be achieved proximally, particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, there is evidence that postoperative radiotherapy can minimise local recurrence, although this does not improve survival. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1141

494.q: Rat tail appearance in contrast radiography is seen in?
494.e: Carcinoma esophagus REF: sabiston's 18' edition chapter 41 See table in the previous question "Rat-tail" appearance on barium study is seen in carcinoma esophagus.

495.q: A 46 year woman is admitted due to a single episode of haematemesis after taking a tablet of ibuprofen 6 hours previously. On examination, she had a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg (lying) and 95/60 mmHg (standing). Her haemoglobin concentration is 7.5 g/dL. What is the likely cause of the haemetemesis?
495.e: The likely answer is gastric erosions because the bleeding occurred after only one dose of Ibuprofen. There is no previous history of dyspepsia or upper GI bleeding. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ( NSAIDs ) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen cause gastric erosions via - Can be direct irritants of gastric mucosa Prostaglandins have a protective role in maintaining mucosal integrity. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production . Because of gravity, the irritants lie on the greater curvature of the stomach, and therefore, gastritis and ulcers are seen distally on or near the greater curvature of the stomach . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 312

495.q: A 52 year old lady complains of epigastric burning pains due to stress. She finally undergoes an UGI endoscopy which shows gastro-oesophageal reflux. Which medication is the most effective for her condition?
495.e: The main pharmacological therapy for GERD is inhibition of gastric acid suppression . Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, lansoprazole and pantoprazole are more effective than H2 receptor blockers such as ranitidine, cimetidine or nizatidine. Healing in oesophagitis is better with a PPI. Bismuth is a mucosal protective agent used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. Magnesium hydroxide is an antacid. It is not as effective as PPI for GERD. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

495.q: A 35 years old male with gastric outlet obstruction presented to emergency with multiple episodes of vomiting. Which of the following fluids is preferred for this patient?
495.e: Treatment of gastric outlet obstruction: Treating the patient involves correcting the metabolic abnormalities and dealing with the mechanical obstruction. The patient should be rehydrated with intravenous isotonic saline with potassium supplementation. Replacing the sodium chloride and water allows the kidney to correct the acid-base abnormality. The metabolic abnormalities may be less if the obstruction is due to malignancy, as the acid-base disturbance is less pronounced.

496.q: A 56--year-old male stomach cancer patient underwent surgery. After surgery, lab reports show Hb = 7.8, MCH= 28, MCV= 120. His anemia is caused by a deficiency of X and can be treated with Y.
o: X = intrinsic factor; Y = folic acid
X = intrinsic factor; Y = vitamin B12
X = extrinsic factor; Y = parenteral iron
496.e: Resection of the stomach does lead to loss of intrinsic factor and the patient will be deficient in vitamin B12. Prevention or treatment of iron deficiency anemia (microcytic cell size) is the only indication for iron administration. Sargramostim is a GM-CSF and is used to stimulate the production of neutrophils and other myeloid and megakaryocyte progenitors. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834-39

496.q: With respect to gastric carcinoma, which of the following statements is true?
o: Aspirin use is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma
Early diagnosis of gastric carcinoma results in a five year survival rate of 20%
Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
Helicobacter pylori infection is not associated with gastric carcinoma
496.e: Incidence of distal stomach tumors is actually decreasing while the incidence of tumors in the proximal stomach is increasing. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use is associated with decreased risk of certain gastric tumors. pylori infection has been associated in a number of studies with increased risk of gastric carcinoma. Screening for gastric carcinoma in Japan detects up to 40% of gastric carcinomas at an early stage and in skilled hands five year survival can be upwards of 90%. Computed tomography (CT) with gastric dilatation is a useful complementary investigation in the staging of gastric carcinoma, but endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning as it is able to assess depth of infiltration and lymphatic dissemination of tumor. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 80, Pg: 629-632

496.q: A visible mass in epigastrium with CD117 positive, but cytokeratin and S-100 negative. What is the diagnosis?
496.e: Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) may arise in any part of the gastrointestinal tract but 50% will be found in the stomach. Previously named leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, the term GIST is now used, recognising the distinct phenotype. They are tumours of mesenchymal origin and are observed equally commonly in males and females. The tumours are universally associated with a mutation in the tyrosine kinase c-kit oncogene. Most GISTs occur due to gain of function mutation in receptor tyrosine kinase KIT or PDGFR-alpha. Most useful marker is CD-117. Carney triad - GIST + paraganglioma + pulmonary chondroma.

497.q: The immediate postoperative period is associated with predictable hormonal and metabolic shifts. Several electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities commonly occur, while some do not. Which one of the following is not typically seen in the immediate postoperative period?
497.e: Explanation: In the immediate postoperative period, patients often develop hyperkalaemia or normal potassium levels due to tissue breakdown, acidosis and decreased renal excretion. Hypokalaemia is not typically seen . Normal metabolic changes in the immediate postoperative period include: Negative nitrogen balance due to catabolic stress hormones (Option A) Glucose intolerance due to increased cortisol, catecholamines and insulin resistance (Option C) Hyponatremia due to ADH surge and water retention (Option D) Potassium tends to be normal or high , not low, because of increased catabolism, acidemia and reduced renal clearance

497.q: Which among the following is helpful in determining organ function after transplant?
497.e: The factors determining organ function after transplantation include - A] Donor characteristics - Extremes of age Presence of pre-existing damage in transplanted organ Haemodynamic and metabolic instability B] Procurement-related factors - Warm ischaemic time Type of preservation solution Cold ischaemic time C] Recipient-related factors - Technical factors relating to implantation Haemodynamic and metabolic stability Immunological factors Presence of drugs that impair transplant function Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 82, Transplantation, Pg: 1549.

497.q: Which among the following statements is false for action of thyroid hormones?
o: Metabolic effects are due to bound T3 and T4
T3 is more important physiological hormone
497.e: The metabolic effects of the thyroid hormones are due to unbound free T4 and T3 (0.03% and 0.3% of the total circulating hormones, respectively). T3 is the more important physiological hormone and is also produced in the periphery by conversion from T4. T3 is quick acting (within a few hours), whereas T4 acts more slowly (4-14 days). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 852

498.q: Nutritional complications are more with which fistula?
498.e: Proximal small intestine fistulas will have high output → so metabolic and electrolyte complications are more common with proximal fistula The maximum malnutrition is caused by duodenal fistulas. Although gastric and duodenal fistulas receive almost the same food and enzymes, duodenum receives extra bile from gallbladder and pancreatic enzymes from pancreas hence duodenal fistula are more notorious for nutritional complications. Fistulas which are difficult to heal: F - foreign body in tract R - radiotherapy I - inflammatory bowel disease E - epithelialised tract N - neoplasia D - distal obstruction S - short fistulous tract ( Principles of management of enterocutaneous fistula (SNAP) S - elimination of Sepsis and skin protection N - Nutrition - a period of parenteral nutrition may well be required. A - Anatomical assessment P - definitive Planned surgery

498.q: A young man met with a motor bike accident and had injury to ileum and jejunum. Therefore the entire ileum and part of jejunum was resected. Which of the following would the patient suffer from?
498.e: If the jejunum is resected, the ileum can assume all the required absorptive functions, but resection of the terminal ileum will result in a diminished bile salt pool, vitamin B12 deficiency and may lead to deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. The ileum also plays an important role in water absorption, possibly because the tightness of the intercellular junctions supports a concentration gradient across its lumen. Significant ileal resection therefore commonly results in very troublesome diarrhea. The small intestine plays an important role in the metabolism of plasma lipoproteins, as it is the main site of synthesis of high-density, low-density and very low-density lipoproteins (HDL, LDL, VLDL).

498.q: A 45 years old male presents with complaints of pain in the abdomen, vomiting on and off and Diarrhea. Measurement of Serum creatinine is high. What is the probable diagnosis?
498.e: In the gastrointestinal tract, especially the small intestine, they secrete excess 5-HT , which is rapidly metabolized by the liver. In the presence of liver metastases, NET metastases secrete 5-HT into the IVC, avoiding hepatic first-pass metabolism and leading to symptoms of 5-HT excess, known as carcinoid syndrome . The cardinal features are sweating, flushing, bronchospasm and restrictive cardiomyopathy secondary to fibrotic right heart valvular disease (Hedinger syndrome ).

499.q: When present with dynamic ileus, the C.difficile infection is identified by
499.e: Diarrhea is the most common manifestation caused by C. difficile. Stools are almost never grossly bloody and range from soft and unformed to watery or mucoid in consistency, with a characteristic odor.
