Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE JUNE 2022; DEC 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 1846

582.q: What is absent in breast milk ?
582.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Vitamin K o Milks from the mother whose diet is sufficient and properly balanced will supply all the necessary nutrients except fluoride and Vitamin D. o The iron content of human milk is low, but most normal term infants have sufficient iron stores for the first 4-6 months. Human milk iron is well absorbed. Nonetheless, by 6 months the breast-fed infant's diet should be supplemented with iron fortified complementary foods. o The Vitamin K content of human milk is low and may cause hemorrhagic disease of newborn.

582.q: Vitamin K is given at birth to prevent the following?
582.e: Neonates have low Vitamin K levels due to Poor transplacental transfer Low Vitamin K in breast milk Lack of gut colonization with Vit K producing bacteria Thus, neonates are predisposed to Vitamin K deficiency, which can cause bleeding manifestations, called as Hemorrhagic Disease of newborn, also called as Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB). To prevent this, Government of India recommends one intramuscular dose of Vitamin K at birth to all neonates. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 183

583.q: Which of the following is not associated feature with zinc deficiency?
583.e: Symptoms associated with zinc deficiency are: Decreased growth Dermatitis of extremities and around orifices Impaired immunity Poor wound healing Hypogonadism Diarrhea Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : MAY KNOW PYQ : FMGE AUG 2020; NEET PG 2023 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 334

583.q: Choose the correct statement/s about Vitamin C and Scurvy A. It is a heat labile vitamin B. Exclusive breastfeeding can cause scurvy in infancy C. Therapeutic dose of vitamin C is 100-200mg/day D. Vitamin C is predominantly stored in Liver
583.e: Vitamin C supplements of 100-200 mg/day orally or parenterally ensure rapid and complete cure of Scurvy. The treatment should be continued for up to 3 months for complete recovery. Breastfeeding protects against vitamin C deficiency throughout infancy . In children consuming milk formula, fortification with vitamin C must be ensured. Children consuming heat-treated milk should consume adequate vitamin C-rich foods in infancy. Vitamin C is easily destroyed by prolonged storage, overcooking, and processing of foods. Vitamin C is not stored in the body but is taken up by all tissues; the highest levels are found in the pituitary and adrenal glands. Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : MAY KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021:FMGE JAN 2023; INICET NOV 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 372

583.q: Low glycemic index is classified as value less than:
583.e: Concept of glycemic index has utility in management of diabetes and obesity. GI range Classification Example Most fruits and vegetables except potatoes and water melon, Low GI 55 or less pasta beans, lentils Medium GI 56-69 Sucrose, brown rice, basmati rice 70 or High GI Corn flakes, white bread, candy bar more Ref: Park 22nd edition, page

584.q: Dosage of intravenous fluid for 2 month old child in diarrhoea with severe dehydration -
584.e: Answer- A. 100 ml/Kg in 6 hour So total fluid to be given 100 ml/Kg in 6 hour.

584.q: Rehydration therapy in a 2 year old severely dehydrated child is -
o: 30 ml/kg in 1 hour, 70 ml in 5 hours
30 ml/kg in 30 min, 70 ml/kg in 2'/2 hours
584.e: Answer- B. 30 ml/kg in 30 min, 70 ml/kg in 2'/2 hours 12 Month - 5 year 30 ml/Kg in 30 min 70 ml/Kg in 2.30 hour

584.q: An 8-month-old child has profuse diarrhea since last 3 days. The stool routine shows absence of blood and stool culture shows no growth. There is no fever and no dehydration. Child is growing fine otherwise. The perianal area shows skin excoriation. What is likely cause of this diarrheal illness?
584.e: The history is very much suggestive of post viral lactose malabsorption. After the viral enteritis, the mucosal brush border cells are lost and these causes lactose malabsorption. Also , perianal excoriation is favorable to diagnosis of lactose intolerance. Other bacterial enteritis might show growth in culture or may have changes in stool routine like pus cells, occult blood. Though, they cannot be ruled out completely, likelihood of lactose malabsorption is more than bacterial. Celiac disease is a cause of chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. Tags: Topic: DIARRHOEAL ILLNESS Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2022; AIIMS JULY 2020; FMGE DEC 2020;AUG 2020 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed, pg no: 2035

585.q: Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome involves which among the following genetic abnormalities?
585.e: Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome. Also known as 4p- (deletion of4pl6), this syndrome is characterized by microcephaly and unusual development of the nose and orbits that produces an appearance suggesting an ancient Greek warrior's helmet. Other anomalies commonly seen include cleft lip and palate and cardiac and renal defects. Seizure disorders are common, and the majority of patients have severe intellectual disability. Reference: CDT Pediatrics 2020/Page 1097

585.q: Which among the following disorders is an example of polygenic inheritance?
585.e: Cleft lip/palate shows polygenic/multifactorial inheritance. Fragile X syndrome and G6PD deficiency show X linked recessive, whereas Cystic fibrosis shows Autosomal recessive inheritance. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed/Chapter 97

585.q: A male boy has a large head, large ears, large jaw and large testes. He also has features of autism and delayed development. Likely diagnosis is?
585.e: The findings of large head, large ears, large jaw and large testes (macro-orchidism) are suggestive of Fragile X Syndrome. More commonly seen in boys, it is considered to be a trinucleotide repeat disorder Involves >200 CGG repeats in FMR-1 gene on Chromosome Xq27.3 Other features include hyperextensible joints, increased risks of ADHD, Autism, Anxiety Disorders Most patients have low IQ, indicating intellectual disability and delayed development milestones during childhood. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Chapter 98.5

586.q: A neonate with hypoglycemia is being managed using IV Dextrose infusion. He needs a bolus or hiking in Dextrose rate every time tapering is tried and more than 7 days have passed with the child being on IV dextrose infusion. What shall be done next?
586.e: Recurrent/ resistant Hypoglycemia This condition should be considered when the infant fails to maintain normal BGL despite a GIR of 12 mg /kg/min or when stabilization is not achieved by 7 days of therapy. High levels of glucose infusion may be needed in these infants to achieve euglycemia. Hyperinsulinism must be excluded because it is the most common cause of persistent hypoglycemia. Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia can be congenital [due to mutations affecting the regulation of insulin secretion from the pancreas] or acquired [neonates with maternal diabetes, birth asphyxia, polycythemia, Rh incompatibility, and severe intrauterine growth restriction, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. etc.] Many patients may have underlying metabolic disorders or hypocortisolism Hydrocortisone is often considered in such cases. Reference: AIIMS Protocols In Neonatology, 3 rd Edition, Volume 2, Page 305

586.q: Which of the following condition you do not expect risk of developing cerebral palsy?
o: A 2 year old child, born at 32 weeks gestation
A 4 year old child, born at term and had birth asphyxia due following obstructed labor
A 14 year old child had significant head injury at 13 years of age
A 12 year old child, who developed kernicterus at 10th day of life
586.e: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent neurological disorders affecting movement, posture, and muscle tone, resulting from brain damage that occurs before, during, or shortly after birth. Risk factors of developing cerebral palsy Prenatal insult Preterm birth Birth asphyxia CNS infections Toxin exposure like bilirubin (Kernicterus) CNS hemorrhage Metabolic disorders KEY TAKEAWAYS: Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive motor disorder that affects a growing brain. Hence, insult after brain growth is nearly complete, does not cause Cerebral palsy. Tags: Topic: CEREBRAL PALSY Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2021 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3168

586.q: You are asked to see a 2-year-old child who has a 12-hour history of severe diarrhoea and vomiting. He is pale and lethargic with a HR 180/min, BP 80 mmHg systolic, and capillary refill time of 7 seconds. What type of shock are they likely to be in?
586.e: This child is likely to be dehydrated from losing fluid through vomiting and diarrhoea, and may not have adequate oral intake to replace losses. This has resulted in severe dehydration, evident from the increased HR (due to compensation for a low blood volume in attempt to increase BP), increased cap refill time and low BP (indicating uncompensated shock), and pale and clammy appearance. KEY TAKEAWAYS: Hypovolemic shock occurs due to a significant reduction in intravascular volume, leading to inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery. This can result in cellular hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, and multi-organ dysfunction if untreated. Tags: Topic: SHOCK Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Manual of paediatric emergencies & critical care, 2 nd ed., pg. 158

587.q: Which among the following conditions presents in infancy with cyclic cyanosis?
587.e: Infants with bilateral choanal atresia who have difficulty with mouth breathing make vigorous attempts to inspire, often suck in their lips, and develop cyanosis. Distressed children then cry (which relieves the cyanosis) and become calmer, with normal skin color, only to repeat the cycle after closing their mouths. This is called cyclic cyanosis. Also note that bilateral choanal atresia is often a part of CHARGE Syndrome. Reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10 th Edition, Page Number-388.

587.q: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the ED for excessive fussiness and colicky behavior. On exam, she has repetitive clusters of stereotyped flexion movements of the trunk, associated with a cry. Her EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. A few flexion movements are captured and are associated with a generalized slow wave followed by an electro-decrement. She has several scattered hypo-pigmented spots on the trunk and extremities. What is the best treatment option?
587.e: The diagnosis is Tuberous sclerosis, with the child having Infantile Spasms. In such a case, Vigabatrin is more efficacious than ACTH. Vigabatrin (VGB) is a structural analogue of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and irreversibly inhibits the GABA degradative enzyme GABA-transaminase (GABA-T), thus increasing brain levels of GABA. VGB is very effective against infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), and it is the first-choice drug of in this case based on many reports. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SE edition, pg. 2879

587.q: What therapy would you recommend for the most effective treatment of the hematologic complications for Gaucher disease?
587.e: ERT has emerged as one of the most important advances in the treatment of sphingolipidoses. ERT with biweekly infusions of recombinant human glucocerebrosidase is invariably effective in reversing the hematologic and early skeletal complications of Gaucher disease. None of the other options listed above are valid treatment options for Gaucher disease. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 708

588.q: A child with HIV presents with features of pneumonia. Which of the following organisms would be most commonly responsible?
588.e: P.jirovecii (previously P. carinii) pneumonia is the opportunistic infection that led to the initial description of AIDS. This is one of the commonest AIDS defining illnesses in children; most cases occur between 3rd and 6th months of life. Reference: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 9 th ed., pg. 225

589.q: A 14 days-old neonate who had bilateral conjunctivitis, now has a cough with chest infiltrates. Which among the following could be the causative organism?
589.e: Chlamydia is the most common cause of neonatal pneumonia associated with neonatal conjunctivitis. Chlamydial genital infection is reported in 5-30% of pregnant women, with a risk for vertical transmission at parturition to Newborn infants of approximately 50%. The infant may become infected at 1 or more sites, including the conjunctiva, nasopharynx, rectum, and vagina. Most commonly these infections manifest as inclusion conjunctivitis and Pneumonia. Rectal and vaginal infections are also seen but most of them are asymptomatic. TLC in these patients is normal to high & CXR often shows interstitial infiltrates. Drug of choice is usually IV Azithromycin Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 1495

589.q: Which of the following is true about DiGeorge syndrome?
o: It results from a duplication of chromosome 22q11.
There is hypoplasia of the second pharyngeal pouch.
Apnea, jitteriness, and high-pitched cry may complicate the course of the disease
Cardiac defect may be a cause of death.
589.e: DiGeorge Syndrome DiGeorge syndrome is a congenital hypoplasia of organs derived from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. It results in hypoplasia or agenesis of the thymus and parathyroid glands, the auricle, and the external auditory canal; congenital cardiac anomalies; cleft palate; and short stature. It is associated with microdeletion of chromosome 22q11 . The main features are hypocalcemia, seizures, congenital heart disease, lymphocytopenia, and multiple minor anomalies. Hypocalcemia can manifest as apnea, jitteriness, crying episodes and tetany. Affected newborns may die from cardiac causes during the first month. Frequent infections due to a defect of cell-mediated immunity and failure to thrive may complicate the course of the surviving newborn. Reference: Nelson 20 th edition, pg-2650

589.q: A baby developed congenital toxoplasmosis. Presence of which among the following will predict a higher risk of severe infection?
589.e: HLA-DQ3+ predicts a more severe and fulminant course of congenital toxoplasma infection. According to Nelson, In monozygotic twins with congenital toxoplasmosis, the clinical pattern of involvement is most often similar, whereas in dizygotic twins the manifestations often differ. The major histocompatibility complex class II gene DQ3 appears to be common even among HIV-infected persons seropositive for T. gondii who develop toxoplasmic encephalitis, as well as in children with congenital toxoplasmosis who develop hydrocephalus. These findings suggest that the presence of HLA-DQ3 is a risk factor for severity of toxoplasmosis, in all patients including congenital toxoplasmosis. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 316

590.q: What is the Most common clinical manifestation of mumps?
590.e: Epididymo-orchitis is the next most common manifestation of mumps (after parotid gland swelling), developing in 15-30% of cases in postpubertal males, with bilateral involvement in 10 - 30% of those cases Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 2st Ed, Ch:207 Pg: 1617

590.q: A mother with no prenatal care gives birth to a term infant with findings of IUGR, microcephaly and hepatosplenomegaly. His hemogram shows thrombocytopenia. BERA test reveals sensorineural hearing loss. Ophthalmic examination shows chorioretinitis. The most important diagnostic study for evaluation in this newborn is
590.e: The newborn in the question shows characteristics of congenital CMV infection. In addition to those findings mentioned above, these patients can have petechiae and purpura, ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, cerebral atrophy, cortical dysplasia, and chorioretinitis. The most important diagnostic study in the evaluation of newborn CMV disease is viral culture, preferably done before 3 weeks of life to help exclude the possibility of perinatal CMV acquisition. Viral PCR is a useful adjunct to culture techniques but does not replace viral culture. Tissue biopsy, while sometimes used for diagnosis, is not standard and is more commonly used in the lung and liver than in the brain. CMV antibody titers are generally not helpful in diagnosis. Tags : Topic : CONGENITAL INFECTIONS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : INICET NOV 2022; JULY 2021; NEET PG 2023

590.q: A mother is very reluctant in giving breast feeding to her newborn. She is lactating well. But she has a fear that her milk is not good for her baby. While counselling the mother about the advantages of breast milk, she must be explained that breast milk protects against multiple types of infections. Which of the following infection is not prevented in exclusively breastfed child?
590.e: Breastfeeding has been suggested to have a possible protective effect in : Diarrhea Otitis media (option a) Urinary tract infections (option b) Necrotizing enterocolitis, Septicemia (option c) Infant botulism Celiac disease Childhood cancer Allergy Hospitalizations and infant mortality Tags : Topic : BREAST FEEDING & NUTRITION Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : INICET MAY 2022 Reference : Nutrition and child development, KE Elizabeth, 5 th ed., pg. 113

591.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Rectal biopsy o Rectal suction biopsy is procedure of choice.

591.q: 24 day neonate with projectile vomiting & failure to gain weight .what is the diagnosis
591.e: Answer- A. CHPS Projectile vomiting in 4th week is quite suggestive of CHPS. In duodenal atresia the vomiting (usually bilious) is right from the 1st day of life. NEC and Hirschsprung's disease have different clinical presentation.

591.q: You are called to the nursery to assess a newborn girl. She was born at 39 weeks via normal spontaneous delivery to a mother who had no prenatal care. APGAR scores are 7 and 9. At four hours of life, the nurse noted respiratory distress. On physical examination, her heart rate is 150 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 70 cycles per minute, temperature is 37.1 C with barrel-shaped chest, a scaphoid-appearing abdomen, and absence of breath sounds on the left chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
591.e: The newborn girl has findings that are suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a developmental defect of the diaphragm that allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the chest. Although routine prenatal ultrasound screening may identify CDH at a mean gestational age of 24 weeks, there is a wide range of reported sensitivity in its detection. Physical findings include a barrel-shaped chest, a scaphoid-appearing abdomen (because of loss of the abdominal contents into the chest), and absence of breath sounds on the ipsilateral side. Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1 st SA ed., pg. 772

592.q: You are teaching a group of medical students the differential diagnosis of edema in children. You take them to the bedside of a patient who has edema associated with hypoproteinemia secondary to proteinuria. Of the following, the feature you are MOST likely to observe in this patient is?
o: Edema that improves throughout the day
592.e: Nephrotic syndrome usually presents with edema that is periorbital and more prominent early in the morning and with minimal systemic symptoms. Edema is the most easily identified clinical feature associated with hypoproteinemia. Impaired cardiac function leads to worsening peripheral edema as the day progresses and is associated with exertion and increased activity. Pitting edema is not pathognomonic for any specific underlying etiology. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2521

592.q: A 9-yr old boy passes hard infrequent stools for the last 2 years. Also, sometimes he soils his under wear. On examination, you found an anal fissure and his rectum is full of hard stools. All other examination is normal. Your most likely diagnosis is functional constipation. What is the most effective initial treatment?
o: Combination of Polyethylene glycol solution & enema
High fiber diet and follow up after 3 months
592.e: The child has now presented with severe constipation with rectal impaction. The 1st step in treatment of severe constipation is disimpaction which requires administration of Polyethylene glycol solution (movicol) (or mineral oil) ± rectal enema As per OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 301, any child with constipation who has hard stools felt on per rectal examination or has abdominal fecoliths or retentive encopresis should undergo immediate disimpaction as the first step in management. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 301; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1765

592.q: A child has been recently diagnosed as Celiac Disease. His parents ask you for foods which are safe to be consumed. You will suggest all of the following foods as safe to eat in this patient, except?
592.e: Since the child has been diagnosed with Celiac Disease, the child should avoid eating foods and grains which contain gluten in them. Among the options, Semolina is puffed wheat and thus should be avoided. Grains unsafe to eat in Celiac Disease- Contain gluten. Mnemonic is BROW Barley Rye Oats Wheat, including whole wheat & semolina (suji/rava) Grains safe to eat in Celiac Disease- Do not contain gluten. Includes Rice, including Puffed Rice like Poha Maize Quinoa Sorghum Chia Seeds Flax Seeds Tapioca Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 320; Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 364

593.q: What is the amount of milk given to a term baby in the first 24 hours after delivery?
593.e: Explanation: On the first day of life, a term newborn usually receives about 60 ml of milk per kilogram of body weight . This volume is tailored to match the limited stomach capacity of the infant and to support a gradual adaptation of the gastrointestinal system , allowing feeding tolerance to improve as digestion matures. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK326679/

593.q: Jaundice due to biliary atresia is suspected when it persists beyond?
593.e: Neonatal cholestasis tends to produce conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a neonate & usually produces prolonged jaundice. Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) is one of the most common causes of neonatal cholestasis and should be suspected in a term neonate if jaundice fails to resolve and persists beyond 2 weeks of postnatal age. EHBA should also be suspected if the neonate has jaundice with dark-coloured urine & clay-coloured stools. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 345-349

593.q: Most common indication of liver transplantation in children is?
593.e: Biliary atresia is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children, followed by metabolic disorders. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Harrison 20 th Ed, page 2415

594.q: Which of the following cells are deficient is a premature infant with RDS?
594.e: Hyaline membrane disease Also called as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) Major cause of this disease is Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant produced by type II alveolar cells Commonly seen in. Premature infants Maternal diabetes (Gestational diabetes mellitus) delivery by cesarean section Reference: Ganong 25th edition page no.631

594.q: In children with respiratory distress, there is deficiency of which of the following lipids:
594.e: Surfactant lipids Account for approximately 90% of surfactant Major surfactant lipids is: Dipalmotoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC) - Lecithin- most abundant component of surfactant Reference: Ganong 25th edition page no.631

594.q: In preterm baby with respiratory distress syndrome which of the following lipid would be deficient?
594.e: Phospholipid Dipalmitoyl Phosphatidyl Choline acts as surfactant and Acts to reduce surface tension, which helps in proper expansion of Lungs. In preterm babies, it is deficient. So preterm babies are prone for respiratory distress syndrome

595.q: Which of the following is a known environmental risk factor for asthma?
595.e: RISK FACTORS FOR ASTHMA IN CHILDHOOD Parental asthma Allergy: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) Allergic rhinitis Food allergy Inhalant allergen sensitization Food allergen sensitization Severe lower respiratory tract infection: Pneumonia Bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization Wheezing apart from colds Male gender Low birthweight Environmental tobacco smoke exposure Reduced lung function at birth Out of all this, only Smoking exposure is environmental factor Tags : Topic : ASTHMA Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : INICET NOV 2022; AIIMS JULY 2020 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 1189

595.q: Which of the following is not a known risk factor for bronchiolitis in an infant?
o: Chronic lung condition due to prematurity
595.e: RISK FACTORS FOR BRONCHIOLITIS Parents who smoke Siblings attending day care or school (risk of transmitting viral infections) Chronic lung disease due to prematurity Breastfeeding given for Tags : Topic : BRONCHIOLITIS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE AUG 2020 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2217

595.q: A 10-year-old boy has a history of recurrent sinusitis and multiple episodes of pneumonia. You suspect CF and order a sweat chloride test. The sweat electrolyte test result is within the normal range. What is your next step in management?
o: Perform DNA testing for CFTR gene mutations.
Perform a pH probe test for gastroesophageal reflux.
Reassure parents that he does not have CF.
Place him on a high-calorie, high-protein diet.
595.e: The child has recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infections suggesting CF. The sweat chloride test can yield falsely low values, so the next step would be to perform DNA testing to identify any of the common CFTR mutations. Negative sweat chloride test results do not exclude CF. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2104

596.q: A 15-year-old adolescent collapses while playing in a high school basketball game without any preceding trauma. He is unconscious and not breathing. Of the following, the BEST sequence of actions is to?
o: Administer a precordial thump and perform a jaw-thrust manoeuvre
Ask someone to retrieve an automatic external defibrillator and start chest compressions
Immobilize the cervical spine and attempt to palpate the carotid pulse
Perform rapid assessment of circulation/airway/breathing and call 108
596.e: As per PALS guidelines and OP Ghai 10 th Edition, if the victim/patient is unresponsive and not breathing, begin CPR immediately. Also call for an automatic external defibrillator (AED) to check for rhythm. If there is VF/pVT, give electric shock and continue CPR If there is Asystole or PEA (Pulseless Electrical Activity), give injection epinephrine and continue with CPR. Effective cardiopulmonary resuscitation includes pushing hard (to 1/3 of the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest), pushing fast (100 compressions per minute) with minimal interruptions, and rotating personnel performing compressions every 2 minutes. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 763, 765; PALS 2020 Guidelines

596.q: During the examination of the child at birth, you observe that the umbilical cord of the baby has single umbilical artery. While counselling the parents of the baby, you explain them the importance of USG abdomen in this child, due to the risk of which of the following defects?
596.e: Single umbilical artery has association with renal agenesis. Hence, all babies with single umbilical artery must be scanned with USG abdomen and KUB to diagnose or rule out the same. Tags: Topic: FETAL CIRCULATION Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2021 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 975

596.q: The MOST common cause of syncope in children is
596.e: Neurocardiogenic syncope, also known as vasovagal syncope, is a common type of fainting or temporary loss of consciousness that occurs due to a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure. This decrease in circulation reduces blood flow to the brain, leading to fainting. Neurocardiogenic syncope can be triggered by several factors, such as: Prolonged standing Extreme emotional stress Pain Heat exposure Physical exertion KEY TAKEAWAYS: In otherwise healthy children, neurocardiogenic syncope is most common . This entity goes by a number of terms, including vasovagal syncope, neurally mediated syncope, and autonomic syncope. Tags: Topic: EPIDEMIOLOGY Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW Reference: Park’s Pediatric cardiology, 6 th ed., pg. 505

597.q: In children, CHF (congestion heart failure) is diagnosed by
597.e: Answer- C. Tender hepatomegaly Heart failure in infants & children results some degree of hepatemegaly which is usually tender & sometimes splenomegaly. Peripheral edema is age dependent : In infants, edema usually eye & over flank. Older childern & adolescent shows both periorbital edema & pedal edema and occurs late.

597.q: Which of the following features is not associated with patent ductus arteriosus?
597.e: PDA is associated with a collapsing pulse Patent ductus arteriosus Overview Acyanotic congenital heart defect Connection between the pulmonary trunk and descending aorta More common in premature babies, born at high altitude or maternal rubella infection in the first trimester Features Left subclavicular thrill Continuous 'machinery' murmur Large volume, bounding, collapsing pulse Wide pulse pressure Heaving apex beat Management Indomethacin closes the connection in the majority of cases If associated with another congenital heart defect amenable to surgery then prostaglandin E1 isuseful to keep the duct open until after surgical repair. Reference: Braunwald's heart disease 12 th edition, page no.1559

597.q: Medical closure of PDA is contraindicated in which of the following?
597.e: Contraindications for medical closure of PDA Platelet count 3 AKI or Sr. creatinine >1. 8mg/dl. NEC/Feed in tolerance Unexplained bleeding. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 122.5

598.q: Which of the following is not true regarding Tetralogy of Fallot?
o: Squatting improve the cyanotic spells in children
Egg on side appearance in chest x-ray
Rastelli procedure is performed for surgical correction
598.e: Tetralogy of Fallot Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease Components: pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding of aorta, RV hypertrophy Characterised by cyanotic / tet spells during childhood while exertion Squatting increases peripheral vascular resistance thereby reducing the magnitude of right to left shunt across VSD Boot shaped heart or 'coeur en sabot' is the characteristic xray appearance Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1833, 1834

598.q: The 'snowman' appearance of heart on chest xray is seen in which congenital heart disease:
598.e: Eponymous chest X ray appearances in congenital heart disease Snowman sign : Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection Egg on side appearance: Transposition of great arteries Boot shaped heart : Fallot's tetralogy Scimitar sign : Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection Figure of 3 sign : Coarctation of aorta Waterbottle sign : Ebstein anomaly (commonly described in pericardial effusion) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264 pg:1831,1832

598.q: Which congenital disease has equal saturation in all four chambers of the heart?
598.e: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connections (TAPVC) is a cyanotic congenital heart disease where all of the pulmonary veins drain directly or indirectly open into the right atrium. O2 saturation of blood in the pulmonary artery is often identical to that in aorta due to complete mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous returns in the right atrium.

599.q: An 8-year-old child presented with periorbital edema and mild oliguria but no hypertension. On evaluation, he was found to have serum albumin <2.5 g/dL, serum creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, urine protein 3+, and no RBCs or RBC casts in the urine. What histopathological diagnosis will you suspect?
599.e: Explanation: The clinical features: significant proteinuria (3+), hypoalbuminemia, and edema; are characteristic of Nephrotic Syndrome . In children aged 2-8 years, the most common histopathological diagnosis is Minimal Change Disease (MCD) . Absence of hematuria and hypertension supports the diagnosis of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Light microscopy typically shows minimal or no changes. Electron microscopy reveals effacement of podocyte foot processes. Oliguria , although more typical of nephritic syndrome, may occur in nephrotic syndrome due to worsening edema and hypoalbuminemia. Explanation of Other Options: IgA nephropathy (Option B): Presents with hematuria, often post-infectious. Membranous nephropathy (Option C): More common in adults; shows thickened GBM on microscopy. FSGS (Option D): Presents with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and may show hematuria or hypertension.

599.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with swelling that has increased over the past week. The swelling is most noticeable around his eyes in the mornings but is most notable in his legs in the afternoon. On examination, he has pitting edema of the bilateral lower extremities. He is also mildly hypertensive. Labs are significant for hypoalbuminemia and 3+ proteinuria. What is the most likely etiology of the child's hypoalbuminemia?
599.e: The child's presentation is consistent with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome results from urinary protein losses, which lead to hypoalbuminemia. The hypoalbuminemia leads to dependent edema. As such, the edema may be most noticeable around the eyes in the mornings with a shift to the lower extremities as the day progresses. Hypertension may occasionally be present. Typical laboratory findings include serum hypoalbuminemia, proteinuria, and hyperlipidemia. Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in childhood. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 500-501; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2523

599.q: A 10-year-old child presented with generalized edema. On investigation, his serum cholesterol level was 238 mg/dl, urine protein was 3+ and stool microscopy revealed oval fat bodies. What is the probable diagnosis?
599.e: Nephrotic range proteinuria is defined as proteinuria >3.5 g/24 hour or a urine protein : creatinine ratio >2. The triad of clinical findings associated with nephrotic syndrome arising from the large urinary losses of protein are hypoalbuminemia (≤2.5 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia (cholesterol >200 mg/dL). Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 2521

600.q: During his 1st physical examination following birth at home with the assistance of a midwife, a 5- week-old male is suspected to have congenital hypothyroidism. His parents refused all newborn screening at the time of his birth. Which of the following may be the earliest clinical sign of congenital hypothyroidism?
600.e: Prolongation of physiologic jaundice, due to delayed maturation of glucuronide conjugation, is often the 1st clinical finding in an infant with congenital hypothyroidism. Poor feeding, partly due to a large tongue, somnolence, and lack of interest are characteristic. Additional clinical findings may include a large protuberant abdomen; umbilical hernia; mottled, cool, and dry skin; extremity edema; and widely open fontanelles. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2668

600.q: A full term baby born to a mother with hypothyroidism, needs to be screened for congenital hypothyroidism ideally at what age?
600.e: A newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism must be done at 3-4 days of life coupled with newborn screening for inborn errors of metabolism. Screening test that are positive must be reassessed with a repeat venous sample and read according to cut-off values for the age. Tags : Topic : CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2022 Reference : AIIMS protocols in neonatology, 2019, pg. 236

600.q: What is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism?
600.e: Causes of permanent congenital hypothyroidism are: Thyroid dysgenesis (most common) Thyroid agenesis TSH resistance Thyroid dyshormonogenesis (2 nd most common) Central hypothyroidism Tags : Topic : CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2022 Reference : Cloherty and Stark's manual of neonatal care, SA ed., pg. 933

601.q: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is due to deficiency of enzyme a. 3β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency b. 5a Reductase c. 17a-Hydroxylase deficiency d. 21-Hydroxylase deficiency
601.e: Enzymes deficiency causing Congenital adrenal hyperplasia are 21-Hydroxylase deficiency 11β-Hydroxylase deficiency 17-Hydroxylase/17, 20 lyase deficiency 3B-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency Lipoid adrenal Hyperplasia Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.366

601.q: An 8-day-old baby presents with vomiting, poor feeding and loose stools. On examination, his heart rate is 190 bpm, BP 50/30 mmHg and respiratory rate 72 breaths/min. Blood tests: Hb 15 g/dl (13-18), sodium 120 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 6.0 mmol/l (3.5-4.9), chloride 80 mmol/l (95-107), bicarbonate 15 mmol/l (21-28), urea 30 mg/dl and creatinine 0.6 mg/dl (both normal). What is the most likely diagnosis
601.e: The features and findings are highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia presenting as salt wasting crisis 21 hydroxylase is the most common enzyme deficiency in CAH and salt wasting crisis. Absence of jaundice and hepatomegaly make the diagnosis of Galactosaemia unlikely. Acute tubular necrosis is ruled out, as urea and creatinine levels are normal. In congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, hypokalemia is the presenting feature and constipation (not loose stools) is the chief complaint. Lactose intolerance would again present with diarrhea or vomiting, thus hypokalemia would be the characteristic finding. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2973

601.q: A 2-month-old infant is presented with failure to thrive, recurrent emesis, hepatosplenomegaly, and adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal calcification is noted radiologically. The most likely diagnosis is?
601.e: Vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal insufficiency and adrenal calcification point to a diagnosis of Wolman Disease. Wolman Disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage diseases that results from deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) and accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides in histiocytic foam cells of most visceral organs. The LAL gene is on chromosome 10 (10q24-q25). Clinical features become apparent in the 1st weeks of life and include failure to thrive, relentless vomiting, abdominal distention, steatorrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly. There usually is hyperlipidemia. Hepatic dysfunction and fibrosis may occur. Calcification of the adrenal glands occurs in about 50% of patients and is an important clue to the underlying diagnosis, when present. Death usually occurs within the 1st 6 months of life. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 104

602.q: A 10-year-old girl is 4 ft 10 in (147 cm) tall. Her father is 5 ft 10 in (178 cm) tall, and her mother is 5 ft 5 in (165 cm) tall. Over the past 3 years she has dropped from the 25th percentile for height to the 5th percentile. Her weight has remained stable. Radiographs show bone age is delayed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
o: Send patient to the emergency department for CT evaluation of the brain
602.e: This child has evidence of possible growth hormone deficiency. Obtaining an IGF-1 level would be the most appropriate initial choice. Growth hormone deficiency is not an emergent condition but the earlier the diagnosis is made the sooner appropriate treatment can be initiated. Obtaining a growth hormone level would not be diagnostically helpful because its secretion is pulsatile. Referral to a pediatric endocrinologist would be warranted if initial screening tests confirm the suspected growth hormone deficiency. Reference: Nelson-Pediatric Symptom based diagnosis, pg. 791

603.q: The following are complications of Neurofibromatosis-1, EXCEPT?
603.e: Complications in NF-1 Learning disability affects approximately 30%. Seizures occur in approximately 8%. The cerebral vessels may develop aneurysms or stenosis resulting in moyamoya syndrome. Neurologic sequelae of these vascular abnormalities include transient cerebrovascular ischemic attacks, hemiparesis, and cognitive defects. Precocious puberty may become evident in the presence or absence of lesions of the optic pathway tumours. Malignant neoplasms affecting approximately 3% of patients. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20 th edition, pg. 2876

603.q: What is the recommended chest compression rate during CPR in a child according to PALS 2020 guidelines?
o: Rates not specified in the new guidelines
603.e: As per CPR guidelines for children in PALS 2020 In CPR, start chest compressions with rescue breaths in cardiac arrest. If unable to give rescue breaths, compressions alone to be given Chest compression rate: 100-120/min Allow adequate chest recoil between 2 compressions Depth of compression: At least 1/3 rd the AP diameter of the chest , approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm) in infants and 2 inches (5 cm) in children. Post puberty, use the adult compression depth 5-6 cm A rhythm check every 2 min , lasting 10 sec Ventilate with 100% O2 Reference: PALS Guidelines 2020; OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 763.

603.q: Which of the following complications is not expected in a child diagnosed with neurofibromatosis (type 1) NF-l
603.e: Complications in NF-1 Option A : Learning disability affecting approximately 30%. Option D : Seizures in approximately 8%. The cerebral vessels may develop aneurysms or stenosis resulting in moyamoya syndrome. Neurologic sequelae of these vascular abnormalities include transient cerebrovascular ischemic attacks, hemiparesis, and cognitive defects. Option C : Precocious puberty may become evident in the presence or absence of lesions of the optic pathway tumors. Malignant neoplasms affecting approximately 3% of patients. Tags: Topic: NEUROCUTANEOUS SYNDROME Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: INICET NOV 2020 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3141

604.q: Commonest tumor of face in chidren is-
604.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Rhabdomyosarcoma Rhabdomyosarcoma o The most common soft tissue sarcoma in children is rhabdomyosarcoma. o The common site of involvement are : - o Head & Neck (25%) 2"d most common Extremities Genitourinary (22%) —> 2nd most common Retroperitoneum

604.q: Which is MC genetic cause of mental retardation -
604.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Fragile-X-syndrome o Down's syndrome is the most common genetic cause of mental retardation, and fragile-X is second to Down's. Also know o Most common inherited cause of mental retardation is fragile-X- syndrome (because down's syndrome is congenital cause but not inherited).

604.q: Most common cerebellar tumor in children?
604.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Astrocytoma o The most common cerebellar tumor in adults is metastasis, whereas in children the most common tumor is an astrocytoma.

605.q: Handedness is established in a child at what age?
605.e: Handedness: dominance of one hand over the other for performing tasks or activities. It is established in children at around 3 years. key takeaways : Bidextrous grasp -4 months Unidextrous grasp-6 months Palmar grasp-7 months Pincer grasp (immature)-9month Pincer grasp (mature)-12month Handedness-3 years Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatric

605.q: Ideal time gap between two live vaccines, if both can't be given together, should be?
605.e: If two live vaccines cannot be given together, there should be a gap of at least 1 month (or 4 weeks) to ensure that the antibodies developed from the first vaccine do not interfere with the effectiveness of the second vaccine. Key takeaways:- -There is no need to keep a gap of 1 month between a live vaccine and a killed (inactivated) vaccine. They can be given at the same time or at different intervals -All live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy & immunocompromised except During outbreaks &travel (YF,OPV,Cholera) & bite case (rabies) -If two live vaccines are given together, they should be administered at different injection sites. ref :Nelson textbook of paediatric

605.q: Which of the following is most common pulmonary tumor in children?
605.e: The most common tumor types are Carcinoid inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor pleuropulmonary blastoma Rare pediatric lung tumors include small cell carcinoma adenocarcinoma pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis KEY TAKEAWAYS: The most common pulmonary tumor in children is carcinoid tumor. Tags: Topic: SOLID TUMORS Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: FMGE JULY 2023 Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics, 21 st ed, page number: 2316

606.q: Which of the following is the most common cause of shock in paediatric patient?
606.e: Dehydration (hypovolemic) shock is the most common type of shock in paediatric population. Common Causes in Paediatrics Gastrointestinal Losses: Diarrhea (e.g., rotavirus, cholera). Vomiting. Hemorrhage: Trauma (e.g., accidents). Post-surgical bleeding. Burns: Fluid loss through damaged skin. Other Causes: Inadequate fluid intake (e.g., neglect, illness). Third-spacing (e.g., sepsis, nephrotic syndrome). Septic shock is most common in neonates. Tags: Topic: SHOCK Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Manual of paediatric emergencies & critical care, 2 nd ed., pg. 158

606.q: Two weeks after a viral syndrome, a 2-year-old develops bruising and generalized petechiae that is more prominent over the legs. He has neither hepatosplenomegaly nor lymph node enlargement. Laboratory testing reveals a normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, and white blood cell count and differential. The platelet count is 15,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
606.e: Immune (or idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is common in children. In most cases, a preceding viral infection can be documented. The platelet count frequently is less than 20,000/mm3, but other laboratory test results are normal, including the bone marrow aspiration (which may show an increase in megakaryocytes). These patients have no hepatosplenomegaly or generalized lymphadenopathy. Treatment consists of observation or possibly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), intravenous anti-D (in Rh-positive patients), immunosuppressives, or steroids. The history must be reviewed for other possible causes of thrombocytopenia, including recent MMR vaccination, drug ingestion, and human immunodeficiency virus. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 2402

606.q: Desmopressin is relatively contraindicated in which type of Von Willebrand disease?
606.e: Type 2B vWD results from gain-of-function mutations that increase the ability of vWF to bind platelets. This leads to increased clearance of both vWF and platelets from circulation and results in the loss of high-molecular-weight multimers and decreased vWF activity, similar to that seen in type 2A vWD. Desmopressin is relatively contraindicated in type 2B vWD as it may accelerate VWF-platelet binding and clearance. Please note that Desmopressin is highly effective in Type 1 vWD Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SE edition, pg. 2390

607.q: Which of the following microorganism is the most common cause of aplastic crisis in Sickle Cell Anemia & Hereditary Spherocytosis?
607.e: Human Parvovirus B19, also written as B19V, is notorious for aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic states. Individuals with chronic hemolytic anemia and increased red blood cell (RBC) turnover, including Sickle Cell Anemia & Hereditary Spherocytosis, are very sensitive to minor perturbations in erythropoiesis. Infection with B19V leads to a transient arrest in RBC production and a precipitous fall in serum hemoglobin, often requiring transfusion. The reticulocyte count drops to undetectable levels, reflecting the lysis of infected erythroid precursors. Humoral immunity is crucial in controlling infection. Specific immunoglobulin (Ig) M appears within 1-2 days of infection and is followed by anti-B19 IgG, which leads to control of the infection, restoration of reticulocytosis, and a rise in serum hemoglobin. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 278

607.q: Type of change seen in sickle cell anemia is?
607.e: Sickle cell hemoglobinopathy occurs due to mutation of beta-globin gene situated on short arm of chromosome 11, where adenine is replaced by thymine in base of DNA coding for the amino acid in the sixth position in beta-globin chain. This leads to an amino acid change in beta chain of Hb molecule, from glutamic acid to valine. The result is profound change in the molecular stability and solubility of Hb "S". Reference: IAP Textbook of Pediatrics 5 th Ed/Page 700, OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 364

607.q: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with sickle cell anemia. He is more susceptible to all the following bacterial infections except
607.e: All patients with sickle cell anemia are at increased risk of infection and death from bacterial infection, particularly encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae Hemophilus influenzae type b Neisseria meningitidis Tags : Topic : BACTERIAL INFECTIONS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2542

608.q: A child was advised yearly vaccination with a vaccine, which is not a part of the national immunization schedule. Yearly vaccination is recommended against?
608.e: Annual vaccination is given against Influenza Vaccine in selected high-risk groups. The type of influenza vaccine currently marketed for use in India is an inactivated, quadrivalent vaccine. The vaccines are highly immunogenic and safe for use above 6 months of age. The vaccine is not part of the National Immunization Schedule, but recommended by IAP in selected high-risk groups like Chronic cardiac, pulmonary, renal, hepatic or hematological disease Asthma or wheezing in the past one year Chronic diseases like Sickle Cell Anemia, DM, SLE and Morbid Obesity Immunodeficiency Prolonged Aspirin Use Laboratory and Health-Care Workers Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 205-206

608.q: A 6-week-old child has just received Pentavalent vaccine today. Components of Pentavalent vaccine shall include?
608.e: Pentavalent vaccines are given according to the National immunization Program at 6-week, 10 week and 14 weeks. It provides protection against 5 vaccine preventable diseases including Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B and H. Influenzae type b. Pneumococcal vaccines and Fractional IPV are also administered along with this but are not part of pentavalent vaccine. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 189

608.q: Which one of the following murmur characteristics supports the diagnosis of an innocent murmur?
o: Maximum intensity at the left lower sternal border.
608.e: The characteristics of innocent murmur are Medium-pitched, vibratory or "musical," Relatively short systolic ejection murmur, Heard best along the left lower and midsternal border Has no significant radiation to the apex, base, or back. The intensity of the murmur often changes with respiration and position and may be attenuated in the sitting or prone position. It is heard most frequently in children between 3 and 7 years of age. Tags: Topic: BASICS OF CARDIOLOGY Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2169

609.e: Oliver Wendel Holmes coined the term Anaesthesia . John snow- administered chloroform analgesia to Queen Victoria for the delivery of her eighth child. This was a success and led to medical and religious acceptance of obstetrical anesthesia. When cholera returned to London in 1853, John Snow undertook an epidemiological study and linked the outbreak in Golden Square to the water pump on Broad Street. WTG Morton is considered as father of Anaesthesia The concept of balanced anesthesia was introduced in 1926 by Lundy and others and evolved to include thiopental for induction, nitrous oxide for amnesia, an opioid for analgesia, and curare for muscle relaxation. The term "spinal anesthesia " was coined in 1885 by Leonard Corning, a neurologist,and Augest Bier used cocaine for spinal anesthesia Reference : Lundy Js . Balanced Anaesthesia .minn .med . 1926;9:399-404

609.q: World Anaesthesia Day is celebrated on ?
609.e: In the Bullfinch amphitheater of the Massachusetts General Hospital. On Friday 16 October 1846 , Morton administed volatile anesthetic Ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott when John Collins Warren was operating a vascular lesion at the left side of Abbott's neck Gilbert Abbott later reported that he was aware of the operation but had experienced no pain . At the moment that the procedure ended, Warren turned to his audience and allegedly announced, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug" To honor this humongous achievement, the day is celebrated as world anaesthesia day Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 1 Page No 4 Table 2

609.q: "Chloroform a lareine", a technique was invented by ?
609.e: John snow administered labour analgesia using Chloroform to Queen Victoria's 8 th delivery, to the birth of, Prince Leopard During the delivery, Snow administered analgesic doses of chloroform on a folded handkerchief, a technique that was soon termed ' chloroform a la reine ' Victoria abhorred the pain of labor and enjoyed the relief that chloroform provided; she wrote in her journal," Dr.Snow gave that blessed chloroform and the effect was soothing, quieting, and delightful beyond measure " Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 1 Page No 4 Table 2

610.q: A 50-year-old patient is being planned for hernia repair. He is a known smoker with history of 20 pack years. His investigations are normal. How long should he be advised to stop smoking prior to surgery?
610.e: Stopping smoking is thought to be beneficial preoperatively, in order to minimize its acute adverse effects. Effects of carbon monoxide and nicotine are significantly reduced after 12-24 h abstinence; up to 6-8 weeks is thought to be necessary for restoration of ciliary and immunological activity. Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 530

610.q: A 38-year-old woman with a history of diverticulosis is scheduled for an exploratory laparotomy for lysis of adhesions. Which of the following is the best way of maintaining core body temperature during the initial hour of general endotracheal anesthetic?
o: Providing warm and humidified inspired gases
610.e: The initial reduction in core temperature during general anesthesia is caused by redistribution of heat from the core to the periphery, which can be attenuated by increasing ambient temperature to minimize the gradient Reference: lippincott's anesthesia review chapter 14.

610.q: You are planning an elective cesarean section for a patient with fetal breech. The patient falls under:
610.e: Explanation: ASA II: This classification is assigned to a patient with mild systemic disease . In this case, an uncomplicated pregnancy is considered a physiological state that alters the woman's baseline health but does not constitute a severe systemic disease. Pregnancy leads to changes such as increased cardiac output, altered respiratory mechanics, and changes in blood volume, which necessitate careful monitoring but generally does not increase the risk category beyond ASA II in the absence of other complications. Key Takeaways: ASA II reflects a healthy pregnan t patient with no significant comorbidities. Understanding the ASA classification helps assess the risk during anaesthesia and surgery. Reference : https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/statement-on-asa-physical-status-classification-system

611.q: While monitoring a patient for return of neuromuscular function after using rocuronium, you notice the patient has regained four twitches using train of four stimulations. With four twitches on train of four stimulations, the patient may still have blockage of acetylcholine receptors of up to
611.e: At the point the fourth twitch reappears, still up to 75% to 80% of acetylcholine receptors may be blocked. Adequate reversal (neostigmine–glycopyrrolate) should be given, and clinical signs for return of neuromuscular function should be used to gauge readiness for extubation. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 134.

611.q: Identify the correct relationship between the cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), intracranial pressure (ICP) and central venous pressure (CVP) from the ones given below.
611.e: Cerebral perfusion pressure is the pressure gradient driving cerebral blood flow. CPP = MAP - (ICP + CVP) Where CPP is cerebral perfusion pressure, CVP is central venous pressure, MAP is the mean arterial pressure and ICP is the intracranial pressure. Reference: Physics, Pharmacology and Physiology for Anaesthetists, Matthew E. Cross, second edition, pg 313.

611.q: A 54-year-old male hypertensive patient underwent laparoscopic lower anterior resection. His blood pressure in the recovery was 190/80 mm Hg and heart rate was 91 beats per minute. He was maintaining saturation of 100% with oxygen mask of 4 liters. Given that, the reason is the pain, step of management will include the following:
611.e: Noxious stimulation from incisional pain, endotracheal intubation, full bladder, or preoperative discontinuation of anti-hypertensive medication, is usually responsible for increased blood pressure in the recovery area. Adequate analgesia preoperatively given with opioids. Mild to moderate elevations can be treated with intravenous labetalol; an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, such as enalapril; or a calcium channel blocker, such as nicardipine. The end point for treatment should be consistent with the patient’s own normal blood pressure. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology, page no 1300

612.q: Which of the following is most likely to be associated with a falsely elevated Sao2 as measured by pulse oximetry (dual wave)?
612.e: Most pulse oximeters illuminate tissue with two wavelengths of light: 660-nm red light and 940-nm infrared light. Because carboxyhemoglobin has an absorbance at 660 nm, very similar to O2 hemoglobin, it produces a falsely elevated Sao2 when present in the blood. Hemoglobin F, bilirubin, and fluorescein dye have no effect on pulse oximetry. Methylene blue, as well as indigo carmine and indocyanine green, lowers the Sao2 as measured by pulse oximetry. Methemoglobin absorbs red and infrared light equally well and gives saturation readings of 85%. Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 702-703; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, p 327.

612.q: A 60-year-old patient undergoes a midline laparotomy for intestinal obstruction. All of the following respiratory effects can be seen in the post-operative period in this patient, except:
o: Increased tidal volume due to pain
612.e: Pain due to abdominal or thoracic incisions compromises pulmonary function because of guarding (splinting). Decreased movement of the chest wall reduces tidal volume and functional residual capacity, promoting atelectasis, intrapulmonary shunting, hypoxemia, and less commonly, hypoventilation. Reductions in vital capacity impair coughing and clearing of secretions. Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition pg 1062

612.q: Capnography can help detect all of the following promptly, except
612.e: It is important to remember that capnography will show a normal capnograph and end-tidal CO 2 immediately following endo-bronchial intubation. Anesthesia providers must be vigilant to always listen for bilateral breath sounds and observe bilateral chest rise to confirm tracheal intubation. Oesophagal intubation will show progressive decrease of etCO 2 with breaths. Bronchospasm will show steep upslope of the trace Sudden decrease in etCO 2 is seen in pulmonary embolism. Reference : dorsch and dorsch 5th edition pg 594.

613.q: All are features of difficult airway except ?
613.e: Ans. D. Increased thyromental distance Decreased thyromental distance predicts difficult airway (not increased TM distance).

613.q: Airway adjust play a vital role in maintaining a patent airway. For selecting a oropharyngeal airway, measurement should be taken from
o: Angle of the mouth to angle of mandible
613.e: Explanation: Measurement for Size Selection: The appropriate size of the oropharyngeal airway (OPA) is determined by measuring the vertical distance from the patient's incisors to the angle of the mandible . This ensures that the OPA fits correctly, allowing for optimal airway patency without causing obstruction. Consequences of Incorrect Sizing: Too small: Can kink the tongue, leading to obstruction of airflow. Too large: May push the epiglottis backward, causing further obstruction or trauma to the larynx. Key Takeaways: Accurate sizing of the oropharyngeal airway is crucial for maintaining a patent airway. Proper measurements help prevent complications associated with incorrect airway adjunct sizing.

613.q: Laryngeal mask airway was discovered by
613.e: Brain demonstrated the first commercially made silicone model of LMA . First commercial devices were made available in the UK Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 16 Page No 197 to 204

614.q: Pre oxygenation replaces the nitrogen in the functional residual volume with oxygen. This can achieved by
o: Tidal respiration for 3-5 mins with 100 percent o2
614.e: The optimal technique is uncertain; 3 min administration is thought to be as effective as 5 min administration, or even four vital capacity breaths. A tightly fitting face-mask (to prevent entrainment of room air) and adequate flow of O 2 are vital. Monitoring of end-expiratory O 2 concentration may be a useful guide during pre-oxygenation; washout of nitrogen from the lungs is indicated by an increase in expired O 2 concentration towards steady state (near 100% in ideal conditions with no gas leaks or mixing). Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 479

614.q: A patient suffering a stab wound to the abdomen arrives in the operating room for an emergency exploratory laparotomy. His BP is 70/40, and his HR is 118. Which of the following fluid regimens are appropriate for his fluid resuscitation?
o: Normal saline, at a ratio of 3 mL per estimated 1 mL of blood lost
Blood at a ratio of 3 mL blood administered to 1 mL of blood lost
Hetastarch (Hespan) in a ratio of 3 mL per estimated 1 mL of blood lost
D5W in a ratio of 3 mL of D5W to 1 mL of blood lost
614.e: Lactated Ringer's solution or Plasmalyte in approximately three times the volume of the blood lost, or colloid in a 1:1 ratio , until the transfusion trigger point is reached is used for fluid resuscitation of a patient. At that time, blood is replaced unit-for-unit as it is lost , with reconstituted packed red blood cells. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition, pg. 1196.

614.q: A 54-year-old woman is undergoing a total thyroid ectomy under general anesthesia. The patient is awak ened in the OR, the mouth and pharynx are suctioned, and after intact laryngeal reflexes are demonstrated, the endotracheal tube is removed. Two days later, the anesthesiologist is consulted because the patient has severe stridor and upper airway obstruction. The most likely cause of airway obstruction in this patient is
o: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
614.e: The symptoms of hypocalcemia, which manifest as laryngospasm or laryngeal stridor, usually develop within the first 24 to 96 hours after total thyroidectomy. After the airway is established and secured, the patient should be treated with IV calcium in the form of either calcium gluconate or calcium chloride Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 352-353, 1330.

o: Increase tidal volume (Vt) and decrease respiratory rate
Increase Vt and increase respiratory rate
Decrease Vt and decrease respiratory rate
Decrease Vt and increase respiratory rate
615.e: At concentrations of 1 MAC or less, volatile anesthetics, as well as the inhaled anesthetic N 2 O, will produce dose-dependent increases in the respiratory rate in spontaneously breathing patients. This trend continues at concentrations greater than 1 MAC for all of the inhaled anesthetics except isoflurane. With the exception of N 2 O, the evidence suggests that this effect is caused by direct activation of the respiratory center in the CNS rather than by stimulation of pulmonary stretch receptors. Additionally, volatile anesthetics decrease Vt and significantly alter the breathing pattern from the normal awake pattern of intermittent deep breaths separated by varying time intervals to one of rapid, shallow, regular, and rhythmic breathing. Reference: Miller’s Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 691-692.

615.q: Anaesthetic breathing systems can be open or closed. To be a closed circuit, which of the following is a pre requisite
615.e: The components of a circle system include: a CO 2 absorber containing CO 2 absorbent; a fresh gas inlet; an inspiratory unidirectional valve and inspiratory breathing tube; a Y-connector; an expiratory unidirectional valve and expiratory breathing tube; an APL valve; and a reservoir. Reference: Morgan, edition 4, page no 40

615.q: Compared to the Mapleson A system, the circle system
o: Has a decreased risk of disconnection
Has decreased resistance to patient breathing
615.e: Advantages of the circle system include economy (low fresh gas flow rates, decreased use of volatile agents), conservation of heat and humidity, and decreased operating-room pollution. Disadvantages of circle system include greater size, decreased portability, increased risk of disconnection, and increased resistance to patient breathing. Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

616.q: When compared to a cylinder manifold, a vacuum-insulated evaporator (VIE) is the most economical way to store and supply oxygen in a large hospital. What is the single most important reason for this?
o: The critical temperature of liquid oxygen is ideal to store as a liquid
Liquid oxygen is easier to store.
VIE does not require rigorous maintenance.
When evaporated, liquid oxygen occupies a large volume as gas.
616.e: Liquid oxygen is stored in a vacuum-insulated evaporator (VIE) at a temperature of -150°C to -170°C and at a pressure of 5-10 atmospheres. In simple terms this works like a giant thermos flask. At 15°C, one volume of liquid oxygen occupies 842 times its volume as gas. Oxygen constantly evaporates from the top of the VIE. As this oxygen is very cold, it needs to be passed through a super heater. When the oxygen flows at a faster rate, the temperature of the liquid falls due to the latent heat of evaporation. To overcome this problem additional heat is provided by a pressure-raising vaporiser. Regular maintenance, monitoring of usage of oxygen and topping up the tank at regular intervals is necessary. Reference: Al-Shaikh B, Stacey S, Eds. Liquid oxygen. In: Essentials of anaesthetic equipment, 3rd ed. London, UK: Churchill Livingstone, Elsevier, 2007; Chapter 1: 9-10.

616.q: True statement about Volatility and vaporization?
o: The more volatile a liquid, the faster it vaporizes
Volatility and vaporization are not related
The more volatile a liquid, the slower it vaporizes
616.e: The more volatile a liquid, the faster it vaporizes and the greater the loss of latent heat of vaporization Liquid cools à rate of vaporization falls Reference : Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 44 Page No .423

The ideal vaporizer should be Lightweight, robust and durable Easy to transport Corrosion and solvent resistant Leak proof Economical and safe to use Require minimal servicing Accurate over a wide range of: Freah Gas Flow Liquid agent levels Ambient pressures Ambient temperatures Unaffected by: Heat loss due to vaporization Pressure changes downstream of the vaporizer Tilting or tipping Compatible with vaporizer interlock systems Reference :Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 44 Page No .423 to 428

617.q: Which of the following are components of High-Quality CPR? 1: Chest compression at a rate of 100-120/min 2: Breathing at a rate of 20-25/min 3: Depth of compression should be 5-6 cm 4: Allow Chest Recoil
617.e: High-Quality CPR in adults includes: Effective compressions at least 100/min, no more than 120/min Minimal interruptions ( Allow for chest recoil, monitoring via capnography *less than 10 is ineffective Compression depth should be at least 5-6 cm Rotate q2mins/5cycles Chest Compression Fraction (CCF) at least 60%, goal of greater than 80%

617.q: Arrange Steps of CPR: A) Check pulse B) Check respiration C) Assess responsiveness D) Start chest compressions E) Start bag and mask
617.e: Assess responsiveness Check pulse Check respiration Start chest compressions Start bag and mask

618.q: Which of the following are methods of invasive ventilation
618.e: Invasive ventilation uses gadgets which pass beyond vocal cords and achieve a definitive airway. In mechanical ventilation, artificial airways provide a vital link between the ventilator and the patient. Two common artificial airways used in conjunction with mechanical ventilators are the endotracheal (ET) and tracheostomy tubes. Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 151

618.q: Incorrect statement regarding the mechanisms of an Ambu bag is
o: It contains a nonrebreathing valve, same as the circle system
It is capable of delivery of nearly a 100% O2 concentration
Patient valve has low resistance to both inspiration and expiration
618.e: While resuscitation devices such as Ambu bags or bag-mask units have nonrebreathing valves, neither the Mapleson (only has adjustable pressure-limiting valve) nor the circle system (only has unidirectional valves and does allow rebreathing) has this component. Ambu resuscitation bags do allow for positive pressure ventilation as the intake valve closes during bag compression. The patient valve has low resistance, but can become obstructed by exhaled moisture. Ambu bags have a reservoir system to prevent room air entrapment and are able to deliver nearly 100% oxygen. Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

618.q: A 65-year-old patient with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and coronary artery disease (CAD) undergoes a laparoscopic nephrectomy uneventfully under general desflurane anesthesia. In the recovery room, ABGs are as follows: Pao2 60 mm Hg, Paco2 50 mm Hg, pH 7.35, and hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL. Which of the following steps would produce the greatest increase in O2 delivery to the myocardium?
o: Administration of 100% O2 with a close-fitting mask
Administration of 35% O2 with a Venturi mask
Transfuse with 2 units of packed red blood cells (RBCs)
618.e: One gram of hemoglobin can combine with 1.34 mL of O2. None of the other choices in this question will do as much to increase the O2-carrying capacity of this patient's blood as a transfusion Reference: Stoelting: Pharmacology and Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, ed 4, pg 787, 849.

619.q: Reason for preferring Cis-Atracurium over atracurium is:
619.e: Cisatracurium This R-Cis, R-Cis enantiomer of atracurium is nearly 4 times more potent , slower in onset (Option A ruled out), but similar in duration of action .(Option C ruled out) Like atracurium it undergoes Hofmann elimination (Option D ruled out), but in contrast to the racemate, it is not hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase and hepatic metabolism is limited, so that less of the toxic metabolite is formed. Most importantly, it does not provoke histamine release and side effects are fewer. Currently, cisatracurium is one of the preferred muscle relaxants, especially for liver/kidney disease patients and for the elderly.

619.q: The atropine is added to neostigmine to?
o: Facilitate earlier recovery from neuromuscular blockade
619.e: Atropine, a tertiary amine, is an anticholinergic drug which is used along with anticholinesterases like neostigmine to minimize the muscarinic adverse effects of anticholinesterases ( Option C is CORRECT ) It has no effect on the reversal of neuromuscular blockade produced by the nicotinic effect of anticholinesterases (Option A, B & D) It counteracts the cardiovascular effects of anticholinesterases like bradycardia and other bradyarrhythmia Glycopyrrolate , a quaternary amine, is another anticholinergic which can be used with the anticholinesterases It has slower onset than atropine but does not cause central effects as it does not cross blood brain barrier unlike atropine Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

619.q: Dose of succinyl choline in infant?
619.e: Neonates, infants, and young children have relatively greater alveolar ventilation and reduced FRC compared with older children and adults This greater minute ventilation-to-FRC ratio with relatively greater blood flow to vessel-rich organs contributes to a rapid increase in alveolar anaesthetic concentration and speeds inhalation induction Furthermore, the blood/gas coefficients of volatile anaesthetics are reduced in neonates compared with adults, resulting in even faster induction times and potentially increasing the risk of accidental overdosage Reference: E Book Morgan and Mikhail’s 6th Edition Chapter 42 Page No 1532.

620.q: A patient was admitted for surgery and halothane is being planned to be used as an anaesthetic agent. The patient was explained about the adverse effect of malignant hyperthermia with this drug. Which of the following drugs may also result in malignant hyperthermia?
620.e: Malignant hyperthermia produced by halothane and isoflurane in rare (genetically predisposed) individuals is more common in patients receiving SCh as well.

620.q: Which of the following inhalational anaesthetic agents is with highest respiratory irritation?
620.e: Desflurane It has minimum blood gas partition coefficient and therefore is the fastest inducing agent. It has very high vapour pressure . Its boiling point is 23°C; therefore it boils at room temperature. It requires special vaporizers due to this property. It produces cardiovascular effects similar to isoflurane except coronary steal phenomenon. Induction with desflurane is unpleasant. It causes maximum irritation to airways . As it can lead to coughing, breath holding and laryngospasm. It can also be used in day care surgery.

620.q: Ratio of 02: N20 in Entonox is ?
620.e: Ans. A. 50 : 50 Entonox contain equal amount (50/50) of N2O and O2.

621.q: Which can replace N20 as 02 carrier?
621.e: Ans. C. Helium Helium can be used to replace nitrogen, as the carrier gas for oxygen (Helium) to reduce the work of breathing.

621.q: Which of the following is a contraindication for the use of Inhalational agents
621.e: Malignant hyperthermia is a contraindication for the use of Inhalational agents and succinylcholine Pseudocholinesterase deficiency can cause prolongation of action of Succinylcholine leading to delayed recovery from the muscle relaxant and scoline apnea Reference: FRCA in a box, page no 188

Enflurane is the most epileptogenic inhalational anaesthetic especially in the presence of cerebral injury and hypocapnia So enflurane is contraindicated in patients with a Known history of seizures Cerebrovascular disease In head injuries as seizure activity can increase the cerebral metabolism manifold Besides enflurane increases cerebrospinal fluid secretion and decreases its absorption which is deleterious in those with poor intracranial compliance Seizures have been associated with the use of sevoflurane in high concentrations, especially in the paediatric population. Epileptogenic Potential : Enflurane >>> Sevoflurane Reference : Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

622.q: What is the correct dose of thiopental?
622.e: The principal clinical uses of thiopental (3–5 mg/kg IV) or methohexital (1–5 mg/kg IV) is for induction of anaesthesia (unconsciousness), which usually occurs in less than 30 seconds. Patients may experience a garlic or onion taste after administration. Barbiturates such as methohexital (20–30 mg/kg) may be administered per rectum to facilitate induction of anaesthesia in mentally challenged and uncooperative paediatric patients. When a barbiturate is administered with the goal of neuroprotection, an isoelectric EEG indicating maximal reduction of CMR O 2 has traditionally been used as the end point. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 442

622.q: Benzodiazepines are usually used as premedication before general anaesthesia. Which are the desired effect of benzodiazepines useful in premedication?
622.e: Benzodiazepines commonly used in the perioperative period include midazolam, lorazepam, and less frequently, diazepam. Benzodiazepines are unique among the group of intravenous anaesthetics in that their action can readily be terminated by administration of their selective antagonist, flumazenil. Their most desired effects are anxiolysis and anterograde amnesia, which are extremely useful for premedication. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 442

622.q: During the course of a complicated cardiac case, the surgeon informs you that he is worried about damage to the right coronary artery in a patient with a right-dominant coronary system. During reperfusion, you are looking for signs of ischemia, and are most interested in leads
622.e: Ischemic changes in leads II, III and aVF suggest right coronary artery disease, leads I and aVL monitor the circumflex artery distribution and leads V3 to V5 look at the distribution of the left anterior descending artery . Reference: objective anaesthesia review 4th edition pg 18

623.q: Which of the following anaesthetic agent is not painful on intravenous administration
623.e: Ketamine is a strong analgesic drug and is water soluble. Its injection is not painful. Propofol and etomidate solutions have to be made in oil due to poor water solubility, so these injections are quite painful.(Option B,C) Methohexitone can cause hyperalgesia.(Option D)

623.q: Which of the following intravenous general anaesthetic agent has cardiovascular stability?
623.e: A characteristic and desired feature of induction of anaesthesia with Etomidate is cardiovascular stability after bolus injection. In this regard, decrease in systemic blood pressure is modest or absent and principally reflects a decrease in systemic vascular resistance.
