Therefore, the systemic blood pressure-lowering effects of Etomidate are probably exaggerated in the presence of hypovolemia, and optimization of the patient’s intravascular fluid volume status before induction of anesthesia should be achieved. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 443

Dexmedetomidine markedly increases the range of temperatures not triggering thermoregulatory defences, Thus proving to be an effective treatment for nonthermally induced shivering Severe bradycardia may follow the administration of dexmedetomidine and cardiac arrest has been reported in a patient receiving a dexmedetomidine infusion as a supplement to general anaesthesia Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 17 Page No 496 to 499

624.q: Which is the reference local anaesthetic agent against which all agents are compared?
624.e: Aside from the issue of a high incidence of TNS with spinal administration, lidocaine has had an excellent record as an intermediate duration anaesthetic, and remains the reference standard against which most anaesthetics are compared. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 460

624.q: Local anaesthetic agents cause neural toxicity. Which of the following is TRUE? 1. Neural injury occurs from voltage gated sodium channels 2. Clinical effect and toxicity is tightly linked.
o: Sentence 1 and 2 both are True and 2 is correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 and 2 both are True but 2 is not the correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 is True but Sentence 2 is False
624.e: It is not clear what role these factors or others play in clinical injury. It is clear, however, that injury does not result from blockade of the voltage-gated sodium channel per se, and thus clinical effect and toxicity are not tightly linked. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 459

624.q: The manifestations of shellfish poisoning are due to the action of the poison on which channel?
624.e: Saxitoxin and Tetrodotoxin are two potent poisons whose mechanism of action is like that of local anaesthetics - blockade of Na channels. Saxitoxin is produced by certain dinoflagellates which are consumed by shellfish → When such shell fish are consumed by humans, fatal shell fish poisoning occurs with hypotension and respiratory paralysis → This is due to blockade of Na channels by the poison in excitable cells preventing action potential generation Treatment consists of Gastric lavage Vasopressors Mechanical ventilation if respiratory paralysis sets in Prognosis is good when the patient survives after 24 hours Tetrodotoxin is a poison found in some fish of the order Tetraodontiformes (puffer fish) and newts Mechanism of action and manifestations are like shellfish poisoning Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

625.e: As previously discussed, this S (–) enantiomer of bupivacaine is somewhat less cardiotoxic than the racemic mixture. It is also less potent, and tends to have a longer duration of action, though the magnitude of these effects is too small to have any substantial clinical significance. Interestingly, recent work with lipid resuscitation suggests a potential advantage of levobupivacaine over ropivacaine, as the former is more effectively sequestered into a so-called lipid sink, implying greater ability to reverse toxic effects should they occur. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 460

625.q: What is the only drawback of lidocaine?
o: Higher incidence of TNS(transient neurogenic symptoms)
625.e: Aside from the issue of a high incidence of TNS with spinal administration, lidocaine has had an excellent record as an intermediate duration anaesthetic, and remains the reference standard against which most anaesthetics are compared. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 460

625.q: An anesthetist injected bupivacaine in a patient for axillary nerve block. Later, the patient developed restlessness, agitation and cardiovascular collapse. Next best step in the management would be?
625.e: Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic At toxic doses, local anaesthetics can result in CNS (convulsions) or CVS (hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias) symptoms. Diazepam is used to treat convulsions. If not responding, thiopentone may be used. Arrhythmias should be promptly treated using bretylium, amiodarone, disopyramide, magnesium sulphate, esmolol or sotalol. Lignocaine should be avoided as antiarrhythmic because it canexacerbate the CNS toxicity. In refractory arrhythmias, intravenous lipid emulsion (like intralipid)has been found to be extremely useful. Bupivacaine induced cardiotoxicity is enhanced by acidosis, hypercarbia and hypoxemia.

626.q: A 32-year-old man is apprehensive of general anesthesia and prefers a regional anesthetic. Decision is made to conduct spinal anesthesia for the repair of inguinal hernia along with midazolam and fentanyl to allay anxiety. During the procedure, he suddenly loses consciousness. There is profound hypotension with systolic blood pressure of 44 mm Hg and a heart rate of 28 bpm. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started. The best appropriate intervention is administration of
626.e: In the clinical scenario described, atropine by itself, may not be able to correct the hemodynamics, and the situations call for initiation of measures required in advanced cardiac life support If there is no pulse → chest compressions along with → administration of epinephrine may be the best course of action Reference : ACLS guidelines AHA

626.q: The surgeon is performing a right total knee arthroplasty under a combined spinal-epidural anesthetic. The surgical team is providing you with information that within the next 15 minutes they plan to place bone cement to anchor the prosthesis. The most likely side effect that may occur is
626.e: The clinical manifestations of bone cement implantation syndrome include Hypoxia (increased pulmonary shunt) Hypotension Arrhythmias (including heart block and sinus arrest) Pulmonary hypertension (increased pulmonary vascular resistance) Decreased cardiac output Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg. 805.

626.q: You are giving caudal block for a lower limb surgery in a pediatric patient. The equilateral triangle is formed between the posterior superior iliac spines and _______
626.e: Caudal epidural anesthesia is a common regional technique in pediatric patients. Caudal anesthesia involves needle or catheter penetration of the sacrococcygeal ligament covering the sacral hiatus that is created by the unfused S4 and S5 laminae. The hiatus may be felt as a groove or notch above the coccyx and between two bony prominences, the sacral cornua. The posterior superior iliac spines and the sacral hiatus define an equilateral triangle Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 987.

627.q: A 21-year-old patient reports tingling in her thumb during her cesarean section under epidural anesthesia. To which dermatomal level would this correspond?
627.e: The thumb corresponds to dermatome C6, the second and middle fingers correspond to dermatome C7, and the fourth and little fingers correspond to dermatome C8. Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 920

627.q: Transient neurologic syndrome (TNS) is MOST commonly seen after the spinal anesthetic injection of which local anesthetic?
627.e: Transient neurologic syndrome (TNS), formerly called transient radicular irritation (TRI), occurs most commonly after spinal anesthesia with lidocaine (Xylocaine). Symptoms include back pain that develops after the block resolves and radiates to the buttocks and legs. The pain is not associated with motor or sensory loss or electromyographic changes. It can be severe, requiring hospital admission of outpatients, and typically resolves within 1 to 4 days. It appears to occur more commonly when outpatients are operated on in the lithotomy position and appears to be less likely when patients are pregnant Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, p 756; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 112-113.

627.q: During performance of lumbar epidural anesthesia for labor analgesia, you experience free-flowing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the advancing 17G Tuohy epidural needle. The epidural needle is removed and a second attempt is successfully performed with an epidural catheter placed at a different level. Which of the following you would not recommend for the patient to practice in the next 72 hours?
627.e: In patients who may experience a "wet tap" during placement of an epidural, conservative therapy should include bed rest and plenty of fluid intake, including caffeine; food diet low in fiber and stool softeners are encouraged to prevent straining. Leakage of CSF can lead to a reduction in intracranial pressure and post dural puncture headache chances are high since the epidural needle is an 16/18 G needle . Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 992.

628.q: A 30-year-old male underwent ACL reconstruction of the left knee under general anaesthesia and adductor canal block. After the surgery, the Inhalational agents were stopped and reversal was giving with Neostigmine (with glycopyrrolate). He did not regain consciousness or spontaneous efforts of breathing. Given that he received high dose of Morphine for premedication, next line of management will include the following,
628.e: When the patient fails to regain consciousness within an expected period of time after general anesthesia, the most frequent cause is residual drug effect. Delayed emergence may occur as a result of absolute or relative drug overdose. The effects of preoperative sleep deprivation or drug ingestion (alcohol, sedatives) can be additive to those of anesthetic agents in producing prolonged emergence. Intravenous naloxone and flumazenil will readily reverse the effects of an opioid and benzodiazepine, respectively. Intravenous physostigmine may partially reverse the effect of other agents. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology, page 1289

628.q: A 30-year-old man presents for open reduction and internal fixation of a left radius fracture as an outpatient. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 12 years. The plan is general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. Which one of the following agents is most appropriate for him?
628.e: Although all agents could be used, sevoflurane would be the preferred choice. Sevoflurane could be used in combination with nitrous oxide Wrong Answers: Option A : Isoflurane could also be used, but because of its high blood: gas solubility it may delay emergence, which is undesirable in outpatients Option B : Desflurane has a lower blood: gas solubility that would provide rapid awakening , but desflurane is irritating to inhale and can cause bronchoconstriction in smokers Reference : Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

628.q: Local infiltration of lignocaine and other local anesthetic agents are less reliable for ankle block of an infected diabetic foot. This is because
628.e: Since local anesthetics are weak bases, they exist largely in the ionic form, making it difficult for them to cross the cell membrane, thus delaying their local anesthetic action. Further they become ionized when the local tissue is infected and the local pH is acidic. Their action becomes unreliable. Addition of sodium bicarbonate promotes nonionized fraction of local anesthetic, promoting more rapid onset of its action. Reference: Stoeltings pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 5th edition pg. 291

629.q: A hyperthyroid patient presents to the casualty room following road traffic accident. He has sustained right leg crush injury that requires amputation. He is taken up for surgery under general anesthesia. Which of the following monitors is likely to indicate precipitation of a thyroid crisis intraoperatively
629.e: Thyroid storm can present during and post surgery with fever (>40°C), sweating, sinus tachycardia (>140bpm), coma, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea. Management involves rehydration with IV saline and glucose, administration of steroid, beta blockers, propylthiouracil and paracetamol. Reference : Oxford handbook of Anesthesia, edition 4, page no 577

629.q: A 37-year-old man with myasthenia gravis arrives in the emergency room confused and agitated after a 2-day history of weakness and increased difficulty breathing. ABGs on room air are Pao2 60 mm Hg, Paco2 51 mm Hg, HCO3 - 25 mEq/L, pH 7.3, Sao2 of 90%. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min and tidal volume (Vt) is 4 mL/kg. After administration of edrophonium 2 mg IV, his Vt declines to 2 mL/kg. What should be the most appropriate step in the management of this patient at this time?
o: Repeat the test dose of edrophonium
629.e: Cholinergic crisis can be differentiated from myasthenic crisis by administering small IV doses of anticholinesterases. With a cholinergic crisis, there are significant muscarinic effects (e.g., salivation, bradycardia, miosis) and an accentuated muscle weakness. Because this patient's Vt decreased with the administration of edrophonium, the diagnosis of cholinergic crisis is made. Although atropine may be needed to treat the cholinergic symptoms, muscle weakness will be worse and these patients need to be intubated until the muscle strength returns. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, p 450

629.q: An end stage renal disease patient has been scheduled for renal transplant. He is on thrice weekly hemodialysis. His blood investigations revealed high potassium levels more than 6.0 mEq/L and he was dialyzed preoperatively, repeat potassium was 5.2 mEq/L. The drugs to be used in caution include all except
629.e: Succinylcholine, depolarizing muscle relaxant can cause an increase in the potassium concentration up to 0.5 mEq/L can be used to facilitate endotracheal intubation only in the absence of hyperkalemia. Meperidine (pethidine), opioid should be avoided because of accumulation of its metabolite normeperidine. Sevoflurane usage for long hours can cause accumulation of compound A, that has been found nephrotoxic. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesia, 6th edition, page no. 689

630.q: A 7-week-old male infant is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (ICU) with a bowel obstruction. His laboratory values are sodium 120 mEq/L, chloride 85 mEq/L, glucose 85 mg/dL, and potassium 2.0 mEq/L. Respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min, and according to the patient's mother, urine output has been 0 for the last 4 hours. The most appropriate fluid for resuscitation of this patient would be
o: D2.5W with 0.45 sodium chloride and 20 mEq/L potassium chloride
0.9% sodium chloride with 30 mEq/L potassium chloride
630.e: The symptoms described in this patient are consistent with severe dehydration. Thus, the vascular volume should be expanded initially with an isotonic saline solution or a colloid solution until the patient voids. When the urine output increases, potassium can be added to the IV fluids. Although glucose administration for long procedures may prevent hypoglycemia, D5W alone or with a crystalloid solution should not be used to replace fluid deficits. Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 126-129.

630.q: A premature male neonate born at 34 weeks of gestation is scheduled to undergo emergency repair of a left-sided diaphragmatic hernia. Which of the following vessels could be cannulated for preductal arterial blood sampling?
630.e: Newborns with diaphragmatic hernia have significant respiratory difficulty. In addition to their hypoplastic lungs, persistent pulmonary hypertension is present, producing right-to-left shunting through the patent ductus arteriosus. To more appropriately administer the anesthetic, a preductal (ductus arteriosus) artery should be cannulated to monitor arterial blood gases and blood pressure. The right radial or temporal arteries arise from vessels that originate from the aorta proximal to the ductus arteriosus. The oxygen saturation monitors should be placed on the right arm as well. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 595-596.

630.q: Main determinant of cardiac output in infants and children?
630.e: Cardiac stroke volume is relatively fixed by a noncompliant and immature left ventricle in neonates and infants The cardiac output is therefore very sensitive to changes in heart rate Although basal heart rate is greater than in adults Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail’s 6th Edition Chapter 42 1521, 1522.

631.q: Which of the factors in adults listed below is the strongest independent predictor of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in most studies?
631.e: PONV is the second most common complaint from patients after surgery (postoperative pain is the number one complaint). Of the many independent predictors of PONV in adult prospective studies, female gender is the strongest predictor for PONV and the need for postoperative antiemetic rescue treatments. It is interesting to note that although patients often experience nausea when smoking their first cigarettes, smokers have a lower incidence of PONV compared to nonsmokers. Other predictors of PONV include nonsmokers, previous history of PONV, history of migraine headaches, use of post[1]operative narcotics, lengthy surgical procedures, use of nitrous oxide, and the use of volatile anesthetics Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2947-2954.

631.q: A 40-year-old woman undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy has an oxygen saturation which rapidly decreases to 80% on 100% inspired oxygen, peak airway pressures increase to 38 cmH2O, and blood pressure reduces to 72/42 mmHg. Examination demonstrates absent breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note on the left side of the chest. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
631.e: This patient is demonstrating clinical features of a tension pneumothorax with hypoxia, elevated airway pressures and hypotension. This is a recognized risk of laparoscopic surgery and requires immediate recognition and treatment with insertion of a cannula in the second intercostal space, midclavicular line on the affected side. An intercostal chest drain should then be inserted for this life-threatening emergency. Optimizing ventilator parameters would not treat the cause and may worsen any tension by increasing the size of the pneumothorax. Administration of intravenous fluid boluses would be of benefit but would not be addressing the underlying cause. Reference: Hayden P, Cowman S. Anaesthesia for laparoscopic surgery. Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain 2011; 11:177–180.

631.q: A 78-year-old woman is anesthetized for a right hemicolectomy for 3 hours. At the end of the operation the patient's blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg, heart rate is 84 beats/min, core body temperature is 35.4°C, and Peco2 on infrared spectrometer is 38 mm Hg. Which of the following would be the LEAST plausible reason for prolonged apnea in this patient?
o: Unrecognized obstructive pulmonary disease and high baseline Paco2
631.e: Hyperventilation to Paco2 of 20 mm Hg or higher for more than 2 hours will result in active transport of HCO3 - out of the CNS. This results in spontaneous breathing at a lower (not higher) Paco2. The other choices should be included in the differential diagnosis of apnea. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 5, pp 359-361; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 62-64, 340; Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 271-273.

632.q: Common causes for lower back pain include all of the following, except
632.e: Chronic lower back pain is one of the top reasons for physician office visits and also one of the greatest reasons for work absence. Lumbosacral strain, degenerative disk disease, and myofascial syndromes are the most common causes, and fibromyalgia is not typically associated with a diagnosis of lower back pain. Reference: lippincott's anaesthesia review pg 212.

632.q: Hyperpathia is the simultaneous presence of which of the following?
632.e: Presence of hyperesthesia, allodynia, and hyperalgesia usually associated with overreaction, and persistence of the sensation after the stimulus is known as hyperpathia. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1050 table 47-1.

632.q: A trauma patient presenting with acute pain can be expected to have all of the following systemic responses to pain except:
632.e: Enhanced sympathetic tone increases sphincter tone and decreases intestinal and urinary bladder motility, promoting ileus and urinary retention and not increased peristalsis. Cardiovascular effects of acute pain often include hypertension, tachycardia, enhanced myocardial irritability, and increased systemic vascular resistance. An increase in total body oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production due to pain, necessitates a concomitant increase in minute ventilation which in turn increases the work of breathing. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1062.

633.q: Which of the following is the correct order of layers of epidermis from deep to superficial?
o: S.basale, S. granulosum, S. spinosum, S. corneum
S. corneum, S. granulosum, S. spinosum, S. basale
S. basale, S. spinosum, S. granulosum, S. corneum
S. corneum, S. spinosum, S. granulosum, S. basale
633.e: Explanation: The correct order of epidermal layers from deepest to most superficial is: Stratum basale -single layer of mitotically active keratinocytes Stratum spinosum -cells with desmosomal "spines" Stratum granulosum- keratohyalin granules present Stratum corneum- outermost layer of dead, keratinized cells Epidermal layers (deep to superficial): S.basale : Stem cell layer, melanocytes, Merkel cells S.spinosum : Thickest living layer, Langerhans cells S.granulosum : Granular layer, barrier formation S.lucidum : Present only in thick skin (palms, soles) S.corneum : Anucleate keratinized layer providing protection

633.q: Which of the following is the most important enzyme in melanogenesis?
633.e: Tyrosinase is a copper dependent enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of L-tyrosine into L-DOPA, the rate-limiting stage in melanin synthesis. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 88, page 5

633.q: The Malpighian layer of the epidermis includes _______.
633.e: The basal layer is the mitotically active layer, divides to give rise to outer population of cells that constitutes the spinous layer. These two epidermal layers together are referred to as the Malpighian layer. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 5

634.q: The epidermis contains multiple specialized cell types with distinct functions, locations, and embryological origins. Understanding where each cell type resides is essential for dermatology and pathology. Which of the following statements about skin structure is NOT true?
o: Langerhans cells originate from bone marrow and are present in granular layer.
Melanocytes are present in stratum basale.
Stratified squamous epithelium with hallmark keratin intermediate filaments.
Merkel cells are present in stratum basale.
634.e: Explanation: Langerhans cells do originate from bone marrow, but they are primarily located in the stratum spinosum, not the granular layer. Key epidermal cell types and their locations: Langerhans cells: Antigen-presenting dendritic cells derived from bone marrow; mostly in stratum spinosum. Melanocytes: Neural crest-derived pigment cells; found in stratum basale. Merkel cells: Mechanoreceptors involved in touch sensation; located in stratum basale. Keratinocytes: Main epidermal cells with abundant keratin intermediate filaments, forming stratified squamous keratinized epithelium.

634.q: A patient presented with multiple hypo-aesthetic patches on limb and trunk with bilateral symmetrical nerve thickening. What is the diagnosis?
634.e: Multiple lesions on limb and trunk with B/L symmetric Nerve thickening are pointing towards lepromatous end of spectrum, which could be BL or LL. BL - hypoesthetic lesions LL - normoesthetic lesions and glove and stocking type anesthesia. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 28, page 10

Combination of giant hemangioma, thrombocytopenia, and consumption coagulopathy KMS is an infrequent but potentially fatal complication of rapidly growing vascular lesions in infants The low platelet count in Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is due to a combination of increased destruction and sequestration of platelets within the expanding vascular tumour. The tumor here is infantile haemangioma. MC vascular tumor in infants Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 101, Page 4

635.q: Which bedside tests helps to differentiate nevus anemicus and nevus depigmentosus ?
635.e: Pressing the lesion with glass slide - diascopy Helps differentiate between ND and NA. The margins of ND remain distinct from normal skin during diascopy. While margins of NA blend in with surrounding skin as normal skin also blanches on pressing with the slide

635.q: The cell seen in Tzanck smear in pemphigus is:
o: Cell with hyperchromatic nuclei and perinuclear halo
Cell with hypochromatic nuclei and perinuclear halo
635.e: Acantholytic cells appear as round cells with perinuclear halo in Tzanck smear: Characteristic of Pemphigus Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 3

635.q: A patient presented to the OPD with dome shaped papules with central umbilication, on face and cytology smear was made. What is the finding observed?
635.e: Dome shaped papules with central umbilication - diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum Tzanck smear can be made from the white pasty core of the molluscum lesion - Giemsa stain done. Tzanck smear reveals the presence of diagnostic intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies (Henderson-Patterson bodies), the largest known inclusion bodies (30-35 m) Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 12

636.q: Eccrine glands are involved in which of the following:
636.e: Syringomas are benign, eccrine sweat duct tumours, typically found clustered on eyelids in a symmetric pattern. Syringomas are skin-coloured or yellowish, generally small, dermal papules. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number-30.

Clinical Presentation of Acne Sites: Face, shoulders, upper trunk Polymorphic eruption: Comedones, papules, nodules, cysts Comedones: Pathognomonic lesions of acne vulgaris Open comedones (Black heads): Block on skin surface Closed comedones (White heads): Block below skin surface Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 90, Page 1

636.q: All of the following are Premalignant lesions except:
636.e: Rhinophyma is a disfiguring nasal deformity due to the proliferation of sebaceous glands and underlying connective tissue. The name itself is broken down into "rhis," derived from Greek meaning nose, and "phyma," also Greek, for skin tumor. Rosacea is the precursor condition to the later development of rhinophyma Rhinophyma has no malignant potential Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 142, page 142.1

637.q: Which of the following is present in both skin and hair?
637.e: Keratin is a protein produced by skin cells Outermost layer of skin cells contains keratin Hair and nails are also made of keratin Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 2.

637.q: Flag sign in hair is characteristic of:
637.e: Skin Manifestations of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM) Crazy pavement 'like skin (parchment) Flag sign' in hair (alternate bands of light and dark colours) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 63, page 5

637.q: Stem cells of the hair follicle are present in?
637.e: The isthmus is the part of hair follicle between the opening of the sebaceous gland and the insertion of arrector pili muscle. Hair follicle stem cells are thought to reside in the bulge area on the isthmus close to the insertion of the arrector muscle. Bulge stem cells are multipotent, migrate in a downward direction, enter the hair bulb matrix and generate the new lower anagen hair follicle. They also migrate distally to form sebaceous glands and to proliferate in response to wounding Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 2, Page 45

638.q: Which of the following is not a NEVUS of melanocyte?
638.e: Ans. D. Becker nevus Becker nevus is appendageal nevi where as other three are melanocyitc nevi. Melanocytic nevi are :- Dysplastic nevus BIue nevus Nevus of ito & nevus of ota Spitz nevus Giant pigmented nevus Mongolian spot Intramucosal neyus

638.q: Inverted Champagne bottle appearance is seen in
638.e: Answer- C. Lipodermatosclerosis The most commonly recognized form of lipodermatosclerosis (LDS), chronic LDS presence with induration and hyperpigmentation of the skin involving the one or both of the lower legs in a characteristic "inverted champagne bottle" appearance. Associated with venous insufficiency, LDS is most common in middle-aged women.

638.q: Which of the following histological type is most sensitive in cold?
638.e: Melanocytes are very susceptible to thermal injury and may die at temperatures below -5 C. As compared to other cells in the skin, including epidermal keratinocytes, merkel cells, langerhans cells, mesissners corpuscles, contact cooling of the skin surface causes selective loss of epidermal melanocytes when the tissue temperature reaches −5 °C or cooler with an exposure time of 10 minutes or longer, leading to partial skin depigmentation Longer exposures combined with colder temperature exposure led to more complete depigmentation in the treated skin surface. This is a reason why cryosurgery procedures on skin - using liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees Celsius - causes depigmentation as a common side effect Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 17

639.e: Profilaggrin is found in the keratohyalin granules present in the stratum granulosum. Profilaggrin breaks down to yield individual filaggrin monomers at the transition between the stratum granulosum and stratum corneum. Deficiency of filaggrin: Atopic dermatitis & Ichthyosis vulgaris Reference : Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number-7.

639.q: In which of the following conditions Parakeratosis most frequently occurs -
639.e: Normally, nuclei are absent in stratum corneum. Retention of nuclei within the cells of stratum corneum - Parakeratosis. Parakeratosis is seen in - Normally → Mucous membrane of mouth and vagina. Disorders → Benign (Psoriasis, Seborrheic dermatitis) Malignant (Actinic keratosis, Squamous cell carcinoma) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 3, page 34

639.q: Which of the following is characteristically associated with Acute eczema?
639.e: Spongiosis: Intraedpidermal intercellular edemaDermal inflammatory infiltrates around the dilated venules of the superficial plexus, edema, and spongiosis Fully developed spongiosis becomes organized in focal micro vesicles Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 39, page 39.3

640.q: Darier's sign is positive in the following :
640.e: Darier's Sign :The skin characteristically urticates within minutes of gentle rubbing in children causing localized pruritus, redness and wheal, which subside within an hour. It is not 100% specific for mastocytosis, since it has been described on rare occasions in juvenile xanthogranuloma and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia of neonates Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 46, page 4

640.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen in urticaria
640.e: Type I hypersensitivity is also known as an immediate reaction and involves immunoglobulin E (IgE) mediated release of antibodies against the soluble antigen. This results in mast cell degranulation and release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Manifestations - anaphylaxis, urticaria, angioedema, food, and drug allergies The allergens that result in a type I hypersensitivity - pollen, mites, or foods, drugs, etc Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 42, page 4
Acute urticaria resolves within 6 weeks . Urticaria longer than 6 weeks' duration is considered chronic. Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 42, page 5

641.q: A patient developed bullae without erythema on elbows, knee & sacral area fib crust formation, scarring & milia. He had no photo sensitivity and negative family history for bullous diseases. On DIF IgG deposition at DEJ with no blood vessel involvement is seen probable diagnosis is:
641.e: Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA) Epidermolysis bullosa - congenital, present from birth EBA is not inherited and usually presents in adult life EBA is a rare disease in which tense blisters appear at sites of trauma EBA blisters tend to be localized to areas that are easily injured such as the hands, feet, knees, elbows, and buttocks Sometimes there is mucosal involvement with blisters forming in mouth, nose and eyes EBA may mimic Bullous pemphigoid Salt split immunofluorescence used to differentiate between EBA and BP Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 45

641.q: What can patient with gluten sensitive hypersensitivity consume as food?
641.e: Gluten is found in grains such as wheat, barley, rye, oats, triticale A gluten-free diet is a diet that excludes the gluten Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 54

641.q: Immediately after eating peanut butter sandwich, a man develops swelling of face and lips, respiratory distress, intense pruritus, hypotension and feeling of impending doom. The most likely diagnosis is:
641.e: Intense pruritus and hypotension is characteristic of anaphylaxis Besides immediate onset, welling of face and respiratory distress is conclusive of Anaphylaxis Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 43, page 4

642.q: Which of the following is the most common sexually transmitted pathogen?
642.e: Genital HPV remains the most common sexually transmitted pathogen in the United States, infecting 60% of a cohort of initially HPV-negative, sexually active Washington state college women within 5 years in a study conducted from 1990 to 2000-i.e., during the pre-HPV immunization era. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 136, Pg: 1079

642.q: What is the Most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis ?
642.e: Most common cause of urethritis in males is N. gonorrhoea. The most common cause of Non-Gonococcal urethritis in males is Chlamydia trachomatis. The most common cause of urethritis in females is Chlamydia. Hence chlamydia is the most appropriate answer. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:136 Pg: 1081, 1083

642.q: Ichy purple papule followed by hayperpigmentation on resolution, is seen in?
642.e: Ans. D. Lichen planus LP is characterized by shiny, violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules which retain the skin lines. White lines, known as Wickham's striae, may traverse the surface of the papules. Linear lesions often appear along scratch marks or in scars (Koebner phenomenon). In most cases, the papules eventually flatten after a 6 months to 2 yrs, often to be replaced by an area of hyperpigmentation.

643.q: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of psoriasis?
o: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland
Defective T cell maturation in the thymus
643.e: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells: This describes Type 1 diabetes, not psoriasis. Hyperproliferation of keratinocytes: Psoriasis is characterized by the rapid turnover and proliferation of skin cells (keratinocytes), leading to thickened skin and scaling. Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland: This is seen in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, not psoriasis. Defective T cell maturation in the thymus: This is related to autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, not psoriasis. Key Takeaway: Psoriasis is primarily due to the hyperproliferation of keratinocytes. Tags: Good to know Tag Line: Moderate Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology . Chapter 17: Autoimmunity, pp. 203-207

643.q: A 19 years old male patient is on treatment for psoriasis. He came to OPD with the complaints of malaise, easy fatiguability, fever with chills. He was diagnosed as malaria fever upon laboratory investigation. Which of the following drug is contraindicated?
643.e: Chloroquine is contraindicated in patients with psoriasis or porphyria, in whom it may precipitate acute attacks of these diseases. It should generally not be used in those with retinal or visual field abnormalities or myopathy. Chloroquine should be used with caution in patients with a history of liver disease or neurologic or hematologic disorders. The antidiarrheal agent kaolin and calcium-and magnesium-containing antacids interfere with the absorption of chloroquine and should not be co-administered with the drug. Chloroquine is considered safe in pregnancy and for young children. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal. Page no. 920

643.q: Which keratin pair is normally expressed in the stratum basale?
643.e: Explanation: The stratum basale expresses keratin 5 (K5) and keratin 14 (K14). These keratins provide structural support to the basal keratinocytes, which are mitotically active and attached to the basement membrane. Mutations in K5 or K14 lead to epidermolysis bullosa simplex. Keratin expression by epidermal layer: Stratum basale: K5/K14 Stratum spinosum & granulosum: K1/K10 Non-keratinizing epithelia (eg. esophagus): K4/K13 Hyperproliferative states (psoriasis, wound healing): K6/K16 Clinical relevance: Keratin profiling helps diagnose blistering disorders

644.q: SAPHO Syndrome components are all except:
644.e: Acronym for the combination of Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, and Osteitis Chronic disorder that involves the skin, bone, and joints Some researchers feel that the SAPHO syndrome is related to the group of arthritis conditions which typically affect the spine, called Spondyloarthropathies Treatment typically involves medications which reduce inflammation Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 90, Page 54

644.q: Loss of Intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes is called as ?
644.e: Ans. B. Acantholysis Separation of epidermal keratinocytes due to loss of intercellular bridge is referred to as acantholysis. Acantholysis is seen in the epidermis (especially in basal layer).

644.q: Tzanck smear in bullous pemphigoid shows:
644.e: Cytologic examination of Tzanck smear in bullous pemphigoid and pemphigoid gestationis shows numerous eosinophils without Tzanck cells (acantholytic cells). Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 18

645.q: Facies leprosa is characterised by all except:
645.e: Nodules on face are not a feature of facies leprosa. Facies leprosa - Seen in lepromatous leprosy Characterized by the resorption of the nasal bone, anterior nasal spine, supra-incisive alveolar region, and anterior alveolar process of the maxilla, with associated sensory or motor damage depending on the type of nerves involved. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 182 International Textbook Of Leprosy, Part I, Section II, Chapter 2.1, Page 16,17

645.q: Which form of leprosy is the Most common form of the disease encountered in India?
645.e: Tuberculoid leprosy(TT) leprosy is the most common form of the disease encountered in India and Africa but is virtually absent in Southeast Asia, where borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy is frequent. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 179, Pg: 1385

645.q: What is The Most commonly affected nerve trunk in leprosy?
645.e: The most commonly affected nerve trunk in leprosy is the ulnar nerve at the elbow, whose involvement results in clawing of the fourth and fifth fingers, loss of dorsal interosseous musculature in the affected hand, and loss of sensation in these distributions Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 179, Pg: 1387

646.e: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome, also known as Ritter disease is a disease characterized by denudation of the skin caused by exotoxin producing strains of the Staphylococcus species, typically from a distant site. Also called as pemphigus neonatorum. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 27

646.q: Which of the following diseases is not caused by Staphylococcus?
646.e: Characterized by a painful bright red appearance of the involved skin, which forms a sharply demarcated plaque. Involve upper dermal lymphatics. Classic cause: group A streptococci.

646.q: What is the most common cause of follicular pyodermas
646.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen of folliculitis and furuncles. Gram-negative pathogens including Klebsiella , Enterobacter , and Proteus species may replace the gram-positive flora on facial skin, nasal mucous membranes, and neighbouring areas, causing gram-negative folliculitis and boils. 'Hot tub' folliculitis is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa contamination of undertreated water in saunas or whirlpools.

647.q: A 25-year-old female presents with red crusted lesions around the mouth and finger pulps, three months after having had small bowel resection for Crohn's disease. What is the most likely cause of her skin condition?
647.e: The features of this patient who had bowel resection suggest zinc deficiency . Zinc deficiency can lead to a condition called acrodermatitis enteropathica which presents with diarrhea, alopecia, muscle wasting, depression, irritability, and a rash involving the extremities, face (perioral), and perineum . The rash is characterized by vesicular and pustular crusting with scaling and erythema. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:333 Pg: 2532

647.q: In Tzanck smear, multinucleated giant cells are seen in:
647.e: A Tzanck smear is a cytologic technique commonly used in the diagnosis of herpes virus infections (simplex, genitalis, varicella-zoster). An early vesicle is deroofed, and the base of the lesion is scraped gently with a scalpel blade. The material is then placed on a glass slide, air-dried, and stained with Giemsa stain. Multinucleated giant cells suggest the presence of herpes. Another finding - presence of acantholytic cells Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 4, Page 22

647.q: Ballooning degeneration is a characteristic feature of:
647.e: Vesicles in herpetic infections (simplex, genitalis, varicella-zoster ) show degenerative changes characterized by ballooning, the presence of multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions. Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 27

648.e: Answer- D. Hypergonadism LEOPARD syndrome Lentigines Electrocardiographic conduction abnormalities Ocular hypertelorism Pulmonary stenosis Abnormal genitalia Retarded growth Deafness

648.q: Pruritus is seen in all except:
648.e: Dermatological Causes of Pruritus: Autoimmune causes: Dermatitis herpetiformis Pemphigoid Sjogren's syndrome Infectious causes: Dermatophytosis Insect bites Pediculosis Scabies Neoplastic causes: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Mycosis fungoides) Leukemia cutis Genetic causes: Darter's disease Hailey-Hailey disease Inflammatory causes: Atopic dermatitis Contact dermatitis Drug reactions Lichen planus Mastocytosis Miliaria Keloid scar Urticaria Pregnancy causes: Pemphigoid gestationis Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 83, page 4

648.q: Besniers sign is a clinical test described in which of the following disease?
648.e: Besnier's sign: Also referred to as the scratch sign or coup d' ongle sign. In this, the indistinct scales of the macules in P.versicolor can be accentuated by scratching with nail . Psoriasis - Auspitz sign Pityriasis rosea - Hanging curtain sign Reference: Madke B, Nayak C. Eponymous signs in dermatology. Indian Dermatol Online J. 2012 Sep;3(3):159-65. doi: 10.4103/2229-5178.101810. Erratum in: Indian Dermatol Online J. 2013 Apr-Jun;4(2):164. PMID: 23189246; PMCID: PMC3505421.

649.q: True about the burrow of scabies is all except:
o: Burrow is present in stratum granulosum
Burrow appears yellow on woods lamp
Burrows are located in the distribution - hebra circle
Burrow is a classical sign of scabies
649.e: Burrow is present in stratum corneum Burrow appears yellow on woods lamp Burrows are located in the distribution - hebra circle Burrow is a classical sign of scabies Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 34, Page 30

650.q: All are true regarding secondary syphilis except :
650.e: Secondary syphilis presents with a variety of symptoms. The cutaneous manifestations are also varied A diffuse mucocutaneous rash (generally coppery red, non-pruritic and bilaterally symmetrical), coppery brown scaly macules on palms and soles are seen. Most often, the lesions are macular, discrete, reddish brown, and 5 mm or smaller in diameter; however, they can be pustular, annular, or scaling. Vesicular rash is typically absent. Generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy is typical, especially epitrochlear LN. Mucosal - condyloma lata, mucous patches, snail track ulcers - they contain a high load of spirochetes, these lesions are highly contagious. Hair - patchy non-scarring alopecia (Moth-eaten alopecia) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 12

Hutchinson's triad : Common pattern of presentation for congenital syphilis Triad: Interstitial keratitis, Hutchinson incisors, and Eighth nerve deafness Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 31

650.q: The lesions not containing Treponema are:
650.e: Late syphilis not infective are Gumma, neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 28

651.q: Correct about stages of LGV is :
651.e: Primary Stage: The patient characteristically develops a painless genital ulcer or papules which are about 1 to 6 mm in size. secondary stage presents with the development of unilateral or bilateral tender inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (also called buboes), which occurs two to six weeks after the primary stage; this is called the inguinal syndrome. Late stage : necrosis of lymph node when left untreated. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 30, page 17

651.q: You are posted as MO on a rural PHC. A patient comes with painful genital ulcer. You issue a STI kit to him. Which of the following will be provided?
651.e: As a PHC MO, follow the guidelines of syndromic management NACO guidelines. According to it, a painful genital ulcer patient should be given red kit- kit no. 5 It contains tab acyclovir 400mg. Dose : Three tablets a day for 7 days (21 tablets total) Reference: NACO guidelines for Syndromic Management of STI

651.q: Which of the following statements is false about disseminated gonococcal infection?
o: It occurs as a result of direct spread by ascending infections
Classic presentations is with a dermatitis - arthritis syndrome
Skin lesions are small, tender and maculopapular
651.e: DGI occurs when the sexually transmitted pathogen Neisseria gonorrhoeae invades the bloodstream and spreads to distant sites in the body, leading to clinical findings such as septic arthritis, polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, petechial/pustular skin lesions, bacteremia, or, on rare occasions, endocarditis or meningitis. The classic triad of features consists of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and migratory polyarthritis DGI is uncommon and thought to occur in 0.5-3% of untreated gonorrhea cases. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 30, page 5

652.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Essential fatty acid In vitamin 'A' deficiency there is toad like skin also known as phrynoderma. o But this is due to associated deficiency of essential fatty acids.

652.q: In congenital dystrophic variety of epidermolysis bullosa, mutation is seen in the gene coding for:
652.e: There are two types of EB Acquired and Congenital The congenital has 3 types (Simple x, Junctional and Dystrophic) Keratin 14 : EB Simplex Laminin 4, Alpha 6 integrin : Junctional EB Collagen type 7: Dystrophic EB Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition Chapter 71, page 2

652.q: Which of the following is/are correct regarding Hailey-Hailey disease? 1. Steroid not ffective 2. ATP2Cl impairment 3. Autosomal recessive 4. Flexural distribution 5. Benign pemphigus
652.e: Hailey-Hailey Disease Synonym: Benign familial pemphigus Autosomal dominant inheritance ATP2Cl enzyme insufficiency Flexural distribution: Painful erosions, vesico-pustules and scaly erythematous plaques appear at sites of friction such as the sides of the neck, the axillae, the groins and the perineum. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 66, page 10

653.q: Which of the following is not nevus of melanocyte?
653.e: Epidermal naevi Keratinocytic/hyperkeratotic/verrucous epidermal naevus Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus (ILVEN) Sebaceous naevus Pigment cell naevi Congenital melanocytic naevus Congenital blue naevus Congenital naevus spilus Congenital Spitz naevus Mongolian blue spot (dermal melanocytosis) Connective tissue naevi - Shagreen patch Muscle naevi Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma Leiomyoma Fat naevi - Congenital lipoma unclassifiable naevi - Becker naevus Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 75, page 2

653.q: The most common site of morphea is:
653.e: Sites of morphea: Upper trunk (MC), buttocks & legs Linear lesions on extremities & fate (en coupe sabre) Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 57, Page 11

653.q: Which of the following is not seen in Dermatomyositis?
653.e: Clinical Features of Dermatomyositis Itchy lesion Facial lesion's: Heliotrope erythema, malar erythema, oedema Gottron's papule: Violaceous, atrophic papules over knuckles and pressure points Gottron's sign: Symmetrical, somewhat linear, lilac papulosquamous plaques Telangiectasia and ragged cuticles Poikiloderma: Hyperpigmentation, hypo pigmentation, telangiectasia and atrophy Mechanic's hand: Confluent symmetric hyperkeratosis along ulnar aspect of thumb and radial aspect of fingers Calcinosis cutis Shawl sign: Symmetrical confluent violaceous erythema extending from dorsolateral aspect of forearms and arms to deltoid region, shoulder and neck Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 53, Page 6

654.q: A naevus present at birth which has predisposition to the development of malignant melanoma is-
654.e: Congenital melanocytic nevi are classified according to their estimated adult size as small (less than 1.5 cm), medium (1.5 to 20 cm), large (20 to 40 cm), and giant (>40 cm). This classification is essential as the size of nevi is one of the main risk factors of melanoma development and neurological involvement. CMNs frequently present with a garment appearance (in a bathing trunk, in coat sleeve, Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 143, page 143.2

654.q: Mycosis fungoides is a malignancy of -
654.e: This is the most common variant of primary CTCL; it is generally associated with an indolent clinical course Mycosis fungoides is characterized by polymorphic patches and plaques usually involving limb/girdle sites, the breast and especially the buttock area. The histological hallmark of the mycosis fungo ides is the presence of the Sezary-Lutzner cells. These are CD4 helper T cells. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 140, page 140.1

654.q: Mycosis fungoides which is not true-
o: It is the most common form of cutaneous lymphoma
Indolent course and good prognosis, easily amenable to treatment
Erythroderma seen and spreads to peripheral circulation
654.e: Mycosis fungoides is an indolent cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (indolent course. but is inevitably fatal (not easily amenable to treatment), except for patients in stage I. MF is the most common primary cutaneous lymphoma. Pautrier microabscess is characteristic of MF. Erythroderma can occur in MF (Sezary syndrome) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 140, page 140.10

655.e: During development of the epidermis, first layer to form is S. Basale and subsequently, layers form from below upwards. The principal function of epidermis is constant replacement of the stratum corneum which is being continuously shed and replaced Total epidermal cell turnover time is 52-75 days. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 2

655.q: All of the following statements are true regarding the skin, except that ____.
o: Langerhans cells originate from bone marrow and are present in granular layer.
Melanocytes are present in stratum basale.
Stratified squamous epithelium with hallmark keratin intermediate filaments.
Merkel cells are present in stratum basale.
655.e: The epidermis is a keratinized, stratified, squamous epithelium and the hallmark filaments are the keratin intermediate filaments. Melanocytes originate from neural crest and are present in stratum basale. Merkel cells originate from ectoderm and are present in stratum basale. Langerhans cells are dendritic cells which originate from bone marrow and function as antigen presenting cells. They are present in stratum spinosum Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 1

655.q: Which of the following component in the skin give protection from UV radiation?
655.e: Present in Stratum Germinativum/ Basal Cell Layer Contains Melanocytes which produce melanin Sun exposure increase melanin production to prevent damage from UV rays (sun tanning) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 17

656.q: All are true regarding Sunitinib except -
o: It is used for renal cell carcinoma
It is used for the treatment of GIST
It is excreted primarily in urine
656.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., It is excreted primarily in urine Sunitinib inhibits multiple Tyrosine kinase receptors. It inhibits PDGF, VEGF and c-kit. o Sunitinib and sorafinib are used in renal cell carcinoma (in RCC there is overexpression of VEGF) and GIST (in GIST there is over expression of C-Kit & PDGF). o It is eliminated primarily by hepatic route with excretion in faeces.

656.q: Meningitis with rash is seen in -
656.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Neisseria meningitidis om

656.q: All of the following are features of juvenile CML except -
656.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Philadelphia chromosome is positive Juvenile CML is mostly seen in children below 2 years of age. Philadelphia chromosome is negative and leukocyte count is less than 100'000/mm3. Features Adult CML Juvenile CML Age 10-12 years 100'000 < 100'000 WBC type Granulocyte Monocyte Normoblastic Unusual Common HbF Normal Increased Immunoglobulins Normal Increased Muramidase levels Normal Increased Response to Busulphan Good Poor Survival 2.5-3 years 9 months

657.q: Most common bone for which nailing is done
657.e: Answer- C. Tibia Most common bones for which intramedullary nailing is done are Tibia and femur.

657.q: Most common organism causing infection after open fracture
657.e: Answer- A. Pseudomonas staphylococcus aureus was the most common organism causing infection in open fractures. More recent studies have shown that gram negative organisms such as pseudomonas aeruginosa and E.coli are becoming more common

657.q: Tension band wiring is indicated in fracture of which of the following ?
657.e: Tension band wiring is indicated in the treatment of two types of olecranon fracture. First type is a clean break with separation of the fragments, and second type is comminuted fracture of the olecranon with displced fragments. A crack in the olecranon without displacement is treated by immobilising the elbow in an above elbow plaster slab in 30 degrees of flexion.

658.q: In a patient with compartment syndrome, which of the following signs would be the last to appear?
658.e: Whenever perfusion to an extremity is inadequate (e.g., trauma or poor perfusion), hypoxic edema develops, producing swelling. When this occurs in a compartment, tissue pressures rise, decreasing capillary perfusion. Symptoms of compartment syndrome include extreme pain unrelieved by analgesics, paresthesias, paralysis, and pallor. Extensive rhabdomyolysis may develop as well as permanent nerve and muscle injury in the compartment. Because the problem is at the tissue level, pulses and capillary refill may still be present. Treatment includes fasciotomy to relieve the elevated pressure Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, p 1514; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 2450.

658.q: Not a common cause of compartment syndrome
658.e: Compartment syndrome is defined as the elevation of pressure in a closed fascial compartment causing a decrease in perfusion to the limb leading to irreversible muscle and neurovascular damage. So in compartment syndrome, by definition there must be a closed fascial compartment for the pressure to build up and rise. In a gun shot injury, there will be bullet wounds, making the fascial compartments open, and hence making compartment syndrome unlikely. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 47

658.q: Which is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome?
658.e: The earliest sign of compartment syndrome pain on passive stretch. Compartment syndrome is defined as the elevation of pressure in a closed fascial compartment causing a decrease in perfusion to the limb leading to irreversible muscle and neurovascular damage. The clinical features of compartment syndrome are summarized as the 6 Ps of compartment syndrome, which are Pain Pallor Pulselessness Paresthesia Paralysis Pain on passive stretch (earliest and most important) Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 47

659.q: A 67 year old woman has neck pains and occipital headaches for 2 years. She is referred to the neurology outpatients for assessment. Investigations showed a normal CT of the brain. Cervical X ray showed degenerative changes of narrowed disc spaces and loss of cervical lordosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
659.e: In cervical spondylosis, several overlapping syndromes are seen: neck and shoulder pain, suboccipital pain and headache, radicular symptoms, and cervical spondylotic myelopathy. Examination findings include neck pain, radicular signs, and myelopathic signs. Cervical spine films can demonstrate disk space narrowing, osteophytosis, loss of cervical lordosis, uncovertebral joint hypertrophy, apophyseal joint osteoarthritis, and vertebral canal diameter. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3452

659.q: Not true about congenital muscular torticollis
o: Can be associated with a mass
659.e: Congenital muscular torticollis occurs because of the contracture of sternocleidomastoid muscle and there is no fusion of vertebrae. Fusion of vertebrae is seen in Klippel Feil syndrome. Sometimes a mass can be palpable in the SCM which is the fibrotic muscle. Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 169

659.q: A 50 year old female presented with sudden onset pain, weakness and wasting of muscles of arm. She gives history of getting a TT injection in the deltoid 5 days back. What is the diagnosis?
659.e: Tetanus toxoid injections can rarely lead to brachial plexus neuritis. This presents as sudden onset pain, paresthesia and weakness of the affected arm. It can also lead to muscle wasting in the long run. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1513

660.q: Proximal humerus fracture which has maximum chances of avascular necrosis
660.e: Answer- D. Four part Neer's classified proximal humerus fracture into 4 types, based on these four segments :

660.q: 32 year old pregnant female with 2 months of amenorrhea comes with mid clavicle fracture. What is your treatment of choice?
660.e: Clavicle fracture is commonly managed conservatively but in young female for cosmetic reasons, some surgeons prefer to perform plate fixation. But in case of young pregnant female, it is an absolute contraindication to operate any fracture in first trimester of pregnancy. Reference- Campbell operative procedure 13ᵗʰ edition, page-3054

660.q: 17-year-old high school tennis player trips while returning a serve and sustains a right mid-shaft clavicle fracture. Which of the following increases the risk of nonunion in the nonoperative treatment of clavicle fractures?
660.e: Displacement and comminution have been shown to increase risk of non- union in nonoperative management. There are no significant differences between outcomes when using sling immobilization versus a figure-of-eight bandage. Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopaedics 1st edition, page no. 44

661.q: True about supracondylar fracture of humerus
661.e: Answer- B. Extension type most common Supracondylar humeral fractures are the most common elbow fractures in children. Most common age group affected is 5-8 years. Boys are affected more than girls. Left side is more common than right. Extension type is most common

661.q: The malunion of supracondylar fracture of the humerus most commonly leads to:
661.e: B i.e. Cabitus Varus Malunion : - It is the commonest complication of supracondylar fracture and results in cubitus varus (Gun stock deformity). Cubitus valgus is rare and may occur occasionally in posterolateral displacement.

661.q: What is seen on x-ray with posterior elbow dislocation
661.e: Answer- A. Coronoid process posterior to humerus AP view : Greater superimposition of distal humerus with proximal ulna and olecranon (normally, only terminal part of humerus is superimposed).

662.q: A 60 year old postmenopausal woman came with reports of DEXA scan which showed a t score of -2.5. She had a history of colles fracture 6 months back which was fixed. She is not a smoker and does not consume alcohol. Which of the following is correct about her further management?
662.e: The patient is a post menopausal female with t score of -2.5, with a past history of Colles fracture, is an indication for anti resorptive treatment. The anti-resorptive agent in the given option is alendronate.

662.q: Most common complication of Colles fracture?
662.e: The complication rate is 55%, with the most common complication being some degree of residual finger and wrist stiffness (39%). Most common complication of Colles fracture → Finger stiffness, 2nd most common complication of Colles fracture → Malunion Complications of Colles fracture: Stiffness of fingers and joints Stiffness of finger; wrist and shoulder are the most common avoidable complication of collie's fracture. This occurs due to lack of exercise. Therefore, patient should be encouraged for active exercise of finger and shoulder. Malunion It is the second most common complication It results in dinner fork deformity Sudek's osteodystrophy (reflex sympathetic dystrophy) Carpal tunnel syndrome: Median nerve may get compressed in carpal tunnel Carpal instability Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus tendon TFCC injury Reference: Maheshwari 4th /e p. 110

662.q: An extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation is also known as a...
662.e: A Colles fracture consists of a fracture of the distal radius at the cortico cancellous junction with dorsal angulation and impaction, but without the involvement of the articular surface. Chauffeur’s fracture is an intraarticular fracture of radial styloid A die-punch fracture is a depressed intra-articular fracture of the lunate fossa of the distal radius Barton fracture is an intraarticular fracture involving the dorsal/ volar lip of the distal radius with subluxation of the carpus and hand bones. Reference: Maheshwari ortho 5th edition page no 111

663.q: A 50 year old male suffers an injury to the right upper limb, resulting in a fracture. He is also unable to dorsiflex his fingers and there is no sensory loss. Which fracture can cause this presentation?
o: Fracture of Humerus at Spiral Grove
Fracture of the Neck of Humerus
663.e: The patient presents with a fracture in the upper limb plus finger drop and no sensory loss. This means that the patient's fracture has caused a Posterior interosseous N (PIN) injury. PIN passes very close to the head and neck of radius and can be injured if there is a fracture or dislocation in this region. So, the answer is fracture of radial neck. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 2038

663.q: Which is the most common muscle involved in pseudotumor formation in hemophilia?
663.e: Sometimes, there is bleeding into a muscle in a patient with hemophilia resulting in the formation of an intramuscular hematoma. This may give the appearance of tumor, hence the name pseudotumor. The most common muscles involved are - Iliopsoas > Quadriceps The most common upper limb muscle involved is the deltoid Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 698

663.q: Content of anatomical snuff box includes?
663.e: The only content of the snuff box is Radial A. As the snuffbox is triangularly shaped, it has three borders, a floor, and a roof: Ulnar (medial) border : Tendon of the extensor pollicis longus. Radial (lateral) border : Tendons of the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. Proximal border : Styloid process of the radius. Floor : Carpal bones; scaphoid and trapezium. Roof : Skin. Reference: Maheshwari 5th edition p. 156

664.q: Why fracture shaft femur is early stabilised
664.e: Answer- A. To prevent blood loss Fracture shaft femur can cause upto 2L of blood loss and severe hypotension, if not immoblized early. the fracture shaft femur should be immoblized early. This can be temporary immobilization by TT splint followed by surgery or can be by immediate surgery.

664.q: The MOST common type of dislocation of elbow joint is:
664.e: In adults, the elbow is the second most frequently dislocated major joint, after the shoulder. It is the most commonly dislocated joint in children. More than 90% of all elbow dislocations are posterior dislocations. This injury entails disengagement of the coronoid process of the ulna from the trochlea of the humerus with movement posteriorly. The mechanism of injury is typically a fall onto an outstretched hand with the elbow in extension upon impact.

664.q: Most common complication of inter trochanteric femur fracture is
664.e: Most common complication of extracapsular inter trochanteric femur fracture is MALUNION. Most common complication of intracapsular neck of femur fracture is nonunion followed by AVN. Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5 th edition page no 139

665.q: Which of the following describes grade 2 fracture neck femur?
o: Moderate displacement of neck, vascularity damaged
665.e: Answer- B. Complete fracture with undisplaced neck Garden stage I: undisplaced incomplete, including valgus impacted fractures medial group of femoral neck trabeculae may demonstrate a greenstick fracture Garden stage II: undisplaced complete no disturbance of the medial trabeculae

665.q: Most common complication of fracture neck of femur
665.e: Answer- B. AVN AVN is the most common complication of femoral neck fracture. Non-union is the second most common complication of femoral neck fracture.

665.q: Which is NOT true about fractured neck of femurs?
o: The leg is shortened and externally rotated in most fractured neck of femurs
The main source of blood to the femoral head is via the vessels running within cancellous bone from the diaphysis
Subcapital fracture cuts off all the blood to the head of the femur resulting in avascular necrosis
The blood supply to the head is increased by vessels in the capsular retinacula and it is this which prevents avascular necrosis of the head after an intertrochanteric fracture the ligamentum teres.
665.e: The leg is shortened and externally rotated in most fractured neck of femurs. The main source of blood to the femoral head is via the vessels running within cancellous bone from the diaphysis. The blood supply to the head is increased by vessels in the capsular retinacula and it is this which prevents avascular necrosis of the head after an intertrochanteric fracture the ligamentum teres. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 554

666.q: An army recruit has pain over both of his feet for the last 3 months since he started training. He has point tenderness and pain in the forefoot which is aggravated by activity. However, his x rays are normal. What is the next line of investigation?
o: No further investigations are required as his x-rays are normal
666.e: From the history, the person has stress fractures. Stress fracture is sometimes not seen on x-ray in early stages. Hence we need further investigations to confirm our diagnosis. For suspected stress fracture in one site, the investigation of choice is MRI. But for B/L stress fractures or multiple stress fractures, bone scan is recommended over MRI as it is easy, effective and economical. Reference- Rockwood and green adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-653

666.q: An army recruit with smoking addiction has pain in his right foot for the last 3 months after he started training. He has point tenderness and pain in the forefoot which is aggravated by activity. What would be the clinical diagnosis?
666.e: Stress fracture occurs due to abnormal loading of a normal bone. This is classically seen in individuals who perform repetitive, strenuous activities that he/she is not accustomed to. The most common site of stress fracture is Tibia followed by 2 nd metatarsal (March Fracture) Reference- Rockwood and green adult fracture 8 th edition, page-652

666.q: Pigmented villo-nodular synovitis most commonly occurs at
666.e: Pigmented villonodular synovitis: Pigmented villonodular synovitis(PVNS) is a rare benign disease of the synovial membrane which is characterised by hypervascular neoplastic proliferation of the synovium with deposition of macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and hemosiderin. Knee joint is most commonly involved joint. On arthroscopy typical brownish pigmentation of synovium is seen due to deposition of hemosiderin pigment. Two varieties have been described: Diffuse variety and localized nodular variety. Chances of recurrence are higher in diffuse variety. Low dose external beam radiotherapy and arthroscopic/open synovectomy have been tried with varying success for the treatment. Malignant transformation has been reported but very rare. Reference: Fundamentals of Ortho Mohindra and Jain, Page no. 268.

667.q: Osteonerosis is seen in all except
667.e: Answer- D. Paget's disease Storage disorders : - Gaucher's disease Caisson disease : - Dysbaric osteonecrosis Hemoglobinopathy & Coagulation disorder: - Sickel cell disease, Familial thrombophilia, Hypofibrinolysis, Hypolipoproteinemia. Congenital disorders : - Perthe's disease, Slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Hematological malignancies : - Leukemia, lymphoma, Polycythemia. Hyperlipedemia : - Nephrotic syndrome

667.q: After chronic use of steroids severe pain in right hip with immobility is due to
667.e: Answer- A. Avascular necrosis Pain in hip and limitatation of movement (immobility) ofter chronic use of steroids suggest the diagnosis of AVN of femoral head.

667.q: A 50 year old male on walker support presents with back pain and weakness of both lower limbs for 1 month. MRI reveals TB spine with abscess compressing the spinal cord. Next line of action is?
o: Emergency surgery and drainage of the abscess
Elective surgery with ALD + fixation of spine
667.e: In, India we follow the middle path regime for treatment of TB paraplegia. All patients with TB paraplegia are first started on ATT and advised bed rest and given a spine brace. These patients are the monitored for improvement. Patients who improve on ATT are continued with it. Those who are not improving are treated with surgery. Indications of surgery in middle path regime are Bowel and bladder involvement Worsening of paraplegia while on ATT Appearance of a new neurological deficit while on treatment No improvement in paraplegia even after 3-4 weeks of ATT In this question, the patient does not have any bowel or bladder symptoms, so he is started on ATT and monitored. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 193

668.q: What is the management in case of a stable cervical spine injury with no neurological changes?
668.e: In a stable cervical spine injuries with no neurological deficit, a rigid cervical brace or halo for 8-12 weeks is usually sufficient. Stable compression fractures of vertebral bodies and undisplaced fracture of laminae, lateral masses or spinous process may also be treated conservatively. Reference: Ebnezar, 5 th edition, Page no. 304.

668.q: Which of the following is not a known complication of TB spine?
668.e: TB produces fibrous ankylosis in all joints except the spine, where it produces bony ankylosis. Complications of TB spine include Kyphotic deformity Neurological deficit Paraplegia Bowel and bladder involvement Bony ankylosis of vertebra Abscess Psoas abscess Paravertebral abscess Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1757

668.q: Indicators of poor prognosis in the pott's spine is/are:
668.e: Factors leading to poor prognosis in potts spine: Inactive disease with poor mechanical compression Complete paralysis/Complete cord involvement Paralysis for more than 1year Presence of severe kyphosis(>60 degree) Older age and poor nutrition Healed vertebral lesion Presence of myelomalacia and syringomyel ia on magnetic resonance imaging(MRI). Good prognosis is associated with: Inflammatory cause of cord involvement Incomplete involvement Short duration of deficit Minimal kyphotic deformity Younger age Good nutritional status. Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 257.

669.q: In scoliosis degree of deformity is calculated by
669.e: Answer- A. Cobbs method Cobb angle is a measurement of the degree of side-to-side spinal curvature, which is a deformity you may know as scoliosis.

670.q: An adult patient with a grade I isthmic spondylolisthesis at L5-S1 is most likely to have weakness of which of the following?
670.e: The clinical findings for fifth lumbar root involvement include: Weakness of EHL, extensor digitorum longus(EDL), knee flexion(hamstrings), tensor fasciae lata(TFL), gluteus medius(hip abduction) Sensory loss over lateral and anterolateral leg and dorsum of foot(typically in the first web space-deep peroneal nerve territory) Weakness or mute posterior tibialis reflex and medial hamstring reflex Positive trendelenburg sign(variable) Trendelenburg gait(variable). Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1 st edition, Page no. 1389.

670.q: Condition in which there is anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra in relation to the vertebrae below:
670.e: Spondylosis - Degenerative osteoarthritis of the joints of the spinal column. Spondylitis - is an inflammation of the vertebra. It is usually seen in inflammatory conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis. Spondylolysis - it is a defect or break in the pars interarticularis of the vertebra. Pars interarticularis is an important structure that links a vertebra to its adjacent vertebrae. Any defect in it can predispose the slipping of one vertebra over its lower vertebra resulting in spondylolisthesis. So, spondylolysis is the precursor of spondylolisthesis. Spondylolisthesis - The anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra or the vertebral column in relation to the vertebrae below it. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 283-284.

671.q: Which of the following drugs can be used in the treatment of GCT of pelvis?
671.e: Denosumab can be used in the treatment of GCT, especially in those tumors that arise in difficult to access areas such as the pelvis and the sacrum. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks RANK ligands. The tumor cells in GCT acts via the RANK ligands to stimulate the osteoclasts. And its this activated osteoclasts that destroy the bone in GCT. Therefore, Denosumab can stop activation of osteoclasts, thereby causing shrinkage of the tumor. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1895

672.e: Answer- B. Joint aspiration Quickest and best method of diagnosis of septic arthritis is aspiration of joint.

672.q: Which of the following is an orthopedic emergency?
672.e: Septic arthritis is an absolute orthopedic emergency as delaying arthrotomy can cause serious joint damage. The pus in septic arthritis contains collagenases and metalloproteinases that start destroying articular cartilage within a period of 8 hours. So arthrotomy and lavage should be done as early as possible. Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 1055

GARRE'S OSTEOMYELITIS Sclerosing non suppurative chronic osteomyelitis Fusiform osseous enlargement. Cortical thickening No discharging sinus There is tenderness on deep palpation Shafts of the femur or tibia are most common site Treatment is guarded. Acute symptoms subside with rest and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Sometimes, making a gutter or holes in the bone bring relief in pain. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7 th edition, Page no. 173.

673.q: Chronic fluorosis is caused by drinking water with fluoride content of
673.e: Chronic fluorosis is seen in localities where the water supply contains > 10 ppm fluoride (Davidson). Fluorosis It is characterized by excessive deposition of calcium in bone & soft tissues due to increased intake of fluorides through drinking water. Clinical features: Dental fluorosis— earliest sign of fluorosis (mottling of enamel) – MC involve the incisors of upper jaw. Skeletal fluorosis— pain in back & joints, stiff spine, paranesthesia, spastic paraparesis & anemia. Radiological findings: Spine: Calcification of posterior longitudinal ligament. Pelvis: Calcification of ischio pubic & sacroiliac ligaments Forearm & leg: calcification of interosseous membrane. Treatment: Defluridation of water (Nalgonda technique) Reference: Maheswari, 55th ed, p. 314
