673.q: Triple deformity of knee includes all EXCEPT:
673.e: Tuberculosis of the knee is classical cause of triple deformity. It includes: Flexion Lateral(external) rotation of tibia Posterior subluxation of tibia Better treatment results are seen with ATT and arthrodesis This condition can also be seen in Rheumatoid arthritis. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5 th edition, Page no. 201.

673.q: Not a part of triple deformity in TB knee
673.e: Triple deformity is seen in advanced TB knee. It has 3 components Posterior subluxation of tibia External rotation of tibia Flexion of knee Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 200

674.q: What is the most common complication after successful treatment of a distal femoral physeal fracture?
674.e: Following are some facts about fractures in children Fractures in children heal faster. Fractures close to the joint heal faster. Sideways displacement will remodel. Angulation in the plane of the adjacent joint is acceptable. Rotational malalignment will never remodel. Physis subjected to compressive forces inhibits growth Reference- Maheshwari 5th /ep. PG NO 59

674.q: Radial head excision is avoided in all except
674.e: The treatment of radial head fractures depend on the amount of comminution and the age of the patient. Comminuted fractures in adults is treated by excising the broken fragments. However the radial head excision is contraindicated in Essex Lopresti fracture - Combination of radial head fracture with interosseous membrane rupture and DRUJ subluxation. Displaced fracture in children - Excision of radial head in children will cause cubitus valgus Undisplaced fractures in adults - These can be treated with POP cast. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 107

674.q: Which tumor is responsible for the most incidence of metastasis in a child?
674.e: Neuroblastoma is responsible for the most incidence of metastasis in children. Important points: Most common malignancy of bone: Metastasis MC primaries for bone mets: Breast > Prostate> Lung MC primaries for mets in children: Neuroblastoma MC bone involved: Spine> proximal femur MC part of spine involved: Thoracic > Lumbar Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 89

675.q: In neglected cases of CTEV, joint fused are
675.e: Answer- A. Calcaneocuboid, talonavicular and talocalcaneal Joints fused in triple arthrodesis for CTEVare i) Subtalar (tolocalcaneal) joint, ii) Calcaneocuboid joint, iii) Tolonavicular joint.

675.q: All are causes of clubfoot at birth except
675.e: Poliomyelitis cause acquired club foot deformity. It is not seen at birth. Club foot can be primary or secondary Primary Idiopathic (MC) Secondary Neurological disorders Spina bifida Meningomyelocele Myelodysplasia Poliomyelitis Syndromes Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita Larsen's syndrome Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 600

According to Ponseti technique cavus is corrected first. The order of correction is given by the mnemonic - CAVE- Cavus followed by Adductus and varus and equinus is corrected as the last step Treatment is started within 1st week of life. The cavus aspect of the deformity is corrected first, followed by the adduction, then varus and lastly equinus. After every manipulation, an above-knee POP cast is applied, which is changed every 5-7 days. It is usually possible to correct all components of the deformity within 6 weeks. The equinus deformity often remains undercorrected, and can be treated by percutaneous tenotomy of tendoachilles. The cut tendoachilles regenerates spontaneous Reference: Essential orthopedics by Maheshwari 7 th edition page no 210.

676.e: Parsonage Turner syndrome is brachial plexus neuritis. It is an uncommon disorder characterized by severe shoulder pain followed by patchy muscle paralysis and sensory loss involving the shoulder girdle and upper extremity. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1513

676.q: Most common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease is
676.e: Bacterial causes of acute hematogenous and direct osteomyelitis include the following: Most common organism causing acute osteomyelitis: Staph. Aureus MCC of osteomyelitis in sickle cell anemia patient: SALMONELLA MCC of osteomyelitis in IV drug abuser: PSEUDOMONAS MC organism causing osteomyelitis in open foot injury: PSEUDOMONAS MC organism causing osteomyelitis in HIV patient: Staph. Aureus MC organism causing osteomyelitis in case of animal bite: Pasteurella Multiocida MC organism causing osteomyelitis in case of human bite: Eikenella Corrodens Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 168.

676.q: All are risk factors of DDH except
676.e: Twin pregnancy is not a risk factor for DDH Risk factors of DDH are First born child Female child Fetal malposition - Breech (MC) Family history of DDH Oligohydramnios Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 558

677.q: A 16-year-old child presented with rickets and deformities. Doctors are planning the surgical correction of these deformities. When can surgery be done?
o: After white line is visible on X-ray
677.e: The methods to evaluate recovery in rickets are X ray There will be an appearance of a white line in the metaphysis. This is called the 'White line of Frankel' Blood tests first change to be seen - increase in phosphate levels End point - normal ALP Surgery should be done only after the rickets have been completely cured and bone healing has completely taken place. This is indicated by normal ALP. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 81

677.q: Stoss regimen is used in the treatment of which condition?
677.e: Stoss regimen is a vitamin D supplementation method used for the treatment of rickets. Here a single dose of vitamin D - 3L to 6L IU is given as an oral dose or as an IM injection. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 311

677.q: All are true regarding osteopetrosis except
677.e: Fracture healing is normal in osteopetrosis. Osteopetrosis is also called Marble bone disease/Albers Schonberg disease It is a congenital condition characterized by defective osteoclastic resorption of immature bone resulting in its accumulation through out the skeleton, causing increased frequency of long bone fractures, cranial nerve palsies, pancytopenia and low back pain. Clinical feature include Low back pain Pathological fractures Progressive anemia Severe infections : Mandible osteomyelitis Easy bruising Failure to thrive Cranial N 2, 7, 8 palsy leading to blindness and deafness Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 688

678.q: The commonest cause of pathological fracture worldwide is?
678.e: Most common cause of pathological fracture is osteoporosis . In India, however the most common cause is Nutritional deficiencies. Reference- Rockwood and green’s adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-671

678.q: In comparison of two patient. Patient-1 is 34yr old female with pathological fracture of shaft of femur due to metastasis of breast cancer and patient-2 is 64year old female with pathological fracture of shaft femur due to osteoporosis. Which of the following is true?
o: Patient -1 will have delayed union compared to patient-2
Patient -2 will have delayed union compared to patient-1
Both fractures will unite in the same time
678.e: Osteoporotic pathological fracture has good prognosis because it follows natural process of bone healing but with some delay. But pathological fracture of malignant lesion has very poor potential for healing and usually ends up in nonunion. Reference- Rockwood and green’s adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-678

678.q: A lady with osteoporosis is on prolonged bisphosphonates. She develops pain in her right hip. Next investigation is?
678.e: In this case, we have to get an x-ray to rule out an atypical fracture. One of the complications of prolonged bisphosphonate therapy is the development of atypical fractures. Atypical fractures occurs after drug usage of more than 5-7 year It occurs due to the defective remodeling of bones, resulting from osteoclast suppression by bisphosphonates. These fractures are commonly seen in the sub-trochanteric region of the femur. These are called atypical fractures because they involve the lateral cortex and not the medial cortex of bone as is typically seen. Reference: Koval's Handbook of fracture's 5th edition, page no. 375

679.q: Woven bone is found in all of the following except
o: Around the growth plate in children
Cancellous bone of femur in adults
679.e: Woven bone is immature bone seen during embryonal development. Woven bone is week and is slowly replaced by stronger lamellar bone during development. Woven bone is almost completely replaced by 2 years of age. However, there are conditions where, woven bone can be seen even after 2 years of age. Eg Around the growth plates in growing children During fracture healing Pathologies of bone Paget's disease Fibrous dysplasia Osteogenic tumors - osteogenic sarcoma, osteoblastoma etc. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 20. Reference: Kulkarni's 3rd edition of Textbook of Orthopaedics and Trauma page no. 161

679.q: Blade of grass lesion is seen in which of the following conditions?
679.e: Blade of grass lesion is an elongated V shaped lytic area in the diaphysis of long bones, seen in Paget's disease. Paget's disease is a disorder of abnormal bone turnover. It is a chronic disease of bone remodeling characterized by abnormal osteoclastic activity(and later by increased osteoblastic activity) resulting in replacement of normal bone with excessive, weak and hyper-vascular bone. X-ray findings depend on the phase of Paget's disease Lytic phase Flame shaped/Blade of grass appearance Osteoporosis circimscripta Mixed phase Picture frame vertebra Ivory vertebra Cotton wool skull Blastic phase Tam O shanter skull Reference: Manish kumar varshney, 1 st edition, Page no.86.

679.q: Which is the drug of choice in Paget's disease?
679.e: Drug of choice in Paget's disease are bisphosphonates which reduce bone turnover and increase lamellar bone formation. The only bisphosphonate in the options is Alendronate. Calcitonin is very useful in relieving the pain in Paget's disease and decreasing bone resorption but the effect is only temporary. Calcium and vitamin D should also be supplemented. Pathological fractures usually require surgery and internal fixation. Reference: Fundamentals of Orthopaedics Mohindra and Jain, Page no. 338.

680.q: Which of the following pairs of structures are antagonist to each other around the ankle joint?
680.e: PL&TA are antagonist to each other as PL plantar flexes and TA dorsiflexes ankle joint. PB & PT are antagonist to each other as PB everts the foot and PT inverts the ankle joint. Reference - Manish Kumar Varshney 1 st edition page no 1242

680.q: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee for the past three days. Also, for the past two days, he has felt feverish. The patient is able to ambulate, but walking exacerbates the pain in his knee. Temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F). On physical examination, the right knee is red, warm to touch, and tender. A large effusion is noted. Which of the following diagnostic studies of the knee is the most appropriate initial step?
680.e: The clinical presentation described, is characteristic of septic arthritis of knee joint. The best method for confirming the diagnosis is to aspirate the knee joint to look for pus. The process of joint aspiration is also called arthrocentesis. Option B- Arthroscopy, is incorrect because this study is not the initial step in diagnosis. Option C- Bone scan, is incorrect because this study is appropriate to nonspecifically localize areas of inflammation but cannot be used to distinguish infectious from sterile processes. Option D- CT scan, and Option (E), MRI, are incorrect because these studies are more sensitive for diagnosing osteomyelitis and periarticular abscesses. Reference- Maheshwari Ortho 5th edition, page no 170.

680.q: Which deformity of tibia is seen in the triple deformity of the knee?
680.e: Triple deformity of knee consists of posterior subluxation of tibia, external rotation of tibia and flexion. The mnemonic ‘P ER F’ can be used to remember this. Triple deformity is classically seen in late stages of TB of knee joint. Rarely rheumatoid arthritis can also produce similar deformity. Reference: Apley’s System of Orthopaedics and Fractures, 8th Edition, Page Number-42.

681.q: A 25-year-old football player sustains a blow to the arm during a match. He develops temporary weakness and tingling, but recovers completely within 6 weeks without surgical intervention. Which of the following best describes neuropraxia?
681.e: Explanation: Neuropraxia is the mildest form of peripheral nerve injury , as described in Seddon's classification . In this condition, the axon remains intact, but there is focal demyelination or damage to the myelin sheath due to compression or ischemia. Conduction block occurs across the site of injury, leading to weakness or sensory loss. Since the axon and endoneurial tubes are preserved, full recovery occurs within weeks to months without Wallerian degeneration. Explanation of other options: Damaged axon, intact nerve sheath (Option B): Describes axonotmesis , where axons are damaged but connective tissue sheaths remain intact. Damaged axon and nerve sheath (Option C): Describes neurotmesis , the most severe form of injury, with a poor prognosis.

681.q: A man slept with head over forearm, next morning he complains of tingling, numbness over forearm. It is caused by ?
681.e: Ans.C . Sensitivity to hypoxia is C>B>A Type C fibers (Type IV Lloyd & Hunt) are least susceptible to hypoxia'

681.q: Which of the following is not an indication of external fixator?
o: Closed fracture of upper tibia with compartment syndrome and blisters over skin
Closed fracture shaft humerus with Radial nerve palsy
Fracture with burns wound over fracture site
681.e: Indications of external fixator Open fracture (grade 3b-3c- absolute indication, grade-2-3a-relative indication) Vascular injury Severe soft tissue injury Damage control orthopedics Nerve injury is not an indication of external fixation Reference- AO manual of principle of fracture management

682.e: Answer- A. Osteoid osteoma Dense, homogenous mineralization (calcification) is typical of osteoid matrix, formed by benign and malignant bone forming lesions. 1265. Which of the following is true about Giant cell tumor a) Usually presents as a lytic lesion with sclerotic rim b) Always beingn c) Epiphyseal origin d) Seen in age less than 15 years Correct Answer - C Answer- C. Epiphyseal origin GCT is an osteolytic tumor arising from the epiphysis and is common between the age of 20-40 years. The commonest sites are lower end of femur and upper end of tibia. Other common sites are lower end radius and upper end of humerus. It may also occur in the spine and sacrum. The radiological features are : -

682.q: Which is not a cause of pain in osteochondroma?
682.e: Malignant change can cause pain in osteochondroma. However the malignancy that arises in osteochondroma is chondrosarcoma and not osteosarcoma. The causes of pain in osteochondroma are Bursitis (most common cause) Fracture of the pedicle Compression of an adjacent nerve Malignant change - chondrosarcoma. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1881

682.q: Which of the following is also called the Codman's tumor?
682.e: Codman's tumor is another name for Chondroblastoma. It should not be confused with Codman's triangle which is a type of periosteal reaction, most commonly seen in osteosarcoma. Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 1109

683.q: Commonest site of occurrence of chondrosarcoma is
683.e: Chondrosarcoma A chondrosarcoma is a malignant tumor derived from cartilage cells and it tends to maintain its cartilaginous character throughout its evolution. Highest incidence is in the fourth and fifth decades and men are affected more often than women. Most commonly involved bones are pelvis(most common), femur(2 nd most common), humerus, ribs and shoulder girdles. It may be at metaphysis or diaphysis. This tumor is slow growing but can metastasise to distant site The usual presentation is dull ache or gradually enlarging mass. Radiological features Expansile, radiolucent lesion in the medullary cavity(concentric) Endosteal scalloping. Punctate comma shaped or popcorn calcification. Treatment Surgery is the treatment of choice Reference: Campbell, 12 th edition, Page no. 914.

683.q: T 10 protocol for the treatment of osteosarcoma includes all except?
683.e: The drugs used in T 10 protocol include High dose Methotrexate Bleomycin Dactinomycin Doxorubicin Cyclophosphamide Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1854

683.q: A 45 year old male presented with an expansile lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis. The lesion shows endosteal scalloping and punctate calcification. Diagnosis?
683.e: The diagnosis is chondrosarcoma. The points in favor are The age of the patient is 45 years. The common age for chondrosarcoma is between 40 to 60 years. The site of origin is the metaphysis. The x ray finding of endosteal scalloping and punctate calcification is seen in chondrosarcoma. Osteosarcoma and Chondroblastoma are commonly seen in the 2nd decade of life Metastasis does not produce endosteal scalloping and punctate calcification Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1885

684.q: A 50-year-old woman has pins and needles sensation that worsens at night and is relieved when she shakes her hand. She also has episodic left knee pain throughout the day. She takes medications for constipation. Her BMI is 35 kg/m2. Her pulse is 57/min and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. Sensation is decreased to light touch in the thumb and index finger. DTR = 1+ and there is mild edema in the legs. Which of the following treatments is most likely to benefit the patient?
684.e: This obese patient has neuropathic pain along the distribution of the median nerve that is consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). The patient presents with classic signs of hypothyroidism: constipation, fatigue, bradycardia, hyporeflexia, and lower limb edema (which is usually myxedematous and non-pitting, but pitting edema can also occur due to excessive albumin in extracellular spaces). While the precise etiopathology is uncertain, it is assumed that the excess deposition of glycosaminoglycans, hyaluronic acid, and mucopolysaccharides in hypothyroidism causes myxedema. These characteristic depositions can subsequently cause compression of the carpal tunnel. With thyroid hormone replacement and return to a euthyroid state, symptoms should improve within weeks to months. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 699

684.q: A professional tennis player presents with shoulder pains especially whilst serving the ball. He has limited passive and active shoulder abduction to less than 60°. His temperature is 36.5°C and he has a normal white cell count. There is tenderness around the anterior portion of the shoulder joint. Which diagnosis is likely?
684.e: Pain during abduction with limitation of movement is suggestive of supraspinatous tendonitis. Palpation or compression around the greater tubercle of the humerus is particularly tender. Glenohumeral joint OA is very rare. Though Rotator cuff tendinitis is often accompanied by a sub acromial bursitis, the more likely answer here is supraspinatus tendinitis, considering the recurrent overhead abduction as in a tennis player. Tennis elbow causes pain the elbow. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 375, Pg: 2878

684.q: A 35-year-old female presents to the emergency room after a motor vehicle collision where her leg was pinned under the car for over 30 minutes. On arrival at the casualty, her BP was 80 systolic. Which of the following is the most accurate way to diagnose compartment syndrome in this patient?
o: Diastolic blood pressure minus intra-compartmental pressure is less than 30 mmHg
Diastolic blood pressure minus intra-compartmental pressure is greater than 30 mmHg
684.e: The classical definition of compartment syndrome is an intracompartmental pressure of 30mm of Hg or above. However, this is not true for hypotensive patients. The best way to diagnose compartment syndrome in a hypotensive patient is to calculate the delta P value. Diastolic blood pressure minus intracompartmental pressure is called delta p, If delta p is less than 30 mm hg patient requires immediate fasciotomy for compartment syndrome Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5th edition, page number 47

685.q: All are causes of recurrent dislocation of shoulder except
685.e: Rotator cuff tear is not a cause of recurrent dislocation of shoulder. The Common injuries causing recurrent dislocation of the shoulder are Bankart lesion Bony Bankart lesion Hill Sach's lesion Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 90

685.q: A young cricket player comes to you with knee pain and inability to extend it fully. He gives a history of twisting injury to his right knee when he collided another player while fielding. His MRI shows a double PCL sign. What is the appropriate management?
o: Application of above knee cast for 6 weeks
Icing, rest, compression and elevation for 2 weeks and then isometric and knee bending exercises
Icing, rest, compression and elevation for 2 weeks and then gradual return to sports
685.e: Double PCL sign on MRI is classically seen in bucket handle tear of a meniscus. The inability to fully extend the knee suggest a locked knee, again pointing towards a bucket handle meniscal tear. The best treatment of acute bucket handle meniscal tear in young athletes is arthroscopic repair. However if the meniscus injury is in the white- white zone, then a partial meniscectomy is done as the meniscus will not heal even if we do a repair because of the poor blood supply at the white -white zone. Reference - Manish Kumar Varshney 1 st edition page no 894.

685.q: Patient with history of knee injury 3 months back presents with knee pain. O/E knee was unstable with knee in flexion but stable in extension. What structure is injured?
685.e: ACL is made up of 2 bundles Anteromedial - which becomes tight in flexion Posterolateral - which becomes tight in extension In this patient, the knee is unstable in flexion but stable in extension. This means that the anteromedial fibres of the ACL are torn but the posteromedial fibers are intact. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 728

686.q: Clostridium perfringens toxin which causes myonecrosis is
686.e: The major toxins used for strain classification of clostridium perfringens are alpha toxin, beta toxin, epsilon toxin, and iota toxin. Alfa toxin is responsible for hemolysis, myonecrosis and gas gangrene in the infected tissue. Reference- Microbiology by Ananthanarayan and Paniker, 8th ed. pg. 251, 263, 634

686.q: Which of the following processes is involved in age-related intervertebral disc degeneration?
o: Increased cell number in the nucleus pulposus
686.e: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF DISK DEGENERATION: Loss of Proteoglycan - The aggrecan molecules become smaller and get leached from the tissue. This reduces glycosaminoglycans and water holding capacity and thus there is fall in the osmotic pressure of the disk matrix. Loss of Collagen Fibers - Type II collagen become more denatured and get replaced by type 1 collagen. Increase in Fibronectin - Fibronectin content increases with increasing degeneration and it becomes more fragmented. Enzymatic Activity - Increased fragmentation of the collagen, proteoglycan and fibronectin is mediated by increased enzymatic activity including cathepsins, MMPs and aggrecanases. Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1 st edition, Page no. 1353.

686.q: The spinal cord terminates as the conus medullaris at what vertebral level in adults?
686.e: SPINAL CORD: The spinal cord extends from the level of foramen magnum to the level of the intervertebral disc between 1st and 2nd lumbar vertebra. The spinal cord is 40-50 cm long and 1-1.5 cm in diameter. By weight the spinal cord contributes only 2% of the central nervous system. All the three meninges namely the pia, arachnoid and dura mater cover the spinal cord. It is attached to the dura mater by a series of lateral denticulate ligaments emanating from the pial folds. Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1 st edition, Page no. 1331.

687.q: All of the following have contributed to defining and developing defense mechanisms except:
687.e: Sigmund Freud focused primarily on repression as the central defense mechanism . Anna Freud greatly elaborated on individual defense mechanisms, including Reaction formation Regression Undoing Introjection Identification Projection Turning against the self Reversal Sublimation. George Valiant classified defence mechanisms into Narcissistic Immature Neurotic Mature levels Victor Frankl however, has no contribution to describing defense mechanisms. (Option D) Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 4 Theories of Personality and Psychopathology, Page number 177.

687.q: A 26-year-old male CT1 psychiatric trainee was put down badly by his consultant in a ward round and the consultant shouted at him. After work, he went to see his mother and started to present childish behavior such as playing with his old toy cars. Which is the most likely defense mechanism?
687.e: Regression is the defence that refers to the reversion to the early stage of ego functioning . Each and every person has defences to deal with stress. Some of them are mature defences → altruism, sublimation, suppression and humour. Some are immature and neurotic defences → displacement, isolation regression and projection. Isolation : thoughts, emotions or behaviour is isolated to break the link with other thoughts or memories ( Option B ) Projection : unacceptable thoughts, emotions and feelings are projected on to some other person ( Option C ) In displacement , emotions or wishes are transferred from the original object or person to a more suitable substitute ( Option A ) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 4, page no. 161

687.q: Which of the following statement is false about Topographical model of mind proposed by Sigmund Freud?
o: Consists of Unconscious, Preconscious and Conscious
Preconscious serves as a censor mechanism
All defense mechanisms operate at unconscious level except suppression
Id, Ego and Superego all operate at unconscious level only
687.e: Id largely operates at unconscious However, ego and superego operate at all three levels of conscious, preconscious and unconscious. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 4 Theories of Personality and Psychopathology, Page number 154.

688.q: All the following conditions result due to problems with basal ganglia except:
688.e: There are four main conditions to be aware of that result from problems with the basal ganglia: Huntington's chorea (caudate nucleus) Wilson's disease (copper deposition in the basal ganglia) Parkinson's disease (substantia nigra) Hemiballismus (sub thalamic nucleus) Multiple sclerosis is a demyelinating disease of CNS. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th Edition, Page Number-8.

688.q: Information about emotion passes through all of the following structures of brain except:
688.e: The Papez circuit consists of the hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → genu of the internal capsule → cingulate gyrus → Para hippocampal gyrus → entorhinal cortex → perforant pathway → back to hippocampus The boundaries of the limbic system were subsequently expanded outside of the Papez circuit to include the amygdala, septum, basal forebrain, nucleus accumbens, and orbitofrontal cortex. The limbic system is thought to be involved in various functions such as mediation of emotional responses (through amygdala), influencing neuroendocrine responses (via hypothalamus) and reward system regulation (via nucleus accumbens). Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 1.2 Functional Neuroanatomy, Page number 13.

688.q: In a patient presenting with headache, all of the following features typically suggest tension-type headache except:
o: Not aggravated by noise or light
Not associated with nausea or vomiting
688.e: Criteria for Tension type headache: At least 10 episodes of headache occurring on 1-14 days per month on average for >3 months and, 1 attack lasting from 30 mins-7 days. 2/4 of following b/l, non-pulsatile (non-throbbing quality), mild to moderate, not aggravated by routine activities None of following Nausea or vomiting, either photo or phono-phobia. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 2.11 Neuropsychiatric aspects of headache, Page number 1647.

689.q: A 16-year-old girl is brought to a physician by her mother, who states that her daughter has been losing weight steadily. The adolescent denies there is a problem and states that she is in no way underweight. The physician determines that the girl is 5 ft 6 in tall and weighs 90 lbs. Which of the following would be the next best step to work this patient up?
o: Complete blood count and differential white blood cell count
Calculation and assessment of patient BMI
689.e: The BMI of a patient is calculated using the patient weight, height and age (in those younger than 18) to create a ratio. BMIs of less than 19 may be the first indication of ANOREXIA NERVOSA. It is an easy, non-invasive calculation that is done in the office quickly so should be done prior to more invasive, expensive, and time-consuming laboratory studies. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 15.4, Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome, Page no. 523.

689.q: Maximum score in MMSE is given to which of the following cognitive functions?
689.e: MMSE assesses the following five cognitive functions and gives them different weightage. Orientation - 10 points Registration - 3 points Attention and concentration - 5 points Recall - 3 points Language - 9 points Max score = 30 ≤24/30 = indicative of cognitive impairment Reference: Mini Mental Status Examination

689.q: A 22-year-old woman is referred for assessment by the obstetric team. She is reported to be feeling depressed following the birth of her first baby three days ago. She has no history of depressive disorder. The baby is healthy, although the woman required a caesarean delivery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Major depressive episode with post-partum onset
689.e: Baby blues typically occur 3-6 days following the birth of the baby in 50-60% of mothers. Post-partum depression occurs in approximately 10% of women after parturition . It usually occurs within 6-8 weeks of birth , most often beginning between days 3 and 14 after parturition Adjustment disorder is usually diagnosed within six months of the occurrence of a significant stressor, and usually resolves within six months of the resolution of the stressful situation ( Option B ) An adjustment reaction is a short-lived anxiety response to a stressful situation. ( Option C ) Given the time frame of this presentation, the birth and the prevalence’s, the most likely diagnosis is baby blues. Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 27, page no. 839

690.q: A severely depressed patient, having undergone six sessions of Electroconvulsive therapy, complains of memory loss following the procedure. Which of the following is false about ECT-induced amnesia in this patient?
o: Both retrograde and anterograde amnesia may occur
690.e: The greatest concern about ECT is the association between ECT and memory loss. About 75 percent of all patients given ECT say that the memory impairment is the worst adverse effect. Although memory impairment during a course of treatment is almost the rule, follow-up data indicate that almost all patients are back to their cognitive baselines after 6 months . (Option A is FALSE) Despite the memory impairment, which usually resolves, no evidence indicates brain damage caused by ECT. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 30th, Brain Stimulation methods, Page number 1071.

690.q: After the complete management for wernickes encephalopathy, which of the following conditions can remain despite the treatment?
690.e: Wernicke's may reversed completely with treatment, residual ataxia and horizontal nystagmus remains there. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 20, Page No.: 632

690.q: A 44-year-old smoker male patient, taking treatment for hypertension, COPD, and Xerophthalmia, starts feeling depressed and suicidal. Which of the following agents included in his treatment regimen, is least likely to cause depression and suicidal ideations in him?
690.e: Antihypertensives like reserpine, propranolol, Corticosteroids, Montelukast have all been associated with causing depression and pose a risk for suicide ( OPTIONS A, B, D ) However, topical application of methylcellulose eye drops has not been associated with depression. ( CORRECT ANSWER C ) Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 23.1 Suicide, Page number 764.

692.q: Which of the following IV anaesthetic agents does not cause cardiac depression
692.e: Etomidate: It is another induction anaesthetic (0.2-0.5 mg/kg) which has a briefer duration of action (4-8 min) than thiopentone; produces little cardiovascular and respiratory depression, but motor restlessness and rigidity is more prominent as are pain on injection or nausea and vomiting on recovery. It is a poor analgesic and has not found much favour except for patients with compromised cardiovascular status. Options B,C,D: Propofol, Methohexitone and Thiopentone have cardiac side effects and hence not used in cardiac patients.

692.q: A young woman recently diagnosed as schizophrenic develops severe muscle cramps with torticollis a short time after drug therapy is initiated with haloperidol. The best course of action would be to
o: Add risperidone to the drug regimen
Discontinue haloperidol and observe the patient
692.e: Acute dystonic reactions are usually very painful and should be treated immediately with parenteral administration of a drug that blocks muscarinic receptors such as benztropine. Option A- Adding risperidone is not protective, and fluphenazine is as likely as haloperidol to cause acute dystonia. Option B- There is no role of observing the patient in acute dystonia. Option C- Oral administration of diphenhydramine is a possibility, but the patient may find it difficult to swallow and it would take a longer time to act. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition by Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 542-543

692.q: A 76-year-old man with history of hypertension and cancer of the colon had colectomy under general anesthesia 24 hours ago. He is receiving an epidural infusion of fentanyl at the rate of 100 micrograms/h. Which of the following is least likely?
692.e: Epidural opioids can cause nausea, pruritus, and respiratory depression Biggest advantage of these agents over epidural administration of local anesthetics is the hemodynamic stability , as there is no inhibition of sympathetic system Hypotension is highly unlikely with epidural fentanyl administration Reference : https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8706199/

693.q: In depressions, there is deficiency of ?
693.e: Ans. A. 5-HT Depression = Decrease in serotonin and norepinephrine. Serotonin is the most imPortant neurotransmitter in depression. Mania= Increased of norepipherine.

693.q: Which of the following drugs acts as competitive antagonist in the 5-HT3 receptors?
693.e: Clozapine competitively inhibits 5-HT3-receptors .( CORRECT OPTION A) Other antipsychotics mentioned in the question inhibit this receptor in a non-competitive fashion. Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29th, Page no. 1029.

693.q: Which of the following medications has the highest propensity to cause QT prolongation on ECG?
693.e: ECG abnormalities occur in approximately 25% of all patients on antipsychotics. The most commonly reported changes are the prolonged QT interval(suggestive of repolarization disturbances), depressed ST segments and abnormal T waves. Thioridazine, pimozide, quetiapine, sertindole and droperidol prolong QTC interval to a higher extent than other antipsychotics . This predisposes to a fatal form of arrhythmia called torsade de pointes (polymorphic ventricular arrhythmia) leading to sudden death . Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29th, Page no. 1027.

694.q: A 70-year-old man admitted in an intensive care unit suddenly develops fluctuation in orientation to time, place and person along with sleeplessness, aggressive behaviour and visualisation of small insects and animals. All of the following terms can be used to describe his condition except:
694.e: The above-mentioned case scenario represents delirium. Various terms describing delirium are as follows: Acute confusional state Acute brain failure Encephalitis Encephalopathy Intensive care unit psychosis Toxic metabolic state Central nervous system toxicity Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis Sundowning Cerebral insufficiency Organic brain syndrome Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 697.

694.q: In a 72-year-old diabetic patient having chronic renal failure, functionally dependent for daily activities on others, and also having moderate hearing impairment, which of the following characteristics carries the highest risk of predisposing the patient to an episode of delirium?
694.e: Advanced age is a major risk factor for the development of delirium. Approximately 30 to 40% of hospitalized patients older than age 65 years have an episode of delirium. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 698.

694.q: A 70-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by the police due to complaints from her neighbours for wandering around the neighbourhood without clothes and poor self-care since last 5 days. When found by the police, she was dirty, foul-smelling, in a half-naked state, with garbage and rotting food all over her house. When interviewed, she appeared confused, disoriented, not able to recognise where she was and was unresponsive. Which of the following neurotransmitter and neuroanatomical area could majorly be implicated for her present confused condition?
694.e: The major neurotransmitter hypothesized to be involved in delirium is acetylcholine and the major neuroanatomical area is the reticular formation. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 699.

695.q: Subcortical dementia is seen in all except ?
695.e: Ans.B. Alzheimer's disease Subcortical dementia is seen in parkinsonism, Huntington's disease, wilson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, idiopathic basal ganglion calcification (Fahr's disease), thalamic lesions, multiple sclerosis, HIV associated dementia and multisYstem atroPhY. Alzheimer's disease causes cortical dementia.

695.q: True statements regarding Marchiafava-Bignami disease are all except?
o: Usual symptoms are personality change or psychomotor impairment
695.e: Marchiafava-Bignami Disease should be considered in patients with chronic alcohol abuse or malnutrition who present with certain neurological symptoms. These symptoms include Dementia Altered mental status Personality change Spasticity Dysarthria Ataxia Gait abnormalities Seizures Other reported clinical findings include desynchronization of bilateral symmetric movements and unilateral signs of agraphia, apraxia, dyspraxia and anomia. Marchiafava-Bignami disease(MBD) is a very rare disorder of demyelination/necrosis of the corpus callosum and the near subcortical white matter that is especially predominant in ill-fed alcoholics. Vitamin supplementation is usually helpful. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526007/

695.q: Which nutrient deficiency is responsible for cognitive decline in elderly individuals?
695.e: Explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a common cause of cognitive impairment in the elderly. It can result in memory loss, confusion, and even dementia if left untreated. The deficiency disrupts myelin synthesis, leading to demyelination and neuronal dysfunction. Explanation for other options: Vitamin C (Option A): Deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by symptoms like bleeding gums and weakness, but it is not associated with cognitive decline. Vitamin B6 (Option C): Deficiency may cause irritability, depression, and confusion but is less frequently linked to significant cognitive impairment in older adults. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) (Option D): Deficiency leads to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's syndrome, which are less common causes of cognitive impairment in the general elderly population compared to vitamin B12 deficiency.

696.q: When exposed to positive events, like going on a holiday or receiving a compliment, transient upliftment of mood is seen in depressed patients. This is termed as ____________.
696.e: Reactivity of mood is the term used to describe the fluctuations in mood that occur in parallel with changes to one's environment Mood will improve on going on holiday or when the stressful situation alters An example, when difficulties with a workmate resolve when that person resigns, but recur when the subject is re-exposed to the stressful situation Reference : Fish's Clinical Psychopathology, third edition, Chapter 5 Disorders of emotion, Page no. 74

696.q: In a patient with Melancholic depression, the mood is characteristically described as _______________.
696.e: A distinct quality of depressed mood characterized by profound despondency, despair, and/or moroseness or by ; so-called empty mood is a characteristic feature of Melancholic depression Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 8, Mood Disorders, Page 362

696.q: How long after a stroke is a patient at a higher risk for developing a depressive disorder?
696.e: Studies of the course and prognosis of post stroke depression indicate that the high-risk period can last up to 2 years. The presence of depression is associated with an eightfold increase in mortality risk. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh Edition, Chapter 21st, Neurocognitive Disorders, Page no. 738.

697.q: What percentage of new mothers is believed to develop postpartum depression?
697.e: Postpartum depression is relatively common, occurring in about 10% to 15% of new mothers. Symptoms are indistinguishable from those characteristics of nonpsychotic major depression and usually develop insidiously over the 6 months following delivery. Some women , however, experience an acute onset of symptoms immediately after delivery and occasionally depression starts during pregnancy. Ambivalence toward the child and doubts about the mother's own parenting abilities are common, but the rate of suicide is low. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh Edition, Chapter 27th, Psychiatry and Reproductive Medicine, Page no. 839.

697.q: What is the feature of atypical depression?
o: The individual shows psychotic symptoms that align with depressive themes
There is a marked decrease in sleep and a high level of energy
Mood brightens in response to positive events, with symptoms like weight gain and hypersomnia
The presence of severe agitation and distinct despair
697.e: Explanation: Atypical depression is defined by mood reactivity (mood improves with positive events) along with features like increased appetite/weight gain, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, and rejection sensitivity.

697.q: All of the following symptoms are a common overlap in grief and Major Depressive Disorder, except:
697.e: Symptoms like sadness, sleep impairment, appetite impairment and weight loss can be similar symptoms in both grief and MDD. (Option A, B & D) However, symptoms like worthlessness, hopelessness and suicidal ideation are infrequent in grief and if present, may be only in context of the bereaved person. Self-esteem (self-worth) is usually preserved in grief. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Chapter 34 End of life issues, Page number 1356.

698.q: A 30 year old female presented to psychiatry OPD with symptoms of hypomania. She has a past history of mania and wants to conceive. Which of the following drugs is most teratogenic?
698.e: Drugs like Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine are safe in pregnancy. Both Lithium and Valproate are teratogenic, but with respect to the risk vs benefit ratio, Lithium is comparatively safer in pregnancy. Adverse effects of Valproate Anorexia, vomiting, loose motions and heartburn are common but mild. Drowsiness, ataxia and tremor occur at high doses. Alopecia, curling of hair, weight gain and increased bleeding tendency have been observed. Rashes and thrombocytopenia are infrequent hypersensitivity phenomena. Administered during pregnancy, it has produced spina bifida and other neural tube defects in the offspring; should be avoided.

698.q: A female came to the psychiatry OPD with a past history of hypomania, now planning to conceive. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
698.e: Drugs like Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine are safe in pregnancy. Both Lithium and Valproate are teratogenic, but with respect to the risk vs benefit ratio, Lithium is comparatively safer in pregnancy. Adverse effects of Valproate Anorexia, vomiting, loose motions and heartburn are common but mild. Drowsiness, ataxia and tremor occur at high doses. Alopecia, curling of hair, weight gain and increased bleeding tendency have been observed. Rashes and thrombocytopenia are infrequent hypersensitivity phenomena. Administered during pregnancy, it has produced spina bifida and other neural tube defects in the offspring; should be avoided.

698.q: A pregnant female presented to OPD in 3rd trimester. She is known case of bipolar disorder with history of 3-4 exacerbation episodes. She's maintained well on lithium from last year. What is next appropriate management?
698.e: Fetal exposure to lithium causes: fetal and neonatal cardiac arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, polyhydramnios, reversible changes in thyroid function, premature delivery, floppy infant syndrome. Small increase in congenital cardiac malformation (ebstein's anomaly). Physiological alteration in pregnancy may affect absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination of lithium. Women with bipolar disorder who are treated with lithium and plan to conceive: Mild and frequent episodes: treatment with lithium should be gradually tapered More severe episodes with moderate risk of relapse: taper dose of lithium and again reinstituted after organogenesis Severe and frequent episodes: continue same dose throughout pregnancy Fetal assessment with fetal echo considered in female who exposed with lithium in first trimester.

699.q: When deprived of food for more than 6 hours, a group of participants in an experiment would be more likely to interpret ambiguous pictures presented to them as something to do with food. This concept is the basis for:
699.e: Apperception means awareness of meaning of a stimulus as modified by one’s own experiences , thoughts and emotions . For example, when hungry, people would more likely interpret ambiguous stimuli as something related to food. This is the basis for projective personality tests like Rorschach inkblot test Thematic Apperception test Children Apperception test. Reference : Morgan and King's Introduction to Psychology, 7th edition, Chapter 13 Psychological Assessment and Testing, Page number 550.

699.q: Identify the hallucinogens whether they are natural or synthetic: 1-Psilocybin 2-Phencyclidine 3-LSD 4-Mescaline 5-Salvia Divinorum
699.e: Hallucinogens derived from natural source are psilocybin mescaline, harmine, harmaline, ayahuasca, salvia divinorum. While synthetic hallucinogens are ketamine, phencyclidine, LSD. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 20.5, Hallucinogen-related disorders, Page number 648.

699.q: Which of the following opioid receptors is responsible for drug dependence?
699.e: The μ-opioid receptors are involved in the Regulation and mediation of analgesia Respiratory depression Constipation Drug dependence The K-opioid receptors with Analgesia Diuresis Sedation The Δ-opioid receptors, with analgesia . Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter number 20, Stimulant-related disorders, Page number 677.

700.q: A 45-year-old man with a history of depression presents with difficulties in ejaculation, particularly during intercourse. He has been taking an SSRI for the past six months. He reports that he feels physically capable of sexual activity but has trouble ejaculating. What is the most appropriate diagnosis for this patient?
700.e: Explanation: The patient has difficulty ejaculating during partnered sexual encounters, which has developed after the initiation of SSRI treatment, suggesting a medication-related issue. Delayed Ejaculation: Duration: Symptoms must persist for at least 6 months. Symptoms: Difficulty with ejaculations: Delayed ejaculation. Absent or reduced frequency of ejaculation. Marked delay or absence of orgasm. Symptoms Needed: At least one symptom must occur. Exclusions: Symptoms should not be attributed to: Relationship problems. Substance use (including prescribed medications). Another medical condition. Another psychiatric condition. Severity Specifiers: Mild: Causes mild distress. Moderate: Causes moderate distress. Severe: Causes severe distress.

700.q: A 30-year-old homeless woman with an 18-year history of daily intravenous heroin use comes into the community rehabilitation clinic asking to be "detoxed" in order to "kick my heroin habit" once and for all. While she is motivated for treatment, she currently is shivering, with rhinorrhoea, tearing, gagging and grabbing her abdomen in pain due to cramps. When questioned about her last use, she claims she used shortly before arriving, but that a peer gave her "something different to shoot up". Which of the following substances would be most likely to cause her current symptoms?
700.e: This patient is suffering from classic symptoms of opioid withdrawal. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist which, when given to a patient actively using another opiate, will precipitate withdrawal. Alprazolam and cocaine would not present with this clinical picture.( OPTION A & C ) Methadone and morphine are opioids which would cause further intoxication, not withdrawal.( OPTION D ) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29, Psychopharmacological treatment, Page no. 1002.

700.q: All of the following receptors are involved in chocoholics except:
700.e: Anandamide , an ingredient in chocolate, stimulates the same receptors as marijuana. Other compounds in chocolate include tryptophan , the precursor of serotonin and phenylalanine , an amphetamine-like substance, both of which improve mood. So-called chocoholics may be self-medicating because of a depressive diathesis. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 20.12, Other Substance Use and Addictive Disorders, Page number 690.

o: Fear that escape might be difficult in specific situations
Fear that panic-like symptoms or embarrassing symptoms may occur in specific situations
No clinically significant distress is present despite the symptoms
701.e: In Agoraphobia, the individual fears or avoids specific situations because of thoughts that escape might be difficult or help might not be available in the event of developing panic-like symptoms or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms (e.g., fear of falling in elderly adults; fear of incontinence). The fear, anxiety or avoidance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9.3, Agoraphobia, Page 399.

701.q: Which of the following is a common symptom of Agoraphobia?
o: Fear of being in crowded places
701.e: Explanation: Agarophobia refers to the fear of being in crowded places Individuals with Agoraphobia often avoid situations where escape might be difficult. Duration: Symptoms last for ≥6 months. Key Symptoms: Fear/anxiety in specific situations (e.g., public transport, open spaces). Avoidance of situations due to fear of panic attacks. Fear and avoidance are disproportionate to potential threat. Exclusions: Not due to another medical or mental disorder.

701.q: Which is true for blood-injection-injury type of specific phobia?
o: One of the Most common type of specific phobia
Bradycardia and Hypotension are characteristically seen as compared to tachycardia seen in other phobias
All of the above are true
701.e: The blood-injection-injury type is the most common type of phobia found (Option A) . It is differentiated from the others in that bradycardia and hypotension often follow the initial tachycardia that is common to all phobias (Option B) . The blood-injection-injury type of specific phobia is particularly likely to affect many members and generations of a family (Option C) . In the special situation of blood-injection-injury phobia, some therapists recommend that patients tense their bodies and remain seated during the exposure to help avoid the possibility of fainting from a vasovagal reaction to the phobic stimulation. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9.4, Specific Phobia, Page 402.

702.q: A 29-year-old male CT3 psychiatric trainee was put down badly by his consultant in a ward round. He couldn't say anything to the consultant when the consultant shouted at him. When he returned home, he became verbally abusive and aggressive towards his wife. What is the most likely phenomenon?
702.e: Anna Freud described 10 defence mechanisms in her work. Reaction formation projection and regression are three of them. In displacement, emotions or wishes are transferred from the original object or person to a more suitable substitute. ( Option A is CORRECT ) Reaction formation is seen in patients with obsessive–compulsive disorder . ( Option D ) Here the attitude is opposed to the oppressed wish and constitutes the opposite reaction Projection : unacceptable thoughts, emotions and feelings are projected on to some other person ( Option C ) Identification : a person takes the attributes of others to him or herself ( Option B ) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 4, page no. 161

702.q: Regarding the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder, which of the following is most correct?
o: Cognitive and behavioural strategies are more effective than serotonergic antidepressants
Group therapy is less effective than individual therapy
More frequent therapy sessions are associated with improved outcomes
Treatment of any kind is more successful if compulsions are present
702.e: Treatment is more effective if compulsions are present . Cognitive and behavioural therapies have similar effectiveness to SSRIs. (Option A) Likewise, group and individual therapies have similar success rates. (Option B) Patients with more bizarre obsessional thoughts are less likely to resist carrying out compulsive acts. The frequency of psychotherapy sessions has not been shown to influence outcome although duration of each session and the therapy overall is associated with better outcomes. (Option C) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 10, page no. 423

702.q: Suicidal tendencies are most commonly seen in: March 2003
702.e: Ans. C i.e. Severe depression 1458. Repetitive irresesistable thought to do something a) Phobia b) Obsession c) Compulsion d) Anxiety Correct Answer - B Ans. is 'b' i.e., Obsession Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) OCD is an anxiety disorder which is characterized by recurrent, unwanted thoughts (Obsessions) and repettive behaviors (compulsions). An obsession has following characteristic : -

703.q: Which among these symptoms must be present to fulfil the criteria for PTSD according to DSM-V?
703.e: The 5th edition of DSM-V criteria for PTSD specify that the following symptoms must have lasted >1 month: Intrusion Avoidance Alterations of mood and cognition Hyperarousal Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th Edition, Page Number-349.

703.q: A 40-year-old man was recently rescued by the fire department from his building which caught fire. He presented with flashbacks, repeated distressing memories and disturbed dreams of the event for about 20 days after the traumatic incident. Which of the following characteristics differentiate acute stress disorder from PTSD in his case?
703.e: According to DSM-5, acute stress disorder (ASD) and PTSD are differentiated by time duration If symptoms are present up to one month of exposure to traumatic event, it fulfils the criteria for ASD However, if symptoms occur more than a month, the criteria of PTSD is fulfilled In this question, the person developed symptoms of flashbacks, distressing memories, disturbed dreams for 20 days after experiencing the fire accident Hence, the diagnosis of ASD would be more appropriate Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 11, Trauma and stressor related disorders, Page 439-441

703.q: In the context of Acute Stress Disorder, which of the following symptoms is not typically included?
703.e: Explanation: Emotional blunting is more commonly associated with PTSD, not typically listed as a symptom of Acute Stress Disorder. Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5) Symptoms occur 3 days to following exposure to trauma. Symptoms arise transiently in response to stress and usually resolve quickly. Required Symptoms: Presence of symptoms from intrusion, negative mood/cognition, dissociation, avoidance, or arousal categories. Nine symptoms needed from these categories. Symptoms Include: Cognitive "daze," narrowed attention, disorientation. Autonomic panic symptoms. May include partial or complete amnesia related to the event. Exclusions: Not due to substance use or other psychiatric disorders.

704.q: The concept of inferiority complex and birth order in relation to personality were given by:
704.e: Alfred Adler’s individual psychology gives the concept of inferiority complex. And he also gave the concept of importance of birth order in personality structure . Reference : Morgan and King’s Introduction to Psychology, 7 th edition, Chapter 14 Personality, Page number 572.

704.q: A 30 year male is over enthusiastic and sensation seeking. He loves to explore new places and dishes of different cities. He makes big list of trying bungee jumping and sky diving and planning to organize camping in a deep forest. His personality trait is considered as:
704.e: Openness to experience (High means adventurous) Conscientiousness Extraversion Agreeableness Neuroticism Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 761

704.q: Mr Mark, who was flying on spicejet. Suddenly he got up and started giving instruction to air hostesses to do pole dance. He instructed everyone in a melodramatic manner to clap for these ladies. He started behaving like a boss. One old man shouted on him and asked him to shut up and sit down. Mr Mark felt insulted and became very anxious. Which type of personality Mr Mark has?
704.e: Excessive sense of self-importance and fragile emotion at the same time: Narcissistic PD. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 753

705.q: Conversion disorder was earlier, termed as 'Hysteria' by Hippocrates due to the belief that:
o: Uterus wanders in the body and presses on different organs thus causing symptoms
Emotionally charged behaviour is seen which seems out of control
Physical symptoms were found to have a psychological cause
Physical symptoms were attributed to demonic possession
705.e: In 1900 BC, Hippocrates coined the term hysteria to describe an illness in which the uterus (hystera) dries up and wanders the body in search of moisture Symptoms would then be caused by the uterus pressing on different organs Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.4, Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder), Page 473

705.q: Terminology for which of the disorders has been modified in DSM-V?
705.e: Term for Conversion disorder was modified to Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (FNSD ) in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition (DSM-5) The term ' Factitious Disorder' has not been modified in DSM-V (Option A) Chronic Fatigue Syndrome is not an entity included in DSM-V (Option C) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.5, Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder), Page 473

705.q: Abnormal prion protein (PrPSc) is seen in all of the following conditions except:
705.e: Prion diseases: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Kuru Gerstman-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome Fatal familial insomnia Prions are infective agents composed of protein. Prion are made of proteins called PrP. PrP exists in a normal form (PrPc) and an abnormal form (PrPSc). PrPSc is resistant to protease and therefore cannot be broken down in the body. PrPSc can change adjacent PrPc into PrPSc (this is how the 'infection' spreads). Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 2.10 Neuropsychiatric Aspects of Prion disease, Page number 1599.

706.q: Factitious disorder is the faking of physical or psychological signs and symptoms in order to maintain a sick role. All of the following clues should trigger suspicion of Factitious disorder except:
o: Unusual dramatic presentation of symptoms that defy conventional medical or psychiatric understanding
Emergence of new and unusual symptoms when other symptoms resolve
Resistance to undergo procedures or testing
706.e: CLUES THAT SHOULD TRIGGER SUSPICION OF FACTITIOUS DISORDER: Unusual, dramatic presentation of symptoms that defy conventional medical or psychiatric understanding (Option A) Symptoms do not respond appropriately to usual treatment or medications Emergence of new, unusual symptoms when other symptoms resolve (Option B) Eagerness to undergo procedures or testing or to recount symptoms (Option C) Reluctance to give access to collateral sources of information (i.e., refusing to sign releases of information or to give contact information for family and friends) Extensive medical history or evidence of multiple surgeries Multiple drug allergies Medical profession (Option D) Few visitors Ability to forecast unusual progression of symptoms or unusual response to treatment Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.6, Factitious Disorder, Page 490

706.q: In a case of Factitious disorder, all of the following methods can be used to detect possibly simulated fever except?
o: Simultaneous recording of temperature from two sites i.e., oral and rectal
Recording temperature of freshly voided urine
Relying on temperature readings given by patients
706.e: METHODS OF SIMULATION OF FEVER IN FACTITIOUS DISORDER: Warming thermometer against a lightbulb or other heat source Drinking hot fluids Friction from mouth or anal sphincter False recordings Injection of pyrogens such as faeces, vaccines, thyroid hormone, or tetanus toxoid POSSIBLE METHODS OF DETECTION OF FALSIFIED HISTORY OF FEVER GIVEN IN FACTITIOUS DISORDER: Simultaneous taking of temperature from two different locals (orally and rectally )- (Option A) Recording the temperature of freshly voided urine (Option B) The appearance of cool skin despite high thermometer readings Normal white blood cell count (Option D) Unusually high or inconsistent temperatures Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.6, Factitious Disorder, Page 494

707.q: A 45-year-old divorced male bus driver was referred for psychiatric consultation for complaints of memory loss for the previous 12 years, behaving and responding to the environment as if it were 12 years previously, e.g., he didn't recognize his 8-year-old son, and denied recollection of current events like name of current president. On mental status examination, the patient displayed intact intellectual function and brain imaging was normal. The patient's mother described a family history of brutal beatings and physical discipline subjected towards the patient. Pick the correct diagnosis.
707.e: The above case scenario is suggestive of dissociative amnesia. The main feature of dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important autobiographical information , usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is inconsistent with ordinary forgetting. Dissociative amnesia can occur in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) , however other symptoms should be present as well to fulfil the criteria for the same. (Option B) In malingering, there is usually a secondary gain. (Option C) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 452.

707.q: All of the following are non-pathological forms of amnesia, except:
707.e: Ordinary forgetfulness, infantile and childhood amnesia, amnesia for sleep and dreaming and hypnotic amnesia are non-pathological forms of amnesia. (Option A, C & D) Dissociative amnesia is pathological. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 452.

707.q: Psychotherapeutic technique proven to be effective in dissociative identity disorder?
707.e: Treatment option out of these, in dissociative disorders is hypnosis. Hypnosis can be useful for accessing specific alter personality states and their sequestered affects and memories. Hypnosis is also used to create relaxed mental states in which negative life events can be examined without overwhelming anxiety. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 461.

708.q: Counter-transference is commonly encountered in all of the following conditions, except:
708.e: Countertransference is the process where the physician unconsciously displaces onto the patient patterns of behaviors or emotional reactions as if he or she were a significant figure from earlier in the physician's life Signs of countertransference: Missed appointment by the psychiatrist Boredom Sleepiness in a session Counter transference by physicians is commonly encountered in disorders in which frequent complaints, non-remitting symptoms are seen: Psychosomatic diseases (Somatic Symptom disorder, Factitious disorder) Personality disorders (Cluster B personality disorders) Impulse Control disorders Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 5, Examination and Diagnosis of the psychiatric patient, Page 194

708.q: A 75 year old man flown to america from Siberia (war zone), to stay with his son. He is having nightmares and flashback. He was brought to hospital by his son. It was informed that he is getting irritated, insomnia and easily forgetting incidences. What is the most probable diagnosis?
708.e: Its old age related disease and patient is forgetting the incidences. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 21

708.q: A 54-year-old man sees a physician complaining of a depressed mood and inability to sleep for the past 3 weeks. He tells the physician that in the past when he has had similar episodes, he was placed on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, which proved effective. The physician diagnoses the patient with major depression and agrees to use an MAOI. Which of the following foods must be completely avoided by this patient while on this medication?
708.e: There is a list of foods that should be avoided due to small amounts of tyramine and rare association with hypertensive episodes while a patient is taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor , but only a few that must be completely avoided. To be completely avoided: Aged cheese Red wine Cured meats To be consumed in small quantities: Anchovies Beets Caviar Chocolate Coffee Colas Curry powder Figs Liquorice Mushrooms Rhubarb Snails Soy sauce Worcestershire sauce Reference : Jacobson, Pg no. 121-22.

709.q: A 19-year-old girl referred for evaluation of menstrual disturbances. She weighs only 38 kg and is 1.78 m tall. She is emaciated, her skin is dry and she has excessive growth of lanugo hair. She has been amenorrhoeic for 9 months. Her cortisol level is elevated, her Free T4 is normal. She has anemia and associated reduced white cell and platelet count. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to fit with this clinical picture?
709.e: Anorexia nervosa has a female to male preponderance of 9:1. It is estimated that around 0.5-1% of women between 15 and 30 years of age have anorexia. The aetiology of anorexia is unknown, but it is likely to be an interaction between environmental and genetic factors, Patient may also have bradycardia and low / low-normal BP Typical laboratory tests include decreased FSH, LH, estrogens and 17-OH steroids. Free T4 and TSH levels are usually normal. Anemia with decreased white and platelet cell count may also occur. There may be metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, hypokalemia and hypomagnesaemia. Treatment may involve complex psychotherapy for a number of years, and referral to a specialist in the field is recommended. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:444 Page number: 3274

709.q: A 17-year-old adolescent suffers from Bulimia nervosa and is very depressed. She is also suffering from insomnia and apathy. Which of the following medications should be avoided?
709.e: Bupropion is a NDRI (norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor). Seizure disorders and eating disorders are contraindications for bupropion because of its possible lowering of the seizure threshold and its anorectic effects. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th Edition, Chapter 29, Page Number-955.

709.q: A 15 year old female is brought to OPD by her mother for evaluation as she has been eating very less and becoming very thin. O/E: her BMI <17.5, russel's sign was seen. Mother is reporting that she is indulged into rigorous exercises and over gymming. During interview, girl is irritated and saying that she is doing good and eating fine. On further enquiry, it was found that she didn't had menses for last 3 months. What is the diagnosis?
709.e: She is image conscious and has BMI Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 511

710.q: A 35-year-old patient reports experiencing sudden, uncontrollable urges to act. This is characteristic of which symptom?
710.e: Explanation: Impulse is a sudden and irresistible urge to take a specific action. Impulse is a strong and often uncontrollable desire to act without much forethought or consideration of the consequences. Explanations of other options: Hallucination (Option B): A hallucination is the experience of sensing something that does not actually exist in the external environment. Delusion (Option C): A delusion is a firmly held false belief that persists despite logical reasoning or evidence proving otherwise. Pseudohallucination (Option D): A pseudohallucination resembles a hallucination but is acknowledged by the individual as originating from their own mind rather than the external world.

710.q: A 38-year-old divorced female professor, belonging to high socio-economic class, was reprimanded many times for charges of shop-lifting, which she had started at the age of 22. She would steal only on impulse, not from pre mediation, and experienced tension prior to, and satisfaction after shoplifting. The stolen items included crayons, spoons, candles, coloured papers, earrings, etc. which she hoarded in her cupboard. In the above case, which of the following statements is false?
o: This disorder is categorised under Disruptive and Impulse Control disorders in DSM-5
The object stolen is usually the goal of stealing
Antisocial personality disorder should be ruled out
SSRI and CBT are usually helpful
710.e: In Kleptomania, the act of stealing is the objective and not the object stolen. It is characterized by mounting tension before the act, followed by gratification and lessening of tension with or without guilt, remorse, or depression after the act. Kleptomania is categorised under Disruptive and Impulse Control disorders in DSM-5 SSRI and CBT are usually considered in management of Kleptomania. In patients with habit of stealing, antisocial personality disorder is an important differential diagnosis; however, in them, the object stolen and violation of norms is the objective. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 19 Disruptive, Impulse control, and Conduct disorders, Page number 611.

711.q: A 27-year-old male CT2 psychiatric trainee was put down by his consultant in a ward round and the consultant shouted at him. After work, he went to the gym and exercised for half an hour more than usual. What is the most likely phenomenon?
711.e: This is the transformation of our instinctual energy to a more socially acceptable one . So, in this case, rather than shouting back at the consultant, the trainee went to the gym and transformed his anger and frustration into exercising . This is a mature defence mechanism. Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 4, page no. 162

711.q: Which of the following drugs is least likely to cause serotonin syndrome?
711.e: Olanzapine is not associated with serotonin syndrome . Other drugs like Venlafaxine, Ecstasy and Fluoxetine have all been implicated in serotonin syndrome.(Option A, B & C) Ecstasy has been associated with serotonin syndrome in combination with venlafaxine. Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29th, Page no. 1020.

711.q: 24-year-old Miss D had come to the Psychiatric OPD with the c/o Unresponsive episodes characterized by clonic movements and weeping spells lasting for 1 hour followed by an interpersonal conflict with her boyfriend. Supportive counselling was provided and she was prescribed with few medications. Two months later, she began to develop galactorrhoea with irregular menstrual cycle. Which of the following medications is more likely to cause it?
711.e: Levosulpiride is an atypical antipsychotic that blocks D2 receptors commonly prescribed in Conversion Disorder Considering the clinical presentation of the patient, all of the above medications can be provided to the patient but Levosulpiride is more prone to cause hyperprolactinemia leading to side effects like amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, anorgasmia Escitalopram and Sertraline are SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake inhibitors) which may also lead to Hyperprolactinaemia but in much lesser propensity while Clonazepam is a Benzodiazepine lacking such effect Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29 Psychopharmacological Treatment, page no. 1014

712.q: A patient is on treatment of depression, complaining of painful coitus/sexual dysfunction. Which drug will you switch him on to address his problem?
712.e: Bupropion is NDRI. Others can increase the level of serotonin, which can cause sexual side effects. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 29, Page No.: 954

712.q: Which of the following is an adverse effect of an antidepressant drug, k/as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor?
712.e: Sexual dysfunction is a well-documented adverse effect of SSRIs. These drugs can cause various sexual problems, such as decreased libido, delayed ejaculation or difficulty achieving orgasm. This adverse effect can significantly impact a patient's quality of life. Other options: B.Dry mouth - Dry mouth is a common side effect of many medications, including some antidepressants, but it is not specific to SSRIs. C.Blurring of vision - Blurred vision is not a commonly reported side effect of SSRIs. D.Constipation - Constipation is also not a common side effect of SSRIs. Key Takeaway: Sexual dysfunction is a common and well-documented adverse effect of SSRIs , which can impact adherence to treatment.

712.q: How to differentiate between psychological and organic erectile dysfunction ?
712.e: Ans. A. Nocturnal penile tumescence One of the important method to distinguish psychogenic impotence from organic imPotence is nocturnal penile tumsescence & early morning erection which are preserved in psychogenic impotence but not in organic cause of impotence.

713.q: Under hypnosis or during psychotherapy, a patient may recover a memory of a painful experience or conflict-particularly of sexual or physical abuse, that is etiologically significant. This is known as:
713.e: Under hypnosis or during psychotherapy , a patient may recover a memory of a painful experience or conflict-particularly of sexual or physical abuse - that is etiologically significant. When the repressed material is brought back to consciousness, the person not only may recall the experience but may relive it, accompanied by the appropriate affective response (a process called abreaction). If the event recalled never really happened but the person believes it to be true and reacts accordingly, it is known as false memory syndrome. (Option A) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 463.

713.q: A 35-year-old businessman enjoys dressing up in his wife's clothes. He says he does so to experience what it feels like to be a woman and it does not cause him sexual arousal. He has no desire to be a woman and he is very much comfortable with his genital organs. What is the correct term to describe his behavior?
713.e: Dual-role transvestism: Patient wears the dress of opposite sex to enjoy the temporary feeling of belonging to other sex. Unlike trans sexualism, there is no desire of permanent sex change. There is no sexual arousal associated with cross dressing. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 17, Page No.: 597

713.q: According to Freud, during psychosexual development a boy focuses his love on his mother. This can reach a stage where a boy becomes jealous of his father and wants to kill him. However, he cannot do this for fear of castration and so represses these urges as he moves to the next stage of development. Which of the following describes the boy's psychosocial development?
